Notice how by these actions he proclaimed the words of the Apostle: "For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out" (1 Tim 7:6).
Notice how the words he uttered served him, not he alone, but will serve us also.
These possessions above all, are they mine? Am I the one who formed them?
This wealth, is it not a deposit? It is foreign to me, for it did not accompany me when I entered this world, and it does not accompany me when I depart...
Let us be dull toward wealth. For this reason God created us naked from the beginning, and made us subject to death.

St. John Chrysostom * When Job's sons died, they found a common grave under the rubble of his house, and all he could do was show his fatherly affection by tearing his clothes and falling on the ground and worshipping, saying: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD" (Job 1:20).
St. Jerome "And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither.
The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD" [21].

The Holy Bible does not mention any hymn of praise sung by Adam and Eve in paradise amid all the surpassing gifts and blessings they enjoyed. But the Book of Job has recorded for us a short hymn that surpasses many hymns, a hymn that gladdens the heart of God and the hearts of the heavenly beings, and remains engraved as on rock, sung by the generations, and in which people through the generations find divine comfort. So we would not have enjoyed the Psalms and the life of inward rejoicing if David the prophet had not been a man of sorrows, and we would not sing the hymn of the three holy youths if they had not been thrown into the furnace of fire.

By saying this Job declares his return to his origin, and as the wise man says: "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was" (Eccl 12:7). Naked we return, when we go back to the dust from which we were taken (Job 34:15). The Latin proverb says that "no one can reach a state of poverty more extreme than that in which he was born."
Job's faithfulness appeared contrary to what Satan claimed, for instead of blaspheming God he blessed Him, acknowledging divine providence whatever afflictions befell him.

He did not say, God gave and the Sabeans and Chaldeans took away, nor did he say, God gave to me and the Lord impoverished me, but said that God who gave has the right to take. He lost nothing, for all that he has, even his children, belong to God; they are His gift.

He blessed God who gave, and blesses Him because He took, for the remaining of the gifts, even for a time, is an expression of God's love for us. And because God, who is all-wise, all-loving and almighty, knows what is for our edification and to the extent that is for our benefit, even the taking from us is for our good.

* When the messengers came to blessed Job one after another, and he heard them announcing deadly news, with the unbearable destruction of his sons added to it, he did not cry out or sigh, but had recourse to prayer and offered thanks to the Lord; imitate him.
* Job not only did not blaspheme, but even blessed! He was not content to bear his calamity in silence, but glorified God, not only at that time but for the future as well.

* If we practice this spiritual wisdom (constant thanksgiving), we will experience no evil, even if we fall under countless sufferings, but the gain will be greater than the loss, and good will overcome evil. By these words you make God merciful toward you, and He defends you against the tyranny of the devil. As soon as your tongue utters these words, Satan flees quickly from you.

* While (Job) was completely surrounded by that wealth, it was not apparent to many what kind of man he was. But when his garments were stripped from him like a wrestler's and he cast them aside, and came naked to the contests for the sake of godliness, he amazed all who saw him. Even the theater of the angels cried out when they beheld his soul steadfast in endurance, and they praised him as having won the crown. And as I noted before, men did not see him as well when he was wrapped in all the wealth as they saw him when he threw it off like a garment, and appeared as one naked on the stage in the midst of the world, and all were amazed at the strength of his soul. They bore witness to him not because he was stripped of everything, but because in his struggle he patiently bore his weaknesses.

* "The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away" [21], to do what seems good to the Lord. See, he believed that it was God who took away... What can be compared with this attitude? He did not ask to know out of curiosity, and did not say: Why does God give to me? And why does He take?
"Blessed be the name of the LORD" [21]. Notice by what means he enjoys consolation...

It is the Lord who decided. You say: Why did God decide in this way...? When He made me rich I did not seek to know why He gave me wealth, and now I do not want to know why He took it from me. For did He give me this because of merit on my part? Did He give me this in return for good works?
He decided to give to me, and He did so. He decided to take, and He is doing this.
It is a sign of a godly spirit to do everything according to the will of God, and not to ask Him for an account, nor an explanation of what He does.

* It is a great thing if we are able to give thanks with great joy. But giving thanks out of fear is one thing, and giving thanks during grief is another. This is what Job did when he thanked God... Let no one say that he did not grieve over what befell him or that he was not affected by it in the depths. Do not take away from him the great praise of his righteousness... Satan harms us not in order to take away what is ours and leave us destitute, but because when this happens we are bound to blaspheme God.

* Job was crowned and became famous, not because he was not shaken despite the countless trials that surrounded him, and despite the opposition of his wife toward him, but because he continued in his thanks to the Lord in every state: not only when he was rich, but also when he became poor; not only when he was in health, but also when his body was struck (with sores); not when these things came upon him slowly, but when a violent storm came upon him, upon his house and also upon his whole person.

* Satan causes us losses, not only to take away our goods, for he knows that these are nothing, but to compel us by this to utter blasphemy. So in the case of blessed Job he did not strive only to make him poor but also to make him a blasphemer.
St. John Chrysostom * Although he was counted as the owner of great wealth, the test presented to him by the Lord showed clearly that he possessed nothing but God alone.

St. Macarius the Great * Praise the Lord on the harp. If you have an abundance of earthly things, give thanks to the Giver. If there is want or you are robbed of what is yours, play the harp with joy. For you have not been deprived of the Giver, even if you have been deprived of the gift He gave you. So I repeat, play with gladness. With full trust in your God, take hold of the strings of your hearts as of a harp, that your voices may resound to their depths, crying out: "The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away."
* Here we find an example of a man who blesses the Lord at all times.

* Let Him take what He has given, but have you lost the Giver...? It is as though he says: Let Him take all, let Him take everything, and let Him send me away naked, but let me keep Him Himself. What do I lack if I possess God? Or what use is everything to me if I do not possess God?

*He could have said: "The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away. What the Lord has taken He can give again, and restore more than He took." But he did not say this; he said: [What seems good to the Lord, let it be]. For what pleases Him pleases me. May what pleases the good Lord not grieve the submissive servant, as what pleases the physician does not grieve the patient.

* From where did such jewels of praise of God come? See a man who was poor outwardly, but inwardly was rich. Could such jewels have come from his lips if he had not carried a hidden treasure in his heart?
* O the inward wealth which no thief can approach! God gave him Himself. He enriched him when He offered Himself to him, in what he loves.

* You take what I have, you do not take what is within me. For he will not become poor who says: [The LORD gave, the LORD hath taken away; as it hath pleased in his eyes, so let it be; blessed be the name of the LORD].

* The mammon of unrighteousness is all the wealth of this world, whatever its source. When the rich man gathers, he is gathering the mammon of unrighteousness, that is, wealth of injustice... If we want true wealth, it is different from this wealth. This wealth was in abundance, yet when Job was naked his heart was full of divine things, overflowing with praises like the most precious jewels offered to his God, and that when he had lost all that he had.
* When you hear this, direct your hearts toward God. Do not deceive your souls.
Seek yourselves... whether you love the world or do not love it, and learn to let it depart before you depart. What does it mean that you let it depart? That is, do not let your hearts cling to it.
When you have something that you will one day lose, whether in life or by death, let it go, for it will not be able to accompany you forever.

Be prepared for the will of God and cling to Him. Hold fast to Him, whom you cannot lose without your own will. If an occasion arises for the loss of temporal things, say: "The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away."

* Job was found worshipping God for God's own sake, loving Him for Himself, and not because He gave him what he needed, but because God Himself had not been taken from him... The fires of temptation approached him, but found him gold and not straw. They removed the dross from him, and did not turn him to ashes!

* If you have sinned, grieve over the loss of your inward treasure. You have nothing in your house, but your heart may be emptier still. But if your heart is full of His goodness, full of your God, why do you not say: "The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; as it pleases the Lord, so let it be! Blessed be the name of the LORD!" What grieves God? Is it from the blows, when He Himself has been struck? Far be it!
* O the jewels of praise to God, which he brought out from his inward treasures! This is his wealth! He brought forth a sweet hymn that glorifies God and commends Job.

* What a courageous, sweet voice! Who does not awake from sleep at this voice? Who does not trust in God in wakefulness, to walk into the battle without fear against the devil, fighting not by his own strength but by the strength of the One who proves him?
St. Augustine * How shall I be fit to be in the company of Job, I who do not accept ordinary trials with thanksgiving?

* It is clear that the virtues become our possessions when they are practically woven into our nature. They do not leave us while we strive on this earth, unless we ourselves drive them away by our will and compel them to go, by opening the door for vice to enter.
They run with us eagerly whenever we hasten toward the other world.
They set those who possess them in the rank of the angels, and shine eternally in the eyes of the Creator.

But wealth and power and pleasure and the whole throng of such follies, which increase daily because of our folly, do not enter this life with us and do not accompany anyone when he leaves this world. For the saying of the righteous man of old: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither" (Job 1:21) is a saying truly established and prevailing for every man.

* Among the men of old and the men of today it is supposed that each of them enjoyed a certain success, as each enjoys a certain virtue: Job received undefeated patience in the midst of affliction, Moses and David meekness, Samuel prophecy looking to the future, and Phinehas zeal (Num 25:7-8)... Peter and Paul zeal in preaching (Gal 7:2), and the sons of Zebedee magnificence of style, so they were called sons of thunder (Mk 17:3).

St. Gregory of Nazianzus * This was something like a cry from him: "I was called a father for a long time, since He who created me wanted me to be so. Now He has wanted in turn to remove from me the crown of offspring. I do not resist Him in what is His. What seems good in His eyes, let it be done. He is the Creator of my children, and I am an instrument. Why should I, the servant, surrender to useless grief and bitter complaint against a decision that I cannot avoid in vain?" With such words he threw Satan to the ground.
St. Basil the Great * Have you seen the arrows that the traitor shot?

The enemy himself was plundered, and was confused in vain. For Job was not affected at all by the events, listening to the reports of the evils falling upon him as though they belonged to someone else, while he was like a rock that repels the waves that dash against it.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem *If anyone bears the Lord's dispensation with patience, and says when he loses something: [The LORD gave, the LORD hath taken away...], he receives a crown for his patience, which pleases God if he is righteous, and forgiveness if he is a sinner.

* The righteous man who suffers destruction (of material things) is rich and naked. St. Job was full of this wealth... He lost all those things that God had given him, but he possessed God Himself, the Giver.

Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * See how he concludes everything he rightly felt by blessing the Lord. By this the enemy experienced shame, and it was counted against him as punishment and defeat. For he himself, though created in blessing, rebelled against the Lord (c), while that one who is mortal utters a hymn of glory even while under His disciplines... With words of patience he praised God when he was struck. He shot many arrows into the breast of his adversary, and wounded him with injuries more bitter than those under which he himself had fallen. For through his trial he lost earthly things, and by bearing them humbly he doubled his heavenly blessings.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Holy Scripture says: "For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out" (1 Tim 6:7). Those who desire to be rich fall into many foolish and hurtful lusts. The disciple who became a traitor is a clear proof of this, for he perished for a little miserable money.

St. Cyril the Great * We are masters of ourselves; it is for us to harm ourselves or not to harm ourselves... (If all our treasures are stolen) it is truly a sad matter, and it seems a loss. But the matter remains dependent on you, for you can make it a loss or a gain for you. You say: "And how can this be a gain?" I am trying to show you how, for if you wish it will be a great gain for you, and if you do not wish, the loss will be harsher than the loss of what was taken from you. For as in the case of artists, when raw materials are placed before them, the one who is skilled in his art uses the materials for a good purpose, but the unskilled one spoils the materials and they become a loss for him. So it is here: how does this become a gain? If you give thanks to God, if you do not lament bitterly, if you utter the words of Job: "The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away..."

* Who can calmly bear to see his only child laid out as a lifeless corpse? He needs a soul like steel to bear that. Such a one must rest from the sighs of nature, and be strengthened to utter the words of Job: [The LORD gave, the LORD hath taken away] (Job 21:1). By these words alone he stands with Abraham himself and Job to be proclaimed a victor. And if he forbids the wailing of women and disperses the groups of mourners to set them up to sing the glory of God, he receives above all countless rewards; men are astonished at him, the angels praise him, and God crowns him.
* These are the words of a living soul, a soul that performs the role fitting for it.

* Suppose that someone lost his son, and another all his possessions... Fruit can be gained from the affliction even if it cannot be remedied, by bearing the circumstances nobly, and instead of using words of blasphemy, offering words of thanks to the Lord; by this the evils that are brought upon you against your will become good works by your choice.
St. John Chrysostom * God is good, and all that He does must be good also.
Has He decided that I must lose my husband? Mourn my loss, but since this is His will, bear it with submission.
Is my only son snatched from me? A harsh blow, but it can be borne, because the One who takes is the same One who gave.
If I become blind, my friend's reading comforts me.
If I become deaf, I escape hearing evil words, and my thoughts are centered on God alone.
St. Jerome "In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly" [22].
This is a living testimony that the Holy Spirit gives us of his good conduct in the midst of affliction. He passed through the trial with success and true victory.

St. John Chrysostom sees in the expression "nor charged God foolishly" that he did not accuse God of injustice, nor did he reckon that what befell him was the product of chance, nor did he murmur, saying that he had not sinned, so why did evils come upon him, does God not care about him. Such thoughts come to some when trials come upon them while they see others enjoying temporal blessings.
* Satan fought (Job) steadfastly, but he was unable to win against the wrestler of God.
He emptied his quiver of arrows, but he was not able to wound his brave, valiant fighter.
He stirred up huge waves, but he could not move the firm rock.
He used his tricks, but he could not demolish the strong tower.
He shook the tree, but he did not shatter the fruit.
He broke the branches, but he did not harm the root.
He pierced the wall, but he did not carry off the treasure.

Now I say that this treasure to which I refer is not of gold or silver, but the faith of the righteous man. For Satan wanted to destroy this treasure when he stirred up against him an unbearable affliction after taking away all his wealth... You see God glorified and Satan put to shame.
Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * Satan and his angels failed to triumph over Job when they launched their attacks on him. He was the man who stands bold, who will not be shaken in his firm faith.

St. Augustine * Notice how Job is described as having come to a greater state through the temptation, while David fell to the ground by temptation. Therefore the virtues of our forebears may strengthen our hope, and their falls support our caution through humility, so that while by the former we are lifted up to joy, by the latter we remain in fear.

* "In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly" [22]... Since he uttered nothing in which there was folly, guarding his tongue from iniquity, while it is said "sinned not," it appears that he removed from himself the sin of murmuring even from his thought, so he did not sin, nor speak foolishly, nor did resentment rise in his silent feeling, nor did his tongue loose itself in cursing.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Give thanks to God and praise the One who tests you in the furnace. Utter praise instead of blasphemy; this is the way in which that blessed man expressed himself.
* This is the way in which Job offered a sacrifice (of praise) although terrible sorrows beyond human strength had come upon him.
St. John Chrysostom
A hymn of praise in the midst of affliction!
* Grant me, O Lord, by Your grace, to enjoy spiritual wealth!
Let me be perfect in Your sight, You who charge Your angels with folly!
And count me upright, because of the work of Your Spirit in me!
Nail Your fear in my heart, that I may live in godliness.
And let Your light shine within me, that I may not bear to walk in the darkness of evil.
* Grant Your Church to be like the family of Job, her days feasts and spiritual banquets that never cease!
Her mark is brotherly love and agreement without division.
She plays the symphony of love that gladdens the heavenly beings!
In the midst of my joys, let the sacrifice of Your cross never depart from me!
I pray for my brethren as for my own lowliness, lest in ignorance or with knowledge I sin against You.
* Let the devil complain against me before You, for I take refuge under the shadow of Your wings!
There is none to support me but You!
* Let the devil strip me of everything!
But I possess You, and he will not draw me away from You.
You are my wealth and my happiness and my sufficiency in everything!
* In the midst of affliction my soul gives You thanks and praises You, for my heart is lifted up to You!
He has no place in the world, nor has the world any place in him!

1 Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them to present himself before the LORD. 2 And the LORD said unto Satan, From whence comest thou? And Satan answered the LORD, and said, From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it. 3 And the LORD said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil? and still he holdeth fast his integrity, although thou movedst me against him, to destroy him without cause. 4 And Satan answered the LORD, and said, Skin for skin, yea, all that a man hath will he give for his life. 5 But put forth thine hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse thee to thy face. 6 And the LORD said unto Satan, Behold, he is in thine hand; but preserve his soul.
“Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them to present himself before the LORD” [1].
The enemy came to obtain permission for harsher and more bitter temptations, for the dragon “accuseth them before our God day and night” (Rev 12:10).
* “Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD” [1]. Why does the writer present the idea of their coming in this way every day?

So that we may realize that the event itself does not escape divine providence, and that the angels give an account of the events of every day, and that every day they are sent to settle matters, even when we fail to realize this; for they were created for this. This is their work, as Paul says: “(Are they not all) ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?” (Heb 1:14)...
Behold, you see for what purpose the angels were present; but as for him (Satan), what was his purpose? To tempt Job, and to have matters proceed toward the fulfillment of this purpose.

Why was he questioned again before the angels? It had to be so, for he had already said before them: [Surely he will blaspheme you to your face] (cf. Job 1:11). What a shame! How did he dare to return and stand among them?
St. John Chrysostom
“And the LORD said unto Satan:
From whence comest thou?
And Satan answered:
From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it” [2].
His answer came exactly as the first time, as though he had never harmed anyone at all, and indeed as though it were his right to wrong others. He did not admit that he had sinned!

* The aim in his temptations was to direct (Job) toward death, yet by the very same blow he gained growth in his life. Our ancient enemy was grieved that Job's virtues were multiplied by the very means by which he aimed to remove them from him. Although he saw that he had been defeated in the first round, he prepared himself to aim fresh assaults of temptations, and he still had the audacity to speak evil of that saint. For the wicked cannot believe in the existence of the good, even when it is proved by experience...

“From whence comest thou?”... (Job 2:2) It is as though the voice of God were saying to him plainly: “Behold, a single man has defeated you; he has defeated you in spite of the weaknesses of the body that he endures, you who struggle to stand before Me, the Creator of all.”
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* “And Satan answered” (then he answered). This means that when he received authority to speak, when the Lord gave the wicked servant permission to open his mouth before Him, when He commanded that one whose tongue had been held like an immovable pillar. He says: “I have quickly observed the whole earth, and I have set snares in every place, and prepared traps. All places are full of my traps, all have been constrained by my nets, and they were caught in my toil. There is no way of escape from my captivity, for my strategic plans take many forms.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Note that he goes about the world at every moment. Zechariah teaches us that the angels go to and fro on the earth (Zech 1:10-11). But this wretched one is not content with going about, for divine providence also does this work; rather, he goes about in order to be condemned the more (for his evils), and so that we may be all the more watchful. For this reason he was called [the ruler of the darkness of this age] (Eph 6:12); that is, the ruler of evil.
Speak, O Satan, what have you done?
He says: I have made a tour of the earth, I have gone around in it, and here I am.
What did you bring?
He brought nothing useful or good; therefore he did not answer why he made the tour.
St. John Chrysostom
“And the LORD said unto Satan: Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth?
A perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil.
And still he holdeth fast his integrity, although thou movedst me against him, to destroy him without cause” [3].
Once again the Judge Himself defends the accused and praises him.

* Since (God) is just, it was not possible for Him to be moved against him without cause. Again, since He is truth, it was not possible for Him to speak other than in this manner: He was indeed moved against him without cause. But the two go together, in that He is both just and true; He speaks the truth and does no injustice. Let us realize that the blessed Job, for his part, was smitten without cause, and also, in another sense, is not smitten without cause... for he could not have been presented to others as an example of virtue had he not been tried...
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Job was not shaken, for he did not retreat from the firmness of his faith.

St. Augustine Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Job is a type of the person of the Lord Christ, who accepted suffering, “wrath,” without cause; He suffered without cause, and as Savior and intercessor, a propitiation for us, He suffered for a cause, that He might cleanse us by His blood from our sins.
* Why does he return to attack? What do we learn from this? Even if we fall a thousand times, Satan will not stop, but continues the war without any hesitation.
St. John Chrysostom
“And Satan answered the LORD, and said:
Skin for skin, yea, all that a man hath will he give for his life” [4].
This proverb was common in ancient times, in the days of Job, and it expresses valuing a man's life above everything in the world; many interpretations of it have been offered.

Perhaps it refers to an ancient custom of bartering the skins of slain animals that hunters pursue. The hungry hunter offers the skins of the animal he has hunted in return for food, and if necessary, when hunger intensifies, he offers all the skins of the animals he has hunted in return for bread to save his life. It is as though this proverb expresses a man's acceptance of the greatest possible losses so as not to lose what is greater, namely his life. The Turkish proverb says: “It is fitting that we offer our beard to save our heads.”

Satan wanted to crush Job's character by saying: “Skin for skin,” meaning that whatever he loses, even if it be his children, so long as he is in health, with no one touching his skin, he does not care. He does not care about the lives of his children, but rises up in rage and loses his faith and his sense if anyone touches his skin. He is like the ostrich, which is hard on her young ones as though they were not hers (Job 39:13). He is selfish, a lover of himself, occupied with his health, his comfort and the soundness of his body and nothing else?

* What he means by this saying is that the most important thing a man has is himself. All the rest are secondary matters... On this basis I wish to hunt him himself, for wealth is not of great value in the eyes of men.

Let us listen, beloved, even if we are ashamed to learn from Satan, that it is fitting for a man to give up everything for his life. And that this is a natural thing for human beings, for no negligence is permitted us when we blaspheme because of wealth. He says that wealth amounts to nothing, so we cast it away entirely for the sake of our life.

St. John Chrysostom *Behold the cunning of the adversary, and how violent he was in sin... He knows the difference between outward and inward things. He knows that even the philosophers of this world call the former (outward) things adiafora, of no value, and that the perfection of virtue does not consist in losing these things and despising them. And that the latter, that is the inward things, are the better, and by losing them a grief that cannot be shaken off occurs. Therefore he boldly contradicted what God had said, and declared that Job does not deserve praise at all, since he had not been subjected to a temptation that touched him himself but touched what is outside him. For he gave his skin in place of the skin of his children, and lost only his money to secure the health of his body.
St. Jerome
“But put forth thine hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse thee to thy face” [5].
Satan asked that God Himself stretch out His hand to strike his bone and his flesh, for the thorn in the flesh is extremely severe, hard to bear without the grace of Christ (2 Cor 12:7-9).
“And the LORD said unto Satan:
Behold, he is in thine hand; but preserve his soul” [6].

The phrase “but preserve his soul” can be understood to mean that the temptation has limits, namely preserving his soul, not destroying it. That is, temptation reveals man's weakness, so he humbles himself before God, and his soul is preserved from pride. But if it exceeds the limits of man's capacity, he falls into despair and frustration afflicts it, and his soul perishes because of his unbelief.

The Lord set a limit to the temptation: “but preserve his soul,” that is, do not bring him to death. Satan was eager to kill him at one of his moments of weakness after driving him to blaspheme. But God bound Satan so that he would not kill him.
Some interpret the expression “preserve his soul” as “preserve his mind,” meaning that He permitted him bodily illnesses without his losing his ability to reason and think.

St. John Chrysostom comments on this phrase to show how weak Satan is, for though he is like a ravening beast, and without a body, he cannot approach to tempt a human being who bears a body except by God's permission.

* “Preserve his soul,” meaning do not kill him. In this he has no authority over that unless he receives permission for it... We understand from this that his authority is conditional upon being permitted or refused... The expression “preserve his soul” is stronger than “do not touch his life.”

* Do not fear, then, Satan, even though he is bodiless, when he draws near to the body. For there is none weaker than that one who draws near in this manner though he is not clothed in a body, and none stronger than the brave and bold one, even if he carries a mortal body!
St. John Chrysostom * It was said to the enemy when he asked for him: “Behold, he is in thine hand.” (Job 2:6) The same person is in the hand of God and at the same time in the hand of Satan...

But how is it said to Satan: “But preserve his soul”? For how can he preserve who always longs to destroy the things preserved? Satan's preserving him here means his not daring to destroy. Just as we speak with the Father in prayer, asking: “Lead us not into temptation,” because God will not lead anyone into temptation, for He always overshadows His servants with His mercy to protect them from temptation. Yet if He does not protect us from the allurements of temptation, it is as though He leads us into temptation. Thus, by not allowing us to be tempted above what we are able, it is as though He does not lead us into the snare of temptation.

In the same way as it is said to God: “Lead us not into temptation” if He permits our adversary to lead us into it, so it is said of our adversary that he “preserves our soul” when he is bound not to overcome us by his temptation.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Now I give you the right to turn things upside down. I deliver him to you (Job 2:6), not that you may change his spirit (his thought), nor that you may have authority over his will, nor that you may destroy his freedom in his decision, because if you used pressure on these things you would easily triumph over him, and the battle would be unfair... Surely you would like to approach the “life” of the righteous man, but you cannot, because the law of the great King avenges this, otherwise the guardian of the flock would have let the wolf loose. I deliver to you the life of those whom you envy, not to do whatever you wish, but in the fear of my laws and my divine will...
You are unable to say that another attacks Job's life, because you are the one who attacks it, you whom I appoint as its keeper. You will be condemned if you lay an ambush for his life.

* Here the protective guard goes hand in hand with permission to strike, and the divine dispensation is accomplished through the protection and through the abandonment of the chosen servant; while He abandons him, He guards him... Thus the saint was delivered into the hand of the adversary, but his soul is kept in the hand of (God) his helper, for he is among the flock of which the Truth said in the Gospel: “neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand” (Jn 10:28).

Moreover, they do not see Lucifer rise, he of whom Isaiah said: [Lucifer, who rose in the morning], then continues [he is cut down to the ground] (Isa 14:12), indicating that he does not return to regain his former dignity. By his fall from heaven to earth he wanted the destruction of man, but God gives the one who is not deceived authority to tread the traitor under his feet, and to shatter him into pieces.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem *The unclean spirit has no authority over human beings. This is shown in his struggle against the blessed Job, for he took authority over his body from the Lord, who said to him: “Behold, he is in thine hand; but preserve his soul” (Job 2:6), that is, do not weaken his spirit and make him mad, and gain dominion over his memory and mind, strangling his inner strength.

Fr. Serenus * He put the saint's body into Satan's hands, but his vital powers were withheld from him. For if Satan had struck that on which his senses and his rational faculty depend, the sin arising from the misuse of the faculties would have arisen and remained at his door, not by his desire to commit it but because of the imbalance of his mind.
St. Jerome St. Ambrose offers us a wonderful interpretation of this phrase, in his discourse on St. Paul's imitation of God:

* Everyone who believes is received by the Lord, but He chastens every son whom He receives (Heb 12:6). And in His chastening of him He does not deliver him to death. For it is written: [The LORD hath chastened me sore: but he hath not given me over unto death] (Ps 118:18).

The Apostle Paul teaches us not to abandon those who have committed sin unto death, but to bind them to the bread of tears (of repentance), yet let their sorrow be moderate. This is what the phrase means: “thou givest them tears to drink in great measure” (Ps 80:5). Their sorrow must be in measure, lest the penitent be swallowed up by excessive sorrow. As he said to the Corinthians: “What will ye? shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?” (1 Cor 4:21). He uses the rod, but without harshness, for it is said: “Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell” (Prov 23:14).

And what the Apostle means by the rod appeared when he rebuked the sin of fornication (1 Cor 5:1), warning against immorality with relatives whom it is forbidden to marry, and reproving their pride, since those who ought to have mourned were puffed up. And finally, in speaking of the offender he commanded that he be removed from the congregation and delivered to Satan, not for the destruction of his soul but for the destruction of his body.

And in this Paul imitates God, who did not give Satan authority over the spirit of the blessed Job, but permitted him to afflict his body (Job 2:6). Paul delivered the sinner to Satan for the destruction of the body, so that the serpent might lick the dust of his body (Mic 7:17), but as for his spirit, it will not harm it...

And if we want to explain what the Apostle Paul means, let us consider his very words, in what sense he said to deliver him to Satan for the destruction of the body, because it is Satan who tempts us, bringing infirmities and diseases upon our bodies. Satan smote the blessed Job with bitter sores from the sole of his foot to his head, because he received authority for the destruction of his body, when the Lord said to him: “Behold, he is in thine hand; but preserve his soul” (Job 2:6). This is also what the Apostle took up in the same words, delivering the fornicator to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, “that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus” (1 Cor 5:5).

Great is this authority!! And great is this gift, by which Satan destroys himself by himself, by urging the tempting of man, for he makes him strong in spirit instead of weak. For when his body is weakened his spirit grows strong, because the weakness of the body resists sin, whereas its delicate living kindles the fire of sin.

Satan was deceived, for he wounded himself by the blows he directed against himself, fighting himself by his thought of weakening the sinner. Thus Satan armed Job the more when he wounded him. For when his whole body was worn away with sores, he truly bore Satan's blow without anything of his venom touching him, and thus it was truly said of him: [Canst thou draw out leviathan with an hook?... Wilt thou play with him as with a bird? or wilt thou bind him for thy maidens?... Lay thine hand upon him] (Job 41:5).

See how Paul mocked Satan, so that he became like the child mentioned in the prophecy who put his hand on the serpent without its harming him. He drew him out of his hiding places and turned his venom into a spiritual antidote against poisons. Turning the poison into a remedy for the poison that is used for the destruction of the body, it became a cure for the spirit!

Then let me leave the serpent to strike what is earthly in (my body), let me leave it to bite my flesh and cause it to turn livid, and righteousness will say to it concerning me: “Behold, he is in thine hand; but preserve his soul” (Job 2:6).

How mighty is God!! He delivers the keeping of man's soul into the hand of Satan who wants his destruction...!! By the Master's commandments He made Satan a keeper of His sheep, so that against his will he came to carry out the commandments of heaven, and in his harshness he obeys the commandments of gentleness!
St. Ambrose

entries.section: 2. Another Adam in the midst of the ashes

paragraphs.text: 7 So went Satan forth from the presence of the LORD, and smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown. 8 And he took him a potsherd to scrape himself withal; and he sat down among the ashes.
“So went Satan forth from the presence of the LORD, and smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown” [7].

As soon as Satan received permission he pounced on Job's body to strike it with an extremely violent disease. He did not strike him with a single sore, nor with several sores, but with sores from the sole of his foot, so that he was unable to walk, to his crown. He could not sleep on either side, nor on his back or even his stomach, nor sit, nor stand, for his whole body except his tongue was full of sores. He did not even find dogs to lick his sores, as happened with poor Lazarus (Lk 16:21).

Origen comments on the divine promise: [If thou wilt diligently hearken to the voice of the LORD thy God, and wilt give ear to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will put none of these diseases upon thee, which I have brought upon the Egyptians] (Ex 15:26). [Since one of their diseases was boils, why did Job fall into this disease? The boils of the pagan Egyptians are their weaknesses toward the love of the world and what is in it. This is what the Lord heals us from, and does not put upon us.]

* [All things work together for good to them that love God] (Rom 8:28). Job, the holy man, was tried. He lost his sons and daughters, his house fell in ruin, and he lost all he had; suddenly everything was gone! He was no longer a father or a master, and there was no sound member left in his body except his tongue, with which he could blaspheme. Behold the tempter, for Scripture says: “smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown” (Job 2:7)...
He left him only his tongue so that he might be able to blaspheme his God. [In all this did not Job sin with his lips] (Job 1:22).

Only realize the dreadfulness of the trial. Consider the greatness of his virtue. Consider well and understand how the saying of the Apostle was fulfilled: [All things work together for good to them that love God]... Before the trial God never spoke with him; and after he was tried God came to him and spoke with him, setting aside formality, as a friend with his friend.
Let calamity strike, let every kind of calamity come, so long as Christ comes after the calamity.

St. Jerome * Perhaps because our God knows that I am exceedingly weak He did not give him authority over my body. Even though I myself desire that. For although I offer myself (to accept a trial in the body), God reckoned me unworthy of this struggle, and tested me with various troubles. But Job did not begin with this struggle; he ended with it.

entries.section: 2. Another Adam in the midst of the ashes

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose “And he took him a potsherd to scrape himself withal; and he sat down among the ashes” [8].

What is this potsherd (fragments of earthen vessels) with which he scratches his body afflicted with sores, if not the use of earthly or temporal means for healing the soul? Instead of offering true comforts and real healing, the person uses a potsherd which causes the sores to be even more contaminated, and wrecks the body; so when we stretch out our hands to treat our spiritual illnesses by human ways apart from God's grace, we wreck our souls all the more and destroy them.

Job became a type of the Lord Christ, for Job found no place to lay his head, and had nothing before him but to sit on a dunghill amid sores that filled his whole body, mocked even by his friends. So the Son of Man has not where to lay His head, and has nothing but to be lifted up on the Cross amid the pains of His whole body; His own received Him not (Jn 1:11).

Job did not go up on a mountain, but sat on a dunghill, to enjoy there victory over the enemy of good, glorifying God his God. So our Christ, the Savior of the world, rests in the humble and the contrite of heart to raise up a temple for Himself from them. He chose the foolish things to put to shame the wise, and the weak things to put to shame the strong, and the base things and things which are despised, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are (1 Cor 1:27-28).

Job found no one to sympathize with him, nor anyone to bandage his sores; perhaps his friends feared the enemy or could not bear the stench of the sores. He did not find a piece of cloth with which to clean his wounds, but scraped them with a potsherd, so the remedy was more painful than the disease itself. There was no one to anoint the wounds of the sores with antiseptic substances nor with ointment to soothe the pain! He complained later, saying that his flesh was clothed with worms and clods of dust (Job 7:5).

As for his sitting in the ashes with his whole body full of sores, it increased the contamination of his wounds instead of cleansing them. Perhaps he did this as a sign of his humility, contrition and repentance.
In the Septuagint it reads: “He sat upon a dunghill outside the city.”

Pope Gregory (the Great) says that we should not marvel if one whom God Himself praised is permitted to be tried until he sits in the midst of the ashes, just as St. John the Baptist, to whom He bore witness that among those born of women there is none greater than he, was permitted to have his life given as the price of a wanton dance.
* Is it not (permitted) so that He may press them down below, in order to reward them on high?
He brings them down outwardly to the level of contempt, so as to lead them inwardly to the heights that cannot be comprehended.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Since human medicines could not heal him, patience and faith healed him. He sat on a heap of dung, but his soul was walking about in Paradise.

St. Jerome * He brought him down from the royal throne to sit on a dunghill. And though resisted by the woes I just referred to, he remained sound. His body was torn, but he kept in the depths of his soul the treasure of godliness inviolate.
St. Basil the Great * O man corrupt (in body), yet innocent! O being branded (with sores), yet beautiful! Wounded, yet your soul is full of health! You sit on a dunghill, and reign in heaven!
If we love, let us imitate him, and let us strive to follow his example.

Fr. Caesarius, bishop of Arles * Do you not see that he truly came to the utmost destitution, so that it is impossible for you to find anyone with whom to compare him? For how could there be anyone poorer than a naked man who has no roof to take shelter under? Indeed, it was not within his power to enjoy even the ground, but he sat on a dunghill.
Therefore, when you find that you have reached poverty, consider the sufferings of the righteous man, and immediately you will rise and shake off from yourselves every thought of despair.

This trial seems to men to be the foundation of all sufferings put together. But the second trial that follows it, or rather precedes it, is the sorrows of the body. Who became so disabled as he? Who bore such a disease? Who ever received or heard of anyone who fell under such great sorrows? No one.

His body wore away little by little, and a stream of worms came forth from his members on every side; this torrent overflowed without ceasing, the foul stench surrounded him powerfully, the body was destroyed bit by bit, and corruption with such putrefaction made his food bitter, and hunger became to him strange and singular.

He was not able to enjoy even the food that was offered him, for he says: [I see my food has become loathsome] (Job 6:7). When you fall under weakness, O man, remember that holy body. It was a holy and pure body even while afflicted with such wounds...

But someone may say, he had great comfort and relief, since he knew that it was God who brought these troubles upon him. This in fact makes his distress greater and more bewildering, that the righteous God whom he served in every way entered into war with him... He says: “Wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous?” (Job 40:8).

When he felt guilty he said: “I will lay mine hand upon my mouth. Once have I spoken; but I will not answer: yea, twice; but I will proceed no further” (Job 40:4-5). Again he says: “I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:5-6).

But if you think there is in this sufficient comfort, you are able to experience the same comfort. And if you suffer nothing of this from the hand of God, but from the arrogance of men, then give thanks to God and do not blaspheme the One who is able to truly restrain them. And if He permitted them to do so, it is for your testing; for whoever suffers sufferings from the hand of God is crowned. So you also are crowned, because you bear with godliness the misfortunes that men brought upon you, giving thanks to the One who is able to prevent them from doing so, but did not will it.
* The wounds of the righteous man (Job) became more profitable than pearls...
Picture this wrestler before you, and imagine him in the mire, sitting in the midst of it.
What a golden statue studded with jewels!

I do not know how to express this, for I am unable to find a material so precious to compare with this body stained with blood. It is far more precious than any material, whatever its cost, for the nature of that body is incomparably precious, and those wounds are brighter than the rays of the sun, for these (the sun's rays) enlighten the eyes of the body, but those enlighten the eyes of the soul! They strike Satan with a total, unrelieved blindness.
* Do you realize, beloved, how great was the reward of the trial?
His body was agile and sound, but it became more dignified when it was pierced with wounds...!
A king sitting on the throne is not, in renown, equal to this man sitting in the mire with great standing... for after the royal throne comes death, but after the mire the Kingdom of Heaven.
* Why did he sit on a dunghill? To hide, on the heap of refuse, his fall (unto death).

Why did he go outside the gates? In order to find some relief, for if he had remained in a closed room, however pure the air of the room, it would be spoiled, and he himself would be suffocated by the foul smell.

In my opinion his sufferings had absolutely no human cause, and he understood that God wished to give a lesson by what happened to him, so he felt neither shame nor embarrassment, but showed himself as having become a laughingstock to all.
St. John Chrysostom * In any case Job did well to sit on a dunghill... for his worn-out body became refuse. He remembered that the body contains the same components (as the dunghill).
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem

9 Then said his wife unto him, Dost thou still retain thine integrity? Bless God, and die. 10 But he said unto her, Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips.
“Then said his wife unto him:
Dost thou still retain thine integrity?
Bless God, and die (blaspheme against God, and die!)” [9].
The Septuagint reads: “And when a long time had passed, his wife said to him: How long will you endure, saying: Behold, I wait a little longer, expecting the hope of my salvation?” [9 (a)]
It is also found in the Septuagint that Job's wife used to wander from house to house, hoping to find a refuge in which to take shelter.
Some of the Jews consider that Job's wife is Dinah the daughter of Jacob.

The enemy is accustomed to strike the faithful through the members of their own household, as he did with Adam using Eve, and with David using his wife Michal, who mocked David her husband, and he even wanted to use the Apostle Peter to strike the Lord Christ when He spoke of the Crucifixion, so that he said to Him: “Be it far from thee, Lord: this shall not be unto thee” (Mt 16:22). So He turned and said to Peter: “Get thee behind me, Satan: thou art an offence unto me: for thou savourest not the things that be of God, but those that be of men” (Mt 16:23).
The righteous Job expressed his wife's view of him, saying: “My breath is loathsome to my wife, and I have become foul (a stench) to the children of my body” (Job 19:17).

* Satan left him nothing but his tongue and his wife. Through his wife he tempts him, and with his tongue he can blaspheme. Satan did not forget his old deception by which he deceived Adam through a woman, therefore he attacked Job through his wife, reckoning that he would always be able to deceive him by a woman, not realizing that if one man was mortally wounded by a woman, now the whole world has been saved through a woman.
You remember Eve; consider Mary.
The first drove us out of Paradise, and the last led us (by Christ her Son) to heaven.

St. Jerome * [And when a long time was passed] [Job 2:9] LXX... The Spirit kept the expressions quite plain for our benefit, as He did not declare the length of this period. For had He specified months and years, those who are placed under trial in the future would be disheartened before reaching the end of the period. They would count the nights and the hours, and focus on this time. Each of them would fall into extreme despair that God's hand had not intervened, and that he had not received help from the heavens as Job did at a set time.
In fact the Spirit said: “a long time.” He expressed it thus in order that you may know that Job was found stronger, not only than the illness and the many sores, but also than time.
He wrestled for a long time in bodily torments and troubles, and yet he remained unconquered in the battles.

By this the Spirit comforts us that however long the time of trial, our heart should not grow weak, for God's hand will come and His right hand will be for our sake (Ps 18:35), for Job was saved from the furnace of trial after a long time.

* Since the adversary did not find the fighter weakened, he enlisted his wife. Perhaps he said to himself: This person (Job) will not be stronger than Adam. If he is rich, yet he does not have “the Paradise of God” (like Adam in the garden). And although righteous, he has not attained “the tree of life.” And although godly, Adam enjoyed conversation with God. This person (Job) has many cattle, but as for Adam, all the beasts of the earth were subject to him. Therefore if I was able to make him lose this through Eve his wife, perhaps this one cannot resist the assaults of his wife. With this thought Satan stirred up Job's wife against him.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * He left his wife to him alone, not as a comforter but rather as Satan's ally.

St. Augustine The continuation of the verse in the Septuagint reads: “Behold, your memory has been blotted out from the earth, even your sons and daughters, the pangs of my travail and the toils of my womb, whom I bore with sorrows in vain; and behold, you sit spending your nights in the open air amid the corruption of worms, and I have become a wanderer and a servant, moving from place to place and from house to house, awaiting the setting of the sun that I may rest from my labors and pains which have encompassed me. Say some word against God, and die” [Job 2:9 - LXX].

* Imagine that you have lost your wealth through which you were famous. The same if you have been deprived of your share in sons; how can your memory remain on the earth after that time? Your goods have been stolen, your possessions destroyed, there are no more sons, no daughters remain, and there will be no children (grandchildren), since the sons have been lost.
(As though Job's wife were saying to her husband): In vain have I sown the field of my womb.

You yourself have been deprived of what you planted, and I too have lost the fruit of my sorrows and the toil of my breasts, and the experience of the womb of pregnant women, the unbearable pangs of labor, which are reckoned as a dreadful memory.
Then is it one sorrow or many sorrows...?
Death has reached the children of my womb, and the fruit of my body has perished in the abyss.
Can I hope to conceive other children?
How? Where? For the sower, who is you, has been ruined and has perished, and you yourself have become food for vermin.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * The more the calamities he brought upon him increased, the more he saw him in strength. Therefore, as you know, after he had used every means, finally he used his instrument; for when he found no way for himself, he ran to his old weapon, the woman, and put on the mask of concern, and presented a tragic picture of his disasters in a tone of the utmost tenderness, and under the pretense of removing his evil offered fatal counsel (curse the Lord and die). But not even by this did he conquer, indeed because that wonderful man recognized his deceit, and with great wisdom silenced the woman who was speaking at his instigation.
* See how she tried by her eloquence to reach all the way to the end. For she has a multitude of arguments with which to persuade him.
As for the length of time, since not one day passed, nor two nor three days, but a great number of months. How long will you endure...?
Note the satanic deception, for he thought of Eve. He says: Behold, you who caused the first man to fall can end the life of Job.
But she was foolish and poor, for finding Adam unable to overcome his weakness, she was able to put poison in good food.
Behold, you see that Job, on the contrary, was a wise man, victorious even over his nature... So do not think that the matter concerns the woman or her recommendations...
Now I suggest to our people that they not take into account the dignity of persons, but rather the nature of the counsel.
For the woman came to help the man, not to be a stumbling block to him... He expects a change, something indicating sound faith and noble hope; he knows God's tenderness.

Thus the main lines of the foundation of her wickedness were laid down. She did not say: “They have died,” according to the common expression used to indicate general grief among all men, for she did not use the usual expression. But what did she say? [Your memory has been blotted out...]
In my opinion she wished to justify the violence of the trial by speaking thus.
This is what she wanted to say to him: “What kind of change do you hope will occur? Can you return to what you were after all that has happened, for can what has utterly vanished return to life?

For we desire children, often so that they may extend our memory in a way that does not pass away. Surely the most important thing men seek is to leave memorials after them. She says to him: You yourself are dead by the loss of your children, for without offspring and without children you perish.
Note to what level she offered this terrible counsel, not to urge him to anger, but to turn him aside to self-pity...
She says: Night and day you find no one to share the roof of your house with you, no one to console you, no one to pity you, no one to share your pains...

What wretchedness! There is no one to pity his wife, nor to soothe her circumstances, she who was in the company of a king has become a slave living in the open under the stars...” For I am without a house or a city or a home, I go about in the city... there is not one house to lighten the shame of my condition, and everywhere I receive mockery and insult from the common people”.

She did not say to him: “Blaspheme,” but said: [Curse God...] Why? So that you may know that by doing this you die, but as for my death, what consolation could it bring you? What correction of the situation by my death...?

What are you saying, woman? When it is necessary to beseech God to grant good things, when it is necessary to appease Him, you are ready to provoke Him! If God is the source of these troubles, then it calls for supplication to Him, not blasphemy against Him. And on the other hand, if He is not their source, then He is not to be blasphemed!

St. John Chrysostom * Job lost his children and all he owned except his wife! (Job 1:13-19), who alone was preserved for his temptation! (Job 2:9-10). And at that time he was covered all over with deadly sores (Job 2:7), and he realized that his friends had not come to console him, but to increase his sufferings and magnify them!

Note the authority that was given to the adversary by the Lord to try him (Job 2:1-6). And although he felt that the arrows of the Lord were in his flesh, and said that they had pierced his body (Job 6:4), yet as a good wrestler he did not yield to the pain, nor refuse the difficulties of the struggle, but continued.
“Since the Lord has begun, let Him wound me, but do not stab me (destroy me) in the end, for what is my strength that I should be silent (wait)?
And what is my end that my soul should endure?
Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh of brass?
Have I not trust in Him? But help has forsaken me, and His visitation has despised me” (Job 6:9, 11-14) LXX.

St. Ambrose * In truth his wife alone had been left until that day. All that he had was completely destroyed, all his children and possessions and even his body, and she was left for the temptation to be a snare for him.

This is truly the reason why Satan did not destroy her along with the children, and did not ask for her death, since he expected that she would contribute the more to making the holy man fall into the snare. Therefore he left her as a kind of terrible instrument in his hand.
He said: “If even in Paradise humanity was driven out by her means, how much more can I cast him down while he is on the dunghill!”

* The building was the same (the one on the rock and the one on the sand), and the trials were the same, but the end was not the same, because the foundation was different. The fall of the building occurred because of the foolishness of the builder and not because of the nature of the trials,...
Do not think that these things were said about a mere building, but the discourse concerns the soul, affirming that by its works it hears the divine Word or rejects it. Thus Job built himself.

The rain came down, because fire came down from heaven and consumed all his flocks, and the floods came, as the messengers came to him bearing news of disasters in continuous succession, telling him of the destruction of his flocks, his camels and his sons. And the wind blew, which is the bitter words of his wife, saying: [Curse God and die]. Yet the house did not fall. His soul was not moved from its place, and the righteous man did not blaspheme, but gave thanks to God, saying: [The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; what is good in His eyes He does].

St. John Chrysostom * The adversary tempted Job through his sons and possessions (Job 1:13), and since he could not conquer him he brought his equipment, coming with him the daughter of Eve who overwhelmed Adam, and through her mouth he said to Job, the righteous husband: [Curse God], but Job refused the counsel.

King Asa also triumphed over the sodomites of the land when (Satan) came to him to fight him through his mother (1 Kgs 15:12-13). Asa knew his cunning, and removed his mother from her high position (queen), and cut down her image and cast it away.
John was greater than all the prophets, but Herod slew him because of the dance of the daughter of Eve (Mt 11:11, 14; etc.).
Haman was rich, third in honor from the king, but his wife advised him to kill the Jews (Esth 6:13).

Zimri was head of the tribe of Simeon, but Cozbi the daughter of the head of the tribes of Midian cast him down, and because of one woman twenty-four thousand persons of Israel fell in one day (Num 25:6-15).
St. Aphrahat “And he said unto her: Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh!
What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?
In all this did not Job sin with his lips” [10].
* Job in the hours of his grief was more watchful than Adam on the throne of his happiness.
One was defeated amid pleasures, and the other conquered amid sufferings.
One agreed to what seemed pleasant, and the other did not wither amid pains of the utmost terror...
He bore his pain in his body, and bore in his heart the faults of others, rebuking his wife for her folly, teaching his companions wisdom, keeping patience in all circumstances.
St. Augustine * Note, beloved brethren, that he never said: “This is the work of Satan.”

Ascribe the chastening directly to your God, for Satan does nothing without the permission of Him who governs your affairs by the power of His authority, whether for punishment or for teaching; for punishment as regards the wicked and for teaching as regards the son. For He “scourgeth every son whom he receiveth” (Heb 12:6).
You need not flee from the rod, unless you do not wish to inherit.

* When his body was covered with sores his wife came to him, who had been left to him as another Eve, to be Satan's companion instead of being a helper to her husband. She was constantly rebuking him sharply to shake his loyalty, saying: [Say a word against God, and die].
But the Adam on the dunghill was wiser than the Adam who was in Paradise.
Adam in Paradise gave his ear to the woman, so that they were driven out of Paradise. And Adam on the dunghill cast the woman aside only that they might enter Paradise.
And what did the Adam on the dunghill have? Inwardly he was begetting immortality; outwardly he was food for worms.
What did he say to his wife? “Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” (Job 2:10).
He repeats that God's hand was upon him when Satan was striking, for he did not look to the one who aimed the blow at him, but to the One who gave him the authority.
For Satan himself in turn called that authority which he begged from the hand of the Lord.

St. Augustine * I choose that the Lord visit my sins and correct my transgressions here in this world, so that Abraham may say to me there what he said about poor Lazarus in his conversation with the rich man: “Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented” (Lk 16:25).
For this reason, when the Lord rebukes us, when He chastens us, we must not be ungrateful.

Let us realize, then, that our being rebuked in the present time is so that we may receive comfort in the future. As the Apostle says: “But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world” (1 Cor 11:32). For this reason Job also accepted all his sufferings willingly, saying: “What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?”

Origen * He became more blessed than anyone, for not only did he do nothing to cause him to stumble, but he practiced what made him more steadfast. His wife troubled him along with all these, and yet he shone in everything.
* A wife is a great good, just as she can also be a grave evil. For the wife is great; note from what point Satan wanted to enter through the strong wall.
St. John Chrysostom The Septuagint reads: [But he looked at her and said to her: Thou speakest as one of the foolish women] (Job 2:10).
* Meaning: You are not speaking what befits you, nor your teaching, nor the formation you received from me.
These words do not befit you.
He did not wish to rebuke her violently, but to turn her back from this corrupt thinking.
“If we receive good things from the hand of God, shall we not endure evils?” Meaning, if indeed these things are nothing but evils, let us bear them.
He is the Lord and Master; does He not have authority over everything He sends upon us?
Why did He give us good things? Not out of any merit on our part.
May we not be anxious from this day on by thinking that we suffer undeservedly.
He is completely free, even if He gave us only evils.
If He gives us good things also, why should we complain?
Note that he never spoke of transgressions, nor of good works, but spoke only of God, who has the authority to do what He wills.

Remember your former good things and you will not find it hard to bear the present troubles. It is enough for us, for our consolation, to realize that the Lord has sent them to us. Do not speak of justice or injustice.
St. John Chrysostom *“He looked at her” (Job 2:10) LXX, he looked at his wife, in order to discern the one who was speaking in her, and to be on guard against the serpent hidden in his wife's speech.
* Shall we not offer our patience as an acceptable sacrifice (Rom 12:1), through which we recover what we lost, and receive other blessings greater than they?
* “In all this did not Job sin with his lips.” Did God deliver Job to this struggle in vain? Did He not truly know His fighter? Does the King not know His soldier...?
As for us, let us imitate his patience. Let us fight with gentleness, let us practice his patience, and equal him in his trust in God.

Let us be formed according to his faith without failure, and let us be steadfast in his spirit, in the truth of his words, in his struggle with an unseen enemy, in his solitude, and in his trials, in his calmness, in facing all that arises, that we may remain strong and firm of resolve.

In all sufferings let us be godly and complete our testing. For by this we share in the crowns, and become partners in his victory, and God will be the witness of our righteousness. To Him be glory forever. Amen.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Let the Almighty be summoned to your aid against the wiles of Satan.
Let Him dwell in you, He who cannot be conquered, for you will surely overcome the one who was accustomed to conquer. But whom does he conquer? Those in whom God does not dwell.

For you, brethren, know this, that Adam in Paradise despised the commandment of God, and lifted up his neck, like one who wanted to be master of himself, and shrank from submitting to God's will. Thus he fell from immortality and blessedness.
But a man was found, a brilliant proven one, though mortal by birth, and though he sat on a dunghill and was corrupt with worms, he conquered Satan.
Yes, Adam himself has prevailed even in Job, because Job is of his race.
Adam was defeated in Paradise, and was overcome on the dunghill.
Being in Paradise, he lent his ear to the persuasion of the woman into whom Satan had entered, but when on the dunghill he said to Eve: “Thou speakest as one of the foolish women.”
There he lent her his ear; here he gave her an answer.
When he was happy he listened, and when he was afflicted he conquered.

Therefore see what followed this, my brethren, in the Epistle (1 Jn 2:9). For this is what we must put in our hearts, that we truly conquer Satan, but not by ourselves, for he says: “If ye know that he is righteous, ye know that every one that doeth righteousness is born of him.”

St. Augustine * It is written: “a man's foes shall be they of his own household” (Mt 10:36), for when the crafty adversary sees that he has withdrawn from the hearts of the good, he seeks out those who are most beloved by them, and speaks to them sweetly with words most dear to them, so that when the power of love steals into the heart the sword of his persuasion can easily break through to the inner defenses of the righteous.

* By good here is meant either the temporal or the eternal gifts of God, and by evil the blows of the present time, those about which the Lord said through the prophet: “I am the LORD, and there is none else, I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil.” (Isa 45:6-7) He does not mean the evil which has no substance by nature as being created by God. Rather, the Lord Himself is reckoned the creator of evil (affliction) when He turns evil into punishment (or discipline), so that these things are evil for the disobedient in their bearing of pain, and at the same time good by nature...

It is a mighty comfort for our trials, when we bear sorrows and remember our Creator's gifts to us... For it is said: [In the day of good things do not forget afflictions, and in the day of afflictions do not forget good things] (Sir 11:27).

For he who receives God's gifts in the season of gifts and does not fear the blows falls by his joy into wandering of mind, and he who suffers punishments, and yet in the season of punishments ignores his comfort in the gifts he had received, falls from the steadiness of his mind into despair on every side.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

His wife mocked him for his simplicity and his attachment to eternal things, and she counted this simplicity as folly and ignorance and deprivation of life and happiness. Therefore she saw his death as far better than his life, and blaspheming God as more fitting than worshiping Him while suffering pains.

* It is as though he says: If we incline toward eternal blessings, what wonder if we face temporal evils? Paul fixed his eyes on these blessings with great attention when he submitted his mind to the evils that befell him. He says: “For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom 8:18).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Job did not sin with his mouth, for he did not utter a word that did not befit him as a believer. St. Peter the Apostle warns us against sinning with the mouth, saying: [Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or one who speaks evil] (1 Pet 4:15) Vulgate.

11 Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him. 12 And when they lifted up their eyes afar off, and knew him not, they lifted up their voice, and wept; and they rent every one his mantle, and sprinkled dust upon their heads toward heaven. 13 So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great.
“Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place;
Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him” [11].

Here he mentioned the names of his three friends who came to sympathize with him and comfort him. Perhaps the young man Elihu was present with them, and he listened to the discussions, and it seems he was not a friend of Job because he was much younger than he, but he attended as a listener. Perhaps he loved to sit with elders, and perhaps the sight of Job in his tragedy attracted him, so that he longed to offer him some service or a word of consolation.

As for the three friends, they were advanced in age, indeed they were elders, famed for knowledge, wisdom and goodness, and they were esteemed, and their opinions were met with respect (Job 32:6). Perhaps they held high positions in the state, as princes or chiefs. Perhaps they were his relatives, for the three were descendants of Abraham, and most likely they inherited from him some teachings and good fruits. Eliphaz the Temanite, king of Teman, was the son of Teman, the grandson of Esau (Gen 36:11). Some see that Eliphaz here is not the eldest son of Esau but his grandson who was called by his name. Bildad the Shuhite was the son of Shuah, whom Keturah bore to Abraham (Gen 25:2). And Zophar the Naamathite is supposed to be Zepho, the grandson of Esau (Gen 36:11). All three were of the Gentiles, and bore some good traits, among them that, unlike most of the friends, they did not leave Job in his trial, but came to share his sorrows as they had shared before in his joys.

They came not out of curiosity, nor at anyone's invitation, but agreed together in doing good. They were sincere in their desire to comfort, though it became clear that they were wearisome comforters because of their lack of wisdom in handling the matter.

We did not hear that any of the poor and needy whom he supported, nor of the orphans and widows whom he cared for, came to ask about him in his trial. Perhaps they heard of the successive calamities and fell into what these three friends fell into, and reckoned that he was a wicked man who had hidden his wickedness with outward gifts and showy concern.
The absence of any of them undoubtedly had its bad effect on Job's spirit, since he reckoned that they had stumbled over his person.
“And when they lifted up their eyes afar off, and knew him not, they lifted up their voice, and wept; and they rent every one his mantle, and sprinkled dust upon their heads toward heaven” [12].

Grief and bitterness often disfigure a person's appearance, so that his elder friends did not recognize him, because his sores deformed his body, and the bitterness of his soul removed his cheerfulness from him. This is what happened with Naomi when grief disfigured her appearance, so that when she returned to her country the people of the city asked: “Is this Naomi?” (Ruth 1:19).

The elders could not contain themselves, so they lifted up their voices like children and wept, and each tore his mantle, and they sprinkled dust on their heads. And they sat with him on the ground. It was as though they shared his humiliation.

They did not meet him on the level of formal courtesies, but as loved ones sharing the bitterness of his soul. As partners in the severe affliction they could not open their mouths for seven days and seven nights; they were silent, astonished. The Latin proverb says: “Light sorrows speak, but heavy ones tie the tongue.”

At first they avoided speaking lest they add weight to his trial, and perhaps because they wanted to take time so that each might examine this baffling riddle, for they knew the works of his great love to which all bore witness, but was there some hidden sin that caused him all these disasters? Does God wish to reveal to him what he had hidden in his heart and mind, or works that no one knows?

* Job's friends did not recognize him, for they did not see the purple robe nor the high throne, nor the royal crown and the soldiers in service, nor the servants at their tasks. Instead of the throne he had the hard ground, the dunghill instead of a bed, and instead of a house the open air.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem “So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great” [13].

They had agreed to come and meet together at Job's, but what astonishes us is that they remained silent seven days and seven nights without uttering a word, and when they spoke they attacked him with great violence, as with one opinion.
They showed at first exaggerated grief, followed by quarreling and bitter arguments amid his pains.
What love was this that moved them to agree together and sit around him amid the unbearable stench for a whole week? And why the sudden change, to the exact opposite?
Were they perhaps sincere in their love for him, but offered a love without discernment? Or was the intention evil, hidden under the guise of intense grief, so that what was inside them burst out?

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that these friends are a type of the heretics, who at first show excessive tenderness, and though sincere in intention to act, lack the spirit of discernment. Therefore Job says to them: “But ye are forgers of lies, ye are all physicians of no value” (Job 13:3-4).
They came every one from his own place (Job 2:11), and the place of the heretics is pride itself. They came by appointment in agreement under the guise of love and friendship.
Thus heretics often agree together against the Church of God, and bear the appearance of friendship and service and conduct in virtue.
