Paul commands us otherwise: "warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men" (1 Thess 5:14).

*"Though ye have ten thousand instructors... yet have ye not many fathers" (1 Cor 15:4)... Paul does not seek any honor here, but rather shows the depth of his love. Honor belongs to the instructor, and love is the mark of the father.
St. John Chrysostom Thy words have raised up him that stumbled, and thou hast established the trembling knees [4].

How much Job strengthened the slack hands for fitting work, took the hands of the stumbling and raised them from the dust, and strengthened their knees to bear them to walk in the way of life by the power of God. So Eliphaz praised him, so that when he rebuked him Job might not think that he was prejudiced against him, or ignoring his past with all its good deeds. Job comforted many, so he deserves to find one who comforts him.
Some commentators see that Eliphaz mentioned this to rebuke Job, as if saying to him:
[You who guided many, why do you not guide yourself?
And you strengthened slack hands, why did you not find rest for your weakness?
And if you helped the stumbling with words, why are you cast down on the ground in your body as in your soul?
If you established the trembling knees, why did you not encourage yourself, but are broken down before the diseases that have come upon you, walking as though paralyzed?

Is this not proof of your hypocrisy, that you offer the medicine to others and refuse to receive it yourself for healing of your sickness? You who taught others not to break down, do you break down? "Physician, heal thyself" (Lk 4:23).
See, your former talk was perhaps vain, and the good that you did contains folly!]
* Our neglect of our brethren is no light fault, but brings upon us great punishment and chastisement without mercy...
Persistent counsel and teaching make a man diligent and bring him to a better state, and in this I cite the common proverb that confirms this truth, that "constant drops of water split the rock."
What is softer than water?! And what is harder than rock?! Yet persistence in work continually overcomes nature. If this is so with nature, shall not human nature all the more be overcome...?!
What a large part of the body of the Church resembles the dead, without movement!!
You say: And what concerns us in this?

You have a very great capacity with regard to your brethren. For you are responsible if you do not counsel them, and ward off evil from them, and draw them here with power, and pull them out of their extreme slackness. For is it fitting for a man to be profitable to himself alone, and not profitable to himself and to many as well?
The Lord Christ made this clear when He called us [salt] (Mt 5:13), and "leaven" (Mt 13:33), and [light] (Mt 5:14), for these things are useful and beneficial to others.

For the lamp does not shine for itself but for those sitting in darkness. And you are a lamp, not to enjoy the light alone, but to bring back a man who has gone astray; for what benefit is a Christian who does not benefit others?! and who does not bring anyone back to virtue?!

Again, salt does not season itself but seasons food lest it spoil and perish... So God has made you spiritual salt, to bind together the corrupt members, that is, the lazy, slack brethren, and to strengthen them and rescue them from sloth as from corruption, and to bind them with the rest of the body of the Church.

And this is the reason why the Lord called us "leaven," for leaven too does not leaven itself, but though small it leavens the whole lump, however great. So do you also. For though you are few in number, be many and strong in faith and zeal toward God. And as leaven is not weak because of its smallness, since it has power and capacity by its nature... so you can, if you wish, draw to yourselves greater numbers than you, and they will have the same level of zeal...

For this reason do not gather here in vain. Rather I do not cease to beseech you with all zeal, as I used to do before, saying: "Come here with your brethren. Guide here. Guide the erring. Teach them by deeds, not by words only"...

May the God of peace and love, who removes from our spirits all rancor, bitterness and anger, condescend and grant us - through our being joined to one another in perfect unity as the members are joined to one another (Eph 4:16) - to offer Him with one accord, one mouth and one spirit the praise of our due thanksgiving.

St. John Chrysostom If we ignore Eliphaz's intention, we find a living testimony to a godly man who did not belong to Isaac the son of Abraham, a king and not a priest of any people, and yet he set in his godly heart the support of the stumbling and the strengthening of the trembling knees. He will judge many of God's servants and priests in the Old Testament as in the New. For there is no pastoral work greater than bending down toward those fallen to the ground to take their hands and rise with them. If the divine Word became incarnate and came down to our earth in humility, and carried us in Himself up to heaven, so it befits every servant, indeed every believer, to support and help so that all may enjoy fellowship with God.

By setting forth Job's traits, Eliphaz presented us with a living method of pastoral care, indeed of the life of faith, and of how every believer cares for the life of his brother through love, without ignoring his concern for the salvation of his own soul and the salvation of his household.

entries.section: 3. His rebuke for his lack of steadfastness

paragraphs.text: 5 But now it is come upon thee, and thou faintest; it toucheth thee, and thou art troubled. 6 Is not thy piety thy confidence, and thy hope the perfection of thy ways?
But now it is come upon thee, and thou faintest!
It toucheth thee, and thou art troubled! [5]

Eliphaz rebukes Job, saying to him that when his turn came to drink the cup of affliction he collapsed, fainted and was terrified. Here begins the attack to accuse him of hypocrisy. As if he were saying to him: When you were in prosperity you taught well, but when you fell into what others fall into, your weakness was exposed and your patience ran out.

* Minds fond of disputation attack the lives of the righteous in two ways: either by asserting that what they utter is wrong, or that they utter the truth which they do not observe in their conduct. Thus the blessed Job was rebuked by his friends over his manner of speaking. They encourage him because he speaks true things, but he does not keep them himself... Observe how they first praised him for his tongue, then complained of the weakness of his life. For the wicked, so as not to show themselves as wicked, sometimes say good things about the righteous, knowing that others know this about them.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

St. John Chrysostom justifies Job's distress and behavior, for it is a natural reaction to the multitude and severity of the calamities and the suddenness of their occurrence, besides the behavior of his friends and their provocative accusations against him.
We cannot ignore that it befits the leader, being in the position of leader, guide and father, not to be quickly disturbed before trials, so as to be a secret of strength and comfort for others.

* No one does more harm to the Church than those who have the appearance and title of holiness yet behave corruptly. And it is a grave error to entrust the place of pastoral care to a deficient person, since pastoral care is an example. A wrong choice of shepherd results in grave consequences, for while in sin he receives honor on account of the position he has taken. Let every unworthy man flee from the weight of this great iniquity and ponder, listening with the ears of his heart to this voice that says: "But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea" (Mt 18:6; Lk 17:2). Here the millstone signifies the whirlpool of life, and the depth of the sea points to eternal perdition. It is far better that a lay person who by himself put on the garment of holiness in outward show should perish alone than that this man should put on himself the garment of pastoral care and destroy others by his wicked example. And I am sure that the punishment of hell will be lighter if this man falls into it alone without being the cause of others' falling with him.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Although a man may keep himself pure from sin, even in lofty degrees, yet I know that one in this condition cannot lead others to virtue. For he who has received the care of a people, it is not enough for him to be free of sin... but he must rise in doing good, as the commandment says: "Depart from evil, and do good" (Ps 37:27).
So he must not only have the traces of vice wiped from his spirit, but also be furnished with virtues, so that he may surpass them in virtue rather more than his loftiness over them in honor.
He must know no limits to doing good or to spiritual growth, nor think it a great gain merely to excel over ordinary people.

He must not measure himself against others, whether wicked or somewhat advanced spiritually, but measure himself by the light of the commandments. Nor should he measure virtue on a small scale, since it flows from God the Greater, for "of him, and through him, and to him, are all things" (Rom 11:36).

entries.section: 3. His rebuke for his lack of steadfastness

paragraphs.text: St. Gregory of Nazianzus Is not thy piety thy confidence, and thy hope the perfection of thy ways? [6]

Here he rebukes him for the piety he showed during his prosperity: where is this piety? And where is your hope and the uprightness of your way? Are not all these vain pretensions with no roots in your depths?

Eliphaz carried out Satan's work and served his interests, for he wanted to stir Job up to blaspheme God by accusing him of hypocrisy, and that this piety, hope and uprightness of his were all vain appearances.

*"Is not thy piety founded on folly, and also thy hope and the perfection of thy way?" (LXX) By this he seeks to distort his former virtuous deeds... He is stabbing at Job's intention while he works. He means either that you did not work, or that your life is full of deceit, or that you did not fear God with an upright intention, but it was all mere talk. Your hope is without reason, it is full of folly... If your deeds were sincere and your life pure, you would not fear these evils...
You see how Eliphaz attacks him, wrestles with him, and makes every effort to prove that his folly brought these troubles upon him...

"By the commandments of the Lord they are destroyed" (9 LXX). Observe another thing.. He says: Do not think that demons and wicked men full of spite are responsible for what has befallen you. For God is chastening you, therefore the chastening is just, beyond dispute.

St. John Chrysostom Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on this phrase: [Where is your fear (piety), your strength, your patience, and the perfection of your ways?] that although he reviled him unjustly, he described precisely the ordering of the virtues and their ladder or degrees, which are the fear of the Lord, then trust in God, then patience, and finally the attainment of perfection:
a. The fear of the Lord, or piety, is the beginning of the way. "In the fear of the LORD is strong confidence" (Prov 14:26).
* Let us not count wealth a very good thing; for the great good is not to possess money, but to acquire the fear of the Lord and all the paths of godliness.
* Fear is no less than a wall, a protection and a mighty tower.
St. John Chrysostom b. Through the fear of the Lord we pass to strength, or "strong confidence in God," which appears only in trial.

* The fear of the Lord contains all those requirements (for continual joy). For the man who fears the Lord as is fitting, and trusts in Him, gathers all the sources of happiness and acquires the perfect fountain of delight. Just as a drop of water falling into a wide ocean quickly vanishes, so whatever befalls him who fears the Lord is dissipated and vanishes in the vast ocean of joy.

It is truly most wonderful that, even with causes of sorrow present, you find the man rejoicing. For since there is nothing at all that brings sorrow, this bitterness is of no value to him compared with his enjoyment of continual joy.

St. John Chrysostom c. Through trust in the Lord the believer enjoys patience. For a man is approved, in the true sense of the word, and grows in strength by bearing the faults of others. He who cannot face his opponent is wounded by the sword of cowardice.

* For four days we have been occupied in explaining the parable of Lazarus (and the rich man), presenting the treasure we find in a body covered with sores. A treasure not of gold and silver, but of wisdom and endurance, of patience and forbearance.
St. John Chrysostom d. Patience leads to perfection. For a man is truly perfect when he is long-suffering toward the weaknesses of others. [In your patience possess ye your souls] (Lk 21:19).

This is the ladder of perfection: the fear of the Lord and piety toward Him give us confidence in Him, and this gives us strength amid trials, this strength gives us patience in bearing others with their weaknesses, and by this patience we reach the ways of perfection.

* There are two forms of perfection, an ordinary one and a higher. One is acquired here, the other hereafter. One is according to human capacities, the other belongs to the perfection of the world to come; but God is just through all, wise above all, perfect in all.

St. Ambrose * The Apostle speaks of himself as perfect and imperfect. He counts himself imperfect, looking at how much righteousness he still lacks, yet perfect in that he is not ashamed to confess his imperfection and that he is advancing to attain perfection.
St. Augustine

7 Remember: who ever perished, being innocent? and where were the upright destroyed? 8 Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same. 9 By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his nostril are they consumed. 10 The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the roarer, and the teeth of the young lions, are broken. 11 The lion perisheth for lack of prey, and the whelps of the lioness are scattered abroad.
Remember: who ever perished, being innocent? and where were the upright destroyed? [7]

Eliphaz presents a practical proof of the accusation he directed at him. For - in Eliphaz's opinion - no righteous man has perished, and no upright man has been destroyed. He asks him for a single example, from Job's long experience throughout his whole life, of a righteous or upright man who suffered what Job has suffered.

This is a theological, moral principle that prevailed in many minds, for even after the Law David was astonished, reproaching the Lord, how the way of the wicked prospers and He allows afflictions to the righteous. But he soon discovers the truth, for the righteous will surely receive their heavenly reward, and the wicked who persist in their evil will fall under judgment. The Psalmist says: "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity. For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb... I have seen the wicked in great power, and spreading himself like a green bay tree. Yet he passed away, and, lo, he was not: yea, I sought him, but he could not be found... But the salvation of the righteous is of the LORD: he is their strength in the time of trouble" (Ps 37).

Eliphaz's speech is true if by perishing and destruction he meant what is eternal, but to apply it to temporal calamities is not correct. Therefore his speech does not apply to Job, for he had not perished eternally.

The prophet says: "The righteous perisheth" (Isa 57:1). And the Wise Man says: "There is one event to the righteous and to the wicked" (Eccl 9:2), until temporal life ends and on the day of the Lord this one is separated from that.

* [What innocent man perishes? and where do the upright perish?] But it often happens in this life that the innocent perishes and the upright are utterly destroyed, yet in their perishing they are kept for eternal glory. If no innocent man perished, the prophet would not have said: "The righteous perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart" (Isa 57:1). If God in His providence did not destroy the upright, Wisdom would not have said of the righteous: [Yea, quickly was he taken away, lest wickedness should alter his understanding] (Wis 4:11).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* The wicked, unbelieving man, even if we suppose that he wraps himself in a heavenly body, remains naked because he does nothing to obtain the garment of the inner man.

St. Didymus the Blind * How beneficial are the trials and sufferings which some consider evil! The saints do not try to avoid them, but truly seek them with all their strength, enduring them courageously, and thus become friends of God, and obtain the crown of eternal life... And the blessed Apostle exults, saying: [I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong] (2 Cor 12:10).
Father Theodore Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity and sow wickedness reap the same [8].
Eliphaz relies in his arguments on two main factors: his personal experience and observations: "as I have seen" [8], and "visions of the night" [13 etc.].

Eliphaz thought that through his observations he was presenting an exact theory, for he found through his statistics that calamities befall the wicked in proportion to their wickedness, that is, justly; but Job refuted this theory (Job 17:21 etc.).

It seems that Eliphaz did not react to the severity of the affliction that had befallen Job, and supposed that what befell him were light pains proportionate to his hidden wickedness, while his grave evil was his excess in murmuring against God.
Thus Eliphaz was hoping that Job would repent of his hidden evils so that the afflictions would be removed from him; but his cursing the day of his birth, this is what utterly crushes him!

This is fulfilled daily, for "whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap" (b), as the Apostle Paul wrote: "Seeing it is a righteous thing with God to recompense tribulation to them that trouble you" (2 Thess 1:6). And it is said: "He that leadeth into captivity shall go into captivity: he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword" (Rev 13:10). But God in His longsuffering waits for the repentance of the wicked, and in His love allows affliction to the righteous so that they may be approved.
Job's friends were pressing him, those who had come to comfort him! And like enemies they were troubling him with bitter words.

* The only comfort for those who find themselves in misery and grief is to be cleared of guilt, lest they appear to have borne their pains and misfortunes as punishment for sin. But his friends seemed to be trying to take away even this comfort from the holy Job, so that he would appear to be the cause of his own misery, as one who brought down the Lord's wrath by his grave iniquities, and that he endures these afflictions as the price of his wicked deeds! And they described the punishments of the wicked (cf. Job 8:4-9), who planted vices and reaped sorrows for themselves! These perished at God's command, for they were consumed by the breath of His wrath, which blew upon those dwelling in houses of clay, and they withered (cf. Job 19:4, 21) LXX, and God frustrates the plans of the crafty and shuts the mouth of the wicked (cf. Job 13:5, 16) LXX; and what the friends alleged was true as regards the power of the Lord, but untrue as regards the merits of that great righteous man.
St. Ambrose By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his nostril are they consumed [9].

All that the wicked devise and plan perishes by a breath from God, and all their wicked schemes fail. This is true: God is longsuffering with the wicked as He was longsuffering with Pharaoh of Egypt in the days of Moses the prophet, but when the cup of their evil is full He destroys them, that the rod of the wicked may not rest upon the righteous; so He destroyed Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea. This does not apply to Job, because what befell him was for his approval and not for his destruction.

Eliphaz wanted to terrify Job that the bitter calamities that had befallen him were only the beginning, and that if he did not confess his hidden evils and put away his pride, his fate would be destruction and annihilation.

*(As if Eliphaz accuses him thus:) You are not as you suppose yourself to be in your pride, for you seek by deceit to make others consider you so. See what you have really done, as is plain from the corruption of your body. Your offspring also perished, and the best of your wealth, and all your property, and the crown of your inheritance. For in truth you are not pure, and in truth it is as you suppose. What a sick man you are in this matter... for it is not unjustly and without cause that these calamities have swallowed you up, but they are in harmony with justice, since God aimed them at you.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem At any rate, if both the righteous and the wicked are exposed to trials and afflictions, the soul of the former exults within him amid the sufferings because he receives the afflictions from the hands of God for his purification and approval. But the wicked groans within, and finds himself as one fallen into a net, and he may examine himself and return to the Lord his Savior, or may persist in folly and distress in his evil, and so fall into bitterness in this world as in the age to come.

*"The LORD trieth the righteous: but the wicked and him that loveth violence his soul hateth" (Ps 5:11)... He approves His righteous by testing them, but the wicked He hates. His soul loathes the wicked who love injustice...

He is the Judge of the righteous and the wicked; the wicked are judged because by their love of injustice they hate themselves... And as Solomon says in Proverbs: "He that refuseth instruction despiseth his own soul" (Prov 32:15). If he who loves injustice despises himself, then he who loves righteousness loves himself; and this agrees with the proverb: [He that getteth wisdom loveth his own soul] (cf. Prov 8:19)...

"Upon the wicked he shall rain snares" (Ps 6:11). Without doubt, for it is the Lord who sets snares for the sinners themselves, to catch those who have corrupted their freedom and must walk the straight way under His bridle, so He gives them the possibility of advancing through Him who said: "I am the way" (Jn 6:14).

*"How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!" (Ps 1:84), in which a man's dwelling is changed from earth to heaven... The mind and heart filled with longing for the Lord's dwelling are fruitful and happy! When death comes upon the sinner, his thought is found occupied not with this dwelling but with punishments. He does not meditate on the Kingdom of Heaven, but on the terror of the flames of hell.

* [The ungodly are like the dust which the wind driveth away] (Ps 4:1). Scripture says that the wicked man will be wretched, not even like the dust of the earth. For dust seems to have no being, yet it surely has a kind of existence in itself... It is scattered here and there and has no single place, but the wind sweeps it away, and it has no power to resist. The same is true of the wicked. As soon as he denies God, the breath of Satan sweeps him away in error and throws him wherever it wishes.
* Wretched is the man who has masks of evil, and happy is the man who has many masks of goodness.
St. Jerome The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the roarer, and the teeth of the young lions, are broken [10].

He likens the unjust and cruel persecutors to roaring, howling lions. Through divine justice the sound of their roaring ceases, and their voice no longer terrifies in the wilderness or the forests. And their teeth are broken so that they cannot tear, that is, God takes their weapons from them, and they are no longer able to prey [11], so they die of hunger and leave no cubs to succeed them.

Perhaps Eliphaz wanted to accuse Job indirectly, declaring to him that he had been like a ravening lion, with none in the region who could stand before his might. His words were like the roar of the fearful lion, plundering and devouring in injustice and tyranny. But behold his might has vanished, his wealth is scattered and his family is lost, and not one son is left him like a cub to occupy his place.
Thus Eliphaz turned from praise to blame.
The lion perisheth for lack of prey, and the whelps of the lioness are scattered abroad [11].
*It is easier for a lion to be cowardly than for the righteous man to walk an easy life.

St. John Chrysostom * Eliphaz compares Job to a lion because of his kingly power, but he rightly adds: "the roar of the lioness" (Septuagint), alluding to the greatness of Job's virtue. He also added "the arrogance of dragons" since he wished to speak of his spirit, calling this beast (the dragon) king among reptiles. At any rate Eliphaz says that all this is broken; it tramples on the sufferings of the righteous...
Father Hesychius of Jerusalem

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: 12 "Now a word was secretly brought to me, and mine ear received a murmur thereof. 13 In thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falleth on men, 14 fear and trembling came upon me, and all my bones shook. 15 Then a spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up. 16 It stood still, but I could not discern the form thereof: an image was before mine eyes. I heard a low voice: 17 Shall man be more just than God? shall a man be more pure than his maker? 18 Behold, he putteth no trust in his servants, and his angels he chargeth with folly: 19 how much more them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, and who are crushed like the moth? 20 Between morning and evening they are destroyed. Without any regarding them they perish for ever. 21 Is not their tent-cord plucked up from them? They die without wisdom."
Now a word was secretly brought to me, and mine ear received a murmur (a whisper) thereof [12].

Here Eliphaz relates to Job a vision he saw, presenting it in order to condemn him. Some see that God gave Eliphaz this vision to calm his soul when he heard what had befallen Job. And that he saw this vision before meeting the tried Job.
This vision was presented to him secretly as a word that stole to him, like one whispering in his ears.
In humility Eliphaz confessed that he had received a small portion of the divine mystery and had not grasped the whole vision as he ought.

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: In thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falleth on men [13].

In the middle of the night, when people were still and fell into deep sleep, that is, slept, Eliphaz was preoccupied with what lay behind what happened to Job, so God showed him this vision. The Psalmist David invites us to speak in our hearts with God, and to be silent until God speaks with us: "Commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still" (Ps 4:4). And as St. Mar Isaac the Syrian says: "Let your mouth be silent, and your heart will speak; and let your heart be silent, and God will speak."

It befits us at night to remember God and meditate on His law, and He will reveal to us His secrets and wisdom. "When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches" (Ps 63:6).

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: Fear and trembling came upon me, and all my bones shook [14].

It seems that before seeing the vision he felt a trembling shake all his bones. His heart was filled with the fear of the Lord, and he realized His greatness and felt that he was too small to reproach God. Thus he was prepared to receive the divine message. The Psalmist urges us: "Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling" (Ps 2:11).
Then a spirit passed before my face.

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: The hair of my flesh stood up [15].

A spirit passed by Eliphaz, most likely an angel sent from God, to serve the Word. And the hair of his skin stood up, for the heavenly beings have been an object of terror to man since Adam's fall; he fears that a painful message will reach him and does not expect good news.

In ancient times the Levites were obliged to shave all the hair of their bodies (Num 8:6-7), since it represents unnecessary bodily matters. So Eliphaz, bearing evil toward Job, could not bear the spirit passing before his face; he lost his peace and his whole being was disturbed until the hair of his body stood up, a sign of the fullness of his disturbance even regarding what is superfluous in his body.
It stood still, but I could not discern the form thereof.

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: An image was before mine eyes [16].
Eliphaz saw the angel clearly; he passed before him as an apparition, "an image before mine eyes," or as one who sees in a mirror, unable to describe him: "I could not discern the form thereof."
The voice came to him softly, for we do not hear the quiet voice of God amid the noise. Elijah did not meet God in the tempest, but in the quiet, gentle breeze (1 Kgs 19:11-13).

Eliphaz bore bitter carnal thoughts toward Job, therefore when the spirit passed by him he could not with his carnal mind see spiritual things, but saw what was more like phantoms, and could not distinguish the voice of the Spirit, which was low; his ears could not distinguish it. Thus Eliphaz confessed without knowing it that he had lost his peace, so the visions of the night became troubling imaginations. He could not sleep and rest while men were sleeping in deep sleep. His bones trembled, the hair of his body stood up, and his mind was confused with phantoms. This is the fruit of the corrupt man who turns truth into falsehood and slanders his brethren unjustly.
I heard a low voice: [16]

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: Shall man be more just than God? shall a man be more pure than his maker? [17]
The message came to rebuke Job for his murmuring; he does not dare claim to be more righteous than God, nor purer than He.
"Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker!... Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou?" (Isa 45:9).
"Righteous art thou, O LORD, when I plead with thee" (Jer 1:12).
"And enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Ps 2:143).
"Let God be true, but every man a liar; as it is written, That thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and mightest overcome when thou art judged" (Rom 4:3).
"Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight" (Rom 20:3).

* For a man to be righteous he must keep the Law in everything, which human nature can hardly accomplish. Since every man is a liar, on that day when the Lord comes to judge mankind, He alone is justified in what He says, for His words are true in everything, they are words of truth.

Origen * I do not trust in myself, but I ask for the mercies of Thy truth and justice. "Enter not into judgment with thy servant" (Ps 2:143). How clearly the prophet declares his confidence in the tenderness of Christ, when he says: [Summon not thy servant to judgment before thee].
St. Jerome * If every man is a liar, and God alone is truth, what befits us, the servants of God and His bishops, but to cast away human errors and obey the Lord's commandments?

entries.section: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

paragraphs.text: 8 But I would seek unto God, and unto God would I commit my cause: 9 Which doeth great things and unsearchable; marvellous things without number: 10 Who giveth rain upon the earth, and sendeth waters upon the fields: 11 To set up on high those that be low; that those which mourn may be exalted to safety. 12 He disappointeth the devices of the crafty, so that their hands cannot perform their enterprise. 13 He taketh the wise in their own craftiness: and the counsel of the froward is carried headlong. 14 They meet with darkness in the daytime, and grope in the noonday as in the night. 15 But he saveth the poor from the sword, from their mouth, and from the hand of the mighty. 16 So the poor hath hope, and iniquity stoppeth her mouth. 17 Behold, happy is the man whom God correcteth: therefore despise not thou the chastening of the Almighty: 18 For he maketh sore, and bindeth up: he woundeth, and his hands make whole. 19 He shall deliver thee in six troubles: yea, in seven there shall no evil touch thee. 20 In famine he shall redeem thee from death: and in war from the power of the sword. 21 Thou shalt be hid from the scourge of the tongue: neither shalt thou be afraid of destruction when it cometh. 22 At destruction and famine thou shalt laugh: neither shalt thou be afraid of the beasts of the earth. 23 For thou shalt be in league with the stones of the field: and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with thee. 24 And thou shalt know that thy tabernacle shall be in peace; and thou shalt visit thy habitation, and shalt lose nothing. 25 Thou shalt know also that thy seed shall be great, and thine offspring as the grass of the earth. 26 Thou shalt come to thy grave in a full age, like as a shock of corn cometh in in his season. 27 Lo this, we have searched it, so it is; hear it, and know thou it for thyself.
But I would seek unto God, and unto God would I commit my cause [8].

Setting aside Eliphaz's intention and his mistaken view of Job, his words are without blemish. If man, because of his transgression of God's commandment, has become born unto trouble, there is no other remedy except returning to God and relying on Him, for He is the true support of the suffering. It is as though Eliphaz says to him: If I were in your place, Job, I would not murmur and curse the day of my birth, but would take refuge in God and submit to His will, as the source of all good and consolation. I would lay my case before God; what seems good in His eyes, He will do (1 Sam 3:18). As the psalmist says: "Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass" (Ps 5:37). "I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust" (Ps 2:91). And the Apostle says: "Is any among you afflicted? let him pray" (Jas 13:5).

* Finding my state to be thus, he says, my confidence is not like yours; rather I wait, knowing that God is the Lord. You trouble yourself, but I wait for God without ceasing to call upon Him and without losing hope. For He is always able to exchange and change circumstances. I find myself in the midst of evils, but God is also able to place me in the midst of good things, transferring me from my former state to this state. He says: [The Lord is the Almighty](d), meaning that He is Lord of all, the Controller of all circumstances, and of all places and things.

St. John Chrysostom * He says to him: You are in fact not worthy to pray. I myself will call upon the Lord of all. For since you are self-assured, you no longer call upon the Lord of all, and for this reason these present evils have attacked you.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * O Lord, You crown us with the shield of Your good will. What does this mean? You guard us, and make us victorious, and after the victory You give us a crown.
St. Jerome * Point out to Him what pains you, point out to Him what you desire!
* [Thou sayest to the Lord, My refuge and my fortress; my God, in him will I trust] (Ps 2:91).

Who is it that says this to the Lord? He "that dwelleth in the shelter of the most High," and not in his own shelter. Who is this who dwells in the shelter of the Most High? The one who is not proud like those two who ate (from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil) to become gods, and so lost their immortality in which they were created. They chose to dwell in their own shelter, not in the shelter of the Most High. Thus they listened to the counsel of the serpent (Gen 5:3), and disregarded God's commandment, and finally discovered that what God had threatened was fulfilled in them, and not the promise of Satan to them. Therefore let you also say: "In him I trust, he will deliver me, and I do not deliver myself.
* No one is helped by God unless he himself does something. He will be helped if he prays.
* The whole effect of faith is this: it makes us ask and receive, seek and find, knock and it is opened to us. Whereas the man who argues shuts the door of God's mercy before himself.
* You made us for Yourself, O Lord, and our hearts will not rest until they rest in You.

entries.section: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine Which doeth great things and unsearchable; marvellous things without number [9].

We do not fear to entrust ourselves, as well as all our affairs, into the hands of God, for He is the Doer of great and marvelous things without limit. He is Almighty; His great works cannot be comprehended. "So that a man cannot find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end" (Eccl 3:11).

* The heretics dared to blaspheme Him... they dared to blaspheme the One whom the prophets proclaimed to be God Almighty. But as for you, worship the one God Almighty, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Flee from the error of believing in many gods. Flee from every heresy, and say: "I seek of the Almighty Lord, who doeth great things and unsearchable, and marvellous things without number"... To whom be glory forever and ever, Amen.

St. Cyril of Jerusalem God is called the Worker of wonders, not as a display of His power by doing what exceeds the nature He created, nor from a desire to break its laws, since He is its Maker, but out of His love for man He works wonders, to make of His people a wonder! His surpassing love for the sons of men is exceedingly wonderful! The men of God find their delight and happiness in praising God that He is a worker of wonders!
"For thou art great, and doest wondrous things: thou art God alone" (Ps 86:10).
"And the heavens shall praise thy wonders, O LORD: thy faithfulness also in the congregation of the saints" (Ps 89:5).
"Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people" (Ps 96:3).
"Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him: talk ye of all his wondrous works" (Ps 105:2).
"Oh that men would praise the LORD for his goodness, and for his wonderful works to the children of men! (Ps 107:8).
"Who is he? and we will call him blessed: for wonderful things hath he done among his people" (Sir 31:9)

* He tells of the wonders of God (Ps 1:9) who sees them accomplished not only openly in the body, but also in an invisible manner in his soul; indeed these wonders are more exalted and lofty. For men, being earthly and led by what they see with the eye, marvel more that dead Lazarus rises in the body than that the persecutor Paul rises in the spirit (Jn 11; Acts 9). But the visible wonder calls the soul to enjoy the light, while through the invisible a man passes over to perceive the invisible, and so speaks of all the wonders of God.

* To rejoice in the (wonderful) works of God is to forget even yourself, since you can delight in Him alone. For what is better than He? Do you not see that when you return to yourself, you return to something sinful? "I will remember thy wonders of old" (Ps 11:77)... "Thou art the God that doest wonders" (Ps 14:77), You alone. In truth You are the great God, You work wonders in the body as in the soul, You alone are their Worker. The deaf hear, the blind see, the weak are healed, the dead rise, the paralyzed are strengthened. But these wonders were accomplished at that time in the body. Let us look at those accomplished in the soul. Those who a little while ago were drunkards have become workers, those who a little while ago were idolaters have now become believers, those who formerly robbed others have now come to give gifts to the poor.

* "The heavens shall praise thy wonders, O LORD" (Ps 5:89)... For in every work of mercy toward lost souls, every work of justification of sinners, what do we praise but the wonderful works of God? You praise Him because the dead rise; praise Him all the more because the lost have been saved. Yesterday, O man, you saw a whirlpool of drunkenness; now you see the beauty of self-control. Yesterday you saw a blasphemer of God; now you see him praising Him. Yesterday he was a slave of the creature; today he has become a worshipper of the Creator. Thus men have turned from these terrible conditions. Would that they did not look to their own merits. Let them become heavens and praise the wonders of Him who made them heavens".

entries.section: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine Who giveth rain upon the earth, and sendeth waters upon the fields [10].

He gives us an example from nature of the great works of God. "Who giveth rain upon the earth." We often take rain lightly, yet it is a great work that reveals God's power; without it life could be destroyed.

In the midst of our pains and afflictions, when we cry to God, the Creator of heaven and earth, He looks upon us and covers our souls with clouds, as being His heavens, and rains upon our lives with the waters of His Holy Spirit, the Giver of heavenly consolations. So we say: "In the multitude of my thoughts within me thy comforts delight my soul" (Ps 19:94). St. Jerome sees that the clouds that cover the heavenly soul are the company of the prophets and apostles, and that the rain God gives us is His joyful commandment or His divine teachings.

* Everyone who is unworthy to understand the divine teaching, for him this teaching is covered with clouds. "Who prepareth rain for the earth" (Ps 8:147). The earth needs rain; if our earth does not receive the rain, which is the fountain of divine teaching, it brings forth no fruit.

* Moses was a cloud, therefore he says: "My doctrine shall drop as the rain" (Deut 32:2). His message is a spiritual rain that comes down upon us. In real fact, what does Paul say in his epistle to the Hebrews? "For the earth which drinketh in the rain that cometh oft upon it" (Heb 7:6). Again he says: [I have planted, Apollos watered] (Col 6:3).
* The clouds are the prophets and apostles who water the barren hearts of men with the rains of their teachings.

St. Jerome Pope Gregory (the Great) translates this verse, "Who sendeth waters upon the fields," as "upon all things," and says that man represents all things. For the greatest of wonders is the creation of man, who represents the whole universe: [Man shares existence with stones, life with trees, sensation with animals, and discernment with angels. He truly represents the title "the universe," for in him the whole universe is contained. Thus the Truth says to His disciples: "Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature" (cf. Mt 19:28-20). For all creation is for man alone, in whom was created what is common to all things.]
* The human man had not yet entered the world of beings (that is, until the sixth day)... For it is not fitting for the ruler to appear before the appearance of the things over which he rules.
But as soon as his dominion was ready, the Creator having prepared all things as a royal dwelling for the coming king, the ruler was announced!
This royal dwelling is the earth, the islands, the sea, and the heaven, which is like an arch encircling above all, like a roof to it.

In this palace He stored up wealth of every kind: the whole world of plants and animals, everything that has body, breath, and life. And if anyone wished to count material things as wealth, he would find also all that is beautiful and valuable in man's eyes, of gold, silver, and precious stones, to enjoy.

The Creator hid these things in abundance in the bosom of the earth, as if they were a royal treasure, so that when the human man appeared in the world, he might contemplate some of them and rule over the others. For when he enjoys these things he thanks the Giver of good things. And when he beholds the beauty of the things he sees and their vastness, he is drawn to the great, incomprehensible power of their Creator.

St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa * The Almighty gives rain upon the earth when He waters the dry hearts of the Gentiles with the grace of the heavenly preaching, and sends waters upon all things, since by the fullness of the Spirit He turns the barrenness of lost man to fruitfulness, as the Truth Himself says with His lips: [Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst] (Jn 14:4).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

paragraphs.text: To set up on high those that be low; that those which mourn may be exalted to safety [11].
The next example is God's power that is manifested in the humble, whom the Most High lifts up, and His work in the life of the mourners, giving them safety.

The successive calamities drove Job down to the dunghill, as he no longer had a place to dwell and rest. But since he humbles himself without murmuring, he comes to be on high, that is, he soars in the heavens, for humility is the ladder by which the soul ascends in Christ Jesus to the bosom of the Father.
Truly sorrow crushes man so that he becomes like one descending into bitterness and destruction, but when he mourns in the Lord he ascends to true safety.

entries.section: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

paragraphs.text: He disappointeth the devices of the crafty, so that their hands cannot perform their enterprise [12].

The third example is God's intervention in the affairs of men; for although He has granted them freedom of will, He does not leave matters to go on without control, for He [disappointeth the devices of the crafty], so their hands are not left to settle upon the heads of the righteous.

By taking refuge in God the believer enjoys the divine truth, so the crafty cannot lay their hands on the believer. Falsehood and deceit cannot appear in the presence of the truth, for the truth is a light that dispels falsehood (darkness). So in the midst of noonday their life becomes an exceedingly dark night. The kingdom of light does not reign over them; rather the kingdom of darkness dominates them.

Often the Jewish leaders, in their craftiness, thought they could trap the Lord Christ, but He allowed them to test Him, and through their craftiness they judged themselves by themselves. For craftiness and deceit cannot stand before judgment, but carry corruption within themselves.
* When they scheme with evil things they show themselves for what they are, and since they cannot accomplish their purposes, (God) preserves those against whom they plot evils.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

paragraphs.text: He taketh the wise in their own craftiness: and the counsel of the froward is carried headlong [13].
The Apostle Paul quoted this verse in his First Epistle to the Corinthians (1 Cor 3:19).

God can with surpassing ease demolish the plots of the crafty, who reckon in themselves that they are wise, so that none is able to stand before them. He has brought to nothing, and brings to nothing, the counsels of many, such as the counsel of Ahithophel, who planned for Absalom to kill his father David and take his throne, and He also brought to nothing the counsel of Sanballat (Neh 4:7-23), and the counsel of Haman (Esth 8). Truly every instrument formed against the Church of God shall not prosper (Isa 54:17).

"In the net which they hid is their own foot taken" (Ps 9:15). "He is fallen into the ditch which he made. His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate" (Ps 7:15-16).

Pope Gregory (the Great) gives us two examples of how God takes the wise in their craftiness, the first from the Old Testament and the second from the New. In the Old Testament Joseph's brothers wanted to be rid of their brother lest he rise above them and they be subject to his authority, and according to their human wisdom they sold him as a slave. God used this action of theirs, and by His divine providence he became great in Egypt, and they bowed down before him. The second is the wisdom of the Hebrews in the New Testament, where the priests and religious leaders wanted to be rid of Him lest the whole world go after the Lord Christ (Jn 19:21); they sentenced Him to death, and behold, by that very means - the Cross - the whole world went after Him.

* How does God take the wise in their craftiness? In that, while they think they are able to work without God, they find themselves all the more in need of Him. They fall into a predicament to show that they are less than fishermen and the unlearned, who now cannot work without their wisdom.

St. John Chrysostom * The ruler flattered Jesus (Lk 18:18), and tried to deceive Him, pretending to take a sympathetic position toward Him. But what did He who knows all things answer, as it is written of Him: [He taketh the wise in their own craftiness] (Job 13:5)?

entries.section: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

paragraphs.text: St. Cyril the Great They meet with darkness in the daytime, and grope in the noonday as in the night [14].

The true believer's life is a continuous day without darkness, and as the Apostle says: "Ye are all the children of light, and the children of the day: we are not of the night, nor of darkness" (1 Thess 5:5). Lot did not know darkness when he received the two angels and urged them to be his guests and spend the night in his house, but the wicked were in darkness and did not realize that they were two angels of light, so they wanted to know them and commit corrupting evil with them, and the men were struck with blindness, and became like those in darkness and were unable to find the door of the house (Gen 11:19). Thus, instead of enjoying the angelic light they fell into the darkness of evil, and lost their inner and outer sight.

* "They meet with darkness in the daytime," because in the presence of the Truth Himself they were struck blind by the deceit of unbelief... Thus the Light Himself counsels them, saying: "Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you" (Jn 35:12).

When the wicked see their neighbors doing something good, they are stricken with the pain of their envy, and suffer the torments of their painful malice, when they see with their envy-filled hearts good things in others. Therefore it was well said: "They meet with darkness in the daytime," when their minds are grieved at the loftiness of another, a shadow is cast from the ray of light...

They busy themselves with zeal and intense examination to find something with which they can accuse others. They truly see all the members sound, but with the eyes of their closed hearts they seek to find in the emotions an affliction for others...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* The worst thing about envy is that it is a disease folded away in secrecy. You see the envious man with lowered eyes and a gloomy face, constantly complaining of an inner torment which withers his face and wastes his body, so that he grows lean and weak. He is ashamed to say: "I am envious, I feel bitterness and grief at the good that another man has obtained, and I am tormented by the happiness of my friends, and cannot bear the success of my peers. I see that the happiness of others is a sword that tears my bowels and stabs me to the heart." This is what the envious man ought to have confessed. But he prefers to keep it in his heart and be silent, and so the disease remains in him, and the torment wastes him, and his body perishes little by little.

St. Basil the Great * Beasts, birds and creeping things grieve at the sufferings of their kinds in nature, and cooperate together against those who oppose them, but the envious man does the opposite; he rejoices at the fall of the brother and the neighbor and the stranger and the relative and the friend.

* The envious man counts the misfortunes of others a benefit to himself more than any success of his own... becoming like a common enemy against mankind and a slap to the members of the Church. For what is nearer to madness than envy?!
* Satan is envious, but he envies mankind, and does not envy another satan, whereas you are a man who envies your brother man, especially those of your own family and clan, which Satan does not do.

* There is no disease worse than envy and malice, for on its basis death entered the world (Wis 2:24), because when the devil saw man honored he could not bear his well-being, and did all he could until he killed him. By envy Abel was slain, and David was nearly killed, and many others of the righteous were killed, and the Jews became the killers of Christ.

entries.section: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom But he saveth the poor from the sword, from their mouth, and from the hand of the mighty [15].

The counsel of the crafty aims at destroying the poor, but God delivers them from their sword as well as from their mouth and their hands. He is the Controller of all, He works on behalf of the poor, and neither the counsels of the wicked nor their strong hands nor their swords stand before Him.

When the believer casts his whole life into the hand of the Lord, he does not fear the devil's sword that kills the soul, nor does he lose his hope because of this mighty one. For although the devil carries the sword of slander and destruction, and is a murderer from the beginning, yet He who is with us is greater than he who is against us. With us is our God, who delivers by Himself, and who also sends His angels to guard us. In Him you enjoy hope, and despair cannot dominate our hearts or our thoughts.

* "The voice of the LORD breaketh the cedars" (Ps 29:5), for Christ is baptized, and the demons that were formerly swollen and haughty are shattered in a heap of ruin [The Lord breaks them. Like a calf, He hurls them into the air like pieces of trees and scatters them to far places in pieces].

* "Hold thy peace" (Mk 25:1)! Let your silence be praise to me. I do not ask for your voice to praise me, but your torment and punishment are praise to me. I am not pleased by your praise of me; I rejoice in your departure. [Hold thy peace, and come out of the man] (cf. Mk 25:1). As if He says: Come out of my dwelling; what are you doing in my guest chamber? I want to enter. Hold your peace and come out of the man (the rational animal). Come out of the man, leave the guest chamber that was prepared for me. The Lord wants His dwelling... It is not my will that you possess him... I have taken a human body... The body that you now possess shares in my body; come out of it!

* They aim to shoot their arrows in the darkness at the upright heart... for I stand in the line of battle, vigilant and girded, ready for the fight. I will not neglect the struggle that has begun, especially since you say that they have bent the strings of their bows, and the arrows are made ready in their quiver, and behold, they wait in the darkness to wound my saints, but they are not yet able to aim them. They have drawn the string, they have filled the quiver. They are ready to aim their arrows in the darkness at the sincere heart. Now that they are fully prepared I place myself among them, and stand opposite their arrows, so that even by my pain my servants may not feel pain, and by my wounds they are healed, and by my sufferings they do not suffer, but say: "Thou compassest him with favour as with a shield" (Ps 5:12).

St. Jerome * He adds that God does the opposite when He shows concern for the weak. [He gives the weak hope, and stops the mouths of the unjust](f)... Eliphaz was busy establishing a dialogue by which he belittles Job. But it is God's custom to lift up the weak, abase the strong and put the deceivers to shame.

entries.section: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom So the poor hath hope, and iniquity stoppeth her mouth [16].

When the afflicted looks at the crafty he collapses in despair, but when he looks to God he is filled with hope, so the mouths of the crafty are stopped, and the sin lying hidden in them cannot utter a word, for God Himself has spoken.

* Even if these (evil) powers rise and prevail, know that this is God's discipline, for although they triumph, they will be judged with a just judgment. Be sure of this, that the beast will be slaughtered at the appointed time. But you, my brother, be zealous in seeking mercy so that there may be peace for the people of God.

entries.section: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

paragraphs.text: St. Aphrahat Behold, happy is the man whom God correcteth: therefore despise not thou the chastening of the Almighty [17].
Eliphaz distinguishes between the Lord's discipline of His believers and the punishment He imposes on the wicked. He esteems God's fatherly discipline of the believer when he falls.
At the end of his first speech Eliphaz offers a consolation which Eliphaz himself needed, namely, accepting the discipline of the Lord Almighty.
What befell Job was nothing but discipline from the loving Almighty God. And it is folly and madness to quarrel with the Lord and ignore His tender fatherhood even in the very moments of discipline.

The Hebrew word translated "despise not" means "do not hate," so it is fitting for the believer to submit gladly to God's will and disciplines, even if they are bitter, for we need the rod of discipline, and let us reckon that what befalls us we deserve, and it is a bitter medicine useful for our healing.
It also means: do not think ill of Him, and do not belittle what He has done, but bow before Him and trust in His wisdom and providence.

It also means: do not overlook Him, as though what has befallen were by chance, and not from a wise and well-ordered divine plan. Reckon discipline to be the voice of the Lord and His heavenly message.

Thus it is fitting for us to accept the Lord's discipline, and appreciate His wisdom, and submit to Him with fear and trembling, confident that it is for our eternal edification. He weans us from the world and temporal goods so that we may cling to the Giver of goods Himself, and He prepares us for eternal glory.

How beautiful it is for a leader to direct himself and those around him to the blessings of the Lord's discipline of His believers. For though it has bitterness and troubles, it is not destructive; it is temporary, and gives strength for the believer to stand even before the beasts of the earth, because he feels that what befalls him is by God's permission for his edification, correction and approval.

But Eliphaz's aim here is not to encourage Job to accept suffering from the hand of God, but he is claiming that God does not seek his discipline but his destruction, because he has transgressed the limits, and thus his sufferings are nothing but punishment, and though they seem exceedingly severe, they are only a pledge of what Job should expect on the day of judgment, because he is the worst of the wicked.

* The pomegranate is covered with a hard and bitter rind; this outer rind is not fit to eat, but the inside is beautiful to look at, and has carefully arranged seeds, and tastes sweet. So also is the life of philosophy (spiritual wisdom): it appears dry and unpleasant from the outside, but when it ripens it is full of good hopes. And when the gardener (God) opens the pomegranate of life at the proper time and reveals its hidden beauty, those who taste it enjoy its sweetness. And the Apostle Paul says: "Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous (that is, the first impression of the pomegranate with regard to its rind): nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby" (Heb 12:11) (that is, the sweetness of the fruit within).

entries.section: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

paragraphs.text: St. Gregory of Nyssa For he maketh sore, and bindeth up: he woundeth, and his hands make whole [18].
Although God allowed the sores in Job's body as bitter wounds, He is a skilled surgeon who binds up the inner wounds of the soul, and grants it the healing consolations of His Holy Spirit.

In His discipline He seems to crush, but He restores to His believers every honor and glory on an eternal level; thus His hands make whole. Moses the prophet sings: "Make us glad according to the days wherein thou hast afflicted us, and the years wherein we have seen evil" (Ps 90:15). And Hosea the prophet says: "He hath torn, and he will heal us" (Hos 6:1).
* In wounding, He heals. For when we are pierced by the spear of His fear, He restores us to a sound mind.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Therefore if anyone at any time sees evil in many persons, yet God's wrath does not fall on all, but only on some, he must realize that discipline is applied with love to the human race. For the blows do not fall on everyone, but the blows that fall on some discipline all, that they may turn back from evil.
St. Gregory of Nyssa * "For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth" (Heb 12:6). First He wounds, and afterward He heals. He brings pain and then binds up.

In the same vein He says: "See, I have this day set thee over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant" (Jer 1:10). However it may be, it is first necessary to remove what is bad from us (from within us), for God cannot build where there is a mean building. For what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? (2 Cor 6:14).
Evil must be uprooted from its roots, the building of evil must be pulled down from our souls, so that the Word may build and plant.

* When evils are not first removed, we do not receive goodness. He breaks down the feeble buildings of unbelief, for He is the Lord who builds the true tabernacle, which He makes and not man (Heb 8:2), of which Paul said: "Ye are... God's building" (1 Cor 3:9).
* "Nevertheless in those days, saith the LORD, I will not make a full end with you" (Jer 5:18)...

God delays His condemnation of those who deserve punishment, to give them a chance to repent. He does not punish sin at once, and does not inflict destruction on the sinner, but delays the punishment.

We find an example of this in the Book of Leviticus: in the curses spoken to those who transgress the Law, after announcing the first punishments, it is said: "And if ye will not yet for all this hearken unto me, then I will punish you seven times more for your sins" (Lev 26:18). Then it also mentions another punishment: "And if ye will not for all this hearken unto me, but walk contrary unto me; Then I will walk contrary unto you also in fury" (Lev 26:27-28). From this it is clear to us that God inflicts punishments very slowly, because He wants to lead the sinner to repentance rather than make him pay the price immediately.

This is also what happened with the people; the Lord threatened them with the sufferings that would befall them, and then said to them afterward: "Nevertheless in those days... I will not make a full end with you."

* "For this is the time of the LORD'S vengeance." Holy Scripture shows that punishments are inflicted on the man who bears them and is patient in bearing them. When a man is not punished on earth he remains so, without punishment, because he is to be punished on the day of judgment. And the Lord says by the mouth of Hosea the prophet: "I will not punish your daughters when they commit whoredom, nor your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery" (Hos 4:14). God does not punish sinners because of His anger against them, as some think, or in other words, when God inflicts punishment on a sinful man, He does not inflict it out of anger at this man, but on the contrary, the sign of God's anger against a man consists in not inflicting punishment on him. For the punished man, even if he suffers under the effect of this punishment, yet the aim is his correction and reformation. As David says: [O LORD, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure] (Ps 6:1). If you wish to discipline me, as Jeremiah says: "O LORD, correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger, lest thou bring me to nothing" (Jer 10:24). Many have been reformed by the Lord's punishments and disciplines of them. As the Scripture says, when the sons of the Lord Christ sin they are punished so that they may have a chance for mercy from the Lord: "If his children forsake my law, and walk not in my judgments; If they break my statutes, and keep not my commandments; Then will I visit their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with stripes. Nevertheless my lovingkindness will I not utterly take from him" (Ps 89:30-33).
From this we understand that if someone commits sins and has not been punished until now, it is a sign that he does not yet deserve punishment.

entries.section: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

paragraphs.text: Origen He shall deliver thee in six troubles: yea, in seven there shall no evil touch thee [19].
The previous speech was general, but now he addresses Job directly, offering him God's precious promises and announcing His great mercies.

Truly Job's friends were not guided by the Spirit of God in all that they said, but they offered divine promises they knew through oral tradition. Though at times they spoke things that were not right about God and about Job.

By saying: "He shall deliver thee in six troubles: yea, in seven there shall no evil touch thee," he affirms the repetition of afflictions and troubles, along with the repetition of help and deliverance. As long as we are in the world we expect afflictions, but we trust in the help of God our Father and His concern for our salvation and peace. The Apostle Paul says: "What persecutions I endured: but out of them all the Lord delivered me" (2 Tim 3:11).
"No evil touch thee": afflictions will not cause real harm, for the wicked one does not touch God's children (1 Jn 5:18), but they are kept in the hand of God their Savior.

* What does the number six, followed by the number seven, indicate but weariness in the period of the present life? For God, after completing everything on the sixth day, created man and rested on the seventh day. This very seventh day has no evening, since there is no end afterward to end the rest that followed. When all things were completed, rest followed; so after the good works of the present life comes the reward of eternal rest. Therefore "in six troubles" the Lord delivers you, and so "in seven there shall no evil touch thee." For by the direction of fatherly tenderness He trains us in the troubles of the present life. But at the coming of the Judge He hides us from calamity... but brings us to His more assured salvation.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* If Job is one of those whom God warns and reforms, and not of those whom He strikes with punishment and destruction, then in six troubles God delivers him, these that wear him out, but since he is His servant and friend and soldier, evil will not touch him the seventh time, for God's help preserves him. But it seems that the case is not so, as Eliphaz meant. Here the calamity that befell you the first time is the burning of the flock, and the second the raid on the oxen, the third the loss of the she-asses, the fourth the plundering of the camels, the fifth the death of the herdsmen, the sixth the sudden death of your sons and daughters, and after that the seventh, evil has touched you, namely the bodily pain and the sores of your members. In any case, God does not deliver you, He who strikes and heals, who causes pain and cures, that you may deserve the divine visitation.

What Eliphaz said he meant to lead Job to despair. He did not know that this encouraged the wrestler all the more. For God delivered him six times from troubles, for the six calamities we have now enumerated came upon him from the enemy. But God, looking at the righteous man, had set beforehand limits that the enemy could not exceed. [Behold, here I deliver him to you, but respect his soul] (cf. Job 12:1). That is: [You may touch what is outside him, but these words will not give you authority to enter into him within]... Note how God preserved Job from these trials, and in vain Eliphaz said to Job the former and the latter things.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Note how he destroys all benefit in what he says and delivers a violent blow. How and by what means? By showing that Job was not a party among those who receive a warning, nor among those who obtain hope. But in reality what he said applies entirely to the person of Job. But his speech had its general application, for he said that this is what we have seen and heard. So if this did not happen in your case, if you remain in your troubles, they are for your benefit, that you may know your error.

entries.section: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom In famine he shall redeem thee from death: and in war from the power of the sword [20].

Famine will not be able to destroy them, for "in the days of famine they shall be satisfied" (Ps 37:19). "To deliver their soul from death, and to keep them alive in famine" (Ps 33:19). Man needs the Word of God - not only as the Savior who restores man's soul to its first nature, but also to satisfy all needs. He presents Himself to man as everything to him. For in the Lord Christ famine cannot destroy us, for the Lord is our satisfaction. Christ offers Himself to those who feel they need Him. For this feeling grants them the worthiness of His presence and dwelling in their hearts. He is one, offering Himself to each believer according to his spiritual state.

* Perhaps, as the Apostle says of those [who have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil] (Heb 14:5), Christ has become each of these things, so as to suit the different senses of the soul.
For He was called the true Light, so that the eyes of the soul may find something that enlightens them.
And He is (the Logos) λόγος, so that its ears may find something to hear.
Then He is the bread of life, so that the soul may find something to taste.
And in a way He was called spikenard or ointment, so that the soul's sense of smell may perceive the fragrant aroma of the Word.

And for the same reason it was also said that He can be felt and held, and He was called the incarnate Logos, so that the inner hand of the soul may touch Him with regard to the Word of life (Jn 1:1-4; 1 Jn 1:1).

But all these things are the One - the Word of God Himself - who adapts to the various passions of the one who prays, according to those many names, and so leaves none of the faculties of the soul empty of His grace.

* Truly, I can say that He becomes everything that every creature capable of being set free needs. Therefore He becomes the light of men, if they - while in the darkness of evils - seek that light which shineth in the darkness and which the darkness comprehended not. He would not have become a light for men had they not been in darkness.

Origen The Lord delivers man from the swords of enemies, however many they may be, so that the wars of the demons cannot destroy us. "A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand; but it shall not come nigh thee" (Ps 91:7).
* Jesus, the Son of God, my Lord, gives me and commands me to crush under my feet the spirit of fornication, and to tread upon the neck of the spirit of wrath and anger, and the demon of greed, etc.
* As the Father [only hath immortality] (1 Tim 6:16), the Lord Jesus, out of love for us, took upon Himself the burden of death on our behalf.

And in the same manner this description applies to the Father alone: "In him is no darkness." For Christ, for the benefit of men, took upon Himself our darkness, so that by His authority He might bring our death to naught and dispel our inner darkness.

* Before the coming of our Lord and Savior, all the demons reigned over the minds and bodies of men, and settled in their spirits. Then the grace of the Lord the Savior and His mercy appeared on the earth, teaching us how the soul of every man should regain freedom and recover the image of God in which it was created...

Who is this, if not Jesus Christ, by whose stripes we who believe in Him have been healed, when He "spoiled principalities and powers" who were in our midst and "made a shew of them openly" upon the Cross? (Col 15:2).

* We fell under the authority of our enemies, that is, "the king of this age" and his helpers from the powers of evil. For this reason arose our need for redemption by Him who buys us so that we may return from the state of estrangement from Him. Therefore our Savior gave His blood as a ransom for us...

And since the "remission of sins," which follows redemption, is impossible before man is set free, we must first be freed from the authority of him who took us captive and kept us under his control, freed beyond the reach of his hand, so that we may be able to obtain forgiveness of our sins and healing from the wounds of sin, so that we may accomplish works of godliness and other virtues.

entries.section: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

paragraphs.text: Origen Thou shalt be hid from the scourge of the tongue: neither shalt thou be afraid of destruction when it cometh [21].

As God protects His children from the sword in battle, so He protects them from the tongue of the wicked, which is sharper than the sword; He protects them from the accusations and slanders falsely directed at them. Thus in time of war as in time of peace the believer lives under the shelter of God in peace, not fearing destruction, even if he sees it coming.

Eliphaz presents an accusation against Job in the form of advice: "Thou shalt be hid from the scourge of the tongue: neither shalt thou be afraid of destruction when it cometh." As if he says: You were defeated in the trial, for when affliction came upon you, you should not have sinned with your tongue, but hidden yourself from this error. Your tongue bears witness to your snare, for you fell into the snare of the tongue, and bowed to its deadly scourges. Eliphaz did not know that what he says does not apply to Job, for God Himself bears witness that in all this he did not sin, nor charge God foolishly (Job 22:1); rather the one who fell into the snares of the tongue and under its scourges is Eliphaz himself, who wanted by them to make righteous Job fall. But to Job applies the saying of the psalmist: [For he shall deliver thee from the snare of the hunter, and from the harsh word] (Ps 3:91).

* The saints of the Lord loved keeping silence, for they realized that the voice of man is the beginning of sin. So the saint of the Lord said within himself: "I said, I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue." For he knew, from what he had read before, that one of the signs of God's protection of man is that he hides from the scourges of his tongue and from the witness of his conscience.
We are disciplined by the rebukes of our thoughts, and the judgment of conscience.

We are also disciplined by the scourges of our voices, when we utter things that strike our souls with deadly blows, and our mind is struck with bloody wounds. But where is the man whose heart has been cleansed of the impurities of sin, so that he does not sin with his tongue?

Thus, seeing that there is no one who could keep his mouth free from evil speech, he set for himself the rule of righteousness by committing himself to the ordinances of silence. He set before his eyes to avoid by silence the fall which it was hard for him to escape by speech.

entries.section: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose * [Neither shalt thou be afraid of destruction when it cometh] [22]. For when the saints see themselves engaged with the adversary in various forms, they equip themselves in different ways for their battle.
They have the help of the Word of God against famine.
And they have the armor of self-control against the sword of war.
And they have the fortress of patience against the scourge of the tongue.
And they have the help of inner love against the harm of outward calamities.
Thus in a wonderful way they pass through the various trials the wicked enemy brings upon them, and so gain greater riches in virtue as soldiers of God.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* "Thou hast consumed them, but they have refused to receive correction" (Jer 5:3). God in His providence and mercy, when He does His purifying work for the salvation of the soul, goes in His work to the end (to consumption), at least on His part. So if all that comes upon us from divine providence aims at our perfection and our discipline, and yet we do not accept the divine disciplines that lead us to perfection, then he who understands the meaning of this passage can say to the Lord: O Lord, You have consumed them (disciplined them), and they refused to receive correction.
Origen At destruction and dearth (famine) thou shalt laugh: neither shalt thou be afraid of the beasts of the earth [22].

The believer looks at the plots of the wicked and the raging of the beasts of the wilderness, and in tranquility makes light of them, for he is kept in God. Such was the Apostle Paul, who did not fear the last enemy, which is death, and completed his hymn saying: "O death, where is thy sting?" (1 Cor 15:55), "Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us" (Rom 8:37).

* [At destruction and famine he shall laugh]... It was well said by the psalmist: [The righteous also shall see, and fear, and shall laugh at him: Lo, the man that made not God his helper] (Ps 6:52-7). Now the righteous look at the wicked and fear, and afterward they look and laugh. They are now held by fear lest they imitate them, but since they cannot reform those who have fallen under the eternal judgment, they do not harbor sympathy for them.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* You find many passages in Holy Scripture in which God is likened to the attributes of man. So if you ever hear the words "the wrath and fury of God," do not think that wrath and fury are emotions and attributes found in God, but they are a way by which God condescends and speaks to discipline His children and correct them.

For we too, when we wish to guide our children and correct their errors, appear before them in a fearsome guise and with a stern and firm face that does not match our true feelings, but matches the method of discipline.

If we showed on our faces the tolerance and leniency that is in our souls and inner feelings toward our children all the time, without changing the features of our faces according to the children's behavior, we would spoil them and drive them to the worse.
