Although I confess that I am wicked, there is none to deliver me out of Your hand but You! To You I flee, so do not be angry with me!

* [There is none that can escape out of Your hand]; it is as though he says plainly: What is left for You but to forgive, You whose power no man can resist? For just as there is no one who enjoys Your visitation by his own merit and loftiness, so it is Your compassion that allows the obtaining of forgiveness.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Even if You bear witness for me, I cannot be saved by my righteousness, and when You wish to strike me I cannot save myself, because [who can deliver me out of Your hands?] All creation is in the right hand of Him who has eternal glory.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem

entries.section: 2. His life in the hand of God

paragraphs.text: 8 "Thine hands have made me and fashioned me together round about; yet thou dost destroy me. 9 Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay; and wilt thou bring me into dust again? 10 Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese? 11 Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews. 12 Thou hast granted me life and favour, and thy visitation hath preserved my spirit. 13 And these things hast thou hid in thine heart: I know that this is with thee:
"Thine hands have made me and fashioned me together round about."
"Yet thou dost destroy me" [8]?
Man owes his existence to God, but when a trial comes upon him he sees as though God wants to swallow him up.

Many of the Church Fathers used this passage to answer the followers of Mani and others who claimed that the human body is an element of darkness, and that it is corrupt by nature and must be gotten rid of.

St. Jacob of Serugh sees that the body cannot live alone, nor can the soul live alone. [The body was not granted permanent life without the soul, and the soul was not granted sensation without the body. The life of the soul is lifeless without the body, and the body laid in the dust remains without life.]

Many Fathers of the Church pointed out that one of the blessings of the divine Incarnation is that God restored dignity to the body which He created, for the eternal Word of God did not disdain to bear a true human body and to perform bodily acts.

* Because the Word came down and came to be flesh with those of flesh, He walked in the way of all who are born, and remained in the world thirty years in humility. Then He began to act with the power of His might.
It is wonderful that He dwelt in the carpenter's house, mingled with them, and lived according to their custom...
The wonder is that the heavens are full of His glorification, and He was content with a small house in which to be brought up...!

He became a child and nursed milk and did not tire... He became a boy and measured the markets with His steps... He became a youth and worshiped in the carpenter's house. He became a man and bowed His head before John, and with the penitents He went down to be baptized in His humility...

Let us believe that He came and became flesh, not in appearance but in truth. He became man so that the world might feel that the second Adam had shown Himself to renew the world in place of the first, whom the serpent bit.

Had He begun to perform mighty works from His youth, they would have wronged Him, saying that He had not truly become incarnate, and that His body was an illusion and was not a body. For this reason our Lord waited thirty years, and then began to walk in the way of mighty works, so that in the body He might be a perfect man like Adam. For He went out to contend with the enemy (Satan) in place of Adam.

St. Jacob of Serugh. * We do not want to be rid of the body, but of the corruption in it. Our body is a burden to us, not because it is a body, but because it is corrupt and subject to pain. But when the new life comes, it removes this corruption; I say this corruption, not the body itself.

* If you wish to learn what kind of body God made at first, let us go to Paradise and look for the man who was created in the beginning. That body was neither corrupt nor dead. Rather it was like a golden statue coming out of the furnace shining with splendor, its frame free from all corruption. Work did not make it weary; no sweat poured from it. Nothing plotted against it, nor was anything of the kind found to trouble it.

St. John Chrysostom. * How great was this saint's grief for the common weakness of all men! How severe is the providence that God made man with His hands! Iniquity may be excused on the plea of (human) weakness, and grace declares its eternal work in us through the tenderness of heavenly protection.

St. Ambrose. * [Thy hands have made me and fashioned me together round about; yet thou dost suddenly cast me down] [8]. It is as though he says to Him in humility: Even if what I do is unfit to satisfy You if it is subjected to a just examination, remember Your mercy, lest the work of Your hands perish... Why do You thus slight me, when You created me in such circumstances of honor?
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* [You have struck me] not as a judge, but as a father who corrects me!
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. What does he mean by the hands of God?

* Since we read that the Holy Spirit is the finger of God (Lk 11:20), we reckon that the fingers refer to the Son and the Spirit. Finally, to indicate that he holds sanctification from both the Son and the Spirit, a certain saint says: "Thine hands have made me and fashioned me" (Job 10:8).
St. Ambrose. * [Thy hands have made me and formed me]. It refers to the divine providence that works after our creation.
Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus. "Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay."

entries.section: 2. His life in the hand of God

paragraphs.text: "And wilt thou bring me into dust again?" [9]
Job resorts to God's surpassing love for man. God raised him from clay and gave him all these surpassing capacities; will God turn back from His love and return man to what he was?
Man must not boast because he was formed from clay, and at the same time he must not belittle himself or despise his life, for he is the work of God, who created him in His image and likeness.
* Job seems to say: Remember the weakness of the flesh, and forgive my iniquity.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Why do You forget Your work? Why do You forget Your visitation?
Yes, why do You forget my weakness?
For what is man but Your visiting him? (Ps 8:4; Heb 2:6).

Therefore do not forget him who is weak. Remember, O Lord, that You created me weak; remember that You formed me as the clay (Ps 103:14; Job 10:9). How can I stand unless Your providence continually directs me to strengthen this clay, so that my strength comes forth from Your face? [Thou hidest thy face, they are troubled] (Ps 104:29).

* The needs of the body generate concerns and bring us into pursuits that hinder the soul's strength and prevent its concentration. Saint Job explained this well: [Remember that you have made me of clay] (Job 10:9). If the body is clay, then surely it defiles us and does not cleanse us. It corrupts the soul and defiles it by excess in satisfying passion. "Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews" (Job 10:11). Thus our souls are bound and tormented by the sinews of the body, and at times become hardened, often when they bow down. "Do not release me from my sin. If I am wicked, woe is me! If I am righteous, I dare not lift up my head, for I am full of dishonor. You bring tortures against me" (Job 10:14-15, 17) LXX.

St. Ambrose. * (Man) is placed in the hand of God (Ps 31:6), who is a safe harbor (Ps 107:30) and a strong tower (Ps 61:3); by nature He is merciful, rescuing and saving. God takes care of those whom He made from clay with surpassing providence... He set up a royal form clothed in glory (Ps 8:6), an image worthy of honor; He gave him features after the likeness of the Creator, since He willed it. Therefore it befits each one of us to keep this image at all times, and especially in time of trial... So now Job depicts precisely the whole history of Adam, giving us a brief teaching, which Moses explained at length.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. * Jonah was distressed after his flight and the reconciliation of the people of Nineveh with God... suffering and agitated in a human way, full of sorrow. So God commanded the earth to cause a gourd to grow for Jonah to shelter his head, then commanded the sun to increase its heat and scorch it. Jonah was angry at its perishing, but when the Lord comforted him and then tried him, hear what He says to him: [Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night: And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand?] (Jon 4:10-11).

This is what He wanted to say: Did you not rejoice in the shade of the gourd? How much more ought I to rejoice at the salvation of the people of Nineveh! Were you not pained at its perishing? So the perishing of humanity pains me...

He did not say to him: "You had pity on the gourd" and stop... but continued: "for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow." For just as the gardener has pity on the tree over which he has labored more than over others, so God wanted to establish His love for mankind through this love. It is as though He says to him: You defend strongly the work of another, in which you did not labor; how much more is it fitting for me to defend the work of my hands! Then He lessens the sharpness of the charge brought against them by saying: "that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand," that is, they sinned without knowledge...

And He reproaches those who groan that they are forsaken, saying: "Concerning my sons, and concerning the work of my hands command ye me" (Isa 45:11), as though saying: Who reminds a father of his son or urges him to think of him? Or who reminds the artist not to spoil his art?!
St. John Chrysostom. Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the earthy man bears an earthy mind that inclines to temporal earthly things, but the Holy Spirit lifts him up to heavenly things.

It is out of God's love that He withdraws the grace of His Holy Spirit from him, as it were, for a time, until he discovers his true state and cries out: "Wilt thou bring me into dust again?" [9]. Man feels his weakness and realizes that without the intervention of the breath of heavenly grace he is dry dust.

entries.section: 2. His life in the hand of God

paragraphs.text: "Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese?" [10]
A wonderful comparison: as a simple person can pour milk or make cheese, so with ease and simplicity God made man.

* When the Lord took a body He was not ashamed of it, since He is the Former of bodies. But who told us this? The Lord says to Jeremiah: "Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee" (Jer 1:5). If He was not ashamed of creating the body of man, would He be ashamed of the body in which He hid His divinity, He who creates infants in the womb, as Job wrote: "Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese? Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews?"

St. Cyril of Jerusalem. Again, when the grace of the Holy Spirit works in it, our mind is drawn away from what it was, and our understanding becomes like poured milk, and is formed by the Holy Spirit anew into tenderness and gentleness, and becomes like a piece of cheese.

* The immortal rational nature is hidden in our worn-out body, and suggests by all its acts in it and through it. And so, since you have this body, which has become an altar on which incense is offered, place upon it all your thoughts and evil counsels before the face of the Lord, lifting up your minds and hearts to Him, beseeching Him to send His holy fire to burn up all that is on this altar and purify it; then your adversaries (the demons and sins), the priests of Baal, will fear you and perish at your hands, as happened with Elijah the prophet (1 Kgs 18:25 ff.). Then you will behold the Holy Comforter in the divine water (Baptism) that rains upon you a spiritual rain.

entries.section: 2. His life in the hand of God

paragraphs.text: St. Anthony the Great. "Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews" [11].

When God created man, He did not create him naked, for He clothed him with skin; nor did He make him weak, for He knit him with bones and sinews. Thus our inner organs are clothed with skin and fortified with bones and nerves. Man could have lived in dignity and strength had sin not stripped him and weakened his power.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the inner man is clothed with skin and flesh, because while rising toward heavenly things he finds at the same time an obstacle, being besieged by bodily movements that hinder him.

And St. John Chrysostom sees that Job touches upon the surpassing providence of God, who created him out of nothing and gave him skin and body, bones and sinews; how then could this Creator, so inventive in His love, care, and powers, fail to care for man, His beloved?

* He means: Are You not the One to whom he gives assurance of the greatness of love toward man and the greatness of this wisdom? If Job refers to the formation of man in some detail, it is only to prove that, after He created him out of nothing, He would deny this great providence of God and His surpassing wisdom? And he has shown that man (in himself) is nothing.
St. John Chrysostom. * He is a wise Maker indeed; who prepared the womb to bear the fetus?!
Who gives life to the lifeless things within you?!
Who bound us with muscles and bones, and clothed us with skin and flesh, and as soon as the child is born the milk overflows from the breasts?!
How does the child grow to be a boy, then a youth, then a man, and remain so until he passes into old age, without anyone noticing this subtle change from day to day?!

entries.section: 2. His life in the hand of God

paragraphs.text: St. Cyril of Jerusalem. "Thou hast granted me life and favour, and thy visitation hath preserved my spirit" [12].

If we have anything to complain about, even of what comes from God, we resort to Him. He permits affliction so that we may learn to resort to Him, for He is the One who created us that we might enjoy Him, not that we might murmur.

Along with the gift of the body in the splendor of its creation and its visible and hidden capacities, God gave us something greater, namely the breath of life from the mouth of God. He granted us life and mercy, and gave us the grace of reason and thought along with heart and emotions.
He established the soul hidden in the body, but what keeps it is not the body with its powers and energies, but the providence of God.

* How powerful is this holy man's lament for the common weakness of all men! How heavy was the charge that God made man with His hands, and yet man offers an excuse for committing sin on the plea that he is weak, while grace declares the eternal work in us through the tenderness of heavenly protection.

St. Ambrose. * "And thy visitation hath preserved my spirit" [12]. It is not enough that you have this by nature, but it requires Your divine providence over us. He says: Throughout all my life I rely on Your divine providence.

* If you doubt God's providence, ask the earth and the heavens and the sun and the moon, ask the irrational creatures and the plants... Ask the rocks and the mountains, the sand dunes and the hills. Ask the night and the day. For God's providence is clearer than the sun and its rays. In every place, in the wilderness and in inhabited cities, on the earth and in the seas... wherever you go you hear a speaking testimony of this crying providence...
In every place voices rise resounding, clearer than the voices of rational men, proclaiming to everyone who wants to hear the watchful love of God!
And when the prophet wished to record the power of these voices he said: [Their line is gone out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world] (Ps 19:4).
Our own language is understood only by the people of our tongue, but creation speaks a language that all peoples understand!
St. John Chrysostom. "And these things hast thou hid in thine heart."

entries.section: 2. His life in the hand of God

paragraphs.text: "I know that this is with thee" [13].

Job was in a struggle between these free divine graces and God's surpassing care to preserve the body as well as the soul, and the unbearable troubles he was permitted to suffer. Therefore he says: "And these things hast thou hid in thine heart," that is, the two agree together through Your will hidden within You, whose depths none of us can fathom. He is certain both of God's providence and of God's permitting him to suffer: "I know that this is with thee."

* [Since You have hidden these in Yourself, I know that You can do all things, and nothing is impossible for You](أ). Do you not see that the possibility of knowing God is revealed in His creation (Rev 1:19); it is enough for my creation to show me God's existence and power, without need of heaven? For since we were created thus, to exist from a seed, and to be under this help, and not to be allowed to fall into dangers, all this suffices to show God's power and authority. Likewise in the fact of the sinner's being preserved and not punished (here), and in the righteous man's being disciplined and punished.
St. John Chrysostom. * How could such a thing (granting life and mercy) not belong to such a Creator?
What could be impossible for Him?

If You made the clay in the image of God (Gen 2:7), and made the dust pass to the rank of a rational being, if You give earthly beings a happiness equal to that of heavenly beings, how could You not work a miracle for me?
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem

14 If I sin, then thou markest me, and thou wilt not acquit me from mine iniquity. 15 If I be wicked, woe unto me; and if I be righteous, yet will I not lift up my head. I am full of confusion; therefore see thou mine affliction; 16 For it increaseth. Thou huntest me as a fierce lion: and again thou shewest thyself marvellous upon me. 17 Thou renewest thy witnesses against me, and increasest thine indignation upon me; changes and war are against me.
"If I sin, then thou markest me, and thou wilt not acquit me from mine iniquity" [14].

Job does not deny that he is mistaken, and that God knows his sins and marks them, and by this Job will not be justified before Him. "If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?" (Ps 130:3)

* If I sin, You mark me, lest I fall into the pit (Ps 28:1), into the utmost sin, and be utterly lost, and lest I stray from the flock (Jn 10:1) and go to the den of wolves. According to the law of justice You do not find me righteous, but find me blameworthy under the stroke of the inherited curse (Gen 3:17).

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. Job realized that he could not be justified by himself, but needs the One who grants it. Like all the fathers of the Old Testament he was longing for the coming of the Messiah, the Savior.
* The Lord Christ suffered at the time when Pontius Pilate was acting as governor and judge...
Who suffered? Our Lord, the only-begotten Son of God!
And what happened to Him? He was crucified, died, and was buried!
And for whom? For the wicked and sinners!
How great is this condescension! How great is the grace!
"What shall I render unto the LORD for all his benefits toward me?" (Ps 116:12).

St. Augustine. * Christ appears to each one according to his need. To those who need joy He comes as a vine; to those who need to be in the presence of the Father He comes as a door; those who need someone to offer their prayers find Him the Intercessor, the High Priest within them; and to sinners He is the Lamb (slain) for their sanctification.

He is all things to everyone without His nature changing, but remains as He is. He remains, and the work of His sonship will not change, but He adapts Himself to our weakness, being an excellent physician or a teacher full of tenderness. He is the Lord Himself; He did not receive lordship by advancement, but the work of His sonship is natural.

* The word "Jesus" means "Savior," and in Greek it means "the Healer," for He is the physician of souls and bodies, the healer of spirits; He opened the eyes of the man born blind, and led minds to the light. He heals the visibly lame, and leads sinners in the way of repentance. He says to the paralytic: "Sin no more," and also: "Take up thy bed, and walk" (Jn 5:14, 8), because the body was paralyzed by the sin of the soul. He ministered to the soul first so that healing might extend to the body.
Therefore if any of you is suffering in his soul from sins, you will find Him a physician for you. And if any of you is of little faith, let him say to Him: "Help thou mine unbelief" (Mk 9:24).
And if bodily pains afflict any of you, let him not be unbelieving but draw near, for Jesus heals such diseases, and let him know that Jesus is the Christ.
St. Cyril of Jerusalem. * Often the mind is disturbed in its depths at the remembrance of sin, and so urges its practice in a worse form than it had when it was first committed.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* "If I sin, then thou markest me" (Job 10:14). Confess your sins, O man, that you may obtain forgiveness: "Declare thou thy iniquities first, that thou mayest be justified" (Isa 43:26) LXX.
Why are you ashamed to confess them, when you were born in them? (Ps 51:5). He who denies his guilt and does not confess it in truth denies his birth.

But do you want to keep what you have received? Why do you think you possess what you have not received? Therefore let the sinner and the unholy confess, and let the righteous not exalt himself nor be proud, lest he lose the reward of his righteousness through pride (Job 10:15).
St. Ambrose. "If I be wicked, woe unto me."
"And if I be righteous, yet will I not lift up my head."
"I am full of confusion; therefore see thou mine affliction" [15].

Without repentance we fall into this woe to which Job refers here. For nothing can rescue me from it, neither moral loftiness nor my worship, whatever it may be, as long as it is without repentance. This is what Job means by saying: "If I be righteous," that is, if I rely on my self-righteousness or on my conduct or service, all this will not lift up my head before my God.
The Holy Bible warns us against sin of any kind, for it brings shame and dishonor: "I am full of confusion; therefore see thou mine affliction" [15].
"Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people" (Prov 14:34).
"Have mercy upon us, O LORD, have mercy upon us: for we are exceedingly filled with contempt" (Ps 123:3).
"The wise shall inherit glory: but shame shall be the promotion of fools" (Prov 3:35).
"When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom" (Prov 11:2).
"Poverty and shame shall be to him that refuseth instruction: but he that regardeth reproof shall be honoured" (Prov 13:18).
"When the wicked cometh, then cometh also contempt, and with ignominy reproach" (Prov 18:3).
"Do not exalt yourself lest you fall, and bring dishonor upon yourself" (Sir 1:38).
"The lot of the lying man is dishonor, and his shame is with him continually" (Sir 20:28).
"A slothful man is compared to a filthy stone, and every one will hiss at his disgrace" (Sir 22:1).
"As they were increased, so they sinned against me: therefore will I change their glory into shame" (Hos 4:7).
"For this cause God gave them up unto vile affections: for even their women did change the natural use into that which is against nature" (Rom 1:26).

* Besides the inherited (ancestral) evils, I added evils of my own... The sin of Adam, without doubt, does not allow a man to look upward with boldness, nor to glorify himself. Therefore Job says: "I am full of confusion."

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. * Yes, for "woe" is for the wicked, and for the righteous "sorrow"; eternal punishment overtakes the sinner who perishes, while each one of the elect is purified by the pains of temporary sorrow...
But if we overlook for a time the sin of our first father, we find ourselves hunted by the evil habit of pride.

It often happens that through the virtues granted him, man is puffed up with boldness and self-righteousness, but through the wonderful dispensation of divine providence it is permitted that certain opposing things be placed before his eyes into which some fall...
When the saint sees what happens to his fellows, a cry comes forth from him personally concerning the dangers to which we are exposed.
In this way, when we read of the lament of a certain person, we learn to grieve over what is within ourselves.
Now when pride rises in the mind, the wounded feeling of love for the heights leaves us, but when grace comes upon us from above, it immediately urges us to long for it with tears.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Rightly he says: "If I be righteous, yet will I not lift up my head, for I am full of confusion" [15]. The righteous man knows his weakness...
The wise man is moved to recognize them, and the fool does not do so.
Truly the wise man is moved toward repentance and remembers his faults, and the ignorant man delights in them.
The wise man is he who accuses himself (Prov 18:17), but the wicked man is the one who defends himself.
The righteous man wishes to precede his accuser in accusing himself of his sins, but the wicked man wishes to silence him.
One hastens from the beginning to speak of his faults, and the other tries to accuse others with his talkative speech so that his sins may not be exposed.

St. Ambrose. In one of the Festal Letters, St. Athanasius the Apostolic depicts for us the dishonor that comes upon the human soul because of sin, while the righteous, who have pure hearts, enjoy glory, that is, the glory of seeing God.

* We say that the wicked are dead, but not in a life of devotion against sin, nor do they, like the saints, bear death in their bodies; rather they bury the soul in sins and follies, so that the soul draws near to death. And as they feed it with deadly pleasures, their souls are like young vultures hovering over the corpses of the dead. The Law declared this when it commanded, in symbolic form, not to eat vultures and all the birds that feed on carrion (Lev 11:13).
These kill the soul with lusts, and say nothing but "let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die" (Isa 22:13).

And the prophet described the fruit gathered by such as these who plunge into pleasures, saying: "And it was revealed in mine ears by the LORD of hosts, Surely this iniquity shall not be purged from you till ye die" (Isa 22:14).
Yes, even while they live they are in shame, for they reckon their belly as their god, and when they die they are tormented, because they boasted of such a death.
Paul also bears witness to this result, saying: "Meats for the belly, and the belly for meats: but God shall destroy both it and them" (1 Cor 6:13).
And the divine Word declares concerning these that the death of the wicked is evil, and those who hate the righteous do wrong (Ps 34:21), for the wicked inherit bitter fire and destroying darkness.

But the saints and those who practice virtue truly have mortified their members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence (Col 3:5). So there is fulfilled in them, because of this purity and undefiledness, the promise of our Savior: "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God" (Mt 5:8).
St. Athanasius the Apostolic. "For it increaseth. Thou huntest me as a fierce lion: and again thou shewest thyself marvellous upon me" [16]!
As though he had become prey in the mouth of a lion, with no refuge and no escape, and no mercy or compassion! One translation reads: "If I am proud and haughty like a lion, You hunt me."

* Man is rightly likened to a lion, for it is a royal beast (Gen 28:8-9). Moreover the righteous man, as he preserves in himself the dignity of the image (of God), is dreadful to his adversaries. It is said of this in the book of Proverbs: [The righteous are bold as a lion] (cf. Prov 28:1). But if he sinks down to covetousness, as his enemies urge him to do, at that very moment he is "hunted like a lion for slaughter." He becomes an object of mockery to those who were tracking him, and is like the lion which, as soon as it falls into their enticement, they hunt down.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. "Thou renewest thy witnesses against me, and increasest thine indignation upon me."
"Changes (calamities) and war are against me" [17].

What multiplied Job's calamity was that he felt God's wrath increasing, which made the trial more bitter and heavy. God does not lack witnesses against Job; if one witness fails, a new witness stands in his place. Since the word "witnesses" in Greek means "martyrs," it is as though those who bear witness to God, to His love, His divine providence, and His work of salvation even unto death, become witnesses against those who doubt God's providence and murmur against Him. The appearance of these holy witnesses condemns us, so that we have no argument or justification for our sinful conduct, and Job expressed this by saying: "and increasest thine indignation upon me; changes and war are against me."
"Changes and war are against me." One translation reads: "Your armies take turns against me."

* God's witnesses are those who bear witness by the practice of holy works... also those who suffer for the truth. In the Greek tongue "martyrs" are "witnesses." The Lord says through John by the voice of the angel: [even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful witness, who was slain among you] (Rev 2:13).

Now the Lord renews His witnesses against us when He multiplies the lives of the elect, so that they challenge our evil with the aim of persuading and teaching us... All that they do is contrary to our evil. Therefore the word of truth is called "the adversary," as the Mediator says in the Gospel: "Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him" (Mt 5:25). And the sons of perdition say in their persecutions concerning the Savior Himself: "He is clearly against our doings," and after that: [his life is not like other men's] (Wis 2:12, 15). Thus God renews His witnesses against us, to show that the good works which we neglect are practiced by others, to rebuke us...

It was fitting to add: "and increasest thine indignation upon me"... as Peter testified, saying: "For the time is come that judgment must begin at the house of God: and if it first begin at us, what shall the end be of them that obey not the gospel of God?" (1 Pet 4:17). Therefore when Almighty God renews His witnesses against us He "increases His indignation" as is fitting, for He sets the lives of the righteous before our eyes, and shows with what severity He will strike our stubbornness while we practice sin, at the judgment.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

18 "Wherefore then hast thou brought me forth out of the womb? Oh that I had given up the ghost, and no eye had seen me! 19 I should have been as though I had not been; I should have been carried from the womb to the grave. 20 Are not my days few? cease then, and let me alone, that I may take comfort a little, 21 Before I go whence I shall not return, even to the land of darkness and the shadow of death; 22 A land of darkness, as darkness itself; and of the shadow of death, without any order, and where the light is as darkness."

The writings of the early Church and its concepts in its worship, asceticism, canons, and every aspect of its life bore a biblical eschatological stamp. The doctrine of the life to come was not merely a principal element of faith, but the very core of the faith itself! The early Church, as a truly biblical Church, was an eschatological Church; it set its heart in heaven, to live as an ambassador of the heavenly Christ, drawing the world toward heaven and bringing it into the life of Paradise, that it might await in hope the fullness of eternal glory and the heavenly inheritance.

As for the view of Old Testament believers toward death, it is expressed in what is found in the Book of Wisdom: [For God created man for incorruption, and made him an image of His own divine self, but through the devil's envy death entered the world] (Wis 2:23, 24). God did not create death, and therefore through righteousness man obtains immortality: [For God made not death: neither hath he pleasure in the destruction of the living. For he created all things, that they might have their being: and the generations of the world were healthful; and there is no poison of destruction in them, nor the kingdom of death upon the earth: for righteousness is immortal] (Wis 1:13-15). As it is also said: [For to know thy power is the root of immortality] (Wis 15:3).

The believing fathers in the Old Testament looked upon death as being gathered or sleeping with their fathers (Gen 25:8; 47:30), and they feared only going down to Sheol in sorrow (Gen 27:35). They counted death in a good old age a blessing (Gen 15:15; 25:8), while the cutting off of a man from the land of the living in the prime of his youth was a fearful thing (Isa 38:10).
Nevertheless the Jews' view of death differed from one person to another, and Alfred Edersheim presented to us a comparison between two Jewish leaders in their view of death.

The first leader is Rabbi Jochanan ben Saccai. It is told of him in the Talmud that his disciples came to him as he lay on his deathbed, and he burst into tears. They were amazed at this, and asked how it was that "the light of Israel, the pillar of the true Temple," should be betrayed in this way by signs of fear. The Rabbi answered them: "If I were being brought before an earthly king who lives today and dies tomorrow, whose wrath and chains are not eternal, and whose pronouncing of the sentence of death is not eternal death, and with whom one can easily enter into dialogue or buy him with money, I would be terrified at this and weep; how much more is my condition, now that I have drawn near to stand before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, who lives and abides forever, whose chains are everlasting chains, and whose sentence of death is an eternal sentence, whom I cannot converse with by words nor bribe with money! And it does not stop at this, but before me are two ways: one toward Paradise and the other toward Gehenna, and I do not know to which of the two ways I shall go: whether to Paradise or to Gehenna; how then should I not shed tears?"
The second example is R. Jehudah, who is called the Saint, for when he died he raised his hands toward heaven, affirming that not one of his ten fingers had broken the Law of God!

The first is utterly without hope, living in great despair and fearing the meeting with God, in spite of his position as head of the greatest assembly among the Jews, and the second, in great pride and certainty, thinks that he will surely enjoy Paradise, because he did not break any commandment with any of his fingers. Two completely extreme pictures: one crushed by despair, the other crushed by pride!
"Wherefore then hast thou brought me forth out of the womb?"
"Oh that I had given up the ghost, and no eye had seen me!" [18]
Job repeats the same desire that he had already declared in an earlier discourse (Job 3:11).
Again Job longed to have been stifled in the womb, not to come out into the world, and for no one to see him.
Perhaps Job felt that he had become a byword and a mockery to all who looked at him, so he wished that he had never seen anyone at all, and that no one had seen him.
"I should have been as though I had not been; I should have been carried from the womb to the grave" [19].

Just as he who sets his heart on temporal life sins, so he who despairs of life and longs for death out of despair sins. The first loves the world and the creature more than its Creator, and the second slights God's plan for him.
"Are not my days few?"
"Cease then, and let me alone, that I may take comfort (smile) a little" [20].
He asks God to cease from discipline so that he may catch his breath and rest a little.
Job knows that the days of man are few, so in this little time he asks for some rest, even if only from time to time.

* Solomon said: "But if a man live many years, and rejoice in them all; yet let him remember the days of darkness; for they shall be many. All that cometh is vanity" (Eccl 11:8). Again he wrote: [Whatever you take in hand, remember your end, and you will never sin]. Therefore when sin tempts the mind, the soul should perceive the purpose of its delight, lest sin hasten it to certain death, since it is clear that mortal life quickly comes to an end.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* O sons of Adam, over whom death has reigned, think of death, and remember life, and do not transgress the commandment like your first father.
O kings crowned with crowns, remember death, which will take away the crowns placed on your heads; it will be king over you until the time comes when you rise for judgment.

O you who are haughty and proud and arrogant, remember death, which will shatter your haughtiness, and loosen your limbs, and undo the joints, and bring corruption upon the body in all its forms. By death the haughty are brought low, and the violent and hard-hearted are buried in its darkness...

O you greedy, who seize and plunder your fellows, remember death, and do not multiply your sins. For in that place sinners do not repent, and he who plundered the possessions of his companion does not even own his own money, but goes to the place where wealth is not used, and becomes nothing; his honor passes away, and his sins remain to stand against him on the day of judgment.
St. Aphrahat. "Before I go whence I shall not return, even to the land of darkness and the shadow of death" [21].

He sets death before his eyes, and asks for some rest, perhaps to prepare for departure, and so as not to sin, even in his thought, under the weight of trials. As the Psalmist says: "Lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death" (Ps 13:3). He asked for a time in which to return to himself, and asked for God's work in his life before he dies and the door is shut. "Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead?" (Ps 88:10)
Job does not ask for rest because he is attached to temporal life, for he knows that he is departing and will not return. "Before I go whence I shall not return."
Job presents to us a painful picture of death and the grave, such as prevailed even among believers before the Resurrection of Christ. "To the land of darkness and the shadow of death."

Job's appearance was a mockery to his friends and to those who passed by him; perhaps he longed for the grave, where there is darkness, so that no one would see his sores, and his body would decay like the rest of the bodies without distinction!

For us, our life is a constant battle, whose site is the land of the heart, the mind, and the senses; it is an inner war between light and darkness. The enemy of good will not rest until the last breath, reckoning himself a king with the right to possess all humanity under his authority. The believer by his departure declares his final victory, or the victory of the grace of God working in him.

* Many of our people die this (bodily) death, and so are freed from this world. This death, which (the people of the world) reckon a catastrophe, the servants of God regard as a departure to salvation.
The righteous die like the wicked, without distinction... but the righteous are called to rest, and the wicked to punishment.
Great peace is granted to the believers, and punishment to the unbelievers.

* As for rest, what do we find in the world but constant war with Satan, and struggle in a continual battle against his arrows and swords?! Our war is waged against love of money, pride, anger, and love of display, and our struggle is constant against the lusts of the flesh and the enticements of the world.

For man's mind is besieged by the enemy on every side, and the assaults of Satan close in upon it from every direction. With effort the mind is able to defend itself, and scarcely can it resist in every spot. If it disdains the love of money, the lusts rise up in it. If it overcomes the lusts, the love of display springs up. If it triumphs over the love of display, anger and pride are kindled in it, and drunkenness with wine entices it, and envy tears apart its agreement with others, and jealousy corrupts its friendships.

Thus the spirit suffers every day from many persecutions like these and from great dangers like these that distress the heart, and yet the heart still delights in remaining long here among the wars of Satan! Though it would have been more fitting for our longings and desires to be directed toward hastening to go to Christ by way of speedy death. For the Lord Himself taught us, saying: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, That ye shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice: and ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy" (Jn 16:20).
Who among us does not wish to be without sorrow?!
Who among us does not long to hasten to obtain joy?!

The Lord Himself also declared the time of turning our sorrow into joy, saying: "But I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh from you" (Jn 16:22). Since our joy lies in seeing Christ... what blindness afflicts our mind, and what foolishness overtakes us, when we love the sorrows of the world and its afflictions and tears more than hastening toward the joy that will not be taken from us?!
St. Cyprian the Martyr. "A land of darkness, as darkness itself; and of the shadow of death, without any order, and where the light is as darkness" [22].
St. John Chrysostom did not wish to speak about the location of Gehenna other than that it is "outside this world," but he spoke in some detail about its torments. In one of his homilies he says:

[It is a sea of fire, not a sea of the same kind with the dimensions we know here, but greater and fiercer, with waves of fire, strange and terrifying flames. There is there a great abyss filled with terrifying flame. One can see the fire coming out of it on every side like a ravenous beast...
There none can resist, none can escape.
There the gentle face of Christ, the giver of peace, is not seen anywhere.

And as those condemned to work in the mines are violent men, who no longer see their families but those who force them to labor, so it will be there. But it is not so simple as this, but far worse. For here a man can present a petition to the emperor asking for mercy, and the prisoner may be pardoned, but there this will not happen. They will not come out but will remain, enduring inexpressible torments.]
St. John Chrysostom says that in spite of all these torments, the chief torment of the condemned is their deprivation of the presence of the Lord and of the communion of the saints in heaven.
The degrees of torment in Hell differ, depending on the extent of man's sins, but all fall under them eternally.

He says: [It is impossible that the torments of Gehenna do not exist.] And he sees that these torments are not merely for the fulfillment of divine justice, but were established to urge humanity to repent and abstain from sin. He says: [If God is concerned that we not sin, and that we enter into such troubles for our correction, it is clear that He punishes sinners and crowns the righteous.] He also says that He prepared Gehenna so that no one would be cast into Gehenna.

* As outward death separates the body from the soul, so inward death separates the soul from God. Thus the "shadow of death" is the darkness of separation, in which each of those condemned by eternal fire that destroys him is in darkness with respect to the inner light.

Now the nature of fire is to give light, and it has the property of destroying; but the fire that is wrathful over former sins has the property of destroying and has no light. Therefore the Truth says to the perishing: "Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels" (Mt 25:41). And as they are all represented in one person, He says: "Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness" (Mt 22:13).

If the fire that torments the perishing could have light, it would not have been said of those cast out, "cast him into darkness." Likewise the Psalmist says: "Fire has fallen upon them and they shall not behold the sun" (Ps 58:8) [Vulgate]. For the fire falls upon the wicked.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

"Without any order": it seems to us that there is no particular order in the grave, but kings are equal with slaves, and the rich with the poor, etc.; each is buried in his turn as God appoints for him; but there is a precise divine plan concerning the chastenings that may come upon us, even if we cannot explain them.

* The words "without any order" are most remarkable, for Almighty God, who rightly punishes evils, will not allow even the torments to be "without order." The very punishments that proceed from the balance of justice cannot in any way be inflicted "without order"; for how could there be no order in the punishments He issues, since the punishment that overtakes those condemned eternally is according to the measure of the crime. As it is written: [But the powerful will have their torment more severe, and more severe torments come upon the strong] (Wis 6:6-7). It is said in the judgment of Babylon: "How much she hath glorified herself, and lived deliciously, so much torment and sorrow give her" (Rev 18:7). If the punishment is according to the measure of the sin, it is an undeniable truth that there is an order preserved in the punishments...

As in our Father's house there are many mansions according to the diversity of the virtues, so there is a difference in crime, and the condemned are subjected to varied punishment in the fires of Gehenna. For although Gehenna is one and the same for all, this does not mean that all burn in the same manner.

* "And where the light is as darkness" [22]. Although the fire in that place gives no light for comfort, yet for the sake of their greater torment it shines with a certain purpose. For the condemned will see by the shining flame their followers with them in torment, those who, for love of the disobedient, preferred the love of fleshly life to the commandments of the Creator...

The Truth shows us that the rich man, whose lot it was to go down into the torments of eternal fire (Lk 17:19-31), is described as remembering his five brothers, and he asked Abraham to send to them to teach them, lest they fall under the same punishment in the future. It is clear without doubt that he who remembers his absent relatives has multiplied his own pains; how much more, when afterward he sees them with his own eyes present with him, does it increase his torment.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* On the day of judgment, there is no doubt that the good will be separated from the bad, and the righteous from the wicked. And to every soul, through the judgment of God, will be assigned a place befitting its worthiness and merit, God willing.
Origen. * We speak of many degrees and various measures in both the Kingdom and Gehenna... For God, as a just judge, gives each one according to the measure of his faith.
* In the light and in the glory there are degrees. And in Gehenna itself and in the punishment it appears that there are sorcerers and thieves, as there are others who committed lesser sins.
St. Macarius the Great
You are my eternity!
* When afflictions hem me in, I feel bitterness and distress.
I loathe my life, longing for death.
Anxiety fills my depths, and my whole inner being trembles.
I cry out with Job: My soul is weary of my life.
Truly, in my weakness I have often longed for death.
I have often wondered why You created me.
But when I lift my eyes to You, in the midst of my trials I will not forget that I am the work of Your hands.
In the midst of my chastenings I will not ignore Your constant care for me.
You are love, wholly wisdom and wholly fatherhood and love!
I look to You, and You carry me in the midst of my chastenings into Your embrace.
I remember Your fatherhood, and I forget all my troubles.
Truly I perceive my hidden sins; instead of thinking about the affliction, my soul is distressed by my iniquities.
Instead of longing for death, I seek Your grace that forgives sins.
Instead of murmuring, I condemn myself.
I confess my sins now, that You may cover me on the day of judgment.
I am exposed before myself, so that I may be covered by Your righteousness.
Affliction turns into peace, as I hide in You and take refuge in You, O refuge of my life.
Instead of the weight of afflictions that crushes the soul, I enjoy the weight of eternal glory that lifts my soul to heavenly things.
I forget all pain, and even long for it, for it is the way of fellowship with You in the Cross, as in the glory of the Resurrection.
* In my affliction and in the midst of my pains I realize that I am a sinner.
But I need Your Holy Spirit to enlighten my insight, that I may know my sin and discover it, and so confess it to You.
I hate it, and cry out to You that Your grace may support me, and I may flee from it.
Who exposes my soul before me but Your light, O Lord.
Let it shine upon me, that I may perceive my weaknesses, and with rejoicing hope for the riches of Your love that forgives all my sins!
Grant me to judge myself here, so that You may not pass judgment on me on the day of Your coming!
* In my weakness sufferings swallowed my soul; I reckoned that You had left the wicked to destroy me.
But when I lift my eyes to You, I realize that You did not permit me affliction beyond my endurance.
In Your love You set limits to affliction, and it does not exceed them.
And by Your grace You grant me the gift of joyful endurance, and pour upon me the fruit of the Spirit, patience, a way of passing over into the glories.
Truly You do not leave the rod of the wicked to rest upon the righteous.
Rather through it You prove them, and bring them over into eternity.
* My God, You know my depths, You are the Creator of time, and You are above time.
You have no need to examine me by trials.
For in my weakness I fear the pressures of the enemy upon me.
Lest he turn me aside to evil!
I flee to You that You may keep me from him!
* My God, I confess to You that I am a sinner.
By Your grace I cry out with the Apostle Peter:
You know, Lord, that I love You.
I do not want to resist You, nor to disobey You.
But this will not justify me, for I am weak.
Support me by Your grace, that I may bear Your righteousness.
* Truly I groan because of my body, yet it is the work of Your good hands.
Scatter the corruption that has crept into it, and sanctify the body that You created and wish to glorify!
You, the eternal Word, became flesh, that by Your incarnation You might sanctify my whole being.
So I do not belittle the body, for it is a partner of the soul in glory!
Glory to You, who honor our bodies in Yourself!
You have honored my body, because it is the work of Your hands!
And when I dishonored it by my sins, You became incarnate to glorify what You created!
* I am the work of Your hands, You cherish me!
I am confident of Your surpassing providence, however the waves rise against me.
But my mind remains in its weakness, unable to comprehend Your wisdom!
Reveal to me the mystery of Your love, that I may not stumble!
Make known to me Your judgments, that I may meditate in Your love!
* You are wonderful in Your care for me, for if I sin You watch me, lest I turn aside further; You lead me with the rod of discipline, that I may not fall into the den of wolves.
You draw me with a love full of firmness, and a firmness full of gentleness!
* Quickly I look to Your Cross, and pass over with You to Your tomb, O my Savior.
So death becomes for me not out of despair and despondency, but a fellowship of love with Him who died for me; indeed I long to die with You, out of love for You and for those You love.
I no longer look to the years of my life, but I await the salvation of the whole world!
I do not fear events, but rejoice in the salvation of many!
You are wonderful in Your love, You who turn even death into a joyful gift!
* I will no longer be preoccupied with my afflictions.
I will no longer cry out in folly, saying:
Lift Your hand from me, for I have sunk in the midst of my bitterness. I will not cry out to You as a fool, reckoning that death is a rest for me from my toils.
* Rise, O Sun of righteousness, upon me and upon humanity, and scatter the darkness of our thoughts, and bring us out of our inner graves, and turn our dry bones into an exceeding great army.
Let me enjoy with Ezekiel the vision of the resurrection of humanity in You (Ezek 38).
So there will be no darkness in my life, and I will no longer suffer from night!
But in Your light I will perceive the mysteries of Your salvation, and enjoy the delight of knowing Your wonderful dispensation.
And I will be always a son of light, and a son of the day!

entries.section: 1. Job accused of pride and falsehood

paragraphs.text: 1 Then answered Zophar the Naamathite, and said, 2 "Should not the multitude of words be answered? and should a man full of talk be justified? 3 Should thy arrogance make men hold their peace? and when thou mockest, shall no man make thee ashamed? 4 For thou hast said, My doctrine is pure, and I am clean in thine eyes.
Then answered Zophar the Naamathite [1]:

entries.section: 1. Job accused of pride and falsehood

paragraphs.text: "Should not the multitude of words be answered? and should a man full of talk be justified?" [2]

Eliphaz began with an introduction of great dignity (Job 4:2), while Bildad was harsher in his speech to Job (Job 8:2). Zophar came and fell upon him without compassion, directing very severe words at him.

It was not possible for Zophar to accept Job's reasoning that it was God who had allowed the trials to come upon him although he was righteous (Job 9:21; 11:4; 10:7). For this contradicts all religious philosophy, both in his own time and before it. Job appeared as one who opposes all the philosophers and those who possess religious knowledge.

He began by saying, "Should not the multitude of words be answered? and should a man full of talk be justified?" Zophar thought Job to be a babbler, a man of words without deeds, not worthy to be answered, a prattler who carries no seriousness, whose speech has no thoughtfulness or balance to deserve an answer.

Bildad had already said to Job, "the words of thy mouth be like a strong wind" (Job 8:2), and in the Septuagint it reads, "The breezes of your mouth overflow in words." Here Zophar the Naamathite accuses him of babbling.

It is true that Zophar presented sound and wise opinions, but he accused Job unjustly, because he did not share his feelings as a man who was suffering greatly, and he did not examine Job's words and circumstances carefully. He accused Job of babbling and of much vain talk in order to justify himself, though what he uttered cannot be counted babbling in view of what had befallen him. And in his speech he did not justify himself, but confessed that he is a sinner (Job 9:20).

Here Zophar calls Job to be wise by sitting at the feet of the elders and listening in silence, rather than being a man of many words. St. James says, "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak" (Jas 1:19). Perhaps by the elders he means his three friends. In other words, Zophar sees that he and his two companions have the right to give Job sermons, advice and counsel, and that Job has nothing to do but sit at their feet and learn from them in silence!

* Zophar did not offer a wrong opinion when he said, [A man of many words will not be able to be justified]. As long as a man lets himself speak on and on, the gravity of silence flees from him, and he loses the safe guarding of himself. For this reason it is written, "The work of righteousness shall be quietness" (Isa 32:17). So Solomon says, "A city broken down and without a wall is the man who has no rule over his spirit in speech" (Prov 25:28) [Vulgate]. He also says, "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin" (Prov 10:19). And the psalmist bears witness to this, saying, [A man of many words shall not be established in the earth] (Ps 140:11); and even the value of a true statement is lost when it is spoken without discernment...

A true statement is against the wicked if it aims at the benefit of the righteous... But the wicked cannot hear good words with patience, ignoring the correction of their life, and so they attach themselves to words in order to answer others.

* Whoever remembers the words of the blessed Job knows how groundless this accusation is... For how could he who said, "If I justify myself, mine own mouth shall condemn me" (Job 9:20) call himself clean (pure)?
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Indeed the Holy Bible urged silence as far as possible if it is holy, just as it urged constructive speech. The psalmist asked for strong divine protection for his mouth, saying, "Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips" (Ps 141:3).
* The Holy Spirit teaches a man to keep his whole body, from head to foot, in harmony:
so he keeps the eyes that they may look with purity...
and he keeps the tongue that it may speak only what is good, giving weight to every word, and does not allow anything defiled or sensual to mingle with his speech.

* Flee from those who bear the name of "monks and virgins" without having true understanding and good discernment. For if you mingle with them, they will not let you advance, and may even quench the warmth of your zeal, since they have no warmth but only coldness, and they walk after their own passions. If they come to you and speak with you about earthly matters according to their own passions, do not be content with this, for the Apostle Paul wrote, "Quench not the Spirit. Despise not prophesyings" (1 Thess 5:19-20), knowing that nothing quenches the Spirit more than vain talk.
St. Anthony the Great * Silence for the sake of God is good, just as speech for the sake of God is good.

Abba Poemen * When your tongue is like the tongue of Christ, and your mouth becomes the mouth of the Father, and you become a temple of the Holy Spirit, then what honor this will be! For even if your mouth were made of gold and precious stones, it would not shine as it does with the ornaments of meekness. What is more lovable than a mouth that does not know how to revile, but is accustomed to bless and to utter good words!
St. John Chrysostom * I have often spoken and regretted it, but of silence I have never once repented.

St. Arsenius the Teacher of the Sons of the Kings * The righteous man is silent, for he teaches that there is a time for silence and a time for speech (Eccl 3:7), yet he does not become dumb. Dumbness is rather a mark of the Sadducees and of everyone who teaches falsehood, for they are made dumb and do not keep silent. Though they are dumb toward the truth, they are not silent. It was thus that the Lord spoke to the sea, and not to a man, to make it dumb, rebuking it when it was stormy.

entries.section: 1. Job accused of pride and falsehood

paragraphs.text: Origen "Should thy arrogance make men hold their peace? and when thou mockest (babblest), shall no man make thee ashamed?" [3]

He called him a scoffer, who mocks God by complaining against Him, and ridicules people, since he is not ashamed to deceive those around him. As he called him a mocker, Zophar thus used harsh words and described him with unseemly epithets.

Some see in Zophar's words here an indirect accusation of Eliphaz and Bildad, for it would have been fitting for them to silence him, and not leave him to babble with violent, mistaken and meaningless speech.
In his opinion, Job had behaved arrogantly with pride and vain lies, and his two friends were not able to silence him, but kept quiet instead of defending the truth.
He accuses him of "babbling," that is, "mocking" or "scoffing," by blaming God in his complaint.

entries.section: 1. Job accused of pride and falsehood

paragraphs.text: "For thou hast said, My doctrine is pure, and I am clean in thine eyes" [4].
He accused Job of words he never uttered. He accused him of saying that his doctrine is pure, and he did not say this.
Job was marked by soundness of faith. It is true that at times he was carried away, longing for death because of the weight of the trial, but he never thought of suicide.
He reproached God, but he did not deny God's justice and mercies.
And he declared that he is neither wicked nor hypocritical, but he did not deny that he is a sinner awaiting forgiveness.
Job's teaching about God was far better than that of his friends.

These friends, especially Zophar, misconstrued Job's words and gave them meanings other than what was in his mind, and they did not take his circumstances into account; and had they been put in his place, they might have sinned against God.

5 "But oh that God would speak, and open his lips with thee; 6 And that he would shew thee the secrets of wisdom! For it is double in understanding. Know therefore that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth.
"But oh that God would speak, and open his lips with thee" [5].

Zophar appeals to God Himself, saying that although He is silent and has not answered Job, it is only for a time; and if He were to speak and open His lips, Job would discover that he deserves far more than what has befallen him.
How hard it is for us to set ourselves as on the divine throne, and to claim that we know what is in His mind, and to judge others, ascribing the judgment to God.

Zophar's wish was fulfilled, and God spoke with Job; He opened His lips in his defense, requiring his friends to apologize to him and to ask for his prayers on their behalf so that he would forgive them.

Truly, there is a great difference between a man opening his mouth to judge and condemn his brethren under the cover of defending the truth and bearing witness for the holy God, and God opening His mouth and speaking with man. God speaks the truth, but it is a truth full of love and practical wisdom. Frankly He rebuked Simon Peter, and even called him "Satan" when he objected to the crucifixion and death of the Lord Christ, yet He was upholding him, and He praised him when he confessed that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.

The weak sinful man opens his mouth to cast his weakness and faults upon others, but God opens His mouth to give the sinner strength to confess, the possibility of repentance, and the power for continual sanctification and constant spiritual growth by the work of the Holy Spirit of God.

* The Truth says to Peter, who was still full of earthly notions, "thou savourest not the things that be of God, but the things that be of men" (Mk 8:33); and yet when he confessed well, it was said to him, "flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven" (Mt 16:17). Thus God opens His lips when He declares His will to men by an open visitation.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Since we cannot arrogate to ourselves the office of judge because of our sins, we ought to withdraw from performing this function; for how can we, being sinners, judge and condemn others?

Therefore no one ought to judge his brother. If your soul tells you to try others, know that the Law has not appointed you a judge and prosecutor, and so by usurping this office you fall under the penalty of the Law, because you violate its sanctity...
Therefore we must take care to examine ourselves before sitting on the judgment seat to pass sentence on others, especially if we are in the position of guide and teacher.
St. Cyril the Great * God will judge in His own proper time. For the judge is insulted when a servant presumes and pronounces a sentence before knowing the decision of the judge.
* Spread your cloak over the sinner and cover him, if you cannot bear and put his burdens upon yourself.
St. Isaac the Syrian "And that he would shew thee the secrets of wisdom!"
"For it is double in understanding. Know therefore that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth" [6].

Zophar sees that Job ought to have kept silent rather than accuse God of injustice for trying him while he is righteous. Zophar assured him that what had befallen him was a punishment lighter than his iniquity deserved. It was fitting therefore that he should expect more calamities.

Since Zophar felt his inability to convince Job, he desired that God would show Job the secrets of His divine wisdom and give him a double understanding, so that he might know that the chastening that had come upon him was less than it ought to be.

Pope Gregory (the Great) distinguishes between the knowledge of the great works of divine wisdom and the knowledge of the great hidden works of divine wisdom. It is easy for a man to enjoy knowing God's great wisdom through the nature He created for man, and His surpassing daily gifts. But the knowledge of His great hidden wisdom is hard to grasp, where God seems to have abandoned man and allows him affliction or trial. Man needs divine grace to perceive the hidden divine wisdom behind the suffering; and when man receives this knowledge it is counted a double knowledge, for he perceives God's wisdom when He gives and also when He takes away, when He grants man what he desires and also when He does not grant his request.
* [And he will declare to thee the secrets of wisdom, and that its law is double] (Job 11:6).

The works of the great wisdom are that when Almighty God governs those whom He created, He brings them to the end of the good things with which He began, and by His inspirations He helps those whom He enlightens with the light of His visitation; so it is clear to the eyes of all men that those whom He created in His utter generosity He supports with His compassions. And when He bestows spiritual gifts, He Himself leads them into perfection, those with whom He began in His "generosity" of compassions.

But the works of the great secret wisdom are when He (seems to) forsake those whom He created, when He does not complete the good works He began with us because of sin, when He enlightens us with the radiance of His shining grace, and yet allows the temptation of the flesh to strike us with a mist of blindness. When He does not care to preserve for us the good gifts He gave us, He lifts the longings of our souls toward Him, and yet presses upon us in a hidden way through the helplessness of our weak nature.

Paul was anxious to reach the secrets of this wisdom when he said, "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?" (Rom 11:33-34)... Since Paul was unable to reach the secrets of God, he returned to the knowledge of his weakness.

Zophar was learned through pursuing knowledge, but he was ignorant because of the insolence of his arrogant speech, not perceiving the truth about himself, looking upon his own weak condition as that of a virtuous person.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Zophar says that where God reveals His hidden wisdom to man, He grants him a double understanding. This is a truth enjoyed by the sincere and faithful believer. He does not cease asking God to grant him wisdom to perceive God's plan, and so he receives a double understanding.
What does he mean by double understanding?

First: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that perceiving God's hidden wisdom is not a purely theoretical, rational perception, but a knowledge of experience and life, where wisdom is bound to love. The wise man receives a double understanding, since he practices a double love, namely the love of God and the love of neighbor. He receives a double love toward God, without limit; and he receives a double love toward his brethren, so that with his whole being he longs to put his brethren before himself in everything, and desires to treat them as he wishes them to treat him.
The law of love is a double law, for we are bound to love either God or our neighbor.
As for our love for God, it ought to be a double love, for we love Him with all the heart, all the soul and all the might, so that we leave nothing for ourselves that we do not offer to God.

And as for our love for our neighbor, it is double: on the one hand we are required not to despise our neighbor through covetousness, or insult with the tongue, or contempt for the bodies of others through the selfishness of fleshly lusts; and on the other hand, to behave toward others as we would have others do to us.

* [And its law is double] (Job 11:6). By what is [the law of God] understood but love? In it we read inwardly how the commandments of life must be supported by outward works. The voice of the Truth says of this law, "This is my commandment, That ye love one another" (Jn 15:12). Paul says of it, "love is the fulfilling of the law" (Rom 13:10). And also, "Bear ye one another's burdens" (Gal 6:2). For by what can the law of Christ be understood more than by love, which we truly fulfill when we bear our brethren's burdens on the basis of love?

This same law is called "double," because love, full of surpassing and zealous care, extends to all works of virtue. It is laid down in only two commandments, yet it reaches to a number beyond counting. For the beginning of the law is the love of God and the love of our neighbor (Mt 22:39-40)...

But "the love of God" is divided into three parts. For we are commanded to love our Creator [with all our heart, all our soul and all our might]. In this we must note that the holy Word commands us to be bound to the love of God. It does not tell us only how, but teaches us how far, by adding "all." For whoever desires to please God perfectly must leave nothing in himself for himself.

And the love of our neighbor comes in two commandments. On the one hand it was said by a righteous man: [Do this, that thou have no man whom thou hatest] (Tob 4:16). On the other hand the Truth says, "Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them" (Mt 7:12). By these two commandments evil conduct is restrained and good conduct is laid upon us.

* Therefore the law of God is rightly called "double," for while it has love as its principle, as soon as it takes possession of the mind it kindles it in double ways with countless works... Paul declares the doubleness of this very law in a fitting way, enumerating the following: "Love suffereth long, and is kind; love envieth not; love vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil; rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth" (1 Cor 13:4-6).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Second: the double understanding means a continual increase without interruption. As long as we are in the body we shall not cease to seek growth in wisdom, knowledge and love. Indeed, some of the Fathers see that this growth does not stop even in eternal life. For the more the believer gazes upon God and receives a deeper union, the more he grows without ceasing in wisdom, knowledge and love. He will never cease to sing continually: [Behold, all things have become new] (Rev 21:5).

* Although everyone constantly seeks more knowledge, it remains incomplete in all things in relation to its true perfection, until the time comes when that which is perfect is come and that which is in part is done away.

St. Basil the Great * He encourages her and urges her not to sit idle there, but to come out to Him, and to try to see Him neither through the windows nor in a mirror, darkly, but to go to Him and see Him face to face (Song 2:9). For now, since she cannot see Him, He stands thus behind her and not before her; He stands behind her back, behind the wall (Song 2:9).

Origen: Zophar did not know his limits. If what he urges on Job is to seek a double knowledge, this is a holy request and good counsel; but by not keeping within bounds he declared in folly that what had befallen Job was less than he deserved, as though it were fitting for Job to expect more blows.

Here Pope Gregory (the Great) likens Zophar to a friend who accompanies his friend and goes with him into the forest to help him cut wood, and then, in his lack of wisdom, he swings the axe, the head of the axe flies off, and it smashes the head of his companion. Instead of helping him to cut the wood, in folly he cut off his head!

It is fitting for us, in wisdom, to understand the limits of rebuke and reproof, and the limits of discipline, so that we do not crush our brethren. As the Apostle Paul says concerning the discipline of the young man who wanted to cling to his father's wife and whom he ordered to be cut off, he returned to say, "So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Wherefore I beseech you that ye would confirm your love toward him" (2 Cor 2:7-8). For he had received enough, and the discipline had reached its goal, and the matter had become extremely serious; for if the penitent does not find the tender embrace of the Church, despair enslaves him and his soul perishes. As they were bound to discipline him by cutting him off, now they are bound to confirm love toward him and renew it, so that his soul may rejoice in salvation.

* "Know therefore that God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth" [6]... Here we should know that Zophar rebuked the righteous man with great iniquity, in that he accused him wrongly... But the word of insult that was offered can be removed if we consider the root from which it sprang. Therefore the Lord rightly commanded through Moses: "As when a man goeth into the wood with his neighbour to hew wood, and his hand fetcheth a stroke with the axe to cut down the tree, and the head slippeth from the helve, and lighteth upon his neighbour, that he die; he shall flee unto one of those cities, and live: Lest the avenger of the blood pursue the slayer, while his heart is hot, and overtake him, because the way is long, and slay him" (Deut 19:5-6). For we go with a friend into the wood when we go with a neighbor to see our iniquities, and we hew wood when we cut off the evil deeds from the wicked with a godly aim; but the axe flies from our hand when the correction is very hard, and it strikes his neighbor and he dies, so that he who gave the rebuke has killed his hearer with the spirit of love. For the mind of the person rebuked is at once driven to hatred if he is condemned without regard for limits.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Rebuke must be preceded by mercy, not by anger.
St. Augustine * It is not fitting for physicians to be angry with the sick, but they ought to oppose the diseases in order to heal the sick.

St. Basil the Great * Tend the flock not with weariness nor with scorn, as though you had authority over them, but as a good shepherd who gathers the lambs into his bosom, and strengthens those that are with young.
The Didascalia - Chapter 4

entries.section: 3. God's perfection cannot be searched out

paragraphs.text: 7 "Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection? 8 It is as high as heaven; what canst thou do? deeper than hell; what canst thou know? 9 The measure thereof is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea.
"Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?" [7]

Zophar portrays the greatness and glory of God just as he portrays the folly and ignorance of man; therefore it is necessary to submit to Him and seek His mercy and care. No man can discover His wisdom, so how can he fault it?

Who can reach the depths of God, and who knows His end? However much you long for Him, however much you cling to Him and come to know His person, your knowledge of Him remains utterly incomplete. Do not imagine that you succeed in searching out His essence and perceiving the perfection of His truth. We perceive the reality of His existence, but we do not reach an understanding of His mysteries. It is like the eye that sees the ocean, but does not reach its end.

St. Cyril of Jerusalem translated the word corresponding to "end" as "least": "Canst thou find out the traces of God, or come to the least of what the Almighty has made?" and he comments on this: [If the least of God's works is beyond comprehension, can the Creator of all these be comprehended?!]

* [Canst thou find a trace of the Lord? or canst thou reach the end of what the Almighty doeth?] That is, if, as you said before, you cannot find the trace of a ship (on the sea), nor of the flight of an eagle (in the air), who can find a trace of God's dispensations, or who can understand the hints of His divine providence which He accomplishes in succession?
* It is good to say this about God, but Zophar did not say it with a pure intention; rather, while glorifying God, he pronounces evil against the righteous man.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * No one has yet discovered, or will discover, what God is in His nature and essence. The discovery takes place in the future. Let those who have thoughts about this search and think about what will come to pass in the future.

My mind, which is in the likeness of God, tells me that when that godlike and divine (I mean the mind and the intellect) is mingled with what is akin to it, when the image returns to its Archetype for which it longs, this seems to me to be the meaning of that great saying, that in the age to come we shall know even as also we are known.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus * Although everyone constantly seeks more knowledge, it remains incomplete in all things in relation to its true perfection, until the time comes when that which is perfect is come and that which is in part is done away.

St. Basil the Great Who can comprehend the depth of God's mysteries and His plan, or understand His works, or who can follow the trace of His steps? Thus man continues to enjoy ceaseless knowledge, and the further he advances, the more he perceives his inability to comprehend the depths of the mystery of God.

Through the Gospel thought, the Fathers give us the way into the mystery of the knowledge of God, namely love. The more our hearts are kindled with the practical love of Him, the more our inner sight is washed to recognize new depths. And the more we enter new depths in the knowledge of God, the more the flame of our love for Him increases, so that we despise temporal things and cling to the eternal.

* "Canst thou find the footsteps of God?" What does he call "the footsteps of God" but the compassions of His visitation? By this he stimulates us to advance toward the heavenly things when we respond to the breezes of His Spirit...
When the spiritual love of the Lord kindles the heart, He gives knowledge of a path to follow, as a kind of footsteps of God, like one who walks and leaves the prints of his feet upon the heart...
