The psalmist was well skilled in following the footsteps of our Creator when he said, [My soul followeth hard after thee] (Ps 63:8), and when he desired to obtain a heavenly vision, [My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God?] (Ps 42:2).

Almighty God is found in a clear sense when we trample underfoot the corruption of our death. Then He is seen by those who are lifted up to heaven in the radiance of His divine nature. In the present time, however, the grace of the Spirit poured out in our hearts lifts the soul from fleshly aims and raises it by despising temporal things, and the mind no longer looks downward at all that is desired from below, but is kindled with longing for the heavenly things.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* The tongue has no power to utter their manner (the divine mysteries); only the pure mind beholds them, and in them it delights and rejoices at seeing them, marvels and exults in their existence, is amazed and delighted at their being revealed to it; and it is amazed and caught up by them into their interior.
And in God it is swallowed up and taken captive by beholding His beauty, and is united with His glory and amazed.
No one who has entered into this looks with desire upon what is seen here.
No one who delights in these (mysteries) also tastes the sweetness of anything that is on earth.
No one who beholds their beauty looks upon the beauty of anything in our world as good.
No one who is made rich by their presence fails to despise the silver coin as dung.
No one who has become familiar with their presence and drunk with meditating on them fails to loathe in his eyes the gatherings of men and their companionship.
No one in whose soul and bones the love of Christ has been set free is also able to bear the filth of loathsome lust.
No one who has become a companion of the angels and familiar with their mysteries fails to reject the company of the world and its snares.
No one whose mind has been taken captive by the beauty of the Lord of all is also able to be taken captive by anything in this world with its desires.
No one who has bound his mind to God and to care for Him is also loosed from it by anything and bound to the worry of it.
The Spiritual Elder (John of Dalyatha)
"It is as high as heaven; what canst thou do?"

entries.section: 3. God's perfection cannot be searched out

paragraphs.text: "deeper than hell; what canst thou know?" [8]

entries.section: 3. God's perfection cannot be searched out

paragraphs.text: "The measure thereof is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea" [9].

If we cannot measure the height of the heavens, nor the depths of the abyss, nor the length of the earth, nor the breadth of the seas, how can we measure the Creator of them all? The psalmist says, "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it" (Ps 139:6), "thy judgments are a great deep" (Ps 36:6).

We lift up our eyes on high toward heaven, and we see God lofty, higher than it. Then our souls long to be freed from the bondage of the love of the world, by the work of the Holy Spirit of God, who flies with us as on the wings of a dove.
We look into the depths of the abyss, and we see the Lord in His love breaking down its bars and carrying us off into the divine embrace.
We roam over the wide earth, and we find it very narrow before the breadth of God's heart toward us, in which He embraces all humanity from Adam to the end of the ages, with a love that has no limit.
We look at the oceans and we count them as nothing before the surpassing deep of God's love.

* [He is higher than heaven, what canst thou do? deeper than hell, what canst thou know? longer than the earth, and broader than the sea] [8-9]. This must be understood in a spiritual sense. If anything pertaining to Him is understood in a bodily way, it is an evil thing. Now He is higher than heaven, since He rises above all things by the impossibility of comprehending His spiritual nature. He is deeper than the abyss, for in His loftiness He helps us who are below. He is longer than the earth in that He surpasses the measure of creation by the infinite continuance of His eternity. He is broader than the sea, being the ruler of the waves of temporal affairs, holding them back and bringing them to pass by His power.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* All these particulars point to man alone, who becomes "heaven" when he desires to attach himself to the heavenly things.
And he himself becomes an abyss when he lies prostrate, bound to the things below, entangled in temptations.
And he becomes "earth" when he multiplies good works through the fruitfulness of a steadfast hope.
And he becomes a sea when he is troubled with anxiety in some circumstances and is confused by the breath of his weakness.
God is higher than heaven in that we submit to the power of His authority, even when we rise above ourselves.
He is deeper than the abyss in that He judges the human mind itself, looking upon it in the midst of temptations.
He is longer than the earth by the fruits of our life which He gives us in the end. Our very hope in the present time grasps nothing.
He is broader than the sea, since the human mind, tossed about here and there, throws up many passions concerning the things to come.

The psalmist set his heart on high, and yet he felt that he had not yet reached God, so he says: [Wonderful exceedingly is thy knowledge of me; it is mighty, I cannot attain unto it] (Ps 139:6). Paul knew that which is deeper than the abyss when he examined his heart, but he feared God's judgment, which searches more thoroughly. He said: [For I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified: but he that judgeth me is the Lord] (see 1 Cor 4:4).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"If he cut off, and shut up, or gather together, then who can hinder him?" [10]

Zophar reached the very conclusion that Job had already reached concerning God's absolute wisdom: "Behold, he taketh away, who can hinder him? who will say unto him, What doest thou?" (Job 12:9) and "Thou knowest that I am not guilty; and there is none that can deliver out of thine hand" (Job 7:10).

If He "cut off" by death, or shut someone up in prison, or gathered him as in a net of snares, who can prevent Him? Who is able to stand before God's judgment or resist His work? Who has the authority to object to God's judgments?

* [If he overturn all things, who shall contradict him? or who can say unto him, Why doest thou this?] [10] The Lord "overturns" heaven when He destroys the height of man's contemplations by His terrible, hidden command. He lays waste the abyss when He allows a person's soul to be terrified under its trials and fall to the utmost extremes. And He casts down the earth when He removes the fruits of good works by pouring misfortunes upon them. And He overturns the sea when He refutes the wavering (waves) of our hesitating spirit by a sudden terror.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem Marcion, in the second century AD, and also his followers, stumbled at the expressions in the Old Testament concerning divine wrath. I have already devoted a special section to the concept of "the wrath of God" in the book Brotherly Love, chapter 8, on wrath. God does not strike anyone down and does not shut anyone up; what the Holy Bible says about God's wrath is by way of presenting some divine matters in human language that we can understand.
God does not have human passions, for He is "love"!

* When we read of the wrath and anger of the Lord, we should not understand the word according to the meaning of an ignoble human emotion, but in a sense befitting God, who is free from every passion or blemish. Hence we should perceive from this that He is the Judge and the Avenger of all the unjust things that are committed in this world.

And by the logic of these terms and their meaning we should fear Him as the One to be feared who recompenses us for our deeds, and fear to do anything against His will. For human nature is accustomed to fear those whom it knows to be angry, and is afraid of offending them, as is the case with certain judges who have reached the height of justice.

The avenging wrath is usually feared by those who are tormented by the accusation of their consciences; certainly not because this tendency exists in the minds of those who will keep fairness in their judgments. But while they are in the throes of this fear, the judge's inclinations toward them are marked by justice, impartiality, and respect for the law which he carries out. And this, however gently and kindly he conducts himself, is stigmatized with the harshest epithets of anger and fierce wrath by those who have been punished rightly and justly.
St. John Cassian

11 "For he knoweth vain men: he seeth wickedness also; will he not then consider it? 12 As for man, he is empty, void of understanding, and man is born like a wild ass's colt. 13 If thou prepare thine heart, and stretch out thine hands toward him; 14 If thou put away the iniquity that is in thine hand, and let not wickedness dwell in thy tabernacle, for he knoweth vain men: he seeth wickedness also; will he not then consider it? [11]

We know of Him the very least, but He perceives all our secrets, even those hidden from us. He knows men of wickedness even if we or they count themselves righteous, and He sees the iniquity we commit in secret. The wicked are exposed before Him, and evil cannot be hidden from Him. "Will he not then consider it?" That is, will He stand passive before the wicked and evil, even if He overlooks it for a time?

* [For he knoweth the vanity of men, and when he seeth iniquity, will he not then consider it?] [11]... Here the order is well observed, for he first describes vanity as being known, and after that iniquity as being considered. For every iniquity is vain, but not every vanity is iniquity. For we practice vain things as long as we do what is transitory. In this the thing passes away from the eyes of him who holds it, and it is said to be "vain." The psalmist says, "Surely every man walketh in a vain shew" (Ps 39:6).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"As for man, he is empty, void of understanding, and man is born like a wild ass's colt" [12].

Zophar says that man himself, after the fall, became empty and void of understanding, because he deprived himself of God's wisdom. He became "like the beasts that perish" (Ps 49:20). He became foolish like the wild ass (the wild ass's colt) that is accustomed to dwell in the wilderness. In his folly he thinks himself wise, and so he does not want to submit to God's judgments, but resists, thinking that he knows truth and justice.

What Zophar said is a truth into which man has fallen in general, but what mars his words is that he means Job and not his friends, counting him in the rank of the foolish and useless wild beasts. Yet when he speaks of himself, he counts himself wise, offering sincere and effective counsel!

* [Mortal, born of woman, like the wild ass's colt] [12]. By these words he points to Job, making him equal to the wild ass's colt. For he said: [For the arrows of the Lord are in my flesh... Doth the wild ass bray without cause, unless he is seeking food?] (Job 6:4-5). Craftily Zophar says: why does he speak of a mortal born of a woman, that is, of a man born of a man, since Job himself compares himself to the wild ass's colt? Therefore Zophar says: [In vain he hides in his reasonings] [12]. By these vain, useless words he brings Job down to triviality, for Zophar says that he must howl very much and not sigh much, avoiding being a man. He compares him to a colt that is starving.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * [The empty (vain) man swells up in pride] this is the end of vanity. Pride corrupts the heart with sin and makes it insolent in iniquity, so that, by ignoring its iniquity, the soul does not grieve over the loss of its innocence, and it is struck with blindness as a just recompense, and perhaps is also separated from humility. The heart often takes back for itself evil desires, casting off the yoke of the fear of the Lord, as though it were becoming free to commit evil. It struggles to bring evil into action, indulging itself.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

If man has descended to the folly of some animals, even of insects, through the pride of his heart and his exalting himself against God, the source of wisdom, then the Wisdom of God became man, in order to lift him up to heavenly wisdom, to enjoy Him and be united with Him. By the divine Incarnation, especially by the Ascension of the Lord Christ, we were lifted up in Him from the degradation of the animals to heavenly wisdom.

* Look at our nature, how it was brought low and then raised up. For it was not possible to descend further than man descended, nor possible to ascend higher than Christ ascended... Paul makes this clear when he says: "He that descended is the same also that ascended." And where did He descend? "Into the lower parts of the earth," and He ascended "far above all heavens" (Eph 4:9-10).
Understand from this who it is that ascended...!
I meditate on the unworthiness of our race until I perceive the honor we have received through the merciful compassions of the Lord, full of tenderness. For we were nothing but dust and ashes...

We have become more foolish than the irrational animals, for man is compared to the irrational animals, and has become like them (Ps 49:20). And when man becomes thus like them, he is worse than they. For they are so by the decree of their nature, but our lack of understanding, we who are a creation adorned with reason, is by our own will...

And so, when you hear of man that he has become like the irrational animals, do not think that he has become equal to them, but lower than they. Not in the sense that he descended to a level below them, but that we, being human beings, have come to this extreme degree of dullness...
This is what Isaiah teaches plainly, saying: "The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib: but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider" (Isa 1:3).
But let us not be troubled because of our former transgressions, for where sin abounded, grace did much more abound (Rom 5:20).
You have seen how we have become more foolish than the animals; do you wish to see how we have become more unreasoning than the birds?!
"The turtledove and the swallow that chirps observe the time of their coming; but my people know not the judgment of the LORD" (Jer 8:7).
See how we have become more foolish than the ass and the ox and the birds of the heaven, the turtledove and the swallow; do you also wish to see to what our folly has reached?!
He sends us to the ant to learn wisdom from it: "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise" (Prov 6:6).

We have become pupils of the ant, we who were created in the image and likeness of God. But our Creator was not the cause; we ourselves are the cause, since we did not wish to remain in His image and likeness.

And why do I speak of the ant only, when we have become more dull than stones? Shall I offer proof of this? "Hear ye, O mountains, the LORD'S controversy, and ye strong foundations of the earth: for the LORD hath a controversy with his people" (Mic 6:2).
He judges man, summoning the foundations of the earth... because men have become duller than the foundations of the earth.

To what extent of folly do they still wish to go?! For they have become more foolish than the ass, more insensible than the ox, more without understanding than the turtledove and the swallow, more without wisdom than the ant (a), duller than stones, and they even resemble the vipers (see Ps 58:4-5)...
And why do I speak any more of the irrational creation, when we have come to be called (in our evil) children of the devil, as He says, "Ye are of your father the devil" (Jn 8:44).
And yet, although we are dull of senses, ungrateful, foolish and harder than stones, and such has become our degradation and unworthiness... today our nature has been lifted above all creation!
St. John Chrysostom "If thou prepare thine heart, and stretch out thine hands toward him" [13].

If God's dimensions cannot be comprehended, so to speak, and He is the One who holds authority and knows all things, then on the other hand man cannot comprehend the perfection of God and the perfection of His knowledge, nor even the mysteries of human nature itself. Therefore it was fitting for man, instead of criticizing God's actions, to turn to Him in prayer and remove everything foreign to God, of iniquity and wickedness, and then God lifts up His face and grants him countless blessings.
"If thou put away the iniquity that is in thine hand, and let not wickedness dwell in thy tabernacle" [14].
Zophar asks, as his two companions did before him, that Job turn to God with his heart as well as in his practical conduct, bearing neither hypocrisy nor deceit, so that God may answer his prayer.
He gave sincere advice about repentance, but we do not know what Zophar's intention was: whether he was truly asking for Job's repentance, or wanted to confirm Job's wickedness and hypocrisy.

He asks him to prepare his heart with purity and to stretch out his hands with perseverance in prayer, like one who wants to hold on to God and not let Him go until He blesses him, as our father Jacob did.

Zophar demands that he cease from iniquity and drive wickedness out of his tent. A strange demand to a man who dwells on a dunghill, whom the worms clothe like a garment, and who is surrounded by sores from the soles of his feet to his head. What iniquity could he practice with hands that bleed without ceasing? And from what tent could he drive out wickedness when he lives on a dunghill?

* Every sin is committed either in thought alone or in thought and deed together. Therefore "the iniquity in thine hand" is iniquity in deed. But "wickedness in the tabernacle" is the injustice in the heart, for our heart is rightly called a tabernacle, in which we are buried within ourselves when our souls do not appear outwardly through deeds.

Zophar was the friend of a righteous man and knew what ought to be said, but since he himself bears a likeness to the heretics, in rebuking such a person he does not truly know how to present even what he knows. For he commands us first to remove the iniquity from the hand, and after that to remove the wickedness from the tabernacle. Yet whoever cuts off from himself all outward evil deeds must necessarily return to himself and examine himself wisely as to his heart, lest the sin which is no longer practiced in deed remain behind in thought. Therefore Solomon said well: "Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in the field; and afterwards build thine house" (Prov 24:27). For what does it mean to prepare the work so that the field is diligently made ready outside, except that we uproot the thorns of evil, so that we may work bearing the fruits of reward? And after the field has been plowed, what then is the return to building our house, except that we often learn from good works the complete purity of life that must be built up in our thoughts.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Repentance is given to mankind as grace upon grace. Repentance is a second birth from God, the pledge of which we receive in baptism, and we receive it as a gift through repentance.
Repentance is the door of mercy open to all who seek it. Through this door we enter into the divine mercy, and by keeping away from this door no one can find mercy.

Since "all have sinned," as the divine Scripture says, [they are justified freely by his grace] (Rom 23:3-24). Repentance is the second grace, born in the heart as the fruit of faith and the fear of God.
Fear is the fatherly rod that leads us even to the spiritual Eden, but as soon as we arrive there it leaves us and goes back.

Eden is found in divine love, in which is the paradise of all the beatitudes. This is the place where St. Paul received power beyond nature. When he tasted the tree of life he marveled, saying: [Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him] (1 Cor 9:2).

St. Isaac the Syrian * There is no sickness that can strike the soul but the word of the Lord offers it a remedy. And just as there are compound medicines which physicians mix and blend to treat bodily diseases, so there are compound medicines prepared by the Spirit of the Lord to treat and confront the passions of sin, so that whoever feels the sickness can find the remedy near him, and enjoy healing.
All diseases are healed by their opposites: diseases caused by cold are healed by hot, warming herbs, and diseases caused by heat are healed by moistening herbs...

Learn therefore from this, O wise one, you who want your soul's diseases healed, and do for your soul what the science of medicine does for the body. For the things on the outward level have been set before our eyes as an example for us to follow with regard to what touches the inward level, so that our souls are healed in the same way our bodies are healed.
Let us then prepare the opposing remedy to meet every passion:

against doubt: faith; against error: truth; against suspicion: certainty; against malice: simplicity; against lying: frankness; against deceit: sincerity; against agitation: clarity; against harshness: tenderness; against cruelty: compassion; against fleshly desire: spiritual desire; against pleasure: pain; against the joy of the world: the joy of Christ; against songs: spiritual hymns...
and against sorrow: joy; against admiring and boasting of ourselves: sincere hope in God; against fleshly desires: spiritual desires; against the fleshly gaze: the spiritual gaze...
and against looking at the things that are seen: thinking on what is unseen...
and against attachment to the fleshly family (for the monk): attachment to the heavenly family; and against living in an earthly dwelling: living and dwelling in the heavenly Jerusalem.
So all these diseases and their like are healed by their opposites.

Whoever longs for the heavenly life must give up earthly, material things, for the desire for one of them does not exist within us unless the other dies. The desire of the Spirit is not born in our thoughts except by the death of the desire of the flesh; by the death of the one the other lives.
When the body lives in us with all its desires and wishes, the soul is then dead with all its wishes.
St. Mar Philoxenus

entries.section: 6. There is no escape from divine wrath except by repentance and prayer

paragraphs.text: 15 "For then shalt thou lift up thy face without spot; yea, thou shalt be stedfast, and shalt not fear: 16 Because thou shalt forget thy misery, and remember it as waters that pass away: 17 And thy lot shall rise above the noonday; the darkness shall turn into morning. 18 And thou shalt be secure, because there is hope; yea, thou shalt dig about thee, and thou shalt lie down in safety. 19 Also thou shalt lie down, and none shall make thee afraid; yea, many shall make suit unto thy face. 20 But the eyes of the wicked shall fail, and their refuge shall perish, and their hope shall be the giving up of the soul."
"For then shalt thou lift up thy face without spot; yea, thou shalt be stedfast, and shalt not fear" [15].

Here Zophar appears to open the door of hope like his two companions, Eliphaz (Job 8:5 etc.) and Bildad (Job 5:8-7, 20-22), in contrast to Job, over whom, because of the severity of the trial, a pessimistic outlook often prevailed, that his former life would not return!

What Zophar said, though it did not suit Job in those circumstances, is nevertheless a true principle for every penitent who is sincere in his repentance. For he cannot lift up his face before the Holy One unless he has removed from himself blemish and shame by the purity of his heart and the holiness of his tabernacle; in this way he stands before God steadfast in his hope and his reliance on God, without fear in his love for God.

* If you offer your prayer with a pure heart [13], blameless as to any unseemly deed, then when you offer sighs over yourself before God you come into a meeting with Him. Instead of sorrow you will have joy, and instead of misfortunes you will receive blessings, and the features of your face will be radiant like pure water [15]... and you will no longer fear other afflictions, for God removes the afflictions from you. You will receive pardon for your troubles, and thanksgiving for the calm that settles over you, and you will not fear trials, but will be like one who has found rest in a safe harbor, not fearing the waves where the sea cannot cause harm.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * Now that we completely wipe away these two (the iniquity of the hand and the wickedness in the tabernacle), we lift up our faces without blemish to God. For the soul is the inner face of man, by which we know our Creator with love and by which we behold Him.
Now the lifting up of this very face is the lifting up of the soul to God by the practice of prayer.

But the stain that spoils the lifting up of the face is the intention of the deed... For it (the soul) is immediately shattered, and loses all confidence in hope. And when it is occupied with prayer it clings to the remembrance of the sin to which it submitted. It loses confidence in obtaining what it longs for, so it carries in the mind a constant refusal to practice what it hears from God. Therefore John says: "Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God. And whatsoever we ask, we receive of him" (1 Jn 3:21-22). And Solomon says: "He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination" (Prov 28:9). For our heart condemns us in offering our prayers when we remember that they stand against His commandments.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* No one is helped by God unless he does something himself. He will be helped if he prays.
* The whole effect of faith is this: it makes us ask and receive, seek and find, knock and have it opened to us. Whereas the man who argues shuts the door of God's mercy against himself.

* There is no means by which a people attains absolute perfection, or by which any man makes the least progress toward true righteousness and godliness, except by the help of our crucified Savior, Christ, and the gift of His Spirit. Whoever denies this cannot, I think, be counted a Christian at all.
St. Augustine "Because thou shalt forget thy misery."

entries.section: 6. There is no escape from divine wrath except by repentance and prayer

paragraphs.text: "and remember it as waters that pass away" [16].

When the sufferer enjoys God's consolations, he forgets his pains and hardship, as a mother forgets the pains of her labor because of her joy over the newborn child. And the sufferings become like a little water poured out of a vessel, leaving no trace of anything.
God alone is able to lift the sufferers above their pains, and carry them over them so that they become as nothing, and even turn into countless blessings.
"And thy lot shall rise above the noonday."

entries.section: 6. There is no escape from divine wrath except by repentance and prayer

paragraphs.text: "the darkness shall turn into morning" [17].

If Job felt that his light had gone out completely, and his life had become like pitch darkness, in Zophar's opinion God will shine His light upon him at his repentance to make of his life a light greater than the light of the sun at noonday, and turn the darkness of night into the joyful light of morning.

* [The rising of noonday at evening] is the renewal of virtue in the time of trial... It is written: [Whoso feareth the Lord, it shall go well with him at the last] (Sir 1:13)... The more outward crosses he faces, the more he shines inwardly with the light of his virtues, as Paul bears witness, saying: "though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day. For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory" (2 Cor 4:16-17).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* O invisible light!
O radiance which no other radiance beholds!
You are the light before which all created lights are hidden!
You are the radiance before which every outward radiance is extinguished!
You are the "light," the source of all lights, and the "radiance," the fountain of all radiance!
You are the light and the radiance, before whom all lights become darkness, and every brightness in relation to You is nothing but darkness!
You are the radiance by which darkness becomes light, and by which the dark gleams with brilliance!
You are the supreme light, no cloud veils You, no vapor hinders You; night is powerless to draw its darkness over You, no barrier obstructs You and no shadows drown You!

Finally, You are the light that continually illumines the inner creation; swallow me up in the abyss of Your majesty, that I may behold all Your depths, by the power of the radiance of Your very divinity, and the work of the radiance reflected upon me from You!
Never leave me, lest my ignorance increase and my evils multiply, for without You I become empty and wretched!
Without You no one has any goodness, for You alone are the truth and the true goodness!
This I confess; and this is what I know, O God my God, that wherever I am found without You I have nothing but misery, within as without, for every wealth that is not my God is to me utter poverty!
St. Augustine "And thou shalt be secure, because there is hope."

entries.section: 6. There is no escape from divine wrath except by repentance and prayer

paragraphs.text: "yea, thou shalt dig about thee, and thou shalt lie down in safety" [18].
God's consolations remove anxiety from the soul and give it reassurance and peace, as the doors of hope open before it instead of despair.
He digs (feels) around him as soldiers do, when they dig trenches and lie down in them in safety, for they rest under the shadow of God's wings, and in Him they enjoy all their needs.

* Hope lifts itself with greater steadfastness in God for the hard things that a man suffers for God's sake. The joy of the reward in eternity cannot be gathered unless it is first sown here in godly sorrow. The psalmist says: "He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him" (Ps 126:6). So Paul says: [If we be dead with him, we shall also live with him: if we suffer, we shall also reign with him] (2 Tim 2:11-12). Likewise he warns his disciples, saying: "we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God" (Acts 14:22).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* To hope in God from God, this is to love God, the Giver of grace.
* How wretched I am!
My God... when will this corrupt nature leave me, and Your perfect power work in me?!
My God... sweet is solitude and stillness and truth and purity, all these which are Yours! But I amuse myself with noise and tumult and vanity and vice!
Again, what more shall I say?! You are the true Good, merciful, holy, just... but I am wicked, self-loving, sinful, unjust...!
You are the light, but I am darkness!
You are life, but I am death!
You are the Physician, but I am sick!
You are joy, but I am sorrow!
You are the faithful Truth, but I am true vanity, like any man on the earth!
In what language do You wish me to speak to You, my Creator?! I beseech You to be pleased to listen to me. I am the work of Your hands, and my destruction is a fearful thing!
I am Your clay, and behold, I am dying! I am the work of Your hands, and behold, I am descending toward nothingness!

If I have existence, You are the One who gave me existence, "Thy hands have made me and fashioned me" (Ps 119:73). Your hands which were nailed to the Cross, let them give me peace; for would You despise the work of Your hands?!
Ah! I look upon Your deep wounds, for You have engraved my name on Your hands! Read my name and save me!
My soul that groans before You is the work of Your hands. Create of me a new creature; this is Your work. Therefore it does not cease to cry out to You, saying: "O Life, make me alive again!"
It is the clay of Your hands, it clings around You beseeching You to restore to it its first beauty!
Forgive me, my God, since You have allowed me to speak with You. For who is man that he should speak with the Lord his Creator?!
Yes. Forgive me! Forgive my boldness! Forgive Your servant who dared to lift his voice before his Master!

Necessity knows no law! Pain drives me to speak with You! The disaster that has befallen me makes me call the Physician because I am sick! I seek the light because I am blind! I search for life because I am dead! And who is this Physician and Light and Life but You?!
Jesus of Nazareth, have mercy on me!

entries.section: 6. There is no escape from divine wrath except by repentance and prayer

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine "Also thou shalt lie down, and none shall make thee afraid; yea, many shall make suit unto thy face" [19].
It is not fitting for a man to be troubled, but to lie down or sleep and rest without disturbance, for he is in the arms of God, surrounded by divine providence.

The person becomes not only secure, with no enemies to overcome him and no disasters to shake his being, but many make suit unto his face, for they find peace and consolation in merely looking upon his face. They see the image of the Savior, our Lord Jesus, imprinted on his face, bearing witness to His dwelling in his heart.
He who entreats the face of God bears the image of the face of God, and so many entreat him.

* Whoever seeks present glory undoubtedly fears contempt. Whoever is always gaping for gain certainly fears loss... But he who is rooted in longing for eternity alone is not exalted by wealth and is not shaken by misfortunes. Since he has nothing in this world that he desires, there is nothing he has to fear from the world.

Did not Paul lie down and rest his heart without fear when he said: "For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Rom 8:38-39).

The power of this love was praised by the voice of the holy Church when it was said in the Song of Songs: "for love is strong as death" (Song 8:6). Love is compared to the power of death, which, when the soul holds to it, makes it die completely to the delights of the world.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 6. There is no escape from divine wrath except by repentance and prayer

paragraphs.text: "But the eyes of the wicked shall fail, and their refuge shall perish (and their refuge shall perish), and their hope shall be the giving up of the soul" [20].

After presenting a magnificent picture of pure repentance and its joyful fruit, he warned against evil and its effects. For the eyes of the wicked fail. The eyes that do not look to God, the source of good, are corrupted.
"And their hope shall be the giving up of the soul" perishes and vanishes, for "When a wicked man dieth, his expectation shall perish" (Prov 11:7).

* By the eyes he means the intention set before us. The Truth bears witness in the Gospel, saying: "If therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light" (Mt 6:22). If the pure intention precedes our deed, then however the deed may appear among men, in the eyes of our inward Judge the deed is counted pure. So the eyes of the wicked are their intentions concerning the fleshly desires within them. These fail because they do not care for their eternal concerns, always looking only toward temporal gains...

[And their hope shall be defilement of the soul]. What is the sinner's hope here, in all his thoughts, but to rise above others in power, to have his storehouses surpass the storehouses of all men, to break his rivals in order to rule over them, to satisfy his lust, and to yield in everything to the satisfying of desire? It is well said that their hope is "defilement of the soul."
Now it might be said that Zophar is right in this, had not the blessed Job declared this more perfectly through his life.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Grant me the living divine truth!
* My soul praises You, for You created it in Your image.
In its depths it longs to know Your divine truth.
Like a bride awaiting the day of her eternal wedding, it wants to adorn itself with the mind of its Bridegroom, and to know His mysteries.
* I confess to You, O wondrous Truth!
A proud thought has often come over me.
I thought myself a defender of You, O Truth, and I took a sword with Peter and struck the opposing servant.
In my folly I cut off his spiritual ear, and made him lose the ability to hear Your word!
I counted myself a churchman, and in folly I defended her with a strange spirit unworthy of her child!
* Grant me the spirit of truth and knowledge, with the spirit of love and tenderness.
What truth can I defend without sincere love for all mankind?
You came, O Truth, to our wicked world.
In bitterness we offered You the Cross, though You are the Lover of all mankind.
In folly we defended the truth, and so we persecuted it.
Grant me to enjoy You and Your Holy Spirit.
For You are the Truth, and You are Love, and You are the Way.
Let Your Holy Spirit work in me, the Spirit who is able to convict of sin and to give divine consolations.
Grant me the ointment of tenderness and contrition in true humility, that by Your love and tenderness and knowledge I may draw many into the net of Your Church!
* Put Your holy words in my mouth, that my tongue may be sanctified and utter only the truth full of love.
Speak in me with my tongue, as with my silence.
Let me bear witness to the truth in my speeches as in my stillness!
* Open Your mouth and speak with me; Your words are light that uncover my darkness and scatter it; grant me enlightenment, so that You save me and glorify me.
Teach me how to speak with my brethren, my partners in weakness.
Instead of condemnation, let me have compassion on them, so that You may have compassion on me.
Let me be weak with their weaknesses, that my heart may be kindled with the fire of Your love.
Let me count myself bound as they are bound, and set us all free, O Giver of freedom!
* Shine upon me with the light of Your divine wisdom, that I may enjoy a double understanding.
Let me perceive Your love through the works of Your surpassing love.
And let me discover the secrets of Your care for me, even in the midst of my chastisements.
Let me praise You for the generosity of Your gifts; when You give and when You take away, I see You the wonderful God in His care.
* Grant me a double wisdom, that I may perceive Your plan, both the manifest and the hidden.
And with Your wisdom let me understand the fellowship in the character of Your love.
With the double wisdom let me bear a double love.
I love You and I love my brethren, who are the object of Your love.
* I love You with a double love, I love You with all my heart and soul and might!
I know no limits to my love for You!
And I love my brethren with a double love; I offer them the spirit of love with generous giving and longsuffering.
I do not know how to hate or envy or condemn.
I want to treat them as I wish them to treat me.
* Grant me, O Lord, a double wisdom, and a double understanding, and a double love.
With every morning I enjoy Your new mercies, and I increase in wisdom, understanding and love.
I will never be content with what You give me until I become an icon of You.
Your gifts kindle my longing for You, and stir up in me fellowship with You and imitation of You, O divine Wisdom and Love!
* Grant me, even in rebuking my beloved, to be compassionate!
So that my words may be anointed with the anointing of Your Holy Spirit, the Comforter.
* I stand before You, O Almighty, and my heart is kindled with longing for more of Your meeting, and my soul groans within me, wanting to know You more.
Tell me, if I do not know the secrets of Your visible creation, how dare I claim to know its invisible Creator?
If I cannot see the trace of the ship after it has passed, nor the trace of the eagle after it has flown, how can I follow Your trace to know Your plan?
* Grant me Your love, in which I may know You and Your plan.
Lift my heart by Your Spirit above every vain love, that it may soar always in Your heavens, and know You?
Let me know You, that my love for You may increase, and that I may despise all the more every earthly love.
* Tell me, where shall I look, O You whom the heavens and the earth cannot contain?
I look at heaven, and I long that Your Holy Spirit would fly with me and soar with me in Your heavens, lifting me from glory to glory, until I settle in Your embrace.
I contemplate the works of the abyss, and I find that I have no place in it.
You descended into it, and broke its bars, and carried me on Your arms, to bring me into the glories.
I look at the earth in all its breadth, and it is very narrow for me before the breadth of Your heart toward me and my brethren.
I tremble on the shore of the ocean, but its vastness is counted as nothing before the surpassing deep of Your love!
Truly, what is the height or depth or length or breadth of Your infinite love!
* We rejoice in Your absolute authority, O Love.
You are the One who has authority; none can resist, and none can stand before You to question You!
But Your authority is the authority of love and tender fatherhood, O Maker of good things.
You desire all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
Your authority is always for edification and glory, as long as we place our lives in Your hands and respond to the grace of Your surpassing goodness.
* I confess to You, O Lord, the degradation to which I have sunk.
I lost true understanding, and my heart suffered emptiness.
Who can fill it but You, O Wisdom of God.
Dwell in me, and carry me in You, that I may enjoy You and walk in the wondrous way of wisdom!
In You I ascend from the abyss of ignorance, and rise with You to the heavens of wisdom and knowledge.
By Your Spirit You continually remove the works of the old man, shatter my ignorance and folly, and renew in me the works of the new man.
So that I may truly become an icon of You, O All-wise!
* Grant me the life of true repentance; let me turn my back on ignorance and my face toward You, O divine Wisdom.
Let me declare my repentance by leaving all evil, and walking in the truth by the riches of Your grace.
Lift my heart to You, that I may receive more than I ask, and beyond what I need.

1 And Job answered and said, 2 "No doubt but ye are the people, and wisdom shall die with you. 3 But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you: yea, who knoweth not such things as these? 4 I am as one made a mockery to his neighbour. He called upon God, and he answered him: the just upright man is laughed to scorn. 5 For the one tried there is contempt in the thoughts of him that is at ease, prepared for them whose foot slippeth.
And Job answered and said [1]:
"No doubt but ye are the people, and wisdom shall die with you" [2].
Job rebukes his friends because they are not wise:

First: because wisdom has fled from their harshness. This rebuke is directed to everyone who is proud and despises his brother, especially in the time of his sufferings. Such a person does not know how to set limits to rebuke, just as he does not know how to choose the right time. "A wise man will hold his tongue till he see opportunity: but a babbler and a fool will regard no time" (Sir 20:7).

Second: because they imagine themselves a people who monopolize wisdom, and that their judgment is the best and highest, by which every person is measured and judged. Therefore the Holy Bible warns us against falling into this delusion, when we count ourselves wise in arrogance and pride. "Be not wise in thine own eyes: fear the LORD, and depart from evil" (Prov 3:7). "Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him" (Prov 26:12). "The rich man is wise in his own conceit; but the poor that hath understanding searcheth him out" (Prov 28:11). "Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches" (Jer 9:23).

* Be a fool in the world, as the Apostle directs you, and you will become wise. Do not be partial (to your own opinion) and do not pass judgment from yourself in what you ask about, but always show obedience with all simplicity and faith. Only take care that these matters be holy, profitable and wise, as they proclaim the law of God and disclose the opinion of your spiritual father in those matters.

St. John Cassian Third: because they thought that after their death wisdom would die, and all mankind without them would be counted ignorant. After their sun sets, the world falls into the darkness of ignorance.

It is folly to imagine that our death causes a great loss, and that we cannot be dispensed with, for God is able to raise up after us one more capable than we. The death of the wise and the righteous does not mean the death of wisdom and righteousness.

Fourth: immoderation in conduct under the cover of wisdom turns even what is good into destruction rather than edification. "Be not righteous over much; neither make thyself over wise: why shouldest thou destroy thyself?" (Eccl 7:16)

Fifth: Pope Gregory (the Great) and other Fathers see that Job's friends represent the heretics who rely on their human wisdom and their intellectual, material and social resources in arrogance and haughtiness, despising the spiritual mind of the Church.
"Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?" (1 Cor 1:20)
"Let no man deceive himself. If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise" (1 Cor 3:18).
"Who is a wise man and endued with knowledge among you? let him shew out of a good conversation his works with meekness of wisdom" (Jas 3:13).
* Job speaks in astonishment... as though he says: Is the honor of rational beings really bound up with you?
Do you know the wisdom of God concerning sinners and the righteous?
Is it fitting for men to know it?
Do you know that God tests the righteous (Sir 2:5), while confirming His longsuffering toward sinners? (Sir 2:11).

This is the reason that some are in prosperity and others in trial, for in the case of some, longsuffering leads them back to repentance (Ezek 33:11), while for others the struggle (with trial) supplies them with the crown (1 Cor 9:25). If you understood this you would no longer condemn the righteous man who is in trial, nor count the sinner who is in prosperity as if he were righteous. But let each one be judged according to his works. If you knew this, it would not be fitting for you to speak in this manner in the judgment to come...

Can the wisdom of this work die with men? Where is astrology? Where is the divination by watching the flight of birds? Where is sorcery? Where is soothsaying? In these you find the defiled wisdom, devised from the folly of deceit. Or does such wisdom remain alive here below?

The wisdom of God, on the contrary, accompanies him who seeks it, for it accords with training in the knowledge of God and His law. By this a man sees two things very clearly: the glory of God, and the power of the Law given to us.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * All the wicked, and all the heretics, are not afraid to teach in a harsh tone those who are better than they, since they see everyone as inferior to themselves. But the holy Church calls every one who is haughty in mind, and every self-assured person, to renew him with the spirit of sound-mindedness by being joined together in equality. Job, who is a member of this same holy Church, when he saw his friends in pride uttering grand words in teaching, answered them, saying: "No doubt but ye are the people, and wisdom shall die with you" [2]. For what does a man who thinks he surpasses all men in the power of reason do but boast that he is "the only man"? It often happens that the mind swells with pride in loftiness, despising all men and admiring itself. For man's flattering of himself springs from delusion, in folly, being deceived by himself, as one who alone has wisdom. He thinks about everything he says and prizes everything he utters, admiring himself and belittling the words of others. So whoever thinks that he alone is truly wise is confined within his own narrow self.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* It is clear that the false apostles had the gift of eloquence which Paul lacked. But it means nothing as long as the substance of the preaching stands, and they cast a shadow over the glory of the Cross, for this (eloquence) is nothing but an attractive appearance.
* Here Paul accuses the false teachers not only of boasting excessively, but also of claiming credit for the labors of others.

St. John Chrysostom * (Satan) invented heresies and schisms in order to destroy the faith, corrupt the truth, and shatter unity. And since he is unable to keep us in the dark paths of the new error, he draws us into a new maze of deception.
He hunts men away from the Church itself, and when they think they have drawn near to the light and fled from the night of the world, he plunges them into a new darkness of which they are unaware.

And although they do not hold to the Gospel and the order of Christ and His law, they claim that they are in the light through the deceptive flatteries of the enemy, he of whom the Apostle says that he transforms himself into an angel of light and adorns his servants as servants of righteousness.
They call night day, and death salvation, and despair hope, and treachery faithfulness, and antichrist Christ, and he undermines the truth by deceit by presenting the truth in a false guise.
This is what happens, my brethren, when we do not return to the fountain of truth, when we do not look to the Head and keep the teaching that comes from heaven.
St. Cyprian "But I have understanding as well as you."
"I am not inferior to you."
"yea, who knoweth not such things as these?" [3]

It was not by way of boasting that he said to them, "I have understanding as well as you," but he wanted them not to fall into arrogance, as though the knowledge of the divine mysteries concerning God's wisdom in His care for creation and in His dealing with the wicked and the righteous were confined to them and no one else. He is not less than they in knowledge, and perhaps many have the same knowledge.
His aim here is to suppress their pride, not to boast of his knowledge and be proud. It reads in the Septuagint: [But I have a heart as well as you].

* [But I have a heart as well as you] [3 LXX]. He says: [I know how to think exactly as you do, and moreover I have the heart of a man like you. But you have darkened your hearts, while I have made mine fruitful by the law of God. This is the reason that, though I have a heart like yours, I see what you cannot see. So I am not surprised if you mock me].

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * "But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you" [3]. Who is ignorant of how great the blessed Job was, and that his experience surpassed the knowledge of his friends? Now in order to correct their pride he affirms that he is not less than they, and lest he should sin and exceed the bounds of his humility, he reserved for himself that he is higher than they.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

How beautiful it is for a man to feel the fellowship of mankind in the enjoyment of reason and thought and also of emotions and heart, each as God has granted him, for the glory of God and the edification of man and of the community. But what distinguishes one from another is the sanctification of what he has received from the hands of God by the work of the Holy Spirit of God, and the kindling of these gifts with faithfulness and diligence according to God's will. This sanctification will not be accomplished by compulsion against our will, nor is it enjoyed by anyone but the humble.

* God gave the rational nature the grace of free will, and bestowed on man the ability to determine what he wills, so that goodness may dwell in our life, not by compulsion or involuntarily but as the result of free choice. Our enjoyment of free will leads us to discover clear truths. In the nature of things, if anyone misuses such free will, then according to the words of the Apostle such a person becomes an inventor of evil things (Rom 30:1). Everyone who is of God is counted a brother to us, but he who refuses to share in good works does so by his own full will.
St. Gregory of Nyssa * May the Lord God give us the grace of humility, which uproots man from many diseases and keeps him from many trials.
Abba Dorotheus of Gaza * Whoever knows the frailty of human nature gains experience of the power of God.
Abba Maximus the Confessor "I am as one made a mockery (a laughingstock) to his neighbour."
"He called upon God, and he answered him."
"the just upright man is laughed to scorn (a laughingstock)" [4].
Job discovered that they treated him with great disdain, belittling him and trampling on him as though he were the object of their mockery or amusement rather than supporting him in earnest.

Indeed they came to comfort him and counsel him, but their way of counseling turned into biting criticism, and they wronged him in his affliction. Job might have accepted this from enemies gloating over him, but to come from dear friends is hard to bear. "For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it: neither was it he that hated me that did magnify himself against me; then I would have hid myself from him: But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance" (Ps 55:12-13), and in this Job was a type of the Lord Christ, of whom it is said: "What are these wounds in thine hands? Then he shall answer, Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends" (Zech 13:6). What increased his wound was not only that they were his friends, but that they were elders, leaders of the people and religious men. He wished that they would pray for him before God and He would answer them, and that they would seek counsel from God and offer words of consolation from God instead of the exceedingly painful rebukes. This is the lot of the prophets and the apostles and all men of God and all the righteous, to be mocked even by those close to them.
* The more the saints acquire love for God, the more they endure everything for His sake.

St. Augustine * [Yes, the just and perfect man is delivered up to mockery] [4]. Not everyone mocks him, but sinners mock him (Wis 5:3); the sensible do not mock him, but the drunken, for it is the habit of the drunken to mock the sensible. This is true, for children often mock old men. So the sinner mocks the righteous (Jer 20:7-8), for they sow in tears and pains (Ps 126:5-6). The sinner does not think of the coming fruits, and that the righteous passes from tears to joy, and from pain to surpassing honor, and that the sorrows of the righteous last only for a time (2 Cor 4:17-18).

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * While the wicked rebuke the souls of the good, they show those whom they rebuke to be witnesses against them. While the groaning soul confines itself to prayer, it is united within to hear the Most High, and that by the very thing it suffers from the self-assurance of men... For the mockery of his fellow creatures makes him near to God (His friend), he whose innocence makes him a stranger to the evil of his fellow creatures...
It is the wisdom of the righteous that makes them seek nothing of outward show, but perceive the meanings in the words; they love the truth as it is, avoiding vain pride.
They do not practice good works in order to bear evil (pride), finding in it more delight than in practicing them.
They do not avenge the injury, counting every insult for the sake of the truth a gain!

But this simplicity of the righteous is laughed at (by the wicked) with contempt, and the wise of this world count the goodness of purity folly. For without doubt everything practiced in innocence they count as stupidity, and the practice of all the laws of truth appears to them as weakness in comparison with fleshly wisdom... But in the eyes of the hidden Judge such a one (marked by innocence) is radiant with virtues, full of splendor springing from the merits of his life. He fears to be honored, he does not shrink when he is despised, he trains his body in chastity, fruitful in love alone in the soul... He rejoices when he is reviled, has compassion from his heart on the afflicted, and rejoices at the success of the good as if it were his own. He considers carefully the provision of the holy Word in the heart, and when tested he is found inexperienced in giving a double answer. He is a lamp, because he shines within, and he is mocked because he does not shine outwardly. Within he gleams with the flame of love, and outwardly he shines without the splendor of (vain) glory. He shines and is despised, he who gleams with virtue and is counted contemptible.

Thus St. David was looked upon with contempt by his father when he refused to present him before the eyes of the prophet Samuel, when he presented his seven sons to receive the gift of anointing. And when the prophet asked him whether he had brought all his sons, he answered with contempt: "There remaineth yet the youngest, and, behold, he keepeth the sheep" (1 Sam 16:11). And when he brought him and he was chosen, he heard the words: "man looketh on the eyes, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1 Sam 16:7).

And also the skilled preacher lessened the glory of his apostleship in the eyes of men, saying: [nor did we use authority when we might have been burdensome as the apostles of Christ, but we made ourselves little children among you] (see 1 Thess 2:6-7).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"For the one tried there is contempt in the thoughts of him that is at ease, prepared for them whose foot slippeth" [5].
It appears in the English translation:
He that is ready to slip with his feet is as a lamp despised in the thought of him that is at ease.)Job 12:5 KJV)

As though he says that he whose foot slips falls into troubles even if he was formerly like a lamp. He is looked upon as a lamp that has gone out, and as a wick that we throw on the ground and trample with our feet.
This is what embitters Job's soul, that those in prosperity and fullness despise those who are tried and suffering and hungry.
* [At the appointed time he is ready to die by the blows of the stranger; he sees his house destroyed by the wicked] [5 LXX].
"At the appointed time," what kind of time? As God appoints the time, He who changes the hours and the times according to His will, moving each one here and there.
He is the One who knows the limits of men immersed in trial, and how far they can bear the trial.

He sets a time [to die by the blows of the enemies], that is, the righteous are ill-treated by the wicked. That is, He will declare by what dealings the wicked wrong the righteous, and how they pass their life in luxury. But as for the righteous, it is clear how they live in perseverance (Jas 5:11), and how they endure sorrows here on earth.

It is not at random that God allows the wicked to destroy the houses of the righteous, but He does not forsake the righteous, nor allow things beyond their ability... For they suffer no harm from this destruction, because the dwellings of the present life and the earthly tents are destroyed (2 Cor 5:1-2), even if they are not plundered.

This then is what we believe, that we experience something of destruction, but find in it our gain very clearly. For we receive the reward for perseverance and the recompense for our diligence, and in place of our earthly dwelling we inherit a heavenly dwelling where we live among the angels and archangels.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * The despised lamp, which is subject to mockery on earth, shines by the judgment of heaven. Therefore it is rightly added: [prepared at the appointed time]. Concerning this time the psalmist says: "For I appoint a time, I judge uprightly" (Ps 75:2). And the Truth declares in the Gospel: [for my time is not yet fulfilled] (Jn 7:6). And Peter says: "Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things" (Acts 3:21).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

St. Mar Aphrahat the Persian Sage tells us how one of the wise men stumbled at Christianity because of the severity of the persecution the Christians suffer, without God intervening to rescue them, and what the saint's answer to him was, as he presented living examples from the Old Testament showing that God allows affliction for His beloved ones in order that they may be glorified at the appointed time.

* It happened one day that a man called a wise man among the Jews asked me: Jesus, who is called your Teacher, wrote that if any one of you has faith like a grain of mustard seed, you say to this mountain, Remove, and it is removed from before you, and it is lifted up and falls into the sea, and it obeys you (a) (Mt 17:19; 21:22). And it is clear that there is not one wise man among all your people whose prayer is heard, so as to ask God to put an end to those who persecute you. So it is evident that this was written for you: [nothing shall be impossible unto you] (b).

* And when I saw him blaspheming and speaking against the Way, my mind was troubled, and I realized that he did not know the interpretation of the words he had quoted and said to me. Then on my part I asked him about sayings from the Law and the Prophets, and said to him: Do you trust that even when you are scattered God is with you...? For He said to Israel: [Even in the lands of your enemies I will not forget you, nor break my covenant with you] (see Lev 26:44).

I answered him: [Well, I hear this from you, that God is with you. But I also speak words against you], for the prophet says to Israel as from the mouth of God: [When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee. For I am the LORD thy God] (see Isa 43:2-3). Thus is there not one wise man among you, righteous and good, out of all the people, who may pass through the sea and live without drowning, and cross the river without being overwhelmed, and who is able to walk on fire and not be burned, and the flame not consume him? And if you offer me an explanation I do not accept it from you, just as you do not accept the interpretation of the words you asked me about.
* Jacob was persecuted, and Esau was the persecutor. Jacob received the blessings and the birthright, while Esau was deprived of both.
* Joseph was persecuted, and his brothers were the persecutors. Joseph was glorified, and his persecutors bowed down to him, and his dreams and visions were fulfilled.
Joseph the persecuted was a type of Jesus the persecuted.
Joseph's father clothed him with a coat of many colors, and Jesus' Father clothed Him with a body from the Virgin.
Joseph's father loved him more than his brothers, and Jesus is the dear beloved of His Father.
Joseph saw visions and dreamed dreams, and the visions and the prophets were fulfilled in Jesus.
Joseph was a shepherd with his brothers, and Jesus is the Chief Shepherd.

When his father sent him to visit his brothers, they saw Joseph coming and plotted to kill him, and when the Father sent Jesus to visit His brothers they said: [This is the heir; come, let us kill him] (Mt 21:38).
Joseph's brothers cast their brother into the pit, and Jesus was brought down by His brothers to dwell among the dead.
Joseph came up from the pit, and Jesus rose from among the dead.
* Moses was also persecuted as Jesus was persecuted.
When Moses was born they hid him from his persecutors lest they kill him, and when Jesus was born they fled with Him to Egypt so that Herod His persecutor might not kill Him.
In the days when Moses was born they were drowning the children in the river, and at the birth of Jesus the children of Bethlehem and its surroundings were killed.

To Moses God said: [for all the men are dead which sought thy life] (Ex 4:19). And to Joseph the angel said in Egypt: "Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel: for they are dead which sought the young child's life" (Mt 2:20).
Moses brought his people out of the service of Pharaoh, and Jesus delivered the peoples from the service of Satan.
Moses was brought up in Pharaoh's house, and Jesus was brought up in Egypt when Joseph fled with Him there.
* Joshua the son of Nun was persecuted as Jesus our Savior was persecuted.
Joshua the son of Nun was persecuted by the unclean peoples, and Jesus our Savior was persecuted by the ignorant people.
Joshua the son of Nun took the inheritance from his persecutors and gave it to his people, and Jesus our Savior took the inheritance from His persecutors and gave it to foreign peoples.

Joshua the son of Nun stopped the sun and the moon and took vengeance on the peoples who persecuted him, and Jesus our Savior made the sun set in the middle of the day, to put to shame the persecuting people who crucified Him.
Joshua the son of Nun distributed the inheritance to his people, and Jesus our Savior promised to give the peoples the land of life.

* These memoirs which I write to you, my beloved, concerning Jesus who was persecuted, and the righteous who were persecuted, are for the sake of those who are persecuted today for the sake of the persecuted Jesus, that they may find rest. For He wrote to us and comforted us Himself: "If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you. They persecute you because ye are not of the world, even as I am not of the world" (see Jn 19:15, 20; 14:17).
St. Mar Aphrahat the Persian Sage

entries.section: 2. The wicked do not necessarily perish in the world

paragraphs.text: 6 "The tabernacles of the spoilers are at rest, and they that provoke God are secure; they bring their god in their hand! 7 But ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee; and the fowls of the air, and they shall tell thee: 8 Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee: and the fishes of the sea shall declare unto thee. 9 Who knoweth not in all these that the hand of the LORD hath wrought this? 10 In whose hand is the soul of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind. 11 Doth not the ear try words? and the mouth taste his meat?
"The tabernacles of the spoilers (robbers) are at rest, and they that provoke God are secure; they bring their god in their hand!" [6]

We should not wonder if we see the wicked living in ease and abundance, their life appearing successful, lacking nothing, mocking the believers who are tried and suffer affliction. They are like the grass that mocks the trees in the winter season when the green leaves have fallen from them and they appear lifeless as though they would never bear fruit, fit only as fuel for the fire. But for everything there is a time appointed by God. Soon the grass dries up, and when the spring season comes we see that the grass has gone and perhaps another has taken its place, while the trees that seemed dry bear leaves and fruit and have a special beauty. So Job looked at his friends who had made him the object of their mockery, and sang that for everything with God there is a time.

Job objected to the principle which his friends held, that the wicked cannot prosper long in the world, but calamities will surely come upon them suddenly. And he determined that God has His wisdom in His dealing with men, and He may postpone the recompense or punishment to the other world. Therefore he says that the tents of robbers are sometimes prosperous; they practice blasphemy, violence and the persecution of others, and yet they are successful. Perhaps he refers here to the Sabeans and the Chaldeans who plundered his possessions and yet appear to be successful.

It is not strange that those who practice evil are like arrogant robbers who care nothing for their relationship with God. They plunder others by treachery and betrayal, and fear no harm that may come upon them.
* "Yet let not the wicked expect to go out unpunished" [6 LXX]. May no one err in estimating the longsuffering of God, or fail to take the coming judgment into account.
May no one believe that the just Judge leaves the deeds of the wicked without chastisement.

Let him learn a lesson from the judgments that came upon Pharaoh (Ex 14:4) and Nebuchadnezzar (Dan 4:31-33) and Jezebel (2 Kgs 9:7-10), and the Amalekites (Bar 3:27-28) and the sons of Korah (Num 16:31), and the company of Dathan (Num 26:9-10) and the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19:24-25), and all the rest of the nations. For looking at these wicked nations and how they despised God's longsuffering makes us pause and fear the punishment that may come upon the likes of them.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem St. Augustine often reassures us that although the wheat is found mixed with the chaff in this world without the chaff being burned, this will not harm the wheat nor deprive it of its crown, for the time will come to separate it from the chaff, when the chaff is burned in the fire.

* This chaff does not destroy those who are the wheat of the Lord, who are few if compared with the others, yet they are a great multitude. God's elect, who are gathered from the ends of the world, from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other (Mt 24:31), do not perish. The elect cry out saying: "Help, LORD; for the godly man ceaseth; for the faithful fail from among the children of men" (Ps 12:1). And the Lord says to them: [he that shall endure unto the end (where evil is bound), the same shall be saved] (Mt 24:13).]

St. Augustine It is not for us to judge and separate the wheat from the tares, and the vessels unto honor from those unto dishonor, but it is also fitting for us to be assured that the wheat is not neglected by God because of the tares, nor do the honored vessels lose their honor because of those unto dishonor, for the Apostle says: "The Lord knoweth them that are his."

* It is not for the sake of the chaff that the wheat perishes (Mt 3:12), nor because of the bad fish is anything from the net not taken into the vessels (Mt 13:47)... He has already predestinated us before we were born, promising us with certainty: "Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified" (Rom 8:30). As he also says: [even if the seed is hidden in the chaff, it is known to the owner of the field. Let no one fear, when he is a seed, even if he is in the midst of chaff, for the eyes of Him who sows us are not deceived.]

entries.section: 2. The wicked do not necessarily perish in the world

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine "But ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee; and the fowls of the air, and they shall tell thee" [7].
Job shows that what these three counted as wisdom to boast of is nothing but natural knowledge, by which all creation is taught, even the beasts and the birds of the air.

* He says: ask even those without speech (Job 12:7); they may lack language, but they point in a natural way, for they know their Creator, and confess that He is their Maker, and that He is the secret of their existence. Now ask the beasts: at whose command did Balaam's ass speak (Num 22:28)? So ask the birds of the heaven: why did the ravens feed Elijah (1 Kgs 17:4-6)?

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * If you are in the bounds of the night, contemplating the captivating beauty of the stars, you see the Artist who designed them and adorned the heaven with these roses. If you are in the early morning, you learn of the wonders of the day, and through the visible things you reach the invisible.

* Let the splendor of these visible things be a reason for us to understand the invisible, which is above all earthly beauty. And let the wonder of these limited sensible things lift us to perceive the loftiness of Him who is eternal, unlimited, whose might surpasses the grasp of our minds and understandings.

* Has the day passed? Give thanks to Him who gave us the sun for the service of our daily work, and gives us fire to light the night and serve our other needs in life. May the night also suggest to us what moves us to prayer.
When you look at the heaven and see the beauty of the stars, pray to the Lord of all visible things, the Creator of the world, who in wisdom made them all (Ps 104:24).

And when you see all nature sunk in sleep, again bow down to Him who even against our will frees us from the pressure of continual labor, and by a little interval of rest restores us again to the activity of our strength.

Do not allow the whole night to be for sleep; do not allow half of your life to pass fruitlessly in dull slumber and torpor. Rather divide the night between sleep and prayer. And let your very light sleep be exercises in godliness. For our dreams during sleep are often reflections of our thoughts in the day.

entries.section: 2. The wicked do not necessarily perish in the world

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great "Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee: and the fishes of the sea shall declare unto thee" [8].

All the dumb creatures bear witness that the big devours the small, like the fish, and the strong preys on the small, like the beasts of prey. Had sin not entered, none of this would have happened, but [the wolf also shall dwell with the lamb] (Isa 11:6).
* Who can know the manner of the eternal begetting? The Father who begot is not in a way that any man can understand, but He alone can understand.

For we know that we should not tell the manner in which He begot Him, but we insist that it is not in this manner; and not only are we ignorant of the birth of the Son from the Father, but we are ignorant of every created nature.

"Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee" (Job 12:8). Although you ask all the things that are on the earth, they are unable to tell you. For the earth cannot tell of the essence of Him who fashioned it as a potter and made it. And not only the earth but the sun also... and the heaven also does not declare it... nor the heaven of heavens.
St. Cyril of Jerusalem * [Ask the fishes of the sea] Who commanded the whale to swallow Jonah (Jon 1:17; 2:10)?

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * There are migratory fish, as though they migrate by collective decision, at a particular signal, to strange regions. When the time of their breeding comes, they depart, these from one gulf and those from another, driven by a general natural law, hastening to the Black Sea. You see these fish at their departure like a torrent pouring through the Bosphorus toward the Black Sea. Who moved them? And where is the king who presides over them? And the orders posted in the public squares, appointing the time of the journey? And where are the commanders? You see divine providence accomplishing everything and caring for the lowest of creatures. The fish do not resist the law of God, but we human beings transgress His teachings.
So do not despise the fish because they are mute and speechless, and fear lest you be less reasonable than they when you transgress the commands of your Creator.

Listen to the fish, which lack nothing but speech, and their conduct tells you: the preservation of the species drives them to undertake this long journey. They have no understanding, but a natural law deeply rooted in their instinct drives them to what they must do. They say: Come, let us go to the Black Sea... its water is sweeter than other waters, and the sun above it is less hot so that it does not absorb all its sweet water; therefore the fish go up the rivers and keep away from the seas, and prefer the Black Sea to receive and rear their young in it, and when each has accomplished his purpose there, all return the way they came. Why? As though by their conduct they said to us: [The Black Sea is shallow, exposed to violent storms, with few refuges, and often turned upside down by the raging winds and stirred up by heaps of sand. And besides it is cold in winter, because of the great rivers that flow into it], so the fish leave it after having benefited from it in summer, and hasten their return to the warmth of deep waters and the regions that have the warmth of the sun, and rest in a calm sea far from the fierce north wind.
I have seen this scene and marveled at the all-embracing wisdom of God.

If the speechless beasts submit to hidden instincts, and know how to provide for their livelihood, and if the fish know what they should choose and what they should avoid, what shall we say, we who have been honored with a rational nature, and cultured by the Law, and called by the divine promises, and have drunk in wisdom by the Holy Spirit? Do we order our affairs with less good sense than the fish?
Do they learn to provide for some things before they happen, while we, on the contrary, hardly care, and spend our life in bestial pleasures?

The fish crosses all the seas in search of some of its benefits, and what do you say, if you live in sluggishness and idleness? Let no one plead ignorance, for in us is a natural mind that shows us the fitness of good and makes us shrink from harmful acts.

entries.section: 2. The wicked do not necessarily perish in the world

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great "Who knoweth not in all these that the hand of the LORD hath wrought this?" [9]
Every rational being, or even irrational, can perceive that God is its Creator and that He is the One who sustains it.

entries.section: 2. The wicked do not necessarily perish in the world

paragraphs.text: "In whose hand is the soul of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind" [10].
* [Is not the life of every living thing in his hand?] Why do all the young ravens call upon Him (Ps 147:9)?
Why do the lions' whelps seek their food from God (Ps 104:21)?

If these creatures take their Creator into account, how much more is it fitting for us whom He brought into existence! We who are ignorant that "the breath of all mankind" is in God's hand, He who from the beginning breathed into us the breath of life (Gen 2:7) (c). David showed this in his prophetic songs: [Thou takest away their breath, and they return to their dust] (Ps 104:29).

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * "The hand" indicates "power"... He gives the soul the power to give life to the body, and on the other hand He quickens the soul to the extent that it attains the understanding of eternity.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* No being is to be credited with its own existence. You alone have not received your existence from another. All of us, that is, all creation, did not exist before we were created. The cause of our existence is the will of the Creator.
* The truth of our existence is not the fruit of the merit of our works, but is grace from our Creator.

* (Concerning the rational creation) Whatever goodness is found in it is not goodness by nature, but a good gift from its Creator... For the Creator gave it reason, and gave it freedom of movement by free will, so that the good in it might be counted as its own good, by its keeping free will.
