The rich are my children, and the poor are also my children. One womb (Baptism) brought them forth in great travail. All are the offspring of her who travailed with them. So if you heap insults on the poor man, I warn you, because the poor man in this case suffers no loss like yours. For he does not fall into error; the loss that befalls him is merely the loss of money, whereas you, as a rich man, suffer loss in your spirit.
St. John Chrysostom Shall not his excellency make you afraid? and his dread fall upon you? [11]

Job warns them about their improper conduct, for while they think they are defending God, they fall under His wrath, because they walk in evil, and the awe of His majesty and His dread fall upon them.

* Now the righteous perceive the awe of God before His wrath is stirred up against them. They fear Him while He is calm (toward them), lest they be compelled to feel Him when He moves in anger. On the other hand, the wicked are terrified of Him for the first time when they are struck with the rod, and terror raises them from the sleep of their torpor, as vengeance disturbs them. So it was said by the prophet: [Vexation alone will be the support for understanding what they hear] (cf. Isa 28:19). For when they begin to fall under the blows of vengeance because of their contempt for God's commandments and their neglect of them, they understand what they hear. The Psalmist says: "When he slew them, then they sought him" (Ps 78:34)...
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Your speeches are like ashes, and your strongholds are strongholds of clay! [12]

Job's friends boasted that they were defenders of God and His justice and His judgments, and behold all their talk is like ashes, trifling and worthless; the wind blows and the ashes vanish. Their thoughts fly away from their earthy bodies; they pass away, and their human wisdom passes with them. They do not heap up wisdom for time, but heaps of clay, from which the children of God want deliverance.

He likens their talk to dust, because it rests on earthly, transient thoughts, and does not depend on heavenly, eternal wisdom. They fortify themselves with human logic, which cannot protect them except for moments.

* [Their remembrance is like ashes] [12]. All who are shaped by the present condition have earthly thoughts, for in all they do they leave a temporary memorial of themselves in the world. Some strive in war, others by erecting towering buildings, and some by recording books that bear the experiences of this world. They toil and struggle and build in order to set up a memorial to their names. But since life runs swiftly toward its end, what can endure in it, when nature itself is swiftly falling away?

A breath of wind scatters the ashes, as it is written: "The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away" (Ps 1:4). Rightly the remembrance of the foolish is compared to ashes, since its place is to be scattered by a breath of wind. The more a man toils to gain glory for his name, the more he places his remembrance, which is like ashes, in the gusts of the winds of mortality that hasten to a moment. In contrast to this it is written of the righteous: "The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance" (Ps 112:6). For by the very circumstances in which he impresses his works on the eyes of God alone, his name remains fixed for his remembrance in the eternal world.

* [And your bodies to bodies of clay] [12]... Thus the neck is brought down to clay, when every proud man goes down to death, and the body that was lifted up in corruption is dissolved. Let us consider the corpses of the rich lying in their graves, what kind of death has come upon the lifeless body, what is the stench of its corruption!
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Hold your peace from me, that I may speak, and let come on me what may [13].

If Job was struck with trials of this magnitude, they are lighter than what befell him from the words of his friends. His trials will not condemn him but vindicate him, whereas their wicked words, their lying and their hatred are greater misfortunes than any disaster or calamity!

It is fitting for them to be silent, for they are lovers of profitless dispute. Let Job speak, and reveal to them what they are, even if he speaks while sitting on the dunghill, wearing a garment of the worms around him.

Job does not care what befalls him: "and let come on me what may," and however they interpret these calamities, and think the worst of him, all this will not stop the testimony of his conscience, which he gives with all uprightness and integrity.

* [Hold your peace from me a little, that I may speak what my mind dictates to me] [13]. It appears that they spoke with a fleshly understanding, those whom he requires to be silent, so that he may speak as his mind dictates to him. As though he says in plain words: I do not speak in a fleshly manner but spiritually, for I hear with spiritual understanding the things that I present through the service of the flesh.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* When you meet a man who loves disputes and begins to argue with you about what is self-evident and true, cut off the conversation and withdraw quickly, for his mind has turned to stone.
For as water spoils the finest wines, so foolish discussions spoil those who are virtuous in their conduct and in their characters.
St. Anthony the Great

14 "Wherefore do I take my flesh in my teeth, and put my life in mine hand? 15 Behold, he slayeth me; I have no hope: only I will justify my way before him. 16 This also shall be my salvation, that the ungodly shall not come before him. 17 Hear diligently my words, and my declaration in your ears. 18 Behold now, I have ordered my cause; I know that I shall be justified. 19 Who is he that will contend with me, that now I should hold my peace and give up the ghost?"
Wherefore do I take my flesh in my teeth, and put my life in mine hand? [14]

Perhaps Job wishes to bring out his desire to bear witness to the truth under all circumstances, not only when he was torn by his calamities, but even if he tore his body with his teeth, and put his life on his palm to hand it over to death; all this will not make him silent about revealing his innocence in the Lord, and about his friends' wrong interpretation of the events.

* It means: why should I condemn myself severely before men, or show what my heart inclines to, since there is no edification of my neighbor in this, whether by condemning my evils or by displaying my good?
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* He says: I am like those who find consolation in devouring themselves; like those who bite their bodies hard, experiencing a kind of relief of their pains; this is what happens with me when I express myself in this way.
St. John Chrysostom * This is the reason that he takes his flesh in his teeth, their vain, provoking words. He speaks in anger, and wants to calm himself.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the teeth here refer to the inner senses, which chew what occupies the mind and present it to the belly of memory. [Therefore it was rightly said: "Every man that eateth the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge" (Jer 31:30). What is the sour grape but sin? The sour grape is fruit before its time. So whoever desires to be satisfied with the pleasures of the present life is like one who hastens to eat fruit before its time. Therefore the teeth of him who eats the sour grape are set on edge, that is, while he feeds on the delight of the present life he has perceptions unable to eat, that is, unable to perceive spiritual things. For the same reason, since they delight in outward things they become dull of sense with regard to inward things, and while the soul feeds on sin it is unable to eat the bread of righteousness. And since the teeth are bound to the habit of sin, they will not be able to chew that goodness so as to listen within.]

As though Job, wishing to take outward things (his flesh) in spiritual meanings, chews them with the teeth of his spirit to enjoy the spiritual pleasures that his friends do not accept, because they seek the glory of the world and the pleasures of the flesh. They oppose him and seek his destruction, for the carnal cannot endure the spiritual.
Behold, he slayeth me;
I have no hope;
only I will justify my way before him [15].

Job resolved to hold fast to his way, and was never willing to give up the rest he had found in walking uprightly with God, however great his afflictions, even to death. So he says with Hezekiah: "Remember now, O LORD, how I have walked before thee in truth and with a perfect heart" (2 Kgs 20:3). Even if trials drive me to my death, I remain trusting in Him, or full of hope in Him, that I may be vindicated before Him. I am His friend and He is my friend; I will not give up clinging to Him, even if He appears as an enemy to me who delivers me to trials unto death.

* [Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him] [15]... A man is truly patient when calamities befall him... Here the righteous mind is distinguished from the wicked; for in the midst of affliction, the former knows that the glory of Almighty God is not shaken by worldly events, and so does not collapse with the collapse of outward glory, but rather affirms that it is stronger when it loses temporal goods.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* "For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ" (2 Cor 1:5)... He lifts up our souls by counting these sufferings as His own; what joy fills us to be partakers with Christ, for whose sake we suffer! By faith we perceive the new birth and the resurrection. Those who truly believe in the risen Jesus must offer themselves to sufferings. And those who share in His sufferings will also rise with Him. "That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death; if by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead" (Phil 3:10-11).

* The loving man who clings to God always is not harmed by waves, however many; on the contrary, he comes out of them with new strength. But the weak, slack man falls often, even when there is nothing to trouble him.

St. John Chrysostom * If as the sufferings of Christ abound, so also the consolation by Christ increases, let us welcome the encouraging sufferings of Christ. Let them overflow in us, if we truly seek the overflowing consolation with which all who mourn are comforted, even if it is not alike for everyone. For if the consolation were alike for everyone, it would not have been written that as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation by Christ abounds exceedingly. Those who share in the sufferings will also share in the consolation, according to their fellowship in the sufferings of Christ.
Origen He also shall be my salvation: for an hypocrite (a hypocrite) shall not come before him [16].

He does not mean here temporal salvation, for his hope of deliverance from his trials in this world and of returning to what he had been was almost nonexistent; rather he hopes for his eternal salvation, where he will meet with God and see Him face to face. As for the secret of his confidence in his eternal salvation, it is that he knows that his relationship with God has in it no hypocrisy or deviation, for God does not cling to hypocrites, and will not allow them to stand before Him enjoying His glory.
* [For a hypocrite shall not come before him] [16]... We must keep in mind that we come before the Lord in two ways.

We call ourselves to account for our sins here, and judge ourselves before Him and punish ourselves with weeping. For whenever we remember our awareness of the power of our Creator, we are like those who stand before Him. Thus Elijah, the man of God, rightly said: [As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand] (a).

The other way is that we come before God when we present ourselves before His judgment seat only at the last judgment. So the hypocrite, in the final reckoning, comes before the Judge; but since he shuts his eyes against looking at his sins here and lamenting them, he refuses to come before the Lord... And since his mind is corrupted by the words of praise directed to him, he does not call it to recognize sin, nor does he realize that he opposes the inward Judge, and does not fear His firmness... Thus his eyes are not directed to the firmness of God, since he is greedy to please the eyes of men.

* [But I reprove my ways before him, he shall be my salvation] [15]. The Apostle Paul says: "For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged" (1 Cor 11:31). The Lord is our salvation insofar as we reprove our sins in the fear of God.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* I will judge myself, so that He may not judge me, who afterward will judge the living and the dead (2 Macc 7:18-19).
St. Augustine * [Consider yourself, then] until you attain the vision of God.
St. Basil the Great * Let this be your first concern, that you do not deceive yourself.
St. Melito, Bishop of Sardis * Hypocrisy is hateful to God and abhorred by men; it brings no reward, and is of no use at all for the salvation of the soul, but rather destroys it.

If anyone escapes by hypocrisy lest his affair be discovered, it is only for a while, for it does not last long, but everything is revealed, and brings shame upon its owner. Thus he is like an ugly woman whose outward adornment, put on her by artificial means, is stripped from her.

Hypocrisy is therefore foreign to the saints, for it is impossible that anything of what we do or say should escape the eyes of the Godhead, since it was said: [For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known] (Lk 12:2). If all our words and deeds will be revealed on the Day of Judgment, then hypocrisy is wearisome and without profit. It is fitting for us to be approved as true worshipers who serve God with sincere and open countenances.
St. Cyril the Great Hear diligently my speech, and my declaration with your ears [17].
He calls them again to cease their accusations and to give ear, so that they may enjoy with him the meeting with God through sincerity, purity and love.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Job repeats the word "hear" because he wants them not to hear only with their outward ears, but also to listen with their inward ears, so that they may understand the depths of his words in a spiritual way.
Behold now, I have ordered my cause;
I know that I shall be justified [18].

He has no need of their testimony, for he has ordered his cause well before God, and has presented to Him the sincerity of his conscience and the purity of his heart, and so enjoys innocence through the grace of God.

* [Behold, I am very near my judgment, I know that I shall be found righteous]. This is the judgment of which it is said in another book: [He shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday] (b). But he did not say: [I am already so], but [I am very near]. For if the judgment he means was not so as he experienced it, it will be so on the last day, when all are judged, and those who pray sincerely are found righteous: [Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors] (Mt 6:12). For through this forgiveness they are found righteous, since the sins they committed here are blotted out by the works of love they practiced (by their forgiveness of others).
St. Augustine * [Behold, I am near my Judge]. It is fitting for the adversary to have his tongue silenced, and for the Judge to be the one who speaks...

* [I know that I shall appear righteous], for I have fulfilled all the Law, and carried out all the commandments. I did not care about my unknown sins, and those I committed willingly, for I have washed them with prayer and tears. [I know that I shall appear righteous]. Although the enemy wishes to hide my righteousness by stirring up my companions to accuse me, even in this I shall appear righteous, when the veil of this present life is opened, while the clouds of the state of this life are corrupt; but even now I appear righteous as long as my patience stands to the end, and I shall show courage in trials to the very end.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that what blessed Job said about himself carries humility, for God Himself testified of him that there is none like him on the earth, and there is a great difference between God's testimony to him and Job's saying about himself in his dispute with his friends, who had become his accusers that he was righteous. He refused to describe himself as greater than others, contenting himself with justifying himself against the accusations of his companions.
Who is he that will contend with me, that now I should hold my peace and give up the ghost? [19]
In assurance of God's wide mercies to sincere believers, he does not care about their contention, nor does he fear divine discipline, but in tranquility gives up his spirit and finds eternal rest.

Job presents to us a living picture of the Christian who enjoys a true vision of the work of the Cross in his life, how it freed him from the devil his adversary, and put him to shame, so that the enemy became under his feet. Thus he does not fear him nor tremble, but mocks him.
* Since he saw in his outward conduct no possibility for anyone to blame him, therefore in complete freedom he looks toward any accuser of his.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* The spirits fall into grief, and since they want our destruction, they are destroyed by us with the same destruction they desire for us. But their defeat does not mean that they leave us for good...

When their strength perishes and they fail in their struggle with us, we say: [Let them be ashamed and put to shame that seek after my soul to destroy it; let them be turned backward and put to shame that rejoice at my hurt] (Ps 40:14). And Jeremiah also says: "Let them be confounded that persecute me, but let not me be confounded: let them be dismayed, but let not me be dismayed: bring upon them the day of evil, and destroy them with double destruction" (Jer 17:18), since no one can doubt that when we have overcome them they perish with a double destruction.

Fr. Serenus * If you say that the opposing power is very strong, and that evil has complete dominion over man, then you ascribe injustice to God when He judges men for their submission to Satan, because Satan is very strong and subjects mankind with an irresistible force. In this way you make Satan greater and stronger than the soul, and then you tell me not to submit to Satan. This is like a fight between a young man and a small child, where the child, when defeated, is condemned for his defeat. This is a great injustice!

St. Macarius the Great * The thoughts of Satan are merely a mental image of something (or a deed) that is evil, and what enables it to take possession of us, or even simply to approach our mind, is the weakness of our faith. For after we have received the commandment, that we cast away from us all distractions and keep our hearts with all vigilance (Prov 4:23), and seek the Kingdom of God which is within us, when the mind has abandoned the heart and the aim we are pursuing, we have at once made room for Satan's imaginations, and the mind has become lax in accepting any evil counsel.

Even to this extent, Satan has no authority to move our thoughts; otherwise he would not have pity on us, but would plant in us all kinds of evil thoughts and allow us no good. Rather, his power is limited to merely offering false counsel at the beginning of every thought, to test to which side our heart inclines: does it incline to his counsel or to God's counsel? For they are opposites.
St. Mark the Ascetic * We go out from the house of our old father... since we were by nature children of wrath, even as others, fixing our eyes upon the things above.
St. Paphnutius

entries.section: 6. A cry to stop the discipline

paragraphs.text: 20 "Only do not two things unto me: then will I not hide myself from thee. 21 Withdraw thine hand far from me: and let not thy dread make me afraid. 22 Then call thou, and I will answer: or let me speak, and answer thou me."
Only do not two things unto me: then will I not hide myself from thee [20].
With all that has befallen Job, he does not want to hide from the face of God like his father Adam, but wants to appear in His presence.

Although Job confesses his sins in more than one place, he wants to be always with God. "Make me to know my transgression and my sin. Wherefore hidest thou thy face, and holdest me for thine enemy?" (Job 13:23-24).
Job desired two things by which he might stand in the presence of the Judge, not in fear of trial, but before a loving Creator of His believers.

entries.section: 6. A cry to stop the discipline

paragraphs.text: This is what drives him to long to stand before God, and not to wish to hide from His presence as our first parents did when they thought that the shade of the fig tree would hide them from their Creator. But what are these two things? He pointed to them in the following phrase [21].
* God Himself says through the prophet: "I am the God who is near, and not the God who is far off" (Jer 23:23) LXX.
Fr. Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus * Wherever you are, God comes to you if He finds chambers in your soul in which He can dwell.
St. Gregory of Nyssa * The Holy Trinity is near to all things, but not all things are near to Him.

The so-called Dionysius the Areopagite * Let the living God be present always in your mind. For your mind itself is in His likeness, also invisible and incomprehensible, and not represented in any form, and yet by its will the whole body is moved.
St. Melito, Bishop of Sardis Withdraw thine hand far from me: and let not thy dread make me afraid [21].

Perhaps by the two things he meant the following: 1. "Withdraw thine hand far from me": perhaps he asked Him not to remove the trial from him, but to lighten it. In lightening it he finds his opportunity for calm and freedom from distress, so that he may be free to speak with God. He does not ask for relief of his pains to boast before his friends that he is not wicked as they claimed, for what concerns him is to stand in the presence of God. 2. Job knows the awe of God; this awe is a source of joy and delight to the faithful believer, and not a source of terror!

* [I need two things, and then I will not hide myself from thy face] [20]. What are the two things that Job needs from God; these two which, he says, if he obtains them he will not hide himself from the face of the Judge?

[Hold back thine hand from me, and let not thy fear terrify me] [21]... Of this David said: [Remove thy strokes from me; I am wasted by the might of thine hand] (Ps 39:10)... You are incorruptible, but I am corruptible (Rom 1:23). You are the Lord, and I am a servant, like a wrestler in training, like an armed soldier. You speak, and I answer; not in boldness do I oppose, but out of desire to obtain wisdom, and to learn through speaking and listening.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in these two requests, that He hold back His hand and not let His fear terrify him, a prophecy of the longing for the age of grace, in which the blows of divine wrath for breaking the Law do not befall believers, and in which believers no longer worship God through fear as in the Old Testament, but through love. [Righteousness cannot be perfected by fear, and according to the voice of John: [Perfect love casteth out fear] (1 Jn 4:18). And Paul offers rest to the children of adoption, saying: "For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father" (Rom 8:15). Therefore, in the voice of humanity longing for the removal of the severity of the stroke of the Law, and with a fervent desire to advance from fear to love, he specifies in prayer two things that God should remove from him, saying: [Withdraw thine hand far from me, and let not thy dread make me afraid]. Remove me from the severity of the stroke, lift the weight of terror; and when the grace of love shines upon me, pour upon me the spirit of assurance. If I am not removed from the rod and from the terror, I know that I shall not be withdrawn from the firmness of Your examination. He who serves You not on the basis of love but on the basis of fear cannot be justified before You.]

entries.section: 6. A cry to stop the discipline

paragraphs.text: Then call thou, and I will answer: or let me speak, and answer thou me [22].

By these two things he is in the presence of God and enters into a delightful dialogue. God speaks and Job answers, and Job speaks and God answers. This is the mutual love between God and His believers. This is the wonderful boldness we have when we stand before the throne of divine grace.

* [Call me, and I will answer; or let me speak, and answer thou me]... God's call to us is His esteem of us in love and His choosing of us, and our answer is our submission in obedience to His love by good works... He who runs eagerly, longing for the eternal world, examines his works, sets himself to act with great precision, and examines himself thoroughly lest there be found in him anything by which he would oppose the face of his Creator.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 7. Why do You hide Your face from me?

paragraphs.text: 23 "How many are mine iniquities and sins? make me to know my transgression and my sin. 24 Wherefore hidest thou thy face, and holdest me for thine enemy? 25 Wilt thou frighten a driven leaf? and wilt thou pursue the dry stubble? 26 For thou writest bitter things against me, and makest me to possess the iniquities of my youth, 27 so that thou hast put my feet in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths; thou hast dug upon the roots of my feet. 28 And I am like a thing that is consumed by decay, like a garment that is moth eaten."
How many are mine iniquities and sins?
Make me to know my transgression and my sin [23].

Now, standing in the presence of the Lord, Job asks God about his iniquities and sins, that He may reveal them to him, so that he may confess them and ask pardon for them in a spirit of humility, not fearing exposure before himself.

Pope Gregory (the Great) says that there is a difference between crimes and iniquities. Crimes are far heavier than the measure of sin, whereas iniquity does not exceed the weight of sin. When an offering is commanded according to the Law, it is without doubt imposed for "sin" and at the same time for "iniquity" also. A crime is not accomplished except by deed, while iniquity is usually committed in thought alone.

entries.section: 7. Why do You hide Your face from me?

paragraphs.text: Wherefore hidest thou thy face, and holdest me for thine enemy? [24]

Job confesses that he is a sinner and iniquitous, but in a spirit of humility and repentance he asks his divine Savior not to hide His face from him, nor to count him an enemy; for with all his weaknesses and sins he will not cease to ask, that he may enjoy fellowship with God his Creator.

* [Why do You hide Your face, and count me Your enemy?] [24] Man enjoyed the light of inward contemplation in Paradise, but when he was pleased with himself he departed from himself. He lost the light of the Creator, and fled from His face to the trees of Paradise. After he had committed his sin, he feared to see Him whom he had formerly loved. But note that punishment was brought upon him after the sin, yet after the punishment he returned to love, for he found the results of his disobedience, and the Face which he feared while in sin, when he awoke to sound understanding, he began to seek anew through the punishment, in order to flee from the darkness of the state of blindness that had come upon him, and he drew back in terror from this solitude that kept him from seeing his Creator.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 7. Why do You hide Your face from me?

paragraphs.text: Wilt thou frighten a driven leaf? and wilt thou pursue the dry stubble! [25]

Job entreats God, making himself very small before God and before himself, so he counts himself like a dry leaf of a tree that flies in haste and falls to the ground, and dry stubble moved by the winds... He is trodden down by his corrupt nature, so is it fitting for God's dignity that he who is already trodden down should be trodden down? Or to crush a person who has no power to resist?
"Thou carriest them away as with a flood; they are as a sleep: in the morning they are like grass which passeth away" (Ps 90:5).
"When the wicked spring as the grass, and when all the workers of iniquity do flourish; it is that they shall be destroyed for ever" (Ps 92:7).
"My days are like a shadow that declineth; and I am withered like grass" (Ps 102:11).
"As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth" (Ps 103:15).
"Let them be as the grass upon the housetops, which withereth afore it groweth up" (Ps 129:6).

"Therefore their inhabitants were of small power, they were dismayed and confounded: they were as the grass of the field, and as the green herb, as the grass on the housetops, and as corn blasted before it be grown up" (Isa 37:27).

"For the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways" (Jas 1:11).
"For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away" (1 Pet 1:24).
* [Has Your authority been shown over a leaf of a tree driven here and there? And will You follow the track of dry stubble (the remains of the harvest)?] [25]
What is man but a leaf that fell from the tree in Paradise?
What is he with whom the wind of temptation plays, whom the storms of his passions lift up, but a leaf of a tree?

The mind of man is stirred by many storms when he suffers temptations. So he is often stirred by anger. And when anger passes, empty merriment follows. He is drawn off by the goad of lust, lifted up by pride, and sometimes plunged by increasing fear to what is under the dust. Thus when a man sees himself raised and carried by many such storms of temptation, he becomes like a leaf of a tree. Therefore it was well said by Isaiah the prophet: [We all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away] (cf. Isa 64:6).

* We see that what we say passes away, while what we write remains; therefore it is said of God not only that He speaks but that He writes bitter things, since His blows upon us remain for a long time. Once it was said to the man who sinned: [Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return] (c), and angels appeared many times and gave commandments to men. And Moses, the receiver of the Law, defined sins by firm means. And the Son of the Father, the Most High and Only-Begotten, came to save us. He swallowed up death by His death. He declared that He had shown eternal life for us in Himself. Yet this sentence that was passed in Paradise concerning the death of our body has remained unchanged from the beginning of the human race to the end of the world. For "What man is he that liveth, and shall not see death?" (Ps 89:48), and also: [Thou, even thou, art to be feared: and who may stand in thy sight when once thou art angry?] (Ps 76:7). For having been angry once when man sinned in Paradise, He established the sentence of death for our body.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* [Their years are as things of no value; in the morning they are like grass which passeth away] (Ps 90:5).. Such are these things which did not exist before their coming, and when they come to be here they soon pass away, for they come here only to pass... They come to fall into death, and dry up in a carcass, and wither in the dust. What is this but the body in which are the hateful fleshly lusts?

* Those who do not think uprightly in their hearts look upon the wicked when they are like green grass, that is, when they are prospering for a time. Why do they look upon them? "That they shall be destroyed for ever." They look to their temporary prosperity and imitate them, and wish to prosper with them for a time, and perish with them for ever.

* While you say that in this age everything passes away like a shadow, you do not pass away like a shadow. "My days pass away like a shadow, and I am withered like grass".. But the grass, when it is moistened with the Savior's blood, flourishes again. I have become dry like grass; for as a man I have suffered from Your just judgment, because "Thou shalt arise, and have mercy upon Zion: for the time to favour her, yea, the set time, is come" (Ps 102:13).

* "As for man, his days are as grass" (Ps 103:15). Let man realize what he is; let no man boast. "His days are as grass." Why should the grass boast, which flourishes now and in a short time withers? Why should the grass boast, which blooms only for a brief period, until the sun grows hot? It is therefore good for us that His mercy come upon us, and make gold of the grass! [As a flower of the field, so he flourisheth] (d). All the loftiness of the human race, honors and powers and wealth and pride and threats, is the flower of grass. That house flourishes, and this family is great, and that family grows; how many flourish, and how many years do they live! To you they are many years, but to God it is a short time; God's reckonings are not like yours. Compared with the length of life through long ages, the flower of any house is like the flower of grass. Hardly does the beauty of the year last throughout the whole year. Everything that flourishes, everything that is filled with the warmth of heat, everything that is beautiful will not last, indeed will not remain even a full year...! He has sent us His Word, His Word who abides for ever... Do not marvel that you will share His eternity, for He shared your grass. Will He who took from you what is lowly begrudge giving you what is exalted?

entries.section: 7. Why do You hide Your face from me?

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine For thou writest bitter things against me, and makest me to possess the iniquities of my youth [26].

entries.section: 7. Why do You hide Your face from me?

paragraphs.text: In his talks with his friends, when he compares himself with mankind, he affirms that he is righteous and not wicked as his friends claim. And when he speaks with the Holy One he confesses the iniquities of his youth, and asks Him to explain to him why He leaves him to be consumed as by decay, or like a garment that the moth eats [28]!

He says to God: If You record my sins and falls, they are bitter, and I will not justify myself from them; and if You record my iniquities, they are the iniquities of my youth. I know them well and do not deny them, but I remember Your love, O Forgiver of sins and iniquities.

The prophet David asks the Teacher not to remember his sins but to remember him as His beloved creature, who has his own particular value, not through any merit of his own, but for the sake of God's mercies and goodness, and for His holy name. He says: "Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions: according to thy mercy remember thou me for thy goodness' sake, O LORD" (Ps 25:7). The thief on the right asked the true Teacher to remember him when He came into His kingdom, and He did not remember his crimes nor his sins, but carried him to Paradise, justified in the merits of the precious Blood. So when we ask the Lord to remember us, He answers, saying: "I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins" (Isa 43:25). St. Paul commands his disciple Timothy: "Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart" (2 Tim 2:22).
* "Why hast thou written evil things against me, and chargest me with the sins of my youth?" (Job 13:26) LXX.
He truly and fittingly makes this period of life (youth) the cause of his complaint, because in general in this period a person is unsteady with regard to sin.

Truly childhood is marked by innocence, and old age by wisdom. And early manhood, which adjoins the stage of youth, is regarded as the stage of gaining a good reputation, and the person feels ashamed if he commits a sin. But the stage of youth alone bears the mark of weakness and feeble counsel, with zeal in sin, and contempt for those who offer them counsel, while they are prepared to be deceived by pleasures. For the same reason David wonderfully asked pardon from the Lord for all that he fell into in that period, when he said: [Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my ignorance] (Ps 25:7). For in that period the majority suffer from the inflammation of lusts and their burning with the heat of hot blood.

St. Ambrose * [Why do You write my evils against me? and charge me with the sins of my youth?] Concerning the writing, He said: "Cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life; thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field; in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return" (Gen 3:17-19). All mankind was condemned by all these, as though for a good reason these lines were written concerning the righteous and the wicked. In the same way God lays upon each one the sins of Adam's youth, for Adam was still young when he tasted the harmful food. This is the reason that not only he, but we also, his offspring, are prevented from gathering from the tree of life (Gen 3:22-24) which is in Paradise.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my ignorance] (Ps 25:7). My transgressions and my impudent boldness and my ignorance, do not keep them for vengeance, but forget them. "According to thy mercy remember thou me" (Ps 25:7). Truly remember me not according to the wrath that I deserve, but according to Your mercy that befits You... not according to my merits but according to Your goodness, O Lord.
St. Augustine so that thou hast put my feet in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths; thou hast dug upon the roots of my feet [27].

I have been disciplined because of my weaknesses and the iniquities of my youth; I have become like a prisoner whose feet are put in the stocks, unable to move. I will not flee from the blows of Your discipline.
You know all my paths, and You discipline me even for my hidden thoughts or my wayward glances. You record on the soles of my feet all that I have committed, and I do not deny what I have done.

* [Thou hast put my feet in the stocks], because our feet have been prevented from walking to enjoy the benefits of Paradise. For God [looks narrowly at our works]. Concerning the disobedience of the commandment that Adam committed, God condemned the whole human race which is his offspring. In any case, since He is a doer of good and a lover of man (Wis 7:23), He [looks narrowly at our works]. If they are evil, we ascribe them to ourselves, as being in the likeness of the old Adam, and we fall under the discipline that came upon him. But if they are good works, we shall be saved from the curse, and set free from the penalties (2 Cor 11:4), in the likeness of the new Adam, and through Him we receive the annulment of our great distress.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [Thou hast put my feet in the stocks]... This means: You have bound them. [You have dug upon the roots of my feet (my heels)] meaning that You attacked me wholly, and searched me to the depths; You struck my feet and my head, and left no part of me sound. Again, he speaks of the seriousness of his trial; he mocks the lowliness of nature.
St. John Chrysostom * God put man's foot in the stocks, in order to bind his evil entirely by a strong, firm judgment.

* [And thou lookest narrowly unto all my paths, thou settest a print upon the heels of my feet] [27]... The prints of the feet may be the many things that are done wrongly, for they perceive... Usually when we do wrong things and our brothers see them, we are a bad example to them, and our feet have turned aside from the way, and we leave all our crooked footprints to those who follow us, so that by our conduct we have led the consciences of others to stumbling.

But all these things Almighty God examines with precision, and weighs each of them in judgment. But when can man, bound as he is by the weakness of the flesh, have the power to stand against all these precisely and keep the straight line of the thought of the heart without moving? Therefore he says: [Who am I? As a rotten thing that consumeth, as a garment that is moth eaten] [28]... For man is like a rotten thing that perishes, for the corruption of his body scatters him. And because the temptation of uncleanness springs up in him from no other source than himself, like the moth, so temptation destroys the body, as the moth spoils the garment from what comes out of it; for man contains in himself the opportunity from which temptation comes forth, therefore the moth spoils the garment, while the moth comes forth from the garment itself.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
And I am like a thing that is consumed by decay, like a garment that is moth eaten [28].

Job confesses that he goes from corruption to corruption because of his sins, as though the worm had worn out his bones and the moth had eaten his garment (his body); his depths are corrupted by the worm of sin and his body worn out by the moth of iniquity... But there is One who rescues the soul from corruption, and gives the body eternal glory when the corruptible puts on incorruption, and the spiritual body takes the place of the earthly.
* If you wish, you can be a slave to the passions. And if you wish, you can be freed from them and not submit to their yoke, for God created you and gave you this authority.

He who overcomes the passions of the flesh is crowned with incorruption. For if there were no passions, there could be no virtues, and consequently God would not give crowns to those who deserve them.

* He who understands what the body is, that it is corruptible and short-lived, understands also that the soul is heavenly and immortal, that it is a breath from God, and is joined to the body until it advances and rises toward likeness to God.
St. Anthony the Great
I fall into Your hand, O my God,

entries.section: 1. The life of man on earth

paragraphs.text: 1 "Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble. 2 He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down: he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not. 3 And dost thou open thine eyes upon such an one, and bringest me into judgment with thee? 4 Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one. 5 Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass; man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble (wrath) [1].

Job agrees with Eliphaz that man is born for toil and hardship. The wise man says, "For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity" (Eccl 2:23). So when a person concentrates on what has befallen him, he looks at life with a bitter eye. But when he lifts his heart to God, he sees in life a divine gift, and he perceives God's plan behind the troubles that befall him, so that his soul rejoices in the spirit of hope.

Job looks at himself as at every man, and finds nothing to boast of, for he is born of a woman, that is, of weak human seed. Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the woman here signifies spiritual weakness, for the man who is born of a woman in weakness is filled with wrath. He is of few days; however long his life, the whole of it is reckoned as few days, and the sum of his whole life is that it is days filled with toil and pain, and rarely does a day pass without distress.
* Truly, the state of man is wretched! He is bound to give an account of his sin, and yet he has not been able to avoid sin.
He has been compelled to enter into judgment, to stand before the sight of Almighty God, declaring the reasons for his conduct... although no one can be clean from sin.
The guilt goes back to the very beginning of childhood, before man has the ability to perceive wrongdoing.
What a wretched state this is, that his life is short, temptation is sweet, trials are multiplied, and anger is a daily work. For even in the midst of a moment of joy there is a constant bitterness.

St. Ambrose St. Augustine comments on the phrase [full of wrath] (Job 1:14) by saying that the wrath of God is prompted only by His mercies and His love, which moved Him to the incarnation of the only-begotten Son in the fullness of time, in order to renew us and remove from us all the guilt of sins, whether the ancestral sin inherited through the generations or those we ourselves commit.

* The human race fell under a just judgment, and all men became children of wrath. Of this wrath it is written: [For all our days are passed away in thy wrath: we spend our years as a tale that is told] (Ps 90:9). And Job also says of this wrath: [Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of wrath] (Job 14:1). And of this wrath the Lord Jesus also says: "He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him" [(Jn 3:36) - the words of St. John the Baptist, not of the Lord Christ]... Every man is born with this wrath, therefore the Apostle says, "and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others" (Eph 2:3).

St. Augustine * Man is "born of a woman, of few days," because God commanded him to return to the dust (Gen 3:19). As for his being full of wrath, (Job is thinking) of the moment when man received the commandment to keep the commandment and disobeyed it (Gen 2:17; 3:6).

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Notice the precision of the expression: "treasurest up unto thyself wrath" (Rom 2:5), showing that judgment does not proceed from the Judge, but is the result of the sinner's own work, for he does not say "God treasures up for you," but "you treasure up for yourself"... He tries to draw you by every means, and if you remain in your stubbornness you treasure up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God. But do not let it come to your mind that His wrath is a violent passion; it is justice, it is a "revelation," where each man receives what he deserves.

St. John Chrysostom * When we read of the wrath and anger of the Lord, we must not understand the word according to the meaning of an ignoble human passion, but in a sense that befits God, who is free from every passion and blemish. Hence we must understand from this that He is the Judge and Avenger of all the unjust things that are committed in this world.

And by the logic of these terms and their meaning we ought to fear Him as the One who is to be feared as the Repayer for our deeds, and we ought to fear doing anything against His will. For human nature is accustomed to fear those whom it knows to be angry, and is terrified of offending them, as is the case with some judges who have reached the height of justice.

The avenging wrath is usually feared by those who are tormented by the accusation of their consciences, not, of course, because this inclination exists in the minds of those who will keep to equity in their judgments. But while they are in the throes of this fear, the judge's disposition toward them is marked by justice, impartiality and respect for the law he carries out. And this, however gently and kindly he acts, is branded with the harshest terms of anger and fierce wrath by those who have been punished rightly and justly.
St. John Cassian St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that Job here calls man "the mortal."

* [The mortal, born of a woman, is of few days, and full of wrath] [1]. The being whom the Holy Bible calls "man" in the history of creation... Job calls the very same being mortal, while some of the pagan writers call him a human being, and others "a speaking, articulate creature."

entries.section: 1. The life of man on earth

paragraphs.text: St. Gregory of Nyssa He cometh forth like a flower, and withereth: he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not [2].

Job likens the life of man to two symbols: 1. The flower of the field, or the grass, which appears for a little while and soon dries up because of the heat of the sun and falls (Isa 40:7; Jas 1:11; 1 Pet 1:24). 2. The shadow, as though it had no being, which soon vanishes. As Bildad said, "For our days upon earth are a shadow" (Job 8:9).

* He is [like a flower that blooms, then falls after it has been shaken]. Man blossomed in Paradise until he gave names to all the animals (Gen 2:20). But he fell after he was shaken, being drawn away by the deceit of the serpent (Gen 3:4-5; 2 Cor 11:3). After this [he fled like a shadow], for when he found himself naked he fled from God, and hid himself under a tree in Paradise when God called him: [Adam, where art thou?] (Gen 3:7-9). Our hope collapsed, and when man was driven out of Paradise he became corrupt, lost all his help, and perished utterly, so that with one blow he was condemned and driven out, with no hope for us of judgment in our favor.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Life in the flesh is a flower in the grass. It was well said by the Psalmist: "As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth" (Ps 103:15). Isaiah also says: [All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field] (Isa 40:6). For man is like a flower that disappears; suddenly he shows himself on an open day, and in a moment he is drawn away by death, where he disappears...

Since man is drawn away daily to death, moment by moment, it was rightly added: [He fleeth as a shadow, and shall not remain in one state]... Why is the life of man likened to a shadow and not to the sun, except because, according to the voice of the Truth: "Because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold" (Mt 24:12)?

It was well said: [He shall not continue in one state]. For he passes from early infancy to childhood, from childhood to youth, from youth to manhood, from manhood to old age, and from old age to death. So in the present life man is bound, by the very steps of his growth, to diminish. And he is always being destroyed by the very causes by which he thinks he acquires what belongs to his life. For we cannot have a lasting abode here; we came in order to pass through, and by the very means by which we live we pass daily out of this life.

The first man was not able to perceive this departure from life, before the disobedience, since time passed over him while he stood firm. But after the disobedience man set himself upon a kind of slope of his temporary state. For when he ate the forbidden fruit he immediately failed to remain.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that this subjection to external change is accompanied by an inner change as well, as man strives to practice better works. For the mind is always in a state of change, unless a person holds to self-control so as not to descend to a bad state.

[The mind that has abandoned the One who stands forever has lost its permanence and its continuing in one state. While it strives to practice better things it is bound to face what opposes the current, but if it slackens in its attempt to ascend, without effort it is carried backward to a state lower than the one it was in.
For ascent requires effort, and in descent there is rest from effort. Therefore the Lord warns us to enter by the strait gate, saying: "Strive to enter in at the strait gate" (Lk 13:24)...
If there is no striving from a burning heart, the waters of the world are not overcome, and the soul sinks to the lower places.]

entries.section: 1. The life of man on earth

paragraphs.text: And dost thou open thine eyes upon such an one, and bringest me into judgment with thee [3]?
Job stands amazed that God, who knows that the life of man is like a shadow that does not last but soon vanishes, nevertheless takes such great care to bring Job to judgment.

David the Psalmist cried out: [LORD, what is man, that thou takest knowledge of him! or the son of man, that thou makest account of him! Man is like to vanity: his days are as a shadow that passeth away] (Ps 144:3-4). Again he says: "What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?" (Ps 8:4).
In great humility Job sees that he is not worthy for God to scrutinize his faults or to judge him. "And enter not into judgment with thy servant" (Ps 143:2).
* Who can be justified in the eyes of God, if the child of one day cannot be cleansed from sin, and no one can boast of his righteousness and the purity of his heart?

St. Ambrose * [Hast thou not given him regard, and brought him to judgment before thee?] [3]. This does not concern Adam alone before his disobedience. For God cared for him so that he would not sin and be driven out of Paradise. Therefore He commanded him before he sinned: "Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat: but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die" (Gen 2:16-17).
As for us too, He has given us regard: He gave us the written Law, and added also the Prophets (Mt 11:13).

What more could He have said than this? Besides this He gave us the grace of the Gospel (Acts 20:24), through which He showed us how we can receive the original dignity, how we may avoid the threat of Gehenna (Lk 12:5), and also seek Paradise (Mk 13:33).
He asked man to enter into judgment, that he might receive the recompense according to his works (Mt 16:27).

Since we know all this, we must pass through our life in a sound way, for each one is punished and crowned according to his works. Those who imitate Adam fall under the penalty, since they did not profit from the lesson given for their discipline. But as for those who keep the commandments of the Law, He shows us how they become better by keeping the commandments (Mt 5:19). We shall be worthy to receive a double reward from the just Judge (Mt 5:12), since we are upheld by the grace given to us through the new Adam (Rom 15:15). For this is the way by which we may enjoy happiness in the Kingdom and in the glory of God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

entries.section: 1. The life of man on earth

paragraphs.text: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one [4].
In true humility Job looks at his life as grass that dries up or a shadow that dissolves, and at the same time he sees his life as unclean. Who can bring purity out of this uncleanness?

As David the Psalmist cried out: [Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me] (Ps 51:5). No one can purify or sanctify man except his Creator, for the work of purification is like a re-creation. "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me" (Ps 51:10).

Job sees that man bears the corruption of sin from his conception, as the Psalmist says: [In iniquities I was conceived, and in sin did my mother bear me]. It is as though Job were telling God that he is a sinner, because all humanity has been defiled since the fall of our first parents, so everyone needs Your sanctifying and cleansing of them; there is none who is justified before You.

* Although the servants and friends of God avoid the sins that lead to death, and practice many good works, we do not believe that they are without trivial sins, for God does not lie when He says: [No child whose life is one day upon the earth is without sin](b). Add to this the blessed John the Evangelist, who is doubtless no less than James in merit, and who declares: [If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us] (1 Jn 8:1). Moreover, we read in another place: "A just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Prov 16:24).
Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * [Who can make clean what has an unclean seed?] He alone who is pure in Himself can cleanse unclean things.

For the man who lives in a corrupt body has the uncleanness of temptation rooted in him, since he derives it from his birth. For his very conception is accomplished through an impure fleshly pleasure. The Psalmist says: [In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins did my mother bear me] (Ps 51:5)... Therefore man is tempted against his will. But whoever masters the passions of secret temptations and overcomes the defilement of thought must not ascribe this purity to himself, for no one can make what was conceived in uncleanness become pure except Him who alone is pure in Himself.

The meaning here is that the blessed Job was looking toward the incarnation of the Savior, and saw that He alone in the world was not conceived of unclean seed, and so He derived nothing from an unclean conception. For He did not come from the seed of a man and a woman, but from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. He alone is truly pure in His body, for He did not come into the world according to the pleasure of the flesh.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

*You quoted the following passage from the Book of Job: "In thy sight no one is clean, even if his life on the earth were one day" (Job 4:14-5) LXX. And you added: "for we are guilty after the likeness of Adam's disobedience," an opinion that your book declares in an honorable and clear way concerning the prophecy of Jonah, where it affirms that the little children of Nineveh were rightly bound to fast with the people merely because of their ancestral sins. Therefore it is not unfitting for me to put the question to you: where did the soul commit the iniquity from which, even at this age, it is bound to be freed by the sacrament of Christian grace?

* No man is without sin, whether his life is one day or he lives many years. For if the very stars are not pure in the eyes of God, how much more the worm and the corruption into which those who submitted to the sin of Adam's disobedience have fallen?

St. Augustine * [Who shall be cleansed from uncleanness? No one, even if his life on earth is one day] (Job 14:4). No one can boast and say, "I am clean," except Christ "who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth" (1 Pet 2:22).

,The child of one day, in whom there is no uncleanness, because he does not know how to discern the good from the evil (Isa 7:15-16), nevertheless bears the corruption of the old Adam (1 Cor 15:42) that lies upon us. But the grace of the new Adam, who put off the old Adam from us (Eph 4:22; Col 3:9), has also cleansed our corruption [by the washing of regeneration] (Titus 3:5).

entries.section: 1. The life of man on earth

paragraphs.text: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass [5].

Job looks at his life and finds that even his span of years is determined by God beforehand. God, who has authority and power, determines the age of man by the day and the month, so that he cannot go beyond what is determined for him. Moses the prophet says: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom" (Ps 90:12).
It is God who [killeth and maketh alive] (2 Kgs 5:7); nothing happens by chance, for the life of man is known to God, and his days are determined with Him.

* "Thou hast appointed his bounds (his time) that he cannot pass" (Job 14:5). For all men it has been determined by our Creator, not only by years and months, but also by days and hours. He has "appointed a time," and the time is fixed and can never be passed. Do you not know that many are saved from a deadly sickness, while others in good health are suddenly snatched from this passing life? Some fall from high places and come down safe and sound, while others, as they walk, are snatched away by death at a vain step. Again, some leave their ship (while it is sinking) and climb upon a bare plank, and arrive in health and safety, while others find death near the harbor, their ship sinking there where no one expects death to be their lot, yet it is fulfilled at the call of the Creator.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * I know that the human soul is spiritual and not bodily, endowed with reason and thought, and that it is not of the substance of God, but created from the life of God, which alone is blessed life; and it is immortal because its sensation must continue forever and form the source of its happiness or woe. Truly, it is not indebted for its being enclosed in the body to works it performed before the body, yet in man it is never without sin, even if its life is one day. Of all those who are born of the offspring of Adam, no man is born without sin. And it is necessary even for infants to be born anew in Christ by the grace of regeneration. I know all this concerning the soul.
* Among those born of the offspring of Adam there is no man who was born without sin, and it is necessary even for little infants to be born anew in Christ by the grace of regeneration.

St. Jerome * As for the swarm of sins of the soul and of free will, what sermon could proclaim them? He says: "From within... proceed evil thoughts" (Mk 7:21; Mt 15:19). And he adds a list of the thoughts that defile us.

If the snares of sins are spread around us on every side, through all the senses and the inner movements of the soul, who can boast that his heart is clean, as Wisdom says (Prov 20:9) LXX? Or as Job testifies to the same thing: "Who is clean from stain?" (Job 14:4) LXX?

The stain that attaches to the purity of the soul is sensual pleasure, which is mingled with human life in various ways through the soul and the body, through thoughts, senses, deliberate movements and bodily actions.
Then whose soul is clean of this stain?
How is there anyone not struck by vainglory and not trodden under the foot of pride?
Who has never been shaken by sinful hands, and whose foot has never run to evil?
Who has never been corrupted by the wandering of his eyes toward corruption, or of his ears that are not restrained?
Who has never been occupied in tasting with pleasure, and whose heart has never been moved by vain passions?

St. Gregory of Nyssa * [No one is without stain, even if his life is one day] (Job 14:4). David groans, saying: [In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins did my mother bear me] (Ps 51:5). The Apostle also declares: "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood" (Rom 3:23-25). Therefore forgiveness of sins is granted to those who believe, since the Lord Himself said: "For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins" (Mt 26:28).
St. Basil the Great Origen uses this phrase to affirm the necessity of baptizing infants, since no one is without defilement, even if his life is one day (*).

* Little children are baptized for the remission of sins (Acts 2:38). Whose sins? When did they commit sins? Or how can the washing of baptism be explained in the case of little children, except according to the interpretation we spoke of a little while ago? [No one is clean from defilement, even if his life upon the earth is one day] (Job 14:4-5). The defilement of birth is removed through the mystery of baptism. This is why even little children are baptized. For except a man be born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.

* Every man who enters this world is said to bear a certain corruption. The Holy Scripture also says this: [No one is clean from defilement (filth), even if his life is only one day] (Job 14:4-5). And this in truth takes place in the womb (Job 3:11) of his mother, when he has received a body from the origin of the parental seed, so that it is said of him that [he was corrupted in his father and mother] (see Lev 21:11). Do you not know that when a male child reaches forty days he is presented at the altar to be purified (Lev 12:2-4), as if he had been defiled in his conception by the parental seed or the womb of his mother? Therefore every man [is defiled in his father and mother] (Lev 21:12).

But Jesus alone, my Lord, came into the world pure in this birth of His and was not defiled in His mother, because He entered into an undefiled body. For He is the One who said long ago through Solomon: [Being good, I came into a body undefiled] (Wis 8:20).

Origen * No one is clean from sin, even if he lived one day. For the Apostles and the saints did not dare to say: We are holy. Nor did they dare to say, "I have pleased" but "I will please." The prophet promises concerning the future and confesses that he has not done so in the past: "I will please the Lord." Where did he please the Lord? "In the land of the living" (Ps 116:9). This land is the land of the dead; the other land is the land of the living.

* Hold the feet of the Savior. Wash them with your tears, and wipe them with your hair. When you do this you reach His head. When you go down into the spring of life with the Savior, then you learn to pour the ointment on the head of the Savior. If Christ is the head of every man (1 Cor 11:3), your head must be anointed, and after your baptism you are anointed.

St. Jerome * [In iniquities I was conceived] (Ps 51:5). Was David born of fornication, being born of Jesse (1 Sam 18:16), a righteous man, and his wife? What does he say about himself but those iniquities that came from Adam? Even the bond of death has been planted in the soul with iniquity itself?
For no man is born without punishment being brought with him; the deserving of punishment is brought with him.
A prophet says in another place: [No one is clean in thy sight, even if he were a child whose life is one day upon the earth] (Job 5:14) LXX.

St. Augustine *Those who want to offer an excuse for their sins claim that there is no one without sin. They resort to the testimony of the Book of Job where he says: "No one is clean from filth, even if his life upon the earth is one day. The number of his months can be counted" (Job 14:4-5) LXX.

They merely utter this phrase and are wholly ignorant of its meaning. We answer them briefly. For a man to be without sin has two meanings in the Holy Bible. One is that a man has never sinned, and the other is that he ceases to commit sin.

If they say that this phrase "without sin" means that there is no one who has never sinned, we agree with them, for there is no one without sin. We all sinned at some time, even if we became virtuous afterward.

But if they take the text to mean that they deny that a person after he sins can practice the virtues and no longer return to sin, then this opinion of theirs is wrong. For it can happen that a man who formerly sinned stops sinning and is said to be "without sin."

Our Lord Jesus Christ [presented to himself a glorious church, not having spot] (Eph 5:27), not because the members of the Church never had any stain, but because they were lately freed from stain. The Scripture adds: "or wrinkle," not because the members of the Church never at any time had the wrinkle of the old man (Eph 4:22; Col 3:9), but because they have ceased to be so.

Origen * This also can be taken concerning the spirit, for we sometimes try to advance in attaining gains in virtue and some of the gifts offered to us, but we are prevented from some of them... For there is no man who reaches the degree he desires, but Almighty God, who discerns what is within us, sets limits to the spiritual gains themselves. So in the matters over which a man tries to rule and is unable, he no longer boasts even of the things that are within his power.

This is the reason why the great preacher who was caught up to the third heaven and pierced the walls of Paradise (2 Cor 12), after receiving this revelation, was not given authority to rest and to be without temptation, but because Almighty God [appointed to man his bounds that he cannot pass], He raised him to perceive heavenly things, then brought him down again to submit to weaknesses. This happened so that he would not be proud of himself, but would keep to humility, and so keep within his limits, and after looking at the measure of his limits would seek to be in safety.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

The Septuagint reads: "No man is clean from stain (filth)." Origen comments on this by saying that the text does not say: "No man is clean from sin," but "from filth." [For every soul that has put on the human body has its filth, but Jesus accepted this willingly, taking the human body for our salvation (bearing in it our stains). [Listen to Zechariah the prophet; he says: [Now Joshua was clothed with filthy garments] (Zech 3:3). Zechariah says this in order to answer those who deny that our Lord took a true body, and claim that His body was of heavenly, spiritual matter.

Origen comments on this phrase by saying that none of the saints holds a celebration of his birthday. On the contrary, we find in the Old Testament that Pharaoh held a celebration of his birth, and at the feast he killed the chief baker and hanged him (Gen 40:20-22), and Herod made a feast on his birthday and beheaded St. John the Baptist.

6 Turn from him, that he may rest, till he shall accomplish, as an hireling, his day. 7 "For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease. 8 Though the root thereof wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof die in the ground; 9 Yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant. 10 But man dieth, and wasteth away: yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he? 11 As the waters fail from the sea, and the flood decayeth and drieth up: 12 So man lieth down, and riseth not: till the heavens be no more, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep. 13 "O that thou wouldest hide me in the grave, that thou wouldest keep me secret, until thy wrath be past, that thou wouldest appoint me a set time, and remember me! 14 If a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come. 15 Thou shalt call, and I will answer thee: thou wilt have a desire to the work of thine hands.
Turn from him, that he may rest, till he shall accomplish, as an hireling, his day [6].

Since the affliction has grown severe upon him, which Job considers to be by God's permission, he asks Him to lift His hand from him so that he may rest from the severity of what has befallen him. As the Psalmist says: "O spare me, that I may recover strength, before I go hence, and be no more" (Ps 39:13).

It is as though he says to God: even my best days are full of toil and misery, so allow me to breathe from the continual distress. The hireling looks with hope to the end of his day, to rest from his labor. Count my days as the days of a hireling! Let there be toil in them, but let there be intervals of rest between them.

* "Turn from him (for a while), that he may rest, till he shall accomplish, as an hireling, his day" [6]. By "turn from him" he means here: remove from him the violence of the blow. But who can rest if he is far from (God), since God alone is rest? And as far as man departs from Him, he departs from rest?

As far as the hireling is from the end of his work, so far is he from the reward of his wages. Therefore every saint who is in this life, while he sees that he is far from departing from the present life, grieves that he is far from the eternal blessing.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
For there is hope of a tree.
If it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch (its boughs) thereof will not cease [7].

Job looks at his life on earth, which is a single life that, once it passes, does not return, while the tree, if it is cut down and its root is left in the soil, puts forth small branches, as though it were newly planted. For the moisture of the earth and the rains of heaven act upon its trunk so that it breathes and lives anew, but man, once he is buried in the grave, does not rise in this world.

Job sees that life is better for trees than for man, for when a tree falls, a new tree can sprout from its trunk. When the prophet Isaiah prophesied about the restoration of the cities of Judah after their ruin, he offered the following comparison: "But as the terebinth and the oak, which even when cut down have a stock, whose stock shall be a holy seed" (Isa 6:13). For the house of Jesse - that is, Israel - is cut down, as a great oak (holm oak) is cut down. But God in His great mercy allows the stump of this oak to sprout again and bring forth a glorious new branch, the Messiah the Savior, who is from the tribe of Judah. "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots: and the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him..." (Isa 11:1-2).
Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us a prophetic interpretation, seeing in these words a prophecy of the death and resurrection of the Lord Christ.

* He was able to die by His sufferings, but by the glory of His resurrection He came again to the greenness of life. His branches that sprout are the believers in Him, who are multiplied by His resurrection and so grow and spread. His root appears as one that has grown old in the earth, since the preaching of Him to the unbelieving Jews was a disgraceful matter. [His stock died in the dust](c), where now are the hearts of His persecutors, held by the spirit of their unbelief, so that He became as one despised and rejected, because He was able to die in the body. But [through the scent of water it budded](d) by the power of God, and His body after His death rose from the dead. This is as it is written: "whom God hath raised from the dead" (Acts 3:15)... [and put forth leaves like a new plant], since the weakness of the Apostles, who feared at the time of His death, and became dry through their denial of Him, was revived anew in faith by the glory of His resurrection. In comparison with this tree, what is every man but dust?
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* If there is hope for the visible tree of new life even after it is cut down, as long as its root is firm, how much more for the tree endowed with reason? Just as there is an axe for this tree, there is also an axe for the tree that has reason (Lk 3:9).
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Though the root thereof wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof die in the ground [8].

* What is the root of the righteous man but the holy preaching, since it is his source, to which he holds fast? And what does he mean by the earth or the dust but the sinner? To whom it was said by the voice of the Creator: [Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return](e). So the root of the righteous man [waxes old in the earth, and his stock dies in the ground]... For according to the words of Wisdom: [In the sight of the unwise they seemed to die: and their departure is taken for misery] (Wis 3:2).

But he whose root waxes old in the earth and whose stock dies in the ground, buds through the scent of water, and that through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, after the pattern of his conduct, and he causes the plant of virtue to grow in the hearts of the elect. For water sometimes signifies the watering of the Holy Spirit, as it is written: "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink," [whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst] (see Jn 7:37; 4:14).

There followed: [and bring forth boughs like a new plant]. It puts forth leaves on the root of the cut tree, for the righteous man dies in the body, and by the example of his sufferings raises the hearts of many, and by his upright faith shows the greenness of truth. Therefore it was well said: [like a new plant]. All that the righteous man does here is a second planting, for it is clear that the first planting does not lie in the practice of goodness but in the foreknowledge of the Creator. While all that the elect do, as if seen for the first time, is settled within them, and afterward is carried out outwardly. It was well said: and bring forth boughs like a new (first) plant, meaning that the greenness appears in the practical carrying out of what was already in the foreknowledge of the Creator.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant [9].

If the waters give life to the root of the dead tree, so that it sprouts again and the tree's life returns, then the Holy Spirit gives the believer new life in the waters of baptism. He offers it resurrection, the resurrection of the soul from its death, so that the body also may enjoy the resurrection on the day of the Lord, and the soul may share with the body in eternal life.

In the waters of baptism the Holy Spirit brings us into burial with Christ and into resurrection with Him also, so that we come out of baptism members of the body of Christ who rose from the dead, who does not grow old or ancient but grows continually without ceasing, enjoying new life. In this our union with the Lord Christ is realized, so that we enjoy sonship to God, becoming through the only-begotten Son sons with Him by adoption, that is, not by nature, but through free grace. This is what the Apostle meant by his words: "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost" (Titus 3:5), "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you" (1 Pet 1:3-4). This is what the Lord Christ Himself meant in His conversation with Nicodemus: "Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God" (Jn 3:5). And Nicodemus, the teacher of Israel, could not understand, because he had not yet perceived that this Jesus who was speaking to him joins those who believe in Him to Himself in baptism by the Holy Spirit, so as to give them His risen life as the gift of the new spiritual birth.

* Was it possible for the rod of the godly Moses to be turned into a serpent, and impossible for the bodies of the godly to live and rise again? And was this done contrary to nature? And will they not return again according to nature?!

Likewise the rod of Aaron, though it was cut off, blossomed without scenting water (Job 14:9). Although it was under a roof, it blossomed with flowers as though it were in the fields. Although it was placed in dry places, in one night it bore flowers and the fruit of a plant watered for many years. Did Aaron's rod rise from the dead, and Aaron himself will not rise?!
Does God work miracles in wood to secure the priesthood for him, and will He not condescend to raise Aaron himself?

St. Cyril of Jerusalem * "Yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs" [9], that is, by the washing of the second birth (Titus 3:5), at the time of the resurrection of the dead.
