That is, as I withdraw and keep far from everything that is worshiped, whether on earth or in heaven, and as I am exalted above every creature, and withdraw from what my hands have made, so also you should reject everything that is not holy or consecrated to God...
And finally, this word, which is called hagios in Greek Αγίου, indicates something far removed from the earth.

* But if you wish to remember other saints, the words of the Holy Bible will answer you: "For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not" (Eccl 7:20). Christ alone has "two perfect hands," "who did no sin" (1 Pet 2:22), that is, His hands have works perfect and complete.
Origen We can say that Job did not commit a sin unto death, but as he himself confesses, he is not a man without sin, even if his life were but one day.
Be my surety with Yourself.

entries.section: 2. A cry for help from the Lord

paragraphs.text: "Who is he that will strike hands with me?" [3]

Although Job says that he did not commit a sin deserving all these blows, he confesses that he is indebted to God and needs a surety or guarantor able to take his place, to stop the seizure and to deposit the bond.

The Holy Bible has often referred to the role of the surety or guarantor: ["A good man will be surety for his neighbour: and he that is impudent will forsake him. Forget not the kindness of thy surety, for he hath given his life for thee"] (Sir 29:19-20).

Job found no man on earth, not even among his dearest friends, to testify to his innocence, and no one standing on his side as a surety or guarantor, but all turned into adversaries to him. Hence he found no one to turn to but God Himself, who knows the secrets of his heart, his intentions, and his hidden and open conduct.

In the name of all humanity he cries out to God, asking Him to be a surety for him. For there is none who can pay our debt and represent us before the divine Presence but the divine Word incarnate, and as St. Augustine repeats in his address to God, saying that there is no refuge to flee to from God except to take refuge in God Himself.

* He (the Lord Christ), who did not sin in thought or in deed, became in bitterness through His sufferings. He was freed by the Resurrection, and by His Ascension came to be beside the Father, where He ascended into heaven and sat at the right hand of God (to be surety for us).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Before the coming of our Lord and Savior, all the demons reigned over the minds and bodies of men and settled in their spirits. Then the grace of the Lord the Savior appeared, and His mercy on earth, teaching us how the soul of every man ought to regain its freedom and recover the image of God in which it was created...

Who is this, if not Jesus Christ, who by His stripes healed us who believe in Him, when He [spoiled principalities and powers] who were among us and "made a shew of them openly" upon the Cross? (Col 2:15).

* We fell under the authority of our enemies, that is, "the prince of this world" and his helpers from the powers of evil. Hence arose our need of redemption by Him who buys us so that we may return from the state of estrangement from Him, and so our Savior gave His blood as a ransom for us...

And since "the forgiveness of sins," which follows redemption, is impossible before man is set free, we must first be freed from the authority of him who took us captive and kept us under his control, freed beyond the reach of his hand, so that we may be able to obtain the forgiveness of our sins and healing from the wounds of sin, so that we may accomplish works of godliness and other virtues.

* "We have peace with God" (Rom 5:1), through our Lord Jesus Christ who reconciled us to God through the sacrifice of His blood... Christ came to destroy the enemies and to make peace, and to reconcile us to God, from whom the barrier of evil that we raised by our sins had separated us.
Origen "For thou hast hid their heart from understanding."

entries.section: 2. A cry for help from the Lord

paragraphs.text: "Therefore shalt thou not exalt them" (glorify them) [4].

As for his friends, because of their ill intent the Lord took away from them wisdom and discernment. The wisdom that was given them by God departed from them, for He took it back, because they did not deserve it. For where there is no compassion toward the suffering, God takes away understanding from their hearts, honor leaves them and shame clings to them, and they come to be in a state of collapse, not in growth and elevation. Consequently they have no ability to perceive God's mercy, nor the discernment to understand His dealings, especially when He permits affliction for His believers.

* It is beneficial for us that our enemies be limited in wisdom and stripped of it. For this reason Paul says: ["But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory: which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory"] (1 Cor 2:7-8).

["Therefore shalt thou not exalt them"]... Why? For what is to our benefit, so the knowledge of the truth is hidden from them (the demons); and since they desire evil, they wish to make us ignorant and to blaspheme the Creator.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem The text in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) reads, "Thou hast removed their hearts from discipline," and in the Septuagint translation: "Thou hast removed their heart from wisdom." So when God took away from Job's friends understanding or wisdom, He took away from them the knowledge of God's wisdom regarding discipline, for He disciplines with afflictions to build up and approve, and not to tear down and destroy!

Those who receive divine discipline with understanding and discernment have their hearts crushed with repentance, and enjoy glory. "For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons; for what son is he whom the father chasteneth not?" (Heb 12:6-7).
* Rejoice while you are under the stripes, for the inheritance is kept for you, because He does not cast off His people. He disciplines for a time, and does not condemn forever.

St. Augustine * ["Thou hast removed their hearts far from discipline"] [4]. For if they had recognized the aim of discipline, and had never despised the commandments of our Redeemer, the very condition of their mortal body (which is under discipline) would have stirred them toward the love of immortal life...

Now some bear stripes but do not shape their lives to be renewed by the fear of the Lord who scourges them. Therefore it was rightly said now: ["Thou hast removed their hearts far from discipline."] That is, although the body is under discipline, the heart is not under discipline as long as the person struck with the rod has not returned to humility of mind. He did not say this as if the Almighty, the merciful God, had removed man's heart far from discipline. Rather, after man's fall by his own will, God permits him to remain in his state of fall...

["Therefore they are not exalted"]; for if the heart is under discipline, it seeks the things above, and does not open its mouth to ask for temporal things... Whereas those who give themselves up to base pleasures long always for the goods of the earth. They will not lift up their hearts toward the delights of heaven; for if they lifted up their minds toward hope in the heavenly city, they would be glorified...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. A cry for help from the Lord

paragraphs.text: "He that delivers his friends to plunder, even the eyes of his children shall fail" [5].

The matter does not stop at depriving these deceivers of understanding or of the inward insight to know God's wisdom, but they also harm their offspring, since they see in their fathers that they dealt wrongly with their friends.

The text in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) reads: "The devil promises his friends plunder, and the eyes of his children fail." It is as though Job compares the children of God with the children of the devil. The former fall under discipline for their exaltation, their glory and their eternal inheritance, while to the latter the devil gives false promises of obtaining spoils, which are temporary, passing gifts, while they perish eternally.

Pope Gregory sees that before he spoke of the wicked in the plural, and now he speaks of their head, the devil, in the singular. As the head, he can at times direct the speech in the name of the wicked, and at times in the name of their father the devil. For what belongs to the head belongs to the whole body, and what belongs to the body is also attributed to the head. He also says that the devil, the chief of all the wicked, makes promises to his friends the demons and evil spirits, that he will give them spoil which is nothing but the sons of men who have become captives to him!

* "He (the devil) promises his friends spoil, and the eyes of his children fail." After the blessed Job uttered a statement concerning the company of the wicked, that is, concerning the body of the ancient enemy, he passes at once to a statement concerning their leader himself (the devil), the head of all the children of perdition. He passes from the plural to the singular, because Satan and all the wicked people are one body. It often happens that the body takes the name of the head, and the head is given the title of the body...
The head takes the title of the body, as was said of the fallen angel himself: "An enemy hath done this" (Mt 13:28).

The chief of all the wicked has some as companions, and some as sons. Who are his companions but the fallen angels who fell with him from the throne of the heavenly city? And who are the others who are his sons but the wicked men, who are born through his evil urging to practice evil? So also it was said by the voice of Truth to the unbelievers: "Ye are of your father the devil" (Jn 8:44).
This wicked one is the source of error; he promises spoil to his companions, as he promises the evil spirits the souls of wicked men, which they hold to the end.

"And the eyes of his children fail," for he sets earthly things as a goal before men to look to, and makes them love what they cannot keep for long. For the tendency of a love wrongly directed cannot endure when it is shown that both the lovers and the things loved quickly become nothing at all.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. A cry for help from the Lord

paragraphs.text: "He hath made me a byword of the peoples, and I have become one to be spit upon in the face" [6].

His friends, who used to desire to sit with him, and sought his favor and praised him, came to mock him in his affliction, and to count him an example and a lesson to every hypocrite and wicked man, that no one may imitate him.

Job became a living image of those who live in the Lord, whom the world mocks, and, if possible, spits in their face. He was also a type of the Lord Christ, whom the wicked mocked, so that He became a laughingstock, and they spat in His face.
"Our soul is exceedingly filled with the scorning of those that are at ease, and with the contempt of the proud" (Ps 123:4).
"I was a derision to all my people; and their song all the day" (Lam 3:14).
"I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting" (Isa 50:6).
"Then did they spit in his face, and buffeted him; and others smote him with the palms of their hands" (Mt 26:67).
"And they spit upon him, and took the reed, and smote him on the head" (Mt 27:30).
"And some began to spit on him, and to cover his face, and to buffet him, and to say unto him, Prophesy: and the servants did strike him with the palms of their hands" (Mk 14:65).
"And they smote him on the head with a reed, and did spit upon him, and bowing their knees worshipped him" (Mk 15:19).
"And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment" (Heb 11:36).

* "We are exceedingly filled with contempt" (Ps 123:3). All who wish to live godly in Christ must endure insult (2 Tim 3:12). It is fitting that they be despised by those who do not choose to live in godliness. They despise those who seek the happiness that cannot be seen with their eyes, and they say to them: "What do you believe, you madman? Has anyone returned from the lower world and given you a report of what happens there? Look, I see and enjoy what I love; you are despised, because you hope for what you do not see."

"Our soul is exceedingly filled with the scorning of those that are at ease (the rich), and with the contempt of the proud" (Ps 123:4). We ask: who are the rich? He explained this by saying "the proud." Scorning and contempt are one, as the rich and the proud are one. Why are the rich proud? Because they want to be happy here... Perhaps they mock when they are happy, boasting in the arrogance of their wealth. When they are puffed up with their condition, filled with conceit because of their vain honor, they mock us. It is as though one says: Look, it is better for me to enjoy the good things before me. Let those who promise what they cannot show keep away from me. What I see I hold; what I see I enjoy, that I may walk prosperously in this life, so that you may be in greater safety, because Christ is risen and you have learned that He will give you another life, so be assured that He will give it to you.

St. Augustine * The Lord of majesty humbled Himself and was rejected by all... He heard mockery on every side, from the Pharisees and from every human being. It is grievous to the heart to look at how they spat in His face, crowned Him with a crown of thorns, and struck His cheeks, as it is written: "I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting" (Isa 50:6). Now if God was willing to humble Himself, and to bear such sufferings, insults and shame, do not think about how far you humble yourself, you whose nature is of the mire, subject to death, and there is no comparison between you and your Lord in this matter. You are proud and puffed up. And God came and took your burden to give you His rest, and you do not wish to bear toils and sufferings; by your toils your wounds are healed.

entries.section: 2. A cry for help from the Lord

paragraphs.text: St. Macarius of Alexandria "Mine eye also is dim by reason of sorrow, and all my members are as a shadow" [7].

Job became a man of sorrows and tears, until his eyes grew dim. Grief so intensified in him that it wore away his flesh, and he became like a skeleton, or like a shadow, with nothing in him but skin and bones.

Job portrays to us his bitter condition: from the intensity of grief his eyes grew dim, or became darkened, unable to see the light of divine truth. Truth had almost disappeared. His friends had turned into enemies resisting him with all their might, supported in this by their resources. And what befell Job himself justifies their conduct, he who had almost become like a shadow without substance. Everything was taken from him, and without cause!

On the other hand, it portrays to us the condition of the believer or the Church, not only during the suffering of the bitter troubles from the wicked, but the intense grief that comes upon the believer or the Church as a whole for every soul that turns aside from the way of truth and strays from true knowledge. For this the Apostle Paul cries out, saying: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not?" (2 Cor 11:29).
These feelings are lived by men of God, whether in the Old or the New Testament, who, having experienced the sweetness of communion with God, cannot bear that anyone be deprived of it.

The psalmist says: ["Dejection has overcome me because of the sinners who forsake Your law"] (Ps 119:53). And Jeremiah the prophet says: "Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!" (Jer 9:1).

* ["My eye is dim with indignation, and all my members are as though they had become nothing"] [7]. The eye becomes dim with indignation when those very persons are granted the light of truth... and see themselves despised for a long time, and made light of by the wicked. They are bewildered in amazement at the shameful judgment, and fail to fathom the mystery of God: why are the wicked permitted to prevail over the innocence of the righteous? Who is not astonished when he sees Herodias, by her daughter's dance, receive from the hand of the drunken king the head of "the friend of the bridegroom," the prophet, and more than a prophet, presented before the faces of his guests on a platter (Mt 14:6-11; Lk 7:26)?
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* If the righteous see a person among the sons of the Law transgress it, they are grieved and saddened, because the pain of one member makes all the members suffer.

Anthimus, Bishop of Jerusalem * Among sinners there are those who sin without the Law (Rom 2:12), because they did not know the Law. And others sin in the Law, because by transgressing it they hold it in contempt. "Dejection has overcome me because of the sinners who have cast away Your law" (Ps 119:53). Truly, if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; and if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it (1 Cor 12:26). So it is fitting for us to suffer for our sinful brethren because they sin, and to take the same attitude as this saint (the psalmist).
St. Didymus the Blind * He who sheds hot tears over the faults of his neighbor is healed by his sorrow for his brother.
St. Basil the Great * Let us weep for them, not one day or two, but all the days of our life.

St. John Chrysostom * Ah, beloved ones! If we are to obtain consolation from sorrows, rest from toils, health from diseases, and immortality after death, it is not right for us to grieve over the sicknesses that befall mankind, nor to be anxious because of the trials that come upon us.

We must not fear if those who fight against Christ (the Arians) plot against the righteous; rather we please God the more because of these things, as we are made readier and trained in the life of virtue. For how shall we obtain patience unless there are troubles and sorrows?
And how can nobility be shown except by our enduring mockery and injustice?
And how can endurance be tested unless there is an attack from enemies (the Arians and others)?
And how can our longsuffering be proved if there are no slanders from those who are against Christ (the Arians)?!
And finally, how can man perceive virtue unless the evils of the wicked first appear?!

So our Lord went before us in this when He wished to show men how to endure... When He was struck, He bore it patiently, and when He was reviled, He reviled not again, and when He suffered, He threatened not, but gave His back to the smiters, and His cheeks to those who struck Him, and turned not His face from spitting (1 Pet 2:23; Isa 50:6).

And finally it was His will to be led to death so that we might see in Him the image of all virtues and of immortality, and so walk following in the steps of His footprints, and truly tread upon serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy (sin).

St. Athanasius the Apostolic * Let us think of the captivity of our brethren as our own captivity. The sorrow of those in danger is our own sorrow. You must be sure that there is one body. Not only love but also godliness urges and encourages us to save the members of our family.
St. Cyprian the Martyr * Paul does not mean that he pretends to be weak with them, but that he sympathizes with their weakness.

St. Augustine * What wondrous tenderness in the shepherd (Paul)! Others fall, and he says, affirming his grief over the stumbling of others, that it kindles the fire of his pains. May all those to whom the care of the rational flock is entrusted imitate him, and prove that they are no less than the shepherd who for many years tends an irrational flock. This does not happen even if some neglect occurs, but in our case, if one sheep is lost or falls prey, the loss is enormous, and the harm and the terror and the punishment are unspeakable. Above all this, if our Lord accepted the shedding of His blood for its sake, what excuse justifies him who allows himself to neglect one who has value in the Lord's sight, and does not exert every effort on his part to care for him?
St. Augustine

8 Upright men shall be astonied at this, and the innocent shall stir up himself against the hypocrite. 9 The righteous also shall hold on his way, and he that hath clean hands shall be stronger and stronger.
"Upright men shall be astonied at this, and the innocent shall stir up himself (rise) against the hypocrite" [8].

When the righteous hear what befell Job of successive afflictions, and of his friends' attitude toward him, they stand in amazement, wondering. They think that God has left the earth and abandoned His believers, so the innocent rises against the hypocrite, that is, he cannot bear this, and seeks out this providence of God which seems obscure. The innocent rises to stand against the ungodly, defending the truth or rejecting every false interpretation.

* ["The righteous are astonished at this, and the innocent is stirred up against the hypocrite"] [8]. The "innocent" in this place is understood as the righteous man who is not yet perfect, who is beginning in good ways. For although he does not think of harming others, he is not able to practice perfect things. When the hearts of the little ones see the wicked flourishing in the present life, they burn with the coals of envy... Now the innocent is inflamed against the hypocrite, since he is not accustomed to harm anyone but envies the glory of the hypocrite.

But if the innocent in this passage means one who is perfect in his goodness, ["the innocent is moved against the hypocrite"] when he sees him thriving and scorns him and his thriving. Then he preaches the true things, and says that he must be despised by others whenever they see in him a longing for things that he cannot keep for long.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity. For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb" (Ps 37:1-2). What seems to you a long time is "soon" in God's sight. When you submit yourself to God, the long time becomes "soon" for you also... You make things trifling and worthless, appearing only on the surface of the earth, with no roots in the depths. In winter they are green, but when the summer sun scorches them they wither. Now it is winter; your glory is not as it appears outwardly, but if your love has a deep root like many trees in the winter, the frost will go and summer will come (the day of judgment); then the greenness of the grass will wither and the glory of the trees will appear.

* I observed the wicked, and I saw them in peace, but what peace? A temporary peace, changing, passing and earthly, and yet I too ask this from God. I saw those who did not serve God receiving what I desired, I who serve God, but my feet were slipping and my steps had slid (Ps 73:2). Now I understood why they have peace and thriving on earth... because their punishment is not temporary, but fixed forever.
St. Augustine "The righteous also shall hold on his way, and he that hath clean hands shall be stronger and stronger" [9].

When the righteous man sees the wicked prospering while trials and afflictions come upon the righteous and the just, the righteous man does not withdraw from the way of fellowship with God, but grows more steadfast in his resolve and advances holding the more firmly to his way. He sees that the troubles that befall the righteous turn to their growth and their enjoyment of greater strength.

The spiritual man experiences the earnest of heavenly life, so he is not shaken before the temporary success of the wicked, nor troubled before trials and afflictions. He finds his happiness in perseverance in the Spirit of the Lord, who gives surpassing sweetness to fellowship with the Lord Christ in His cross, and always kindles the depths of the believer toward seeking heavenly things, despising every temporal gift.
The true believer does not cease to persevere against sin and in enjoying the holy life, because of his enjoyment of fellowship with the Lord.
* The hypocrite obtains the things of this world by an evil will. But the righteous man is bound and fettered more strongly by the love of heavenly things.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* If we keep the rule of perseverance and practice discernment with knowledge, where the fruit of life is harvested, then the struggle is with the attacks of passions that are in no way able to approach our mind.
St. Isaac the Syrian * We to whom eternal life has been given do good works, not for the sake of reward, but to preserve the purity that has been given us.

St. Mark the Ascetic * It is very beneficial to read the Holy Bible, for it makes the soul wise, directs the spirit toward heaven, moves man to thanksgiving, destroys the desire for earthly things, and lets our minds continually contemplate the world to come.

St. John Chrysostom * ["(The judgments of the Lord) are sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb"] (Ps 19:10). As the soul is bound to become pure honey, freed from the bonds of mortal life, it awaits in simplicity the blessings of the divine banquet; or it is in the honeycomb, wrapped in this life as in the cells of the wax, which it fills without becoming like them (that is, without becoming wax). And in this it needs the help of God's hand, which presses not to crush, but to make it drip honey. The judgments of the Lord become for such a soul sweeter than its own being, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

St. Augustine * Consider the Orthodox manner in the battle and appreciate the achievements of spiritual battles, how the Christian combatant, having conquered his rebellious body and put it under the weight of his feet, is carried forward as a victor on high. Therefore he does not run as uncertainly, because he trusts that he will enter at once into the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem.
St. John Cassian

10 "But as for you all, do ye return, and come now: for I cannot find one wise man among you. 11 My days are past, my purposes are broken off, even the thoughts of my heart. 12 They change the night into day: the light is near to the darkness. 13 If I wait, the grave is mine house: I have made my bed in the darkness. 14 I have said to the grave, Thou art my father: to the worm, Thou art my mother, and my sister. 15 And where is now my hope? as for my hope, who shall see it? 16 They shall go down to the bars of the pit, when our rest together is in the dust."
"But as for you all, do ye return, and come now: for I cannot find one wise man among you" [10].

Job demands that they turn back from what they are thinking, and realize that there is not one wise man among them, because they ask him to repent so that prosperity and the comfort of the world may return to him, thinking that in this is the consolation of the suffering. They are not wise, because they have turned their eyes from the consolations of heaven to the comfort of the world. The happiness of the righteous is in their hope in eternity, not in their obtaining a temporal good.
It is as though he tells them that it would be foolish for him to listen to them and answer their requests, and so grant them what is temporal.
* "Well, come now, rise up all of you, for I do not find truth in you" (Job 17:10) LXX. It is as though he says: Come, and you who are cooperating together, enter into a heated debate against me.
Job knows that one alone pursues a thousand, and two can put ten thousand to flight (Deut 32:32). There is no need of a great number of combatants, especially when they are armed with falsehood.
I see decisively that there is no truth in you; therefore I surely urge you all to the battle.

One must marvel at the bold spirit in Job's words. For after his friends trampled him underfoot, so that we cannot imagine how he suffered, yet he did not cease to contend with them, nor did he abandon his patience, which made him fearsome to his enemies.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem The text in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) reads: ["But as for you all, change your way and come now"] [10]. It is as though Job answers them by saying: If you ask me to repent of sins I have not committed, you fall into the sin of slander and unjust accusation. I advise you to turn back from this way of yours, and your evil conduct, then you may come to me, and we can come to an understanding together.

The Pope sees here that Job calls them to two works: the first negative, which is to cease from sin, and the second positive, which is doing good. This is what he meant by their changing their evil way and coming to him bearing good works.

* Paul asks us to be dead to the world, for this death is beneficial to us, being the beginning of a new life. So also he commands us to be fools to the world, that by this we may enter into true wisdom. You become fools to this world when you despise earthly wisdom, and trust that it contributes nothing to our understanding of the faith.
St. John Chrysostom * The wisdom of this world is that which lacks the grace of God; it is wholly human in its characteristics.

Theodoret * They must change their way, and come. The change is by faith, and the coming by practice; or they must change by leaving evil works, and come by practicing good works. As it is written: ["Depart from evil, and do good"] (Ps 37:27).

["Perhaps I shall not find one wise man among you"] [10]. What does it mean that he exhorts them to wisdom, and at the same time longs not to find them wise, except that they cannot come to true wisdom when they are deceived by their trust in their own vain wisdom?
It is written of this: "Be not wise in thine own eyes"(a) (see Isa 5:21). It was also said: "Be not wise in your own conceits" (Rom 12:16).

In this the great preacher (Paul) gives counsel to those whom he found carnally wise, that in order to obtain true wisdom they must first become fools, saying: "If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise" (1 Cor 3:18). And the Truth Himself says: "I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes" (Mt 11:25). So, because those who are wise in their own eyes cannot come to true wisdom, the blessed Job, longing for the change of his hearers, truly desired that [no wise man be found among them]. It is as though he says plainly: "Learn to be fools in yourselves, that you may be truly wise in God."
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Do not let abundance of wisdom become a stumbling block to your soul, and a snare in your path; rather, firm trust in God makes for you the beginning of the way filled with blood (the way of spiritual striving against sin), lest you be found continually in want and bare of the knowledge of God, for the fearful man who watches the wind never sows.
St. Isaac the Syrian "My days are past."
"My purposes are broken off, even the thoughts of my heart" [11].

They ask Job to repent of his evil and hypocrisy so that what he lost may return to him. As for him, these matters have no place in his heart. His days have passed or are hastening to the end, and the former purposes of his heart, works of reform and care for the poor, have been taken from him. Job has come to see death not far from him, so he does not think about what he cannot do.

Pope Gregory sees that Job is a symbol of the persecuted Church. When tribulation greatly intensifies upon her, her thought rises all the more toward heaven, so she is not occupied with earthly matters, not even with purely social service, but is confined to eternal glory. And what we say of the Church as a holy company is fulfilled in the life of each member in her, when he meets affliction with thought of heavenly things.

* ["My days pass away, my thoughts are scattered, they pain my heart"] [11]. The holy Church sees that the periods of her life pass in periods of day and night, for when she is in distress she has night, and when she is in prosperity she has day. For the light dawns in the calm of peace. At times she listens to the service of temporal matters... So also the blessed Job, whether by his own voice or by the voice of the universal Church, after experiencing that his days had passed, went on: ["My thoughts are scattered, they pain my heart."] When temporary glory departs from the minds of the righteous, even obligations to earthly matters are taken away from them... At times in their earthly obligations they are bound to descend to thinking of lower things, and feel within themselves that they are in torment. And it also happens that the very hostile work of persecution turns for them into great rejoicing because of the rest of heart they obtain.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* ["My soul is in my hand"]... A man's soul is between his hands when he is in the midst of dangers... So the righteous man says: As for me, I die daily, I am in constant danger because of (my attachment to) Your word, and for the sake of the truth... But I have not forgotten Your law, for the danger of death cannot make me forget Your law.
We can understand this statement in another way, namely that my soul is always in my palm, that is, it is always practicing good works, for the "hand" or the "palm" always denotes work.
Origen * You gain the world of light instead of a bitter pain that you bear for His sake for one day.
If you endure hunger a little for love of Him, your desire to see His face will then be kindled.
If darkness appears on your face from works done for Him, He will adorn you with His glory forever without end.
If you strip yourself of what is yours, He will clothe you with His light, and hide from you what is yours.
If you leave what you possess, you will possess it in yourself eternally.
The Spiritual Elder (John of Dalyatha)

* The toil of all the long years of this present life disappears when we look to the eternity of the glory to come, and all our sorrows will vanish by thinking of the great blessing, and become like vapor that dissolves as though it had never been; like lightning that disappears as soon as it flashes.

St. John Cassian * They (the martyrs) renounced all the things that are on earth, and saw with the eyes of faith the King of heaven, and the ranks of angels standing before Him. They pictured in their minds heaven and its unutterable blessings. They transferred their thoughts to heaven, and gave no more attention to anything they could see with their bodily eyes...

They were never affected by the visible things (the instruments of torture), but passed beside them, counting them dreams and shadows, and their minds gained wings because of their desire for the things to come.
* We do not fear poverty or sickness or any affliction of this kind, for we know that we are on our way to a better life, which is invulnerable to death and destruction, and free from all injustice.
St. John Chrysostom "They change the night into day: the light is near to the darkness" [12].

They speak to him about the night, where his days had almost passed, as though it were day, but it is not a day cheerful with its light; rather its light is near to the darkness. While he was not expecting anything on earth, they focused their talk on prosperity in the world as the Lord's reward to the righteous, and so they prepare for him in their minds the world as a house of rest, but he sees death before his eyes, and has no hope in the temporal matters of the world. He welcomes death as a house in which to settle. There in the grave his bed is made ready.
"If I wait, the grave is mine house: I have made my bed in the darkness" [13].
"I have said to the grave, Thou art my father: to the worm, Thou art my mother, and my sister" [14].

In bitterness Job looks to exchange his friends in the world for the grave, which becomes a father to him, since it is more merciful than they, and in place of their promises of temporal blessings he finds in the worm his mother and his sister. Job complained that his relatives had failed him and become strangers to him (Job 19:13-14), therefore he mentions here relatives who do not leave him or disown him, namely death and the worm.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem sees that Job called corruption a mother and a sister, because on account of sin the sentence was passed against man to dissolve and decay and return to his dust.

* If we understand this in the spiritual sense, nature is not unfittingly called our mother, and habit is called our sister, for we were born from the one and grew with the other. The same mother and sister are the worm, for because of corrupt nature and evil habit we are bound to a kind of worm, or stirring thoughts, that eat the mind. For the corrupt nature of the body and evil habit give birth to many cares in the heart of our weakness, and so rightly they were called a worm.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* May we rid ourselves of the filth of sin, so that the first beauty of virtue may appear. David the prophet says in the Psalm: ["O Lord, by Your beauty You gave strength to my beauty"] (Ps 30:7). Let us be purified so that the image of God may appear in us, and this is what God wants of us, that we be without defilement, without lack and without blemish.

Fr. Dorotheus * All the saints grieve with daily sighs over this weakness of their nature. And while they search out their wandering thoughts and the hidden things of their consciences and their deep retreats, they cry out in supplication: "And enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Ps 143:2)....

See, then, how all the saints truly confess that all men, as they themselves also are, are sinners, and yet they never despair of their salvation, but seek complete cleansing by the grace and mercy of God...

There is no one, however holy, in this life without sin. The teaching of the Savior, who gave His disciples the pattern of perfect prayer..., also told us this, for He says: "And forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us" (Mt 6:12).

Therefore, since He gave this as a true prayer practiced by saints, as we must believe without the least doubt, who can remain stubborn, impudent and puffed up with the pride of Satan, supposing that he is without sin.
Fr. Theonas * Just as the saint is the temple of God, so the sinner makes of himself a tomb.
St. Jerome "And where is now my hope?"
"As for my hope, who shall see it?" [15]

Job sees that all his former hopes go down with him into the grave, and he laments them. Truly, if in this life only we have hope, we are of all men most miserable (1 Cor 15:19). There is no one who can see our hopes that console us, for we look not at the things which are seen and temporal, but at the things which are not seen and eternal (2 Cor 4:18).
The hopes his friends offered him go down with him into the grave, to be buried with him and not return. They are mortal and offer what is perishable.
* ["What then is my hope?"] [15]. Or where is the hope of man in whom this way of weakness is fulfilled? "Where shall I see my good things?" when we depart from it.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * ["Where is now my expectation?"] [15]. What can be the righteous man's expectation but God, who justifies the righteous, who by His own will descended to human punishment, and by His righteousness freed the captives of death? For they will not cease from the rest of the expectations that are full of hope. They know that this is coming, but they ask for the speed of the coming. Therefore he did not say, "Where is my expectation?" but added the word "now," showing that he wishes that what will one day come may be fulfilled without delay.

["And who considers my patience?"] [15]... The Truth bears witness: ["For I tell you, that many prophets and kings have desired to see those things which ye see, and have not seen them"] (Lk 10:24). And so, "who considers my patience?" The breaths of ardent desire have become open... Let him say: "Who considers my patience?" For what the Ruler of the matter (God) counts a short time, the one who loves sees as a long time.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* We ought to lay up in heaven what we lose now on earth. The enemy can dig through our houses, but can he break the door of heaven?! He kills the guard here, but can he kill God, its keeper?!

* If an architect told you that your house is falling down immediately, would you not move quickly before you are occupied with lamenting over it?! Behold, the Founder of the world tells you that the destruction of the world is near, and do you not believe Him...?! Listen to the voice of His prophecy: "Heaven and earth shall pass away" (Mt 24:35)... Listen to His counsel!
St. Augustine "They shall go down to the bars of the pit, when our rest together is in the dust" [16].
* ["Or will they go down with me to hell, or shall we go down together to the dust?"] [16]. Why then do we put up buildings?
Why do we trouble ourselves with costly coverings for couches and various garments? Why do we "lay field to field" (Isa 5:8)? Why do we seek riches that do not go with us?

And why do we not believe the plan of the Judge, and obey Him, who says: ["Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal"] (Mt 6:19-20). For our angels guard our treasures, and above all the Lord of the angels.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * ["Do you not think that at least there will be rest for me there?"]... Here is what it profits us to meditate in great fear as a guarantee for us of eternal rest, for even Job was terrified of it... "And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?" (1 Pet 4:18). For the blessed Job knew that he would receive rest after the blows of affliction, but as he shakes our hearts with fear, he seemed to be in doubt regarding the reward of eternal rest by saying: ["Do you not think?"]
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Some see their houses in which they live as their kingdom, and although they know that death is certain, and that one day it will force them to leave them, in their hearts they feel that they will remain forever. They boast of the size of their houses, and the excellent materials of which they are made. They find pleasure in decorating their houses with bright colors, and in choosing the sturdiest and best furniture to fill the rooms. They imagine that by owning a house that will last long... they will find in it their peace, that is, whenever they are sure that its walls and roofs remain solid for many generations.

But we, on the contrary, know that we are merely guests living temporarily on earth. We realize that the houses we dwell in are like hotels on the road to eternity. We do not seek peace or security from the material walls around us or the roofs over our heads. Rather we wish to surround ourselves with the walls of divine grace. And we look up to heaven on high as our roof. As for the furniture in our life, it should be good works, which we do in the spirit of love.
St. John Chrysostom
I look forward to meeting You
* Whenever I remember the day of my departure, or the day of my meeting with You, my soul is crushed within me, groaning because of every weakness that comes upon me.
Behold, the wicked grow fat, for they think they will live here forever.
But as for me, the day of Your last coming is engraved on my heart, and never leaves my memory.
By what shall I be justified before You?
* In the midst of my sorrow over my weakness, my heart rejoices within me.
Yes, I long to return to my eternal home!
My eyes look to You; when shall I meet You face to face?
* My God, behold, around me are those who seek dry debate.
They spoil my repentance, and my longing for the meeting with You.
No, rather the enemy of good, a stranger to me and to all the human race, has no work but to rob me of the enjoyment of thinking of You, and of preparing for the fellowship of the eternal glories.
He is a stubborn adversary, who does not rest until he brings me down with him to his eternal dwelling.
In this I do not justify myself, for You know that I am a sinner.
I am wounded by sin, but I have found You a healing Physician!
I am a sinner, I have found You the Holy One, sanctifying my whole being!
I am a debtor, and You are my surety and guarantor.
Your blood tears up the bond written against me.
Your cross frees me from my captivity.
You alone spoil principalities and powers, by Your cross You make a show of them openly, so I escape from their hands, and bow no more to their authority.
I depart from the ruler of this age, to take refuge under Your wings, O King of kings and Lord of lords.
The enemy of good thought that by wisdom he had captured and humbled me.
But his wisdom became malice and craftiness!
My Lord has taken from him true wisdom, since he cut himself off from the wisdom of God.
The wicked one became foolish, and lost his abilities.
But as for me, in my ignorance I cry out for help.
I long for union with You, O Wisdom of God.
I possess You, and so through You I become truly wise, and am made worthy to dwell in heaven, the dwelling of the wise!
* What grieves my soul is that the enemy of good captures many.
Every soul that loses Your light, I count myself in darkness with it!
And every soul that makes light of its salvation, I count myself as one who perishes with it!
Every soul that the enemy takes captive, I count myself a captive with it!
* Why does my soul groan when I see the wicked, who oppose the truth, prospering?
However long the time of their life, they will pass quickly, and like the grass they wither!

Your children are like a tree in the season of winter, appearing as dead trees without leaves or fruit, but the spring of Your day will come, and the frost of the world will go, and Your trees will be glorified with their wonderful fruit!
Truly. The world will soon pass away, and the eternal glory of Your children will appear!
However severe the frost of the world, and however the trials pile up, the earnest of heaven fills me with Your joy!
And fellowship with You even in Your sufferings fills me with peace!
* Behold, my days pass quickly.
Grant me to possess divine wisdom and truth.
That I may renounce arrogant human wisdom.
I enjoy You, O All-humble One!
* My soul is in my hands, and I walk in the midst of dangers.
I look forward with joy to my departure from the world at any moment!
I do not cease to accomplish Your work with my hands, for I am Your ambassador.
Until, when I depart, I am found with You, and enjoy Your splendor!
* Finally, let all my hope be in You.
Let my treasure be in Your heavens!
There is no place as safe as they!

1 Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said, 2 "How long will you set snares for words? Be sensible, and afterward we will speak. 3 Wherefore are we counted as beasts, and reputed vile in your sight? 4 O you who tear yourself in your anger, shall the earth be forsaken for you? or shall the rock be removed out of his place?
Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said: [1].
"How long will you set snares for words?"
"Be sensible, and afterward we will speak" [2].

Bildad shoots an arrow into Job's heart, accusing him of speaking empty words without sense. In this he includes others with Job, perhaps meaning the two friends Eliphaz and Zophar, or some of those present who perhaps defended Job now and then.

Bildad had grown weary of hearing speech, and when his turn came he poured out all that was in his heart of distress, without compassion. Sadly, Bildad often thought that wisdom was the monopoly of his own mind and no one else's, so he was hasty in attacking with words.
The Apostle commands us that "every man be swift to hear, slow to speak" (Jas 1:19).

After Job, in his prosperity, used to give the final, decisive word like a wise man whose opinions all respected, he now directs to him and those with him that they should speak only after they have become sensible.

* Look at those who were busy condemning him. Look at those who want to silence his mouth. This is not the attitude of people seeking consolation for him, but on the contrary those who provoke him and mock him... Do you not see their envy? They count silence a disgrace, and the height of folly.

St. John Chrysostom The text in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) reads: "Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said: To what extent will you utter your words and spread them abroad? First understand, let us speak" [1-2]. In most of his interpretation of the Book of Job, this Father sees Job as a symbol of the holy Church, and his friends as symbols of the heretics who oppose her.

Here Bildad, as a representative of the heretics, brings two accusations against the Church: the first, that her views are not original, and the second, that she is without understanding, as she does not grasp their views and thoughts. In every age, since the Church holds to the living faith without laxity, some accuse her of arrogance, pride and rigidity, and since she rejects dissolute views, they accuse her of narrowness of outlook, unable to be contemporary, as she does not understand what is going on around her.

In St. Jerome's comment on the words of the Apostle Paul: "fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind" (Eph 2:3), he distinguishes between the sin of the flesh and the sin of thought, saying: [There is a difference between the sin of the flesh and the sin of the mind. The sin of the flesh is immodest and licentious, and acts as an instrument for the fulfillment of its lusts. But the iniquity of the mind concerns teaching against the truth and the decline of the heretics.]

* All heretics think that the holy Church, because she knows some things, is full of pride, while they count her as not understanding some things which they imagine. Thus Bildad the Shuhite was like one asserting that the blessed Job had been broken down in pride, when he declared that he "spreads words abroad." But (Bildad himself) bears a sign of his own pride, for he was puffed up, supposing that the blessed Job utters things he does not understand.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Whatever accusations are directed against the Church, she does not cease her continual striving until she brings all the believers to the unity of the faith, which the Apostle Paul counts as attaining to perfection: "Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ: that we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine" (Eph 4:12-14).

St. John Chrysostom comments on these words, saying: [We mature when we attain to the unity of the faith, that is, when there are partakers in the one faith, for this is the unity of the faith, when we all become one, when we all know the same covenant.]
"Wherefore are we counted as beasts, and reputed vile in your sight?" [3]

It is true that Job called his friends deceivers (Job 17:2), and portrayed them as unwise and without mercy, but he never called them animals or beasts as Bildad claims here. Bildad was offended by Job's rebuke, and counted it a grave insult, so he returned insult with a bitterer and harsher insult.

* "Why are we silent before you like beasts?" (LXX) Because you have a beastly spirit, you bow your head toward the earth. Surely your thoughts are not sound, and do not suit honest men, but those of whom David said: ["Man, being in honor, does not understand; he is compared to the irrational herd, and is like them"] (see Ps 49:12).

As for Bildad, when he realized that he was unable to answer Job, he turned to abuse, and became a threatening figure at the wrong moment. For this reason Job's words, which he addressed to the adversary (the devil) and not to God, Bildad counted as being against God, and so he was not ashamed to wrong the righteous man.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Since all heretics complain that the holy Church despises them in her estimate of them, he added: ["So we are counted as beasts, and as corrupt in your eyes"] [3]. It is natural for the human mind to suppose that the things it does come back upon it. So they believe that they are despised, as they are accustomed to despise the ways of the righteous... The Church proves against the heretics that what they do is unreasonable, so they think within themselves that the Church looks upon them as beasts.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"O you who tear yourself in your anger, shall the earth be forsaken for you? or shall the rock be removed out of his place?" [4]

Bildad became still more enraged and counted Job a fierce animal: "O you who tear yourself in your anger." If Job was a beast of prey, he tore himself. Perhaps Bildad wished to answer Job, who had accused God: "His wrath has devoured me and persecuted me," by saying: [Do not blame God as though He had devoured you; rather by your own savagery you have devoured yourself.]

Bildad accused Job of arrogance, as if he could legislate for God: "Shall the earth be forsaken (abandoned) for you?", as if he wished the laws of nature to be changed for him alone. Or as if the world could not stand without him, so that if he perished the world would perish with him, and the earth be emptied with him.

Some see that Bildad rebukes Job thus: either he confesses that he is wicked and deserves what has come upon him, or he supposes that God has abandoned His divine providence and forsaken the earth, and that the rock of ages has been removed.

In mockery the heretics speak with the Church as Bildad speaks here with Job. It is as though they say to her: [Do you think that you alone are the ark of salvation, and that without you no man will enjoy divine salvation? What you proclaim is a kind of madness and pride.]
Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on this text, saying:
[The heretics count that the strong feelings of good order or of the spiritual grace of holy preaching are not good as a virtue, but are the madness of anger...

"Shall the earth be forsaken for you?" (Job 18:4)... The holy catholic Church declares that God cannot be worshiped except through her, affirming that all who are outside her will not be saved. And the heretics, on the other hand, trusting that they can be saved even without entering her bounds, assert that divine help reaches them everywhere...

"Or shall the rock be removed out of his place?" The heretics call these persons rocks, those who in their view, by the loftiness of their thoughts, stand in the human race boasting of being teachers. But the holy Church offers herself to gather together the erring preachers so that they may enter together into the bosom of sound faith. What is this counted as but that she [moves the rock from its place]. And when they gain a sound view of things, they submit humbly within her, those who formerly took a stubborn stance, holding fast to erroneous concepts...?
Thus Bildad bore a symbol of the heretics who were exalted on the ground that their life is happy, puffed up over the blows that befell the blessed Job.]

Rahab and her household would not have enjoyed salvation had they gone out of the house on whose window the scarlet thread was hung, for there is no salvation outside the Church redeemed by the blood of Christ.

* Rahab represents the Church, and the scarlet cord signifies the blood of Christ, and only those in the house were saved. Whoever wishes to be saved, let him come to this house where the blood of Christ is the sign of redemption... Let no one deceive himself, for no one is saved outside the house, I mean outside the Church.

Origen * Do you think you can stand and live if you withdraw to set up for yourselves various houses and places, when it was said to Rahab: "Bring thou thy father, and thy mother, and thy brethren, and all thy father's household, home unto thee into the house: and it shall be, that whosoever shall go out of the doors of thy house into the street, his blood shall be upon his head, and we will be guiltless"?!

* In this the mystery was declared, that those who wish to live and escape the destruction of the world must gather together in one house alone, that is, in the Church, but whoever goes out from among those gathered there together, that is, if anyone, although he received grace in the Church, leaves it and goes outside, his blood is upon his own head; he is responsible for the destruction of his own soul, which Paul made clear when he commanded us to avoid the heretic (Rom 16:17).
* Whoever remains outside the Church is outside the camp of Christ.
* He is not a Christian who is not within the Church of Christ.
* For how can anyone be with Christ if he does not walk within the Bride of Christ, and is not found in His Church?!
* He who does not have the Church as his mother cannot have God as his Father!
St. Cyprian

entries.section: 2. The light of the wicked is put out

paragraphs.text: 5 "Yea, the light of the wicked shall be put out, and the flame of his fire shall not shine. 6 The light shall be dark in his tabernacle, and his lamp above him is put out.
"Yea, the light of the wicked shall be put out, and the flame of his fire shall not shine" [5].
Bildad's speech here is true, but it is not fulfilled immediately and in a visible, public manner.

By saying "Yea," Bildad refers to what Job suffers of the intense grief under which he has fallen. He says to him: What you say is true, for you ought to be as you are, as a natural thing fitting for a wicked man. So do not be astonished if the little light you had has been completely put out. Perhaps by the light of the wicked he meant the good things and joy he had for a short time before the trials came. The light of the wicked is not the light of the eternal Sun of righteousness, the light of the Lord which will never go out, but is ["the light of his fire, and the spark he kindled"] (Isa 50:11).

Job speaks of the days of his prosperity when the lamp of the Lord shone upon his head (Job 29:3). And the psalmist David says: "For thou wilt light my candle: the LORD my God will enlighten my darkness" (Ps 18:28). On the other hand, the righteous Job expresses his intense pain by saying: "How oft is the candle of the wicked put out!" (Job 21:17). And Solomon says: "Whoso curseth his father or his mother, his lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness" (Prov 20:20). "The lamp of the wicked shall be put out" (Prov 24:20). The Lord Christ pointed to deprivation of the Kingdom of God, or the kingdom of light, by entering into outer darkness or hell (Mt 8:12; 22:13).
It is said in the Proverbs: "The light of the righteous rejoiceth: but the lamp of the wicked shall be put out" (Prov 13:9; see Jer 25:10).

* ["Shall not the light of the wicked be put out, and the flame of his fire not shine?"] [5]. If he says this of the present life, he is mistaken, for often light is seen flourishing in the life of the wicked, while the darkness of shame and poverty envelops the life of the righteous... And if this is said regarding the wicked man, it is not directed against the holy man upon whom blows fall...

But "the light of the wicked is put out" in that the happiness of the present life soon ends with life itself. Therefore it is fitting to add: "and the flame of his fire shall not shine." For every wicked man has "the flame of his fire," which he kindles in his heart from the heat of temporal lusts, as long as he burns with various desires, and scatters his thoughts in a greater flame with the manifold illusions of the world. But if the fire is without flame, it does not shine by giving off any light... For even the righteous have the flame of their fire, but it is a flame that lights with brightness, since their desires shine forth in good works. But the light of the wicked does not shine, at least as they would wish in evil, and they are bound to enter into darkness.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

The enemy of good, the devil, cannot give light, and if he appears to give light, he bears a counterfeit light. For he is the ruler of the kingdom of darkness, and appears as an angel of light to deceive mankind and bring it into the kingdom of darkness. So the wicked, who persist in their disobedience, will not be able to give light, for they offer of what is theirs and their father's, that is, darkness.

* Since we know Christ to be the true Light (Jn 1:9), He is not comprehended (1 Tim 6:16) by falsehood. We learn this, that it is necessary for our life also to be enlightened by the rays of the true Light. But the virtues are the rays of the "Sun of righteousness" (Mal 4:2), sent forth for our enlightenment, through which we put off the works of darkness (2 Cor 4:2). When we do everything in the light, we ourselves become light, shining upon others (Mt 5:15-16), for this is the characteristic of light.
St. Gregory of Nyssa * Satan does not aim his arrows in the daytime lest he be seen, for everything done in the light is made manifest by the light.

* The heretics do not have Christ, the Truth, on their lips, because He is not in their hearts... They mean one thing in their hearts, and promise another on their tongues. They speak of godliness, and hide evil. They speak of Christ, and conceal the antichrist, for they know that they will not succeed in deceiving if they show the antichrist. They offer light only to hide the darkness, for by the light they lead into darkness.

entries.section: 2. The light of the wicked is put out

paragraphs.text: St. Jerome "The light shall be dark in his tabernacle, and his lamp above him is put out" [6].
He means here the tabernacle of the soul (2 Cor 5:1), that is, the body, which is wholly corrupted and becomes darkness.
If the tabernacle is the body, then the removal of the lamp refers to death, for "when a wicked man dieth, his expectation shall perish" (Prov 11:7).

The wicked think that life is the enjoyment of fleshly lusts, pleasures and amusement, and that deprivation of them is loss of life, or they see them as their light, without which they would be like dwellers in gloomy graves. What they count as light grows dark, and what they think a lamp is put out.
This is the light of the wicked and their lamp, but the light of true believers is the word of God, which dispels the darkness, and makes the believers a true light in the Lord.

* The lamp is a light in an earthen vessel, but the light in the earthen vessel is the pleasure in the body. So the lamp that is above him is put out, since the recompense for his evil comes upon the wicked man, and bodily pleasure becomes nothing in the heart.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"The steps of his strength shall be straitened, and his own counsel shall cast him down" [7].

Since the wicked man devotes all his energies to temporal goods, heedless of eternal blessings, his days pass like a shadow, and the steps of his life are counted very short, and he goes out empty-handed. And since he spends all his effort thinking about temporal things, his plans turn into an enemy to him, depriving him of true, eternal life.

* "And his own counsel shall cast him down" [7]. Every wicked man's counsel aims at temporal things, leaving eternal things aside, so he practices injustice and mocks righteousness. But when the Judge of the righteous and the unjust comes, every wicked person is cast down by his own counsel, for his choice of the things to come was with evil intent, therefore he is cast down, sunk in the darkness of eternal woe.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* The love of this world is a harlot, who seduces by the desire of her beauty those who hold her to love her. The man whom the love of the world possesses and who falls into her snares cannot save his soul from her embrace until his soul is plundered. When the world strips man of everything, and throws him out of his dwelling on the day of his death, only then does man understand that he has truly been deceived and led astray.

* As long as man approaches this world on the path of his life, love of material things strikes its roots in him. He is always troubled and anxious over them, and for their sake he fights others, and the friendship of certain persons captivates him... Let us remember this, beloved, and let us make light of the things that are here as far as possible, and so withdraw our thoughts gradually toward the things to come. If we do not control ourselves little by little, we shall have no strength to renounce bodily things so as to look to God St. Isaac the Syrian * If the fashion of the world passes away (1 Cor 7:31), then without doubt everything in the world will come to an end. All will pass. Every day the world grows older Fr. Ambrosiaster

8 For his feet push him into the net, and he walks into a mesh. 9 The snare grasps him by the heel, and the nets hold him fast. 10 The snare is laid for him in the ground, and a trap for him in the way.
"For his feet push him into the net (into the snare), and he walks into a mesh" [8].

The wicked man's strong plans and mighty efforts fail, for his sinful ways drive him into evil, so he does not accomplish his purposes. The more effort he puts into his counsel, the more he is entangled in the nets, and hastens to his destruction.

* ["For he puts his foot in the net, and walks in its threads"] [8]. He who puts his feet in a net cannot take them out when he thinks to (except by asking God's grace). He who allows himself to sink into the habits of sin cannot rise from them when he wishes. And he who walks in the threads of the net hinders his steps in walking. And when he tries to free himself in order to walk, he finds himself bound and tied, and is unable to walk. It often happens that a man is distracted by the pleasures of this world in order to reach the glories of its honor... but he learns, by obtaining them, how trivial what he sought is. If he returns to himself he sees how he fell into the nets of sin. The very power that entangles him holds him, and he cannot escape from sins... Then he sees in the true light what hard bonds he is bound with. For we do not know even that we are bound, with a sound understanding, until we struggle to be freed, and try to lift our feet...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

And as many Fathers of the Church affirm, such as St. Macarius the Great, that sin carries its corruption within it, the wicked man who is set on his wickedness perishes as a natural fruit of evil, certain of corruption.

The wicked man does not need someone to restrain and punish him, rather what he does gives him bitterness and death! He drinks from the very cup that he has filled for himself, unless he throws away the cup during his enjoyment of fellowship with his Savior, and his earnest striving through the holy will in the Lord.
* If you remain in what concerns the dust, you will in the end be turned into it. It is fitting for you to change, you must be transformed, you must become heavenly.

Origen * We have all become one lump of clay, a lump of sin. And since we lost our reward through sin, in the absence of God's mercies we deserve, as sinners, nothing but eternal destruction. What man, then, from this lump thinks he is able to ask God, saying: "Why hast thou made me thus?" If you wish to know those things, do not be clay, but be a son of God through the mercy of Him who gives to those who believe in His name the power to become sons of God.

* Truly by sin we slide into death. For where the Law forbids, sin is graver than if the Law had not forbidden it. At any rate, where grace is added we can fulfill without difficulty and with our whole will what the Law strictly commands. We are no longer slaves of the Law through fear, but friends and servants of righteousness through love.

St. Augustine He who eats and drinks sin falls into snares, and his will is loosened and weakened, and he finds himself a slave to it in humiliation, unable to be saved from it, but thirsting for it. We should not wonder at this, for he who uses drugs, the more he uses them becomes the more a captive in their snares, and his attachment to them increases all the more.

Many think that the practice of sin gives them a bitter experience, so they flee from it through their own bitter experience. This reasoning is not sound, for he who tastes sin while perceiving its destruction desires it all the more at the expense of his inner joy and his peace and eternal glory. Sin, like fire, inflames man and shatters his will, so that he cannot be free from it unless God's surpassing grace supports him.
"The snare grasps him by the heel, and the nets hold him fast" [9].

The wicked man who is set on his evil and on not returning to God cannot escape drinking the bitter cup of evil and reaping its deadly fruit. This is what the Holy Bible sometimes calls divine wrath, or the fulfillment of divine justice. This is the translation of the cherishing of freedom of will, for when man chooses evil by his will, he only keeps for himself the fruit of evil. "The Lord knoweth how ... to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished" (2 Pet 2:9).
The text in the Septuagint translation reads: ["And the snares hold him, and those who thirst strengthen themselves toward his destruction"] [9 LXX].

* ["And the thirsty burn strongly against him"] [9]. When our ancient enemy catches someone alive in the snares of sin, he thirsts for his death. This statement can also be understood in another sense. When the wicked mind sees that it has fallen into sin, it seeks with superficial thought to escape from the snares of sin. But fearing the threats or rebukes of men, it chooses to die eternally rather than suffer slight trials for a while. So the mind surrenders itself entirely to the ways of evil when it sees itself already bound... and the sinner despairs of his return. By this very despair he burns more fiercely in the lusts of this world, the heat of desire rises within him, and the mind fallen in the nets of former sins is inflamed toward a more bitter disobedience. Therefore it was added: ["And the thirsty burn strongly against him"]...
The one afflicted with dropsy, the more he drinks, the more his thirst increases, and every covetous person doubles his thirst the more he drinks (of money).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"The snare is laid for him in the ground (a cord is hidden for him in the ground), and a trap for him in the way" [10].

The misleading enemy of good does not cease to fight mankind by every means of deception, hiding his cords and snares in the paths men walk. His war is hidden and full of deceit, he does not despair of resisting servants and people, old men, children and youths, women and men, virgins and married, rich and poor, sick and healthy. To each one he offers a war that suits him. But as we look to the heavenly One who gives victory, we do not fear the tricks and deceptions of the devil.

* "Their snares are hidden in the ground, and all their cords are in the way" [10 LXX]. This is true, for Satan hides the nets in the earth in such a way that he uses those who are deceived, that is, those who live according to the wisdom of the world (1 Cor 2:6; 3:9), and according to the lusts of men (1 Pet 4:2; 2 Pet 1:4). He (Satan) sets the accuser, those around him, on the way, that is, by all the ways of men. For he wants to catch them and take them captive by every means. He catches the righteous man by self-righteousness, and the sinner by his greed. David sings prophetically: ["They spread their cords as a net for my feet, they set a stumbling block for me beside the way"] (Ps 140:5). Even Bildad, who uttered what was upright in his earlier statements, came to lie in the following words.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * His snare is hidden in the ground when sin is concealed under earthly concerns, because our enemy, in carrying out his plans, shows the human mind a longing for earthly gain, and hides the snare of sin until it binds itself completely... The enemy of mankind surveys the inclinations of each individual to see with which evils he is allied, and the enemy places these things before his face, where he sees the mind drawn to them. To those of a gentle and cheerful temperament he often suggests dissoluteness, and sometimes vainglory, but to those of a violent temperament he suggests pride or violence. He sets the snare where he sees the way the mind is heading.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* We have warned you beforehand to take care lest the evil spirits deceive you and turn you away from reading and understanding what we say. For they strive to hold you as slaves and servants. At times they use appearances in dreams and magical deceptions to subdue all those who fail to exert strong opposing efforts for the salvation of their souls.
God the Word urges us and strengthens us to keep away from the demons, and to follow the living God alone through His Son.
We who for a time wallowed in fornication, now accept chastity alone.
We formerly used the arts of magic, and now we dedicate ourselves to the good, living God.
Our concern above all was to gain wealth and possessions, and now we bring what we own to be common property for every needy person to take from it.

We hated and destroyed one another because of the difference in our manners, for we refused to live with those of another tribe, but today, since the coming of Christ, we live together in familiarity.

Today we pray for our enemies, and try to urge those who hate us without cause to submit to the good principles of Christ and His commandments, in order that they may share with us the same joyful hope of receiving a reward offered by God, the Ruler of all.
St. Justin the Martyr * Satan is always diligent, even when danger comes upon him of losing his prey.

* Satan can destroy even under the appearance of godliness. For he can destroy not only by leading to fornication, but also on the contrary, by the excessive grief that accompanies repentance for fornication. This is his fitting work, to possess us by sin, but to catch us in the net in our repentance is a shame accomplished with great malice, for repentance is our weapon, not his.

St. John Chrysostom * The problem is not in recognizing the devil's schemes, but in making a mockery of them. Paul knows the schemes of the demons, not to be occupied with them, but so as not to fall into their snares.

St. Didymus the Blind * "And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light" (2 Cor 11:14)... These deceptions are appearances of that spirit who seeks to cast wretched souls into the nets... and turns them away from the true worship of the true God, who alone can cleanse and heal.

* At times Satan changes himself into an angel of light, to test those who need testing, or to deceive those who deserve to be deceived. Only God's great mercies are able to rescue man from the mistaken understanding of evil spirits, so that he thinks them good angels, and of false friends as though they were true, and rescue him from the troubles of all the losses that come because of the utterly deadly satanic deceptions, which cannot be expressed.
St. Augustine

11 Terrors shall make him afraid on every side, and frighten him at his feet. 12 His strength shall be hungerbitten, and destruction shall be ready at his side. 13 He eats the members of his body. The firstborn of death eats his members.
"Terrors shall make him afraid on every side, and frighten him at his feet" [11].

He speaks here of the very ruin reserved for the wicked in the world to come, which in some form befalls them in this world. The first of this ruin is what comes upon his heart of terrors that shake his whole being, reaching down to his feet, which cannot bear him. These terrors, which arise from his sense of guilt, are a foretaste of the terrors he will suffer after his death.
Everything around him terrifies him, so that it is said of him, "The wicked flee when no man pursueth" (Prov 28:1), because what pursues him is not what is around him but what is within him.
"There is no peace, saith the LORD, unto the wicked" (Isa 48:22).
"The way of peace they know not; and there is no judgment in their goings: they have made them crooked paths: whosoever goeth therein shall not know peace" (Isa 59:8).
"They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace" (Jer 6:14; 8:11).
"We looked for peace, but no good came; and for a time of health, and behold terror!" (Jer 8:15).
"Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there was no peace; and one built up a wall, and, lo, others daubed it with untempered morter" (Ezek 13:10).
"To wit, the prophets of Israel which prophesy concerning Jerusalem, and which see visions of peace for her, and there is no peace, saith the Lord GOD" (Ezek 13:16).

* And now those who do not keep the feast... these are heading toward days of sorrow, not happiness, for "there is no peace, saith the LORD, unto the wicked" (Isa 48:22). And as Wisdom says, joy and gladness are taken from their mouth. Such are the joys of the wicked.

* For what does the feast mean but the service of the soul?! And what is this service but constant prayer to God and continual thanksgiving?! So the ungrateful, who are far from this, are truly deprived of the joy that flows from it, for joy and gladness are taken from their mouths, and therefore the (divine) Word does not allow them to be at peace, for there is no peace for the wicked, saith the Lord (Isa 48:22), but they work in pain and sorrow.
St. Athanasius the Apostolic * ["Terrors make him afraid on every side"], for he imagines that all men are turned against him in this way, and so he struggles with all.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"His strength shall be hungerbitten, and destruction shall be ready at his side" [12].

The wicked man does not feel satisfied, for what he thinks is the source of his satisfaction, whether his wealth or honor or power, etc., shames him and brings him into a sense of emptiness. Beside this inner famine, ruin comes upon the wicked man, drawing near to take control of him. "They are brought into desolation, as in a moment" (Ps 73:19).
The text in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) reads: "Let his strength be stricken with hunger, and let famine invade his ribs" [12]...

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that man, being composed of soul and body, has the soul representing the strong element, while the body represents the weak element. So the wicked man, since he gives leadership to the body and its lusts, however strong he may seem, is weak, losing his inner strength and his inner satisfaction, and lives in weakness, famine and emptiness. But the spiritual man, since he gives leadership to the soul sanctified by the Spirit of God, lives in a spirit of strength and inner satisfaction, lacking nothing.

* Every man, being composed of soul and body, is as though made of strength and weakness.
