For by virtue of that element by which he was created a rational spirit, he is not unfittingly called strong, but with regard to the element belonging to his bodily being, he is weak. So man's strength is in his rational soul, able to resist the tendencies of evil that face him. So it is also said by the blessed Job: ["I strengthened him for a time, that he may pass away forever"] (Job 14:20), where man withdraws with his rational soul to live eternally. So the strength of this wicked man is smitten with hunger, since his soul is not fed by any inward food that refreshes it. God says of this hunger through the prophet: ["I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD"] (see Amos 8:11).

It is well added: ["Famine invades his ribs"]... Everyone's ribs are the senses of his mind which swim about his hidden thoughts. So famine invades his ribs when all spiritual food is taken away, and the senses of the mind weaken, and cannot control their thoughts or protect them.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Someone may think that the people of Israel are rich, for they have the adoption as sons, and the divine service, and the promises and the fathers. At any rate, they became poor because of their sins against the Lord. "But they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing" (Ps 34:10). They came to be in need of food in a certain sense, and suffer hunger. For since they killed the Bread of life, hunger for bread came upon them... they were in need and hungry.

St. Basil the Great * When Joseph was about thirty years old, he was freed from his bonds and interpreted Pharaoh's dream. He became ruler of Egypt. And in the time of plenty he gathered wheat so as to distribute it in the time of famine. I believe that Joseph's thirty years came beforehand as a type of the Savior's thirty years. For this second Joseph did not gather wheat of the same kind that the first Joseph gathered in Egypt. Jesus gathers the wheat and distributes it when famine comes upon Egypt, ["not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD"] (Amos 8:11).
Origen "He eats the members of his body."
"The firstborn of death eats his members" [13].

Death draws near to the wicked man and eats the members of his body, that is, brings him into corruption. But for the righteous, death prepares eternal glory, where the body shares in the glories of the soul.

The text in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) reads: "May it remove the beauty of his skin, and may the firstborn of death scatter his arms." What is the beauty of his body but temporal glory, which is eaten and passes away, for it is beauty on an outer skin, with no place in the inner depths? But of the righteous it was said: ["The king's daughter is all glorious within"] (Ps 45:13). And it was said in Zechariah the prophet: "And will be the glory in the midst of her" (Zech 2:5).

Moreover the matter does not stop at the passing of temporal glory, but death comes upon the human soul, as it withdraws from God, the source of its life and resurrection. Spiritual death kills the soul's arms, that is, makes it unable to work!
* "The beauty of his skin" is the temporary glory which he desires as something external to us, and which remains as beauty on the skin...

And what is death but sin that kills the soul in its inner life? Therefore it is written: ["Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection"] (Rev 20:6). By this resurrection a person afterward enjoys a joyful resurrection in the body, he who, while in this life, rises again from the death of his soul...
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* ["The king's daughter is all glorious within"] (Ps 45:13), as one moves to the level of the mind, he discovers the beauty of the soul.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 6. The wicked are driven from their tents

paragraphs.text: 14 He is cut off from his tent, from his confidence, and is driven to the king of terrors. 15 One who is not his dwells in his tent. Brimstone is scattered on his dwelling.
"He is cut off from his tent, from his confidence, and is driven to the king of terrors" [14].
The man who lives in this world for the body and its lusts loses even this body, or this tent, and death comes upon him, not as a joyful passage to heaven, but as the "king of terrors."

Everything he depended on as his master is taken from him, and nothing is left to him of what he depended on, not even his tent. His soul was his confidence, but it is uprooted from the tent of the body, so the body has no support at all. This is what was said to the foolish rich man: "This night thy soul shall be required of thee" (Lk 12:20).

The text in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) reads: "Let his confidence be uprooted from his tent, and let death tread upon him as a king." He sees that death here is Satan, to whom the wicked man surrenders himself and submits as to a king, as it also refers to sin, which humiliates the wicked man and enslaves him.

* The title "Death" in this place refers to (the devil), the enemy of the human race himself, who brought in death. He spread by a certain servant of (the enemy), of whom it was said to John: "and his name that sat on him was Death" (Rev 6:8). So this death treads upon the wicked man as a king, on the day of his departure from here. For the one who deceived him before with gentle allurements carries him in the end to punishment in chains by violence, and brings him down harshly, binding him by force with evil works.

And here also, when death takes possession of the heart of the lost sinner, it treads upon him at the very time when it presses upon him with the feeling of pleasure. It is as though he sets on him the feet of his tyrannical authority.

But if we understand by death not the devil openly but sin, whose fruit is death on the day of judgment, then truly such a death treads upon the mind as a king, when it reigns over a person without resistance from him. For the temptation of sin cannot be far from a man who stands in this life. But resisting the temptations of sin is one thing, and being enslaved to its tyranny over us is another. So the wicked man, since he does not learn to resist the enticements of sin, and does not fear to submit to its authority, of him it is said: ["Death as a king treads upon him"]. It is the reign of this death that Paul guarded against, lest it rule over the hearts of his disciples, when he said: ["Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body"] (Rom 6:12).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Those who live in pleasures fear death, but the sorrowful long for it that they may depart quickly.
The rich fear death, and the poor desire it that they may rest from their toils.
The strong are terrified when they remember it, and the sick look to it in hope that they may rest from their pains.

Fr. Aphrahat * He who loves earthly things and their lusts does not think of being with Christ after his departure, and cannot say: ["I am a stranger in the earth"](a), for he is concerned with the things of the earth. But he who says, "hide not thy commandments from me," is a saint... Therefore the prophet asks God to reveal to him the great things of His commandments for the heavenly life.
Origen * Surely he fears death who has not been born of water and the Spirit, for he is delivered to the fires of hell.
He fears death who has not experienced the cross of Christ and His sufferings.
He fears death who awaits another death after death.
He fears death for whom the fires of eternity and endless punishment are waiting.
He fears death who finds benefit in postponing his death so that his sighs and groans may be delayed.
St. Cyprian the Martyr "One who is not his dwells in his tent."

entries.section: 6. The wicked are driven from their tents

paragraphs.text: "Brimstone is scattered on his dwelling" [15].

God created man to be the storehouse of His love and tenderness and rich grace and goodness, but if man persists in refusing to cleave to God, a curse comes upon his tent, where his body, like his soul, becomes a dwelling for the enemy of good, who usurps what is not his own. Man turns into a lair for the devil, receiving brimstone and fire like Sodom and Gomorrah, instead of being a holy temple of God.

St. Macarius sees that the inner man is either a land that God inhabits as His sanctuary, or the enemy of good occupies it and makes it his land, and it becomes satanic. By "land" he means "dwelling."

* ["Let brimstone be scattered on his dwelling"] [15]. What is brimstone but the fuel that kindles fire and sends out of it a very foul smell? What then do we understand by brimstone but fleshly sin, which, as it fills the mind with evil thoughts, like a kind of corrupt odor kindles an eternal fire for itself. And while the clouds of its smell spread in the lost soul, it is as one who supplies fuel to the flame of its destruction. By this the foul smell of the flesh is understood as brimstone.
The history of the Holy Bible itself records this, telling us that the Lord rained fire and brimstone on Sodom (Gen 19:14)... Thus "let brimstone be scattered on his dwelling."

entries.section: 6. The wicked are driven from their tents

paragraphs.text: The wicked man, by corrupting leniency toward the body that exercises authority within him, is occupied by evil thoughts without ceasing, and they prevent him from producing the fruit of good work. Therefore it was rightly said: ["His roots shall be dried up beneath, and above shall his harvest be corrupted"] [16].
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* There is a land inhabited by wild beasts, and a land in the air in which birds move and live. If the birds wish to stand and walk on the ground, the hunters snare them. The fish also have a land, the waters of the sea. The place in which any creature is born, whether on the earth or in the air, in it it lives, in it it feeds, and finds its delight and rest.

In the same way there is a land of Satan and a house for him, in which the powers of darkness and the spirits of evil live. In it they move and find their rest. As there is also a land of light, the land of divinity, where the camps of angels and holy spirits ascend and descend upon it and find their rest in it.

The eyes of the body cannot see the dark land or touch it, and so also with the land of light, which is the land of divinity... But to the spiritual, the satanic land of darkness and the land of divinity are revealed to the eyes of their hearts.
St. Macarius the Great * You should know that we become bodies for them (the demons) when our souls accept their dark, evil thoughts, and when they become manifest through our body in which we dwell.
St. Abba Anthony the Great * Do not be a companion of the quarrelsome, lest a chorus of demons dwell in your house.
Beware of the one who bears a grudge, for he is a devil incarnate.
The Spiritual Elder (John of Dalyatha)

* It is clear that unclean spirits cannot find a way into the bodies of those whom they have seized by any means unless they first reign over their minds and thoughts, robbing them of the fear of God and of remembering Him and meditating on Him, and by this they dare to approach them as those who have no divine protection, and bind them easily, and find a place in them, as if they had the right of ownership over them.

Fr. Serenus Some see that Bildad heard of the fire that came down from heaven and burned Job's sheep and servants, so he supposed that Job, with all his possessions, had reached in his wickedness what Sodom and Gomorrah had reached, and deserved the fires of God's wrath to burn what Job did not deserve or what he had usurped, for he was dwelling in a house not his.

* (The godly man) the beauty of his virtues is not changed by a savage death. The health that is brought to him by his prayers is not removed from his tent (his body), as long as he is indeed rich in practicing good works, and if his wealth is lost he remains radiant with the splendor of righteousness through his patience...

["His loftiness is scattered with brimstone."] This is what truly happened to the sinners in Sodom and Gomorrah, for what happened partially to the wicked (in Sodom and Gomorrah) the other wicked expect to happen to them in this present world or the world to come.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem

entries.section: 7. The remembrance of the wicked removed

paragraphs.text: 16 His roots shall be dried up beneath, and above shall his branch be cut off. 17 His remembrance shall perish from the earth, and he shall have no name on the face of the land.
"His roots shall be dried up beneath, and above shall his branch be cut off" [16].

When man, by his persistence in evil, loses the riches of God's surpassing grace, he becomes like one stripped of his roots, that is, of his blessed fathers, and is like a tree whose roots are dried up, with no life left in it. He also loses his offspring, like a tree whose branches are dried up, so that there is no fruit in it. This is what many wicked men fell into, such as Jeroboam, Baasha and Ahab, and not one of their offspring was left alive.

If our roots have dried up, the Lord Christ has offered Himself as a root overflowing within us with His divine life, and our branches are refreshed to bear the fruit of His Holy Spirit: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance (Gal 5:22-23).
The text in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) reads: "Let his roots dry up beneath, and let his harvest be corrupted above."

* What do we understand by the title "his roots," hidden from sight, which put forth a branch that is seen openly, but the unseen thoughts in the heart, which produce visible works? So also by the title "harvest" he refers to that visible practice which comes from the hidden root... The wicked man puts his thoughts on lower things, and ignores seeking the delights of eternal greenness, and what is this but that he leaves [his roots to dry up beneath]? ["Let his harvest be corrupted above"], since his patience is counted as nothing in the eyes of heaven, even if it is counted good in the eyes of man. Thus the roots are beneath, and the harvest above, in that we first send good thoughts here, so that we may one day be made worthy to receive the fruit of our good works in an eternal reward.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 7. The remembrance of the wicked removed

paragraphs.text: "His remembrance shall perish from the earth, and he shall have no name on the face of the land" [17].

Nothing occupies the mind of the devil like vainglory; because of it he rebelled against God and fell. And because of it he fights the children of men, supposing that he reigns over their hearts and thoughts, and that his reign over them will last forever.

His children imitate him, so they seek temporal glory, and think that the world will immortalize their names, offering every human work that will establish their memory through history. But evil blots out their name from the book of life. And when the name of the wicked man is removed from the book of life in heaven, his honor is buried in the dust, and his name bears nothing but contempt and disdain even on earth, "he shall have no name on the face of the land." He receives here a foretaste of the eternal shame and disgrace that he will face on the great day of the Lord. "The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot" (Prov 10:7).
It was said of the wicked:
"O thou enemy, destructions are come to a perpetual end: and thou hast destroyed cities; their memorial is perished with them" (Ps 9:6).
"When he maketh inquisition for blood, he remembereth them: he forgetteth not the cry of the humble" (Ps 9:12).
"The face of the LORD is against them that do evil, to cut off the remembrance of them from the earth" (Ps 34:16).
"Let them be before the LORD continually, that he may cut off the memory of them from the earth" (Ps 109:15).
"For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten" (Eccl 9:5).

["They shall fall hereafter a shameful fall, and be a reproach among the dead for evermore: for he will dash them speechless, with heads bowed down, and shake them from the foundations; and they shall be utterly laid waste, and be in sorrow; and their memorial shall perish"] (Wis 4:19).
"He dried up some of them and destroyed their inhabitants, and removed their memory from the earth" (Sir 10:20).
And it was said of the righteous:
"His memorial shall not depart away, and his name shall live from generation to generation" (Sir 39:13).
"Let their memorial be blessed, and let their bones flourish again out of their place" (Sir 46:14).
"And Nehemias, whose memorial is for all days, who raised up for us the walls that were fallen, and set up the gates and the bars, and raised up our ruined houses again" (Sir 49:15).

* "Let his memory be removed from the earth, and let his name not be found in public places" (LXX). It is clear that this concerns those who must dwell in this darkness, those whom Christ appointed [to be in outer darkness (Mt 8:12; 25:30)], those who take part in the wedding feast in filthy garments, and the king says: Bind his hands and feet... and cast him into outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth, for many are called but few are chosen (see Mt 22:13-14).

["And their name is not found"], because the wicked are driven out of the land of the righteous, and are taken to be with those whose names are blotted out forever (Deut 32:26). Therefore David sang elsewhere on the harp: "Thou hast put out their name for ever and ever" (Ps 9:5).

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * ["His memory perishes from the earth, and his name is not heard in the streets."] It is fitting to notice that Bildad the Shuhite expressed himself about each one of the wicked, so that his words are secretly directed against the chief of all the wicked. For the chief of the wicked is Satan. He himself enters in the last times into this vessel of destruction, who is called the "antichrist," and who seeks to spread his name everywhere. Every person, even now, likens himself to the antichrist when he strives to spread the memory of his earthly name through the glory of praise and by exalting himself with temporal fame. Therefore may every wicked person understand these words, and may they also point especially to the chief of the wicked himself.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

18 He is driven from light into darkness, and chased out of the world. 19 He has neither son nor descendant among his people, nor any survivor in his dwellings. 20 They that come after him shall be astonied at his day, and they of old shudder. 21 Surely such are the dwellings of the wicked, and this is the place of him that knoweth not God.
"He is driven from light into darkness, and chased out of the world" [18].

The wicked man is driven from what he thinks is light in this world, because of the comfort he obtained, into the darkness of the grave, and from it into outer darkness, where "they shall never see light" (Ps 49:19), and have no hope at all.

The wicked man is chased out of the world, that is, out of the pleasures of the world which he thought inhabited, and he goes out as with his first parents Adam and Eve from Paradise. So he is driven from the chamber of the heavenly Bridegroom, where there is no place for him, and remains in outer darkness eternally.

* "Thou hast put out their name for ever and ever" (Ps 9:5). You destroy them utterly, uproot them from their roots, and blot them out so that their memory also disappears... "Their memorial is perished with a crashing" and in another text "their memorial is perished with them." What does he mean by saying "with a crashing"? He speaks of total destruction, or of the hideousness of the evils. And this in fact is a sign of God's providence, that He does not do this in secret, so that He may reform men through the misfortunes of others. Therefore he points to the fame of the destruction that comes upon them.

St. John Chrysostom * "The eyes of the LORD are upon the righteous, and his ears are open unto their cry" (Ps 34:15)... Perhaps you will say: I have cried to Him, yet I am still in distress. Only hold fast to His ways, and when you are in distress He hears you.

He is a physician, and gives you a kind of cleansing. You cry out, but He keeps cutting and does not lift His hand until He has cut as He pleases. For a physician who listens to the person and stops wounding and cleansing is cruel.

Mothers keep on bathing their children for their health. Do the children not cry in their hands? Are these mothers cruel because they do not stop and do not care about their children's tears? Are they not full of tenderness...? So God also is full of love, but He seems like one who does not hear. For He does not stop until He heals us eternally.

Perhaps the wicked man will say: I do evil and I am safe, for the eyes of the Lord are not upon me, but the Lord listens to the righteous, and not to me; I do what I want and I am safe. Since the Lord sees the thoughts of men, it was said: "The face of the LORD is against them that do evil, to cut off the remembrance of them from the earth" (Ps 34:16).

St. Augustine * ["He drives him from light into darkness"] [18]. Man is driven from light into darkness when he falls under eternal judgment because of the love of receiving the honor of the present life.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Bildad and his friends thought that Job's name would perish from the earth, because he was wicked. So also the Jews wished to destroy the name of Jesus by crucifying Him, so that in its place the name of the robber Barabbas might arise. But their name perished and the name of Jesus remained glorified, and will be glorified forever. And what was directed against Job and against the Lord Christ the world continues to direct against the Church, that her name may be destroyed from the earth, bringing continual accusations against her. But the Church remains the holy Bride, her life bearing witness to the surpassing riches of God's grace, and enjoying fellowship of glory eternally.
"He has neither son nor descendant (heel) among his people, nor any survivor in his dwellings (nor any remaining in his habitations)" [19].

The spiritual man is a living witness to the Gospel of Christ, and gains many as offspring for himself in the Lord. The Apostle John calls those he serves "my little children." And the Apostle Paul speaks of his disciple Onesimus, saying: "whom I have begotten in my bonds" (Phlm 10). But the wicked man, even if he has many children according to the flesh, has no son or grandson who enjoys any wealth and bears his name and memory.
Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that this saying does not apply to the righteous Job, but to the wicked devil, as it applies to the antichrist who thinks he rules the whole world.

This saying applies to all the wicked, especially Judas, who betrayed his Lord because of his love of silver, for it was said of him: "For it is written in the book of Psalms, Let his habitation be desolate, and let no man dwell therein: and his bishoprick let another take" (Acts 1:20).
"O thou enemy, destructions are come to a perpetual end" (Ps 9:6).
"Let their habitation be desolate; and let none dwell in their tents" (Ps 69:25).

* ["He has neither son nor descendant among his people, nor any remnant in his sides"] [19]. For it is written that the Lord Jesus "shall consume with the spirit of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming" (2 Thess 2:8). And so, since his evil ends at the same time as the end of the world, [he has no offspring among his people], for he and his people together are driven on the same level to punishment. All the wicked who walked in evil by his evil counsel are struck by the brightness of the Lord's coming with eternal ruin, together with this their chief (Satan). He has no offspring remaining in the world, for the just Judge ends his evils at one time with the end of the world. Now these words are understood as specifically about the antichrist, since there was added to them: ["They that come after him shall be astonied at his day, and they of old shudder"] [20].
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* "But strangers dwell in his place" [19 LXX]. The blessings of the age to come have been prepared wholly for all, if they will walk in the way of God (Ps 25:10). Places there have been prepared for all (Jn 14:2-3), if they will be watchful. But those who do not walk in the way of God can open themselves so that they (demons or sins) may enter into them. Therefore he said: ["Strangers also live in his place"], meaning that those who walk in the way of God live far from the wicked (the evil spirits).
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem "They that come after him shall be astonied at his day, and they of old shudder" [20].

When the curse comes upon the wicked man and he falls into a sudden bitter change that no one expected, and of which neither those before him nor those after him had heard, they cry out in amazement: ["How terrible are Thy judgments, O Lord!"] (see Ps 66:3).

The element of surprise at what will befall the wicked, especially on the day of judgment, amazes the righteous who preceded him, and also his contemporaries. For however the distress that comes upon them is described, it cannot express what they will suffer. And in the same way with the righteous, for no human mind can imagine the glory prepared for them.

Perhaps, while speaking here of the wicked, he is speaking of the most dangerous of them, the antichrist, who appears as a king with authority, to whom many peoples submit, and who controls the outlets of the world, but he suddenly collapses when God sends help to His Church, and destruction comes upon the antichrist.

* ["They that come after him shall be astonied at his day, and they of old shudder"] [20]. For he (Satan) will be loosed to stand against the righteous with such evil, that the hearts of the chosen will be struck with no little terror. It is written: "insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect" (Mt 24:24). This was said clearly not because the chosen will fall, but because they will be terrified by fearful dangers.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* ["Those who come later groan deeply over him, and astonishment seizes those of old"] [20]. Bildad calls those who are made worthy to receive the wages at the eleventh hour (Mt 20:9), through repentance, the latecomers. Rightly they sigh over the wicked, asking themselves why these also did not desire to obtain spiritual prosperity through profitable repentance.
["And astonishment seizes those of old"], those who from the beginning fulfilled the commandments of God... meaning how even at the end of time these (the wicked) did not submit to God's commandment.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem "Surely such are the dwellings of the wicked, and this is the place of him that knoweth not God" [21].

This is what comes upon the dwellings of the wicked of desolation and ruin, misery and wretchedness. ["Those who know not God await vengeance"] (2 Thess 1:8). What is the dwelling of the wicked who persisted in not knowing God but eternal hell.

St. Hippolytus says in his treatise Against Plato, on the Cause of the Universe, if this work is authentic, that souls after death are led by a guardian angel to Hades, to a wide and dark place, where they remain until the day of resurrection, some of them wicked souls deserving temporary punishment for their wickedness, as a foretaste of the eternal punishment that awaits them. They remain beside the lake of fire which is hell, see its flame, smell its smoke, and are filled with terror because of the coming judgment, but the righteous are led to a place more radiant, and more joyful than the lower world, called "Abraham's bosom," where they enjoy fellowship with the angels and the patriarchs (the Fathers), and rejoice at seeing the reward to come.
St. John Chrysostom did not wish to speak of the location of hell other than that it is "outside this world." But he spoke in some detail of its torments. In one of his homilies he says of it:

[It is a sea of fire, not a sea of the same kind and dimensions as we know here, but greater and fiercer, with waves of fire, strange, terrifying fires. There is a great abyss there filled with terrifying flame. One can see fire coming out of it on every side like a ravening beast...
There none can resist, none can escape.
There the gentle face of Christ, the giver of peace, is seen nowhere.

And as those condemned to work in the mines are violent men, who no longer see their families but those who put them to forced labor, so it will be there, but not so simply, but far worse. For here a man can present a petition to the emperor asking for mercy, and the prisoner may be pardoned, but there this will not happen. They will not go out but remain, enduring torments that cannot be expressed.]

Again he says that the fires there do not consume the person, and give no light, but burn continually. For the resurrected bodies of the condemned are changed to incorruption, therefore they remain suffering torments eternally.

St. John Chrysostom sees that the degrees of torment in hell differ, depending on the extent of man's sins, but all fall under it eternally. He also says that God prepares hell so that no one may be cast into it(b).
* It is impossible that the torments of hell do not exist.
* These torments are not merely for the fulfillment of divine justice, but were established to urge mankind to repent and abstain from sin.
* If God is concerned that we not sin, and that we enter into troubles such as these for our correction, it is clear that He punishes sinners and crowns the righteous.

St. John Chrysostom * I wonder how man makes light of the fire on the day of judgment. They fear the flame of the furnace, and do not care about the fire of hell, as though it were nothing. Why are they so insensible and heedless of the matter? Why are their hearts so perverse?

St. Augustine * ["Is this also the place of those who know not the Lord?"] [21 LXX]. Who are those who did not accept this (place)? And how? The Only-Begotten Son declares this (place) to us plainly: "Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels: for I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me no drink" (Mt 25:41-42)... But you do not doubt that Bildad was able to understand this or utter it, for the natural law proclaims the judgment of God. All men, when they receive the natural law in their lives in a sound way, know what awaits the righteous and what awaits sinners. And also those who disobey cannot make excuse before the great and awesome Judge. But Bildad deserves blame and contempt all the more, because, while knowing what belongs to the wicked, he basely confused them with Job. In this he is like those who call fornicators chaste, the covetous righteous, and hypocrites humble...

As for us, let us distinguish the good from the wicked, and as we praise the righteous let us sanctify our words and cleanse our hearts. And at the same time let us consecrate our bodies and our souls and the temples of our souls with our zeal, together with our esteem for the righteous and our glorifying of God, who is pleased with the honor of His servants. To Him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * The gnashing of teeth (as the Lord described it in eternal hell) is not a gnashing of bodily teeth, nor is the worm a bodily one. These things were written only because the worm appears with severe fever (sickness), and so he who does not repent and is not cleansed of his sins will burn in his fire and be eaten by his worm (his works). Therefore Isaiah wrote: Walk in your fires, and in the sparks that ye have kindled (Isa 50:11). They are the fires of the dejection of sin and its result. It is like a worm, because the sins of the soul pierce the mind and heart, and eat the bowels of the conscience.

St. Ambrose * ["Surely such are the dwellings of the wicked, and this is the place of him that knoweth not God"] [21]. For he had said before: ["He drives him from light into darkness, and chases him out of the world"] [18]. And to his miseries there follows: ["Surely such are the dwellings of the wicked, and this is the place of him that knoweth not God."] He who now boasts of not knowing God is driven to his dwelling, when his wickedness thrusts him into woes, and he finds himself one day in the darkness of his place, while he made himself happy here in the false light of the righteous, and so occupied another's place. For the wicked in all that they do with deceit strive to gain for themselves the title "righteous," as those who occupy another's place. But then they are brought to their own place when they are tormented with eternal fire as the fruit of their iniquity.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
You are my life, and without You I have no life
* My God, You are the eternal Light, You enlighten my depths, and turn me into a light for the world; without You my lamp goes out, and my house turns into a tomb.
And I lose all warmth and life!
* Lead my soul, for You are the Way.
Without You I stumble in the darkness, I fall and do not rise.
By You I set out to heaven, and walk the journey of my life in safety!
* You are the Truth, in You I set out to true knowledge.
Without You I become like a straying beast.
Or like an animal without awareness.
I fall into the snares of the devil, and become a laughingstock to him!
Rescue me from the snares of the enemy, and I will be like a bird that escapes from a broken snare, flying in complete freedom!
* You are the Life.
Without You death possesses me.
It devours me, and there is no deliverer!
I live as in an unbearable hell.
Come, O Life, and fill my depths with Your peace!
* You are my treasure and my wealth.
I possess You, and so everything is in my hands.
I will not feel want, and no trial will be able to crush me.
* You are my Father!
You counted me a son to You!
I draw near to You, and I find You in my depths, not far from me.
Who can separate me from You?
Finally, grant me to possess You, O Holy One, and evil will flee from me, and the enemy will find no place in me.
Rather, let me taste the earnest of Your heavens!
* My God, You are my all!
You are my light, dispelling the darkness.
You are my mighty Leader.
You are the Truth that cannot be resisted!
You are the mystery of my salvation.
You are my treasure that cannot be stolen, and my wealth that cannot be taken from me.
You are my heavenly Father, You embrace me in Your arms!

1 Then Job answered and said, 2 How long will ye vex my soul, and break me in pieces with words? 3 These ten times have ye reproached me: ye are not ashamed that ye make yourselves strange to me. 4 And be it indeed that I have erred, mine error remaineth with myself. 5 If indeed ye will magnify yourselves against me, and plead against me my reproach: 6 Know now that God hath overthrown me, and hath compassed me with his net. 7 Behold, I cry out of wrong, but I am not heard: I cry aloud, but there is no judgment.
Then Job answered and said [1]:
How long will ye vex my soul, and break me in pieces with words [2]?

None of the bodily pains and calamities that befell Job held any psychological suffering like that which came upon his soul from his friends. The trials moved him to offer a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving to God, but the words of his friends crushed him. It is as though he cried out with the psalmist: "O Lord, heal me; for my bones are vexed" (Ps 6:2).

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem sees in the words of righteous Job here a rebuke addressed to his friends, who had almost destroyed his hope, which the devil had not been able to do to him. For the utmost that the enemy of good can do is to pour out upon him trials of bodily suffering that end in death. In all this Job does not care about the pains and does not fear death, since he sees in his battle with the devil that he receives a multitude of crowns as the trials increase. But his friends aimed their arrows not at his body, which will one day dissolve, but at his soul, to destroy his hope, and this is more dangerous. It is as though what the wicked friends did was more evil and more dangerous than what the enemy of good aimed against him.

The Holy Bible often speaks to us of the danger of violent words that shatter the soul, and it warns us as well of smooth words that hide a deadly, deceitful heart. The sharp tongue is a deadly arrow, and its blows are more dangerous than being killed by the sword or beaten with whips; and the lying tongue is set together with haughty eyes and hands that shed blood.
"Many have fallen by the edge of the sword: but not so many as have fallen by the tongue" (Sir 28:22).
"Their tongue is as an arrow shot out; it speaketh deceit: one speaketh peaceably to his neighbour with his mouth, but in heart he layeth his wait" (Jer 9:8).
"The stroke of the whip maketh marks in the flesh: but the stroke of the tongue breaketh the bones" (Sir 28:21).
"A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood" (Prov 6:17).
"A man of an ill tongue is dangerous in his city; and he that is rash in his talk shall be hated" (Sir 21:8).
"His mouth is full of cursing and deceit and fraud: under his tongue is mischief and vanity" (Ps 10:7).
"The Lord shall cut off all flattering lips, and the tongue that speaketh proud things" (Ps 12:3).
"My soul is among lions: and I lie even among them that are set on fire, even the sons of men, whose teeth are spears and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword" (Ps 57:4).
"Who will set a watch before my mouth, and a seal of wisdom upon my lips, that I fall not suddenly by them, and that my tongue destroy me not?" (Sir 22:33).

* The first commandment: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile" (Ps 34:13; 1 Pet 3:10). For the sin that the tongue causes is exceedingly active and many-sided, and it has its part in anger, vainglory, hypocrisy, condemnation and deceit. Would you have me list the many names of the sins of the tongue? For from the tongue come slander, mockery, extreme folly, false accusations, bitterness, oaths and false witness. The tongue is the inventor of all these evils and more.
St. Basil the Great * A horse cannot tame itself, and neither can a man do this. A man must necessarily tame a horse, and in the same way God must tame man.

St. Augustine * The sword kills the body, and the tongue kills the soul. The tongue knows no moderation: it is either very good or very evil. It is very good when it knows that Christ is God, and very evil when it denies this. Let no one deceive himself, thinking that he has never sinned, for I sin, and I do so with my tongue.
* The more the tongue sins, the more wretched it becomes!

St. Jerome * The practical proof of a sound mind and a perfect thought is that no error is found on our tongues, and that we keep our mouths shut when necessary. It is better that we be led by fitting speech, which is able to know and express the perfection of every praise. For the most useful of gifts is to be able to speak wisdom when talking about the good life. Evil speech must be foreign to the saints.

St. Cyril the Great * Guard the tip of your tongue, for it is like a royal steed. If a bridle is put in its mouth and you teach it to walk with discretion, it submits to this and is content. But if you leave it to run without restraint, it becomes a chariot for Satan and his angels.
* The tongue is a sharp sword. Let us not wound anyone with it, but rather cut with it the "gangrene" that is within us.

St. John Chrysostom * When the body is weary, I feel no pressing need; I count my pains as nothing, and I do not care for my body when this clay is spent and passes away. Do not torment my soul, and do not trouble my spirit, for since my soul carries a (spiritual) melody, my enemy is struck by it. I am victorious in the battle, and I do not fear the pains. But you crush me with your words, and you take from me the hope of obtaining the crowns, and you make me turn back my steps like one who has not run well.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Understand the words of the holy man as spoken at one time about his own person, at another time by the tongue of the Head (Christ), and at another time as a type of the universal Church.

Now the soul of the righteous man is in deep sorrow when people hurl words against him without having learned to practice the good life, and with words they ascribe righteousness to themselves, though in practice they are his enemies...

Job speaks about his own person, so as to speak, confessing, with the tongue of the universal Church: "But in truth I am ignorant, and my ignorance is with me" [4 Vulgate]. It is as though he says of the heretics: "All your knowledge is not with you, but against you, since it lifts you up in foolish pride. But my ignorance is with me, for it works on my behalf, since I do not presume to inquire into the things of God with pride of heart. Keep my soul in the truth, in the spirit of humility..."
Pope Gregory (the Great)

If the wounds of righteous Job were exceedingly bitter because of the harsh words of his friends, more than any other bitterness, then it is fitting for us, as believers who care for the safety of our brethren, their salvation and their joy in the Lord, not to utter wounding words, but to have good words that heal their wounds and comfort their hearts in the Lord. The Holy Bible urges us not only to guard against the sharp tongue, but also that God may grant us a gentle tongue that supports us and supports our brethren with its healing sweetness.
* The Apostle said this (Jas 3:8), not that we should be indulgent toward this evil of the tongue, but that we should ask for divine grace to tame our tongues.

St. Augustine * The fountain is the heart of man, the channel in which the water overflows is his speech, and the opening from which it comes out is his mouth. The sweet water is sound teaching, and the bitter water is that which is contrary to it.
Fr. Hilary, Bishop of Arles * It is a great thing to be able to control the tongue, for failure in this is the greatest of evils.
St. Cyril the Great "Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones" (Prov 16:24).
"He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour" (Ps 15:3).
"My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue is the pen of a ready writer" (Ps 45:1).
"A wholesome tongue is a tree of life: but perverseness therein is a breach in the spirit" (Prov 15:4).
"Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof" (Prov 18:21).
"By long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone" (Prov 25:15).
"Be not hasty in thy tongue, and in thy deeds slack and remiss" (Sir 4:34).
"Sweet language will multiply friends: and a fair-speaking tongue will increase kind greetings" (Sir 6:5).
"If she have kindness and meekness in her tongue, her husband is not like other men" (Sir 36:25).
"The flute and the psaltery make sweet melody: but a pleasant tongue is above them both" (Sir 40:21).
These ten times have ye reproached me.
Ye are not ashamed that ye make yourselves strange to me (rebuke me) [3].

They put him to shame by the evil qualities they ascribed to him and by what they accused him of, time after time, without hesitation. Their words were like a deadly sword and like heavy stones that crushed his soul. They were not ashamed to despise him, for they made themselves strangers to him and pretended not to know him (Job 2:12). They did not deal with him with the same familiarity they had in his prosperity. Therefore the wise man says: "A friend loveth at all times" (Prov 17:17).

They had spoken five times, and each of them multiplied his reproach, so Job counted what they had done to him, saying: "These ten times have ye reproached me." The number ten points to completeness in time, which is why the commandments in the Law are ten, signifying the believer's obligation to the commandment throughout the span of his life. Here it is as though he did not leave the friends a single moment of their sitting with him without its carrying a spirit of biting criticism and rebuke with which to put him to shame.

* "Only that ye may know that the Lord dealeth thus with me" [3 LXX]. He says: at least let the honour of Him who disciplines me change your view of me. For it is not fitting for you to trample on people whom God disciplines, but to sigh and grieve over such, especially since it is not fitting for anyone to rejoice at another's death, for this conduct is not left without punishment.
St. John Chrysostom And be it indeed that I have erred.
Mine error remaineth with myself [4]!

"And be it indeed that I have erred" means: suppose that your accusations are true and that I have indeed erred, whether through ignorance or mistake, for every man is exposed to this, and this touches my own life; for my error - if I err deliberately, with malice and deceit - remains with me and not with you, so why all this deadly attack?

Perhaps it means: if I am truly in the wrong and wicked, and I suffer because of my wickedness, and all these calamities have come upon me, leave me in my bitterness; why do you add pains to my pains?

* [You rise up against me], as though he says to them: "It would have been fitting for you, on the occasion of my being struck (by trials), to rise up against yourselves. This is the good ordering of rising up on the side of what is good, that we stand first against ourselves, and afterward against the wicked. We rise up against ourselves when we look at our evil works, and strike ourselves with the harsh punishment of remorse, and never leave ourselves in our sins, and are not partial toward ourselves by any foolish thought.

We must first track down our evils within us with severity. Then it is just that we rise up to resist evil in others for their benefit, and the evil that we punish in ourselves we apply also to others...

The wicked know nothing of this kind of rising up, for they leave themselves alone and attack the righteous... Therefore it was rightly said to the friends of blessed Job, who were haughty toward him while he was under punishment: [You rise up against me]. In other words, it was said to them: "You leave yourselves, who deserve blame, and you rebuke me with harsh expressions." For whoever does not judge himself first does not know how to judge others rightly... So it was said to those who acted deceitfully when they brought an adulteress to fall under judgment: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her" (Jn 8:7). For they came to punish the sins of others and left their own sins behind them.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* "Or how wilt thou say to thy brother, Let me pull out the mote out of thine eye; and, behold, a beam is in thine own eye? Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye"(a).

Remove hatred from yourself so that you may be able to correct the one you love. The Lord rightly says "Thou hypocrite," for only the man who loves may complain of the sins of others, whereas the wicked man, when he complains of others, is a hypocrite, since he shows himself in a form other than what he is... For there is a kind of pretenders who complain of the sins of others, such as hatred and grudge, with the aim of appearing to be men of counsel... Let us take care lest we fall into this. Likewise, if you are compelled to expose the faults of others or to rebuke them, let us look at ourselves to see whether we commit the same sins, or have committed them before. If we have not committed them, let us know that we are human beings exposed to sin. But if we have committed the sin before and have been freed from it, let us remember our weakness continually. Therefore we must hold love, not hatred, for those whose faults we expose... and let us take care lest we be occupied with their sins... Let us not blame the sinner or rebuke him, but grieve deeply over this state of ours, not asking him to obey us, but to strive together with us.

* We should use rebuke only rarely. And if we are compelled to use it, we must eagerly seek to serve God and not ourselves. Let us have one aim, so that we do nothing with a double heart. Let us take out of our eyes the beam of envy or malice or pretence, so that we may be able to see and take the mote out of our brother's eye. Let us look at the mote with the eyes of the dove, which belong to the bride of Christ (Song 1:4), whom God chose for Himself as a glorious Church, without spot or wrinkle, that is, pure, with no guile in her (Eph 27:5).

St. Augustine * Christians must strive... not to judge anyone, not even one of the adulteresses, nor the wicked who are notorious for their sins, nor the disorderly, but to regard the whole human race with simplicity of intention and a pure eye, so that a man becomes by his nature and foundation one who despises no one and neither judges nor hates anyone, nor even makes distinctions among people. If you see a one-eyed man, do not despise him in your heart, but give him the attention that is his due, which you would have given him if he had no defect... For true purity of heart is that when you see sinners or the weak, you pity their state and show them mercy. For this is what befits the saints of the Lord, that they sit in the watchtower (Hab 2:1; Isa 21:8), and behold the error and deceit of the world, and speak to God by the inner man.

St. Macarius the Great * Do not wrong a man, who is the image of God, because of the evil in him, for evil is an accident, a trial, an illness and a satanic deception, but his being, as the image of God, remains.
Fr. John of Kronstadt If indeed ye will magnify yourselves against me, and plead against me my reproach [5].

Job felt that they had not only taken an inhuman stand toward him and turned away from his friendship, but that they had truly exalted themselves over him, counted themselves higher than he, and magnified themselves against him to humiliate him. Instead of removing his reproach from him, they confirmed his reproach as proof of his lack of integrity, sincerity and perfection. They took from his disgrace an argument to establish his wickedness.

The proud Pharisee saw in the adulterous woman an unbearable uncleanness and an intolerable evil, so that he thought it too much for her to dare to enter his house. It was as though he wished he could drive out our Lord Jesus so that such as these would not enter with Him. But our Lord Jesus saw in her broken heart and the tears of her eyes much love, and so He forgave her many sins.

And the crowds saw in Zacchaeus, the chief of the tax collectors, a traitorous man, a lover of money, who did not deserve to live among them; but the Lord Christ saw in him his longing for salvation and for freedom from material things, so that he deserved the entrance of the Lord of glory not only into his house but into his very heart.

The look of our holy Lord Jesus, who loves the soul that confesses its blackness, is: [Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair] (Song 1:15). But her sisters look at her blackness, and so she rebuked them, saying: "Look not upon me, because I am black, because the sun hath looked upon me" (Song 1:6).

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem holds that blessed Job, to whose righteousness God bore witness, cannot have erred; he who received wisdom from above does not utter what is foreign to the truth; there are no vain thoughts in him. And yet, even if he had erred, it was not fitting for his friends to exalt themselves over him while he was in humiliation.

It is as though he says to them: "Why do you deal arrogantly with a man in humiliation? Why do you attack a person who has collapsed to the ground? Why do you hurt a person whom you ought to have pitied and prayed for? And suppose that you do exalt yourselves over me, why do you exalt yourselves over God? For His surpassing providence rests upon me."

St. Cyprian says: [It is pride and arrogance for anyone to dare to think himself able to do what God did not grant even to the apostles, supposing that he can distinguish the tares from the wheat... And whoever thinks that he chooses the vessels of gold and silver, and despises and casts out the vessels of wood and earthenware, though the wooden vessels are not burned except on the day of the Lord by the consuming divine fire, and the earthen vessels are not broken in pieces except by Him to whom a rod of iron was given.]

* The Lord counsels us not to judge anyone rashly or unjustly, because He wishes us to do everything with a simple heart that is always turned toward God. This is so since the disposition of one who judges others is to search out the sins of others in order to rebuke and condemn them, not to correct and train them in love... all this because of their pride or envy; therefore the Lord of glory added: "And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?"

So if your brother falls into the sin of anger, you fall into the sin of hatred (by your condemnation of him). And there is a vast difference between anger and hatred, as between the mote and the beam. For hatred is anger grown chronic; with the passing of time the mote (anger) has grown so strong that it is rightly called a beam (hatred). For if you are angry with a man, you surely desire his return to the truth, but if you hate him, you cannot long for his return.
St. Augustine Know now that God hath overthrown me, and hath compassed me with his net [6].
Perhaps he wanted to say that what befell him was by God's permission, so his life was torn down and he fell into a net, like game in a hunter's net, and there is no escape. Leave God to judge me...

Some see here an allusion to what the Persians, Romans and Goths were accustomed to do in their battles. In some Roman battles one soldier held his sword and shield while beside him another held a spear and a net. The latter made every effort to throw the net over his opponent's head, and if he succeeded in this, he immediately dragged him by the net wound about his neck, which had a snare in it, pulling him along the ground and striking him with the spear in his hand. Once the net was thrown over his head and he was inside it, he became helpless and powerless, and his fate was in the hand of the victor.
Behold, I cry out of wrong, but I am not heard.
I cry aloud, but there is no judgment [7].

Job felt as though God had taken a stand against him and that there was nothing to explain what had befallen him. He feels that he is under wrong, and here he calls upon God, and God does not answer. It is as though he says to them: why do you trouble my soul and crush it? Leave me to cry to my God and to press Him, and He will explain to me the cause of what has befallen me.

* [Behold, I cry out of wrong, but I am not heard] [7]. This concerns Him who said to the officer who struck Him: "If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil: but if well, why smitest thou me?" (Jn 18:23). It is clear that the judgment was neither upright nor just, for with the great number of judges, not one pronounced according to the truth.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Perhaps Job's cries here were a type of the cry of the Lord Christ in the midst of His sufferings on the Cross: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" (Ps 22:1; Mt 27:46; Mk 15:34)

* In His most tender humanity, and through the form of a servant that He has, we learn what we despise here in this life and what we hope for in eternity. In His very sufferings, in which His proud enemies thought they were victorious, He took the words of our weakness, where our sinful nature was crucified with Him (Rom 6:6), in order to destroy the body of sin, saying: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"... And this is how the psalm began that was sung long ago as a prophecy of His sufferings, and an announcement of the grace by which He raises up His believers and sets them free.

St. Augustine * Since He (the incarnate Divine Word) took a human soul, He took also the feelings of the soul. As God He was not in pain, but as man He was able to suffer. He died not as God but as man. It was in a human voice that He cried: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" As man He spoke on the Cross, bearing with Him our terror. For in the midst of dangers we respond as human beings, counting ourselves forsaken. Therefore as man He suffered and wept and was crucified.

St. Ambrose * He was forsaken, because His humanity had to pass through death. It must be carefully and precisely observed that He gave up the spirit with a loud cry after He drank from the sponge filled with vinegar and offered to Him on a reed (Mt 27:46-48)... The fact that it was offered to Him to drink from a sponge on a reed means that He took from the bodies of the Gentiles the sins that had destroyed eternity, and turned our sins to Himself, so that He might unite us with His immortality.
St. Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers

8 He hath fenced up my way that I cannot pass, and he hath set darkness in my paths. 9 He hath stripped me of my glory, and taken the crown from my head. 10 He hath destroyed me on every side, and I am gone: and mine hope hath he removed like a tree. 11 He hath also kindled his wrath against me, and he counteth me unto him as one of his enemies. 12 His troops come together, and raise up their way against me, and encamp round about my tabernacle.
He hath fenced up my way that I cannot pass, and he hath set darkness in my paths [8].

He began to comment on the bitterness that God had permitted for him, hoping they would have mercy on him and leave him. He portrays God as one who blocks his way, not allowing him to pass to escape even by death, and as one who has made his path darkness, so that he does not know where to go. He reproaches God and asks Him about the secret behind these events.

Perhaps Job expected, in the midst of all the hardness of their hearts and their harshness with deadly words, to find at least a little tenderness, so he wanted to stir them so that they would cease what they were doing to him and have pity on his state.

* [He hath fenced up my way round about me, so that I cannot by any means escape]. This is because of the cohort of Pilate's soldiers and the crowd of the Jews. They "encompassed" the Lord, pursuing Him, as Pilate ordered (Mt 27:26-27). Some spat in His face (Mt 27:30), others struck Him with their hands (Jn 19:3), and others beat Him. In any case He did not escape from the midst of the people who surrounded Him...
[He hath set darkness before my face]. There was darkness from the sixth hour until the ninth. He took away the light of day, so that creation might not see the unveiled face of the Creator.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * But the soldiers who gathered around Him were mocking Him. He became a laughingstock to them. "They look and shake their heads at me." His kingship appeared even in their mockery of Him, for they knelt before Him.

And before the Crucifixion the soldiers put on Him a robe of purple and a crown on His head. Why did they put a crown on Him, though it was of thorns? Because every king shows his kingship by means of his soldiers. So Jesus as King was crowned symbolically through the soldiers. For this reason the Scripture says in the Song of Songs: [Go forth, O ye daughters of Zion, and behold king Solomon with the crown wherewith his mother crowned him](b). The crown was a mystery, for He is the forgiver of sins and the remover of the curse.

Adam received this sentence: [Cursed is the ground for thy sake... thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee](c). For this reason it was fitting for Jesus to accept the thorns, so as to remove this sentence. And for this reason Jesus was buried in the earth, so that the earth that was cursed might receive the blessing instead of the curse.
St. Cyril of Jerusalem * The crucifiers stripped Him of His garments like shearers, but He was silent like the sheep before her shearer!
He left His garment in joy, so that those who went out of Paradise naked might put it on!
He clothes them with His garments and He Himself remains in mockery! For He knew that they were fit for exposed Adam!
They stripped off His garments and put on Him a scarlet robe, the colour of blood, that the slain Bridegroom might be adorned with it!
* They gave Him a reed to hold like a judge, and for their sake He was constrained to write the bill of divorce of the daughter of the Hebrews, because she hated Him!
She gave Him the reed to write her divorce, because she saw that He loves holiness greatly, like His Father.
* They blindfolded His eyes and mocked Him, and struck Him, and said to Him: Prophesy to us, who is it that smote thee!
They struck with the reed the exalted Head, and the angels were terrified!
With these corrupt and evil things they repaid Him in madness...!
They went mad in order to veil the face of the Sun of Righteousness, lest He shine, and the world see their corruption.
The foolish bride veiled the Bridegroom, lest He see her lewdness and corruption.
They veiled the Physician, lest He bind up their wounds and heal them!
Look at Christ, how much He endured from the wicked!
That fool, how did he dare to spit in His face!
St. Jacob of Serugh He hath stripped me of my glory, and taken the crown from my head [9].
It is as though God had taken from him his wealth and his former honour, and every opportunity for doing good, and his authority and his kingly crown, so that he became without strength.

Without doubt Job spoke these words in bitterness of heart, under the pressure of the severity of the trial, not in pride and arrogance against the judgments of God, but in bitterness and sorrow. For this reason, although the words seem to contain boldness, God looked to his meek spirit. As Pope Gregory (the Great) says: [He who ceases from his righteousness because of sorrow is not righteous, but blessed Job, because of his meek spirit, did not sin even in uttering harsh words. For if we say that he sinned by this saying, we make Satan to have achieved his purpose when he said: "Touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse thee to thy face" (Job 2:5).]

* "He hath stripped me of my glory" [9]. For there was need for the word of the prophet Isaiah to be fulfilled: [He hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him... his visage was so marred more than any man] (cf. Isa 53:2-3).
[And taken the crown from my head], so that they might prepare for Him a new crown made of thorns (Mt 27:29).

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * He says: "He has stripped me of my glory," because the glory of every man is his righteousness. Now just as a garment protects from the cold, so righteousness protects from death. Thus it is not unfitting to liken righteousness to a garment, for it was said by the prophet: "Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness" (Ps 132:9).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* They plaited a crown of thorns and put it on Him. This is fitting for Him, for He came to uproot the thorns from the earth!
He bore the curse of the earth by the crown that they placed on His head, and bore the weight of the whole world like a mighty one!
Sins and transgressions, pains, sufferings and blows were plaited into the crown and set on His head that He might bear them!
And by the thorns the curse of Adam was loosed!
He became a curse, so that the heirs who return might be blessed through Him.
By His crown He uprooted the accursed seed of the serpent!
By His crown of thorns and the curse of the earth that killed the generations... He removed the curse of Adam and his sweat!
By the crown of thorns He pulled down the crown of Satan, who wished to be god over creation!
By His crown of thorns He plaited a crown for the daughter of the Gentiles, the bride whom He betrothed from among the idols and wrote in His name!
* The great Saviour was scourged, and by the sentence issued by the governor He went out to be crucified!
He came to His own, and His own received Him not, but cast Him out from among them with mockery!
He went out to die with the wicked without any fault; then Judas - the lamp that was put out from among his companions - repented and was ashamed of the evil deed that he had done.

He who betrayed Him returned the silver to those who had seized Him, since he despised himself, and confessed that he had betrayed Him with evil... and the crucifiers also fled like those who are not near, and said: What is that to us? See thou to that.
The pure blood cast terror upon those who shed it, and they began to be afraid and to tremble before it even before they shed it!
St. Jacob of Serugh He hath destroyed me on every side, and I am gone: and mine hope hath he removed like a tree [10].

He did not merely leave him in a closed way, nor as a humiliated slave, but pulled down his whole being on every side. It is as though he were a tree that had been uprooted. He became torn down on every side, and the devil heard this complaint, he of whom he had said that God had set a hedge about him and about his house and about all that he had on every side (Job 1:10).

* "He hath destroyed me on every side, and I am gone" [10]. This was when the disciples who had formerly been at His side were scattered (Mk 14:50). As for Himself, He delivered Himself to those who seized Him; He went!

[And mine hope hath he removed like a tree]. He did not say that He uprooted it from its roots, but that He cut it off, for when a tree suffers somewhere above the roots, other trees come forth from the root after it is cut.

As soon as Christ was crucified, the hope that many had in Him was cut off, although He had spoken with His disciples before about His resurrection (Mt 16:21). Since they were troubled by His sufferings, they despaired of the Saviour.

This is exactly what happened when Cleopas said: "But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel" (Lk 24:21). The Saviour rebuked him firmly for reaching this degree of despair, when Christ said: "O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken" (Lk 24:25). And since He showed that there was no need to lose hope in Him, He added: "Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?" (Lk 24:26).

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Despair almost mastered Job when trials surrounded him on every side, and he became like a tree that had been cut down, yet its root stayed alive, so that it returns and puts forth small shoots that grow and flourish. As for the Lord Christ, all rose up against Him, He was sentenced to death, and those around Him almost lost hope in what they had expected of Him as the Saviour of Israel.

Now when tribulations surround the Church and some of the weak fall, some think that she fails in her mission. But God, who permits her troubles so that she appears like a tree cut down, is her support; He works by His Holy Spirit in her, so that she gains many through weakness, and remains in the world like the leaven that seems to have died in the midst of the dough, yet leavens the whole dough! So it is fitting for us not to lose hope, but always to rejoice in those who join her to enjoy eternal salvation, through the living word of God.

* The Church is torn down on every side as she is dissolved in her weak members, when those who appear to be strong perish. And the crown is taken from the head, in the sense that the eternal rewards are neglected by those who occupy the place of the head. Therefore he rightly adds, concerning the fall of the weak: "And mine hope hath he removed like a tree."
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Leaven is a small quantity, but it takes hold of the dough and spreads through all of it, and quickly passes on to it all its properties. The word of God works in us in a similar way, for when we receive it within us, it makes us holy and blameless.
St. Cyril the Great He hath also kindled his wrath against me, and he counteth me unto him as one of his enemies [11].

The wrath of God upon Job became like a fire that was kindled, and it blazed and burned him. It is as though he cries out with the psalmist: "Remove thy stroke away from me: I am consumed by the blow of thine hand" (Ps 39:10).

This is what was prefigured when Moses struck the rock with the rod. "Behold, I will stand before thee there upon the rock in Horeb; and thou shalt smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it, that the people may drink. And Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel" (Ex 17:6). It is said: "And Moses lifted up his hand, and with his rod he smote the rock twice: and the water came out abundantly, and the congregation drank, and their beasts also" (Num 20:11). Therefore the psalmist says: "He opened the rock, and the waters gushed out; they ran in the dry places like a river" (Ps 105:41). "Which turned the rock into a standing water, the flint into a fountain of waters" (Ps 114:8).

This is what the prophet Isaiah saw in the Lord Christ on the Cross, when he said: "Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed" (Isa 53:4-5).

* "He hath also kindled his wrath against me," by the condemnation of Adam. The new (Adam) came (1 Cor 15:45) to pay the debt (Col 2:14) of the old Adam. For this reason Job added: [And he counteth me unto him as one of his enemies]. It is clear that He demanded from me the debt that is upon the disobedient.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * To be sure that it is He Himself whom Moses saw, hear the testimony of Paul, who says: "For they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ" (1 Cor 4:10).
St. Cyril of Jerusalem * For those, water burst forth from the rock, but for you blood flows from Christ. The water was enough for them for an hour, but today He waters you for eternity.

St. Ambrose * Consider the word of the Creator and liken it to the rock that went with the people of Israel in the wilderness. It was not a reservoir of water that held within it what flowed out upon them in glorious streams. There was no water in the rock, but oceans welled up from it. Such is the act of the Word, who formed creatures out of nothing.

St. Ephrem the Syrian * Again the cloud rose up and led them to another place (Ex 17:1-7). But this place was a barren desert with burning sands, and there was not a drop of water in it. And here again thirst afflicted the people. But when Moses struck a protruding rock with his rod, it brought forth sweet water, good to drink, in greater abundance than all this great multitude needed.

* It is not difficult to reconcile the historical sequence with the spiritual contemplation. The man who left the Egyptians dead behind him in the water, and was purified by the wood, and delighted in the springs of the disciples, and rested in the shade of the palm trees, is indeed able to receive God. For the rock, as the Apostle says, is Jesus Christ. And this rock is hard and resistant to unbelievers, but if a man uses the rod of faith, the rock turns into water for the thirsty, and flows to those who receive the Lord Christ, for He says: "(I and my Father) will come unto him, and make our abode with him" (Jn 14:23).

St. Gregory of Nyssa * The rock was struck twice with the rod so that it might pour out water, because the Cross has two beams. All these things, then, were done as a type, and they have been revealed to us.
St. Augustine His troops come together, and raise up their way against me, and encamp round about my tabernacle [12].

The attack of the raiders upon him was by God's permission, so he called them "God's raiders" or "His troops." They came to him without hindrance and encamped around his tent without resistance. They besieged him like an army that deprives a city of provisions until it perishes of hunger and thirst!

* It often happens that evil spirits instil many things into the hearts of those who suffer, and along with the blows that come upon them from outside, they instil evil thoughts in their hearts, calling down the wrath of God. Therefore it is rightly added: [The robbers come together, and make themselves a way through me] (Job 19:12). His robbers are the evil spirits who are busy hunting for the death of men. These make themselves a way in the hearts of the sorrowful when they suffer from outside because of dangers, and do not cease to pour in evil thoughts as well. Of these it was said: "They encamp round about my tabernacle" (Job 19:12)... and that is when they surround the mind on every side with temptations...

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * It is strange: why does he speak of robbers (raiders) and add that they are his, showing that these raiders are ascribed to him? In this place we must distinguish between the authority of the evil spirits and their will, for this shows why he calls them "God's robbers." For the evil spirits always pant and run to do us harm, but they have no authority to harm us unless they receive permission from the supreme will. Of themselves they long to harm us unjustly, but by Almighty God they cannot harm anyone except through justice.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* The devil planned not to draw us away from the blessings that we have, but he tries to draw us to a steeper cliff. But God in His love did not fail to care for mankind.

He showed the devil how foolish he is in his attempts. He showed man the greatness of the care that God shows him, for by death He gave man eternal life. The devil drew man out of Paradise, and God led him to heaven. So the gain is far greater than the loss.
St. John Chrysostom * Satan's temptations are directed all the more against those who have been sanctified, because he longs all the more to gain victory over the righteous.
St. Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers

13 He hath put my brethren far from me, and mine acquaintance are verily estranged from me. 14 My kinsfolk have failed, and my familiar friends have forgotten me. 15 They that dwell in mine house, and my maids, count me for a stranger: I am an alien in their sight. 16 I called my servant, and he gave me no answer; I intreated him with my mouth. 17 My breath is strange to my wife, though I intreated for the children's sake of mine own body. 18 Yea, young children despised me; I arose, and they spake against me. 19 All my inward friends abhorred me: and they whom I loved are turned against me.
He hath put my brethren far from me, and mine acquaintance are verily estranged from me [13].
Our Lord Jesus Christ did not come into this world to reject the Jews, His own, but through their unbelief He opened the doors of faith to the Gentiles.

* [My brethren are gone far from me, and they that knew me are strangers to me] (Job 19:13) LXX. The grace of the Gospel bears witness to this... for John says of the Lord: "For neither did his brethren believe in him" (Jn 7:5), when they said to Him: "Depart hence, and go into Judaea, that thy disciples also may see the works that thou doest" (Jn 7:3-4). They said this because they did not know His power, [and they knew strangers more than Him]. This is what the Jews saw plainly.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Consider John's saying: "He came unto his own," not because of any need of Christ, for it is impossible for the divine Self to be in need, but He came for the sake of doing good to His own.

John made the blame of these Jews sharper when he said: "and his own received him not." Although Christ is the one who came to them for their benefit, they rejected Him, and they did not do this to Him only, but cast Him out of His vineyard and killed Him.

St. John Chrysostom * I will show this more easily when we bring forward the testimony of John, who says: [He came unto his own, and his own received him not] (Jn 1:11), for His brethren departed far from Him, and His acquaintances became strangers to Him. These are the Hebrews, who had the Law and were taught prophecy, and yet when He was present they did not know Him at all.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* He did not come with the aim of bringing about the unbelief of the Jews. But by His foreknowledge of what was to happen, He used beforehand the denial of the Jews and told us what would happen, namely the calling of the Gentiles to the faith.
The divine economy was wonderful... for He used the sin of the Jews to call the Gentiles into the Kingdom of God through Christ, though they were strangers from the covenants of promise (Eph 12:2).
Origen My kinsfolk have failed, and my familiar friends have forgotten me [14].

God permitted that his relatives and acquaintances should not return his love, but the spirit of kinship, brotherhood, friendship, kindness and tenderness departed from them. They gave him their backs and not their faces, forgot him as though he had no existence in their lives, and cared nothing for any blood relationship or old friendship. They failed him, since he lost all hope in them. They were not moved by all the calamities that had come upon him.

* Not only was there no one to soothe his pains, but many frustrated him on every side with mocking rebukes. For the nature of trials is not such that those who rebuke us for them should stir up and agitate our souls. You see the bitterness of his grief and his saying: "Even ye have fallen upon me" (Job 5:19) LXX. And he called them "cruel," saying: my kinsfolk have failed, and my servants have conspired against me, I called the sons of my concubines and they went far from me (cf. Job 19:14, 17)... Some mock, others rebuke, and some despise, not only enemies but even friends. Not only friends, but even servants, who not only mock and rebuke but are also disgusted with him. And this not for two or three days or ten days but for several months... He found no rest even at night, and the terrors of the night were more fearful than the trials of the day. He suffered what was bitter in his sleep; hear what he says: [Then thou scarest me with dreams, and terrifiest me through visions] (Job 14:7). What man of iron or heart of steel could endure such miseries?
St. John Chrysostom They that dwell in mine house, and my maids, count me for a stranger.
I am an alien in their sight [15].

Even those whom he had brought into his house as sojourners and maids counted him a stranger to them. Not one of them stretched out a hand to serve him in the midst of his severe illness. If he called one of his servants and asked him for something, he left him without answering him a word, though he had been a merciful master to them and had not refused their right in their cause against him (Job 31:13).

* "They that dwell in mine house, and my maids, count me for a stranger" [15]. This is about the incarnate Lord, whom those who had long before announced Him in the words of the Law refused to know and honour...
"I am an alien in their sight" [15]. For our Redeemer, since the synagogue did not recognize Him, became like a stranger in His own house.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
