* "No prophet is accepted in his own country" (Lk 4:24). Since Anathoth was the homeland of Jeremiah (Jer 11:21), it did not receive him well. And Isaiah and the rest of the prophets were rejected by their homeland, that is, the people of the circumcision... But we, who did not belong to the covenant but were strangers from the promise, received Moses and the prophets who announce Christ, we received them with all our hearts more than the Jews, who rejected Christ and did not accept the testimony concerning Him.
Origen I called my servant, and he gave me no answer.
I intreated him with my mouth [16].
He is the master, entreating the servant and begging him, and the servant does not care and pays him no attention.
* "I called my servant, and he gave me no answer" [16]. It is clear that (Christ) was speaking about Judas.

* "I intreated him with my mouth; I besought my wife" [17]. (Christ) is speaking about Jerusalem, for He betrothed her to Himself so that she might serve the Law. He entreated many times for her sake in order to save her. He besought her many times to change, until He said: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together... and ye would not!" (Mt 23:37).

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Who are the Jewish people but a "servant" who did not obey the Lord out of love as a son?... God calls us when He brings us near by His gifts, and we answer the call when we serve Him worthily according to the benefits that we receive.

"I intreated him with my mouth" [16]. It is as though He says more clearly: I Myself, who accepted My incarnation, gave commandments to be practised, by the mouth of the prophets, and I came to him incarnate, entreating him with My mouth. Thus when Matthew (the Evangelist) told of the commandments that (the Lord) delivered on the mountain, he said: [And he opened his mouth, and taught them] (Mt 5:2). It is as though he says plainly: then He opened His mouth, He who had opened before the mouths of the prophets.

So too it was said of Him by the bride who longs for His tenderness: "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth" (Song 1:2), through all the commandments that she learns by preaching. It is as though the holy Church receives the many kisses of His mouth. Now it was well said: "I intreated," since He appeared in the flesh, uttering the commandments of life in humility, as though seeking His servant who was full of pride, that perhaps he might come...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* O company of the Jews, when you come to Jerusalem and find that it has been laid waste and turned into dust and ashes, do not weep like children (1 Cor 14:20)(d). Do not grieve, but seek for yourselves a city in heaven instead of the one that you seek here on earth. Lift up your eyes, and you will find on high the Jerusalem which is free, which is the mother of us all (Gal 4:26).

Do not grieve over the absence of the temple here, and do not despair at your lack of a priest. For in heaven you will find an altar and the priests of the good things to come, after the order of Melchizedek, in their procession before God (Heb 5:10). For the love and mercy of the Lord willed to take from you the earthly inheritance, so that it might be possible for you to seek the heavenly.
Origen My breath is strange to my wife, and I am loathsome (and foul) to the children of my own body [17].
As for his wife, she could no longer bear to come near him or endure the smell of his sores. Although he treated her with conjugal love, she made light of him and despised him.

* "I besought the sons of my concubines" [17 LXX]. In the same way as we understand the servant to be the synagogue of the Jews, so also the concubines. As we spoke of the associates (Job 19:15) as being the scribes and Pharisees, on account of the Holy Scripture, so also here [the sons]. It is about this (the synagogue established for Christ) that the Jewish people cries out through the prophet Isaiah: "I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me" (Isa 1:2). Often I called them, lamenting, and rebuking in anger, and comforting, and correcting.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * "My wife shudders at my breath" [17]. What is this wife of the Lord but the synagogue of the Jews, subject to Him by the covenant of the Law in a carnal understanding? Now breath comes from the body, and unbelieving people understand the incarnation of the Lord in a carnal way, counting Him a mere man.

* "I besought the sons of my womb" [17]. God, who cannot be limited in a bodily way, is spoken of in such a manner, using members to show forth His power... Here the womb (the bowels) that conceives brings forth this life. Now what are we to understand by the "womb" but His counsel?
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* The prophet Zechariah took up the harp of the Spirit and ran before Him with prophetic hymns; with joy he tuned its strings and moved his voice, and said: "Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion"... Rejoice and cry out with the glory on high, for He comes to you as I told you by prophecy.

But the contemptible bride (the company of the Jews who refused to be His bride)... did not rejoice as she was called, but was crushed and grieved at the coming of the Bridegroom. And for this reason she did not rejoice in receiving Him.
Her heart was captured by the (golden) calf, her beloved, and with it she bargains, and she does not want to listen to the prophet who says to her: "Rejoice greatly."
She did not go out to carry branches with the children...!
The prophets knock at her high gates and awaken her, but she is asleep in her love for her many companions!
The children glorify the coming (heavenly) King and bless Him, while the old woman is busy cleaning her idols (their self-love and the pride of their hearts).
She grieved at the coming of the Father's heir. She knew that He would expose her, so she hated Him, and was not willing for the children to glorify Him!
Envy struck her mouth dumb, so she became mute, silent from glorifying, and was busy with silencing those who glorify!
It was not enough for her that she did not want to glorify; she also strove to silence those who glorify!
These glorified Him, but she was angry at their voices.
Isaiah cried out: Awake, awake, put on strength.
Zechariah cried out: Rejoice and be glad at the coming King.
The children cried out: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.
She listened neither to the prophets nor to the children, but grieved at their voices and was angry.
O Jews, haters of the light, how can you keep silent about the glorification that fills heaven and earth?
St. Jacob of Serugh Yea, young children despised me.
I arose, and they spake against me [18].

Perhaps he means here the children of his servants, who were born in his house and whom he counted as his own children; they mocked him and spoke evil against him. When he had authority over them he showed them all love, and when he lost his authority they insulted him and mocked him.

* [When I departed from them, they spake against me] [18]. It is as though the Lord drew near to the hearts of men when He wrought wonders for them. And it is as though He departed from them when He did not show them signs. But they spoke against the Lord as against one who had departed when they refused to submit to Him by faith... Moreover he added that the teachers of the Law and the Pharisees [and those whom he loved much are turned against him]. For by their readiness for unbelief they turned away from faith in the truth... and even persecuted Him.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
All my inward friends abhorred me: and they whom I loved are turned against me [19].
None of those around him offered him anything any longer but hatred; all the scales had been overturned.

entries.section: 4. The loss of anyone to show him tenderness

paragraphs.text: 20 My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth. 21 Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me. 22 Why do ye persecute me as God, and are not satisfied with my flesh?
My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth [20].

After complaining of what God had permitted for him, in that He hemmed in the way before him and besieged him so that he had no outlet, and kindled the fires of His wrath against him; stirred up strangers (raiders) against him and gave them power against him; and all his relatives, friends, household, servants and slaves took a stand of hatred - now he complains of his body, which had almost dissolved. His freshness, beauty and strength were gone from him, and no health was left in him, until his bone cleaved to his skin, and he became a skeleton. Even his skin had almost dissolved, so that nothing was left to him but the skin of his teeth.

* "My flesh is corrupted under my skin, and my bones are held by the teeth" [20]. It is understood from these words that he speaks of the mystery of the Lord, for the whole of humanity may fittingly be called "skin," especially the churches and their assemblies. In them and for them the body of the Lord did not see corruption, for His body would not see corruption (Ps 16:10). But in respect of the truth of His descent from the heavens for the sake of suffering, He shared in some way in the food of the pious. For Job is not speaking of a dissolution that belongs to corruption, but is speaking of the part of food (spiritual), for Christ became food that is offered and taken by our teeth. We could not have partaken of the Lord's body had He not willed to draw near to us and to let us taste His body.

entries.section: 4. The loss of anyone to show him tenderness

paragraphs.text: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me [21].

After giving the preceding painful description of his state, he asked his friends to have pity on him. He had fallen under the wrath of God, and this is the harshest of all calamities, so let them have pity on him and show him practical love by prayer and supplication to God for his sake, instead of their persecuting him.

* How noble Job was when he was in trial, for he said: "Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends" (Job 19:21). It is not a cry as from misery, but rather from one who reproaches. For when his friends rebuked him unjustly he answered them: [Have pity upon me, O my friends], that is, it was fitting for you to show tenderness, but you attacked and crushed a man on whom you should have had compassion in his sufferings for the sake of friendship.

St. Ambrose * Notice that he calls them "friends," those who insult him, for to pious minds what is against them is counted for their benefit. For any wicked man either is changed by the sweetness of the righteous, so that he turns back from his wickedness and thereby becomes a friend, or he holds fast to his wickedness and becomes a friend against his will...

Job was struck by Satan, and yet he did not ascribe the stroke to Satan but called it "the hand of God hath touched me," just as Satan himself said: "But put forth thine hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse thee to thy face" (Job 2:5). For the holy man knew that what Satan himself did from his own evil will, he received authority for not from himself, but from the Lord.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Friendship cannot be strong unless you are united with your friend and cleave to him by that love which the Holy Spirit, given to us, pours out.

* We must conform to all in order to gain all, following the Apostle, who said of himself: "I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some" (1 Cor 9:22). Be sorrowful with the sorrowful, for there is nothing that comforts a sorrowful man like seeing someone grieve with him over his hardship, and joyful with the joyful, and weak with the weak. But this accompaniment is necessary to help one's neighbour and to save him from his evil, not to share in his evil.

See how a man bends down to raise up with his hand one who has fallen; he does not fall with him in order to raise him, but stands firm with his feet on the ground lest he fall because of the one who has fallen, then stretches his hand to him a little, as far as he needs help, and thereby lifts him from his fall.

Let this be a fitting picture for us: we must bend down a little, and accompany them a short way in their circumstances, in order to save them from their falls and to gain them for God. But for this we must keep our hearts firm lest they draw us after them.

entries.section: 4. The loss of anyone to show him tenderness

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine Why do ye persecute me as God, and are not satisfied with my flesh? [22]

If God is pursuing him, it is for a reason that no one knows; is this not enough? Why do they also pursue him? God has absolute authority over him, and His wisdom surpasses all human thought, so why do they too bring distress upon him?
If they rejoiced in his calamities, let them be content with his flesh, which was about to dissolve completely; why do they wound his spirit and shatter his psyche?

* He did not say that God persecuted him in a way opposed to his godliness. For there is a good persecutor, as the Lord says of Himself by the lips of the prophet: [Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off] (Ps 101:5). And when the saint suffers the stroke he realizes that he suffers a persecution in return for the evil he committed inwardly...
It is as though he says: why do you persecute me for my weaknesses, as if you yourselves were without weakness in the likeness of God...?

He rightly added: [And are not satisfied with my flesh]. For the mind that hungers to punish its neighbour necessarily seeks to be satisfied with the flesh of another. Moreover it must be known that those who feed on slander of the life of others are surely those who [are satisfied with the flesh] of others. So Solomon says: "Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh" (Prov 23:20). For one who brings a body to eat it is, in the language of baseness, to tell what is bad in the features of the brethren, and his punishment is: "For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags" (Prov 23:21). Those who get drunk give themselves up to cups, but the gluttons are those who utter slanders, contributing with words, like one who contributes to providing supplies to be eaten... And as it is written: [Every talebearer shall be rooted out](e), but the sluggard (the sleeper) clothes a man with rags, and his death finds him an object of mockery, empty of all good works.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

When Fr. Dorotheus spoke about [not judging our neighbour], he spoke at length about our obligation not to usurp God's right of judgment, for He alone knows every soul, its strength and its inclinations, a man's gifts, his biological make-up and his abilities, and the circumstances that surround him. On the basis of all this it is He who condemns or justifies. We may indeed know a man who has committed a certain sin, perhaps one so clear that it needs no investigation, but can we judge the man as a whole because of a sin or sins that he committed at some time, when we do not know his depths or his circumstances?!

* God alone judges; it is for Him to justify and for Him to condemn. He knows the state of each one of us, our potentials and our deviations, our gifts, our circumstances and our dispositions, so He alone is to judge according to His unique knowledge. He judges the works of a bishop in one way, and the works of a superior in another; He judges an abbot of a monastery or his disciple differently; the old person (who has his experience and knowledge) differently from the one who seeks monasticism, and the sick differently from the one of sound health. Who can understand all these judgments except the Creator of all things, who knows all matters?

Fr. Dorotheus * See, my brethren, that the work of the servants at the wedding of the king's son (Mt 22) was nothing but to draw the good and the bad to the feast, and the Lord did not say of them that they judged those invited and distinguished between the good and the bad, nor did He say of them that they found one who had not on a wedding garment, but the king himself saw him; the master of the house alone discovered him and cast him out.
St. Augustine * Judging others is regarded as impudently robbing the divine right, while rebuking (without love) demolishes a man's soul.
St. John Climacus

23 Oh that my words were now written! oh that they were printed in a book! 24 That they were graven with an iron pen and lead in the rock for ever! 25 For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: 26 And though after my skin is destroyed, yet without my flesh shall I see God: 27 Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another; my reins yearn within me.
Oh that my words were now written!
Oh that they were printed in a book [23]!

The following expressions reveal the splendour of Job's life, his hope, his thoughts and his concepts, and they lead us to reconsider the interpretation of all that has gone before, for even his speeches that seemed to carry sharp reproach, and which many commentators criticized as having overstepped his bounds, came from a heart that longs to see God.

In all the words of dialogue in this Book between Job and his friends we find nothing more eloquent than what is before us now. He speaks to us wonderfully of the Lord Christ and of heaven as a better homeland. He speaks of his faith in God the living Redeemer, and of the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come.
In the preceding expressions we smell the scent of despair and cut-off hope, but here the Spirit of God lifts him up, enlightens his insight, and grants him life-giving words.

Some hold that from these moments we no longer hear murmuring or complaint against God or His divine providence as before. For this reason they hold that the Holy Spirit of God, who knew the sincerity of his heart, the truth of his intention and his faith, lifted him up and tore the veil before him so that he might know the mystery of salvation and God's surpassing love; so the tone of his speech changed completely, and his soul found rest in Him in the midst of his sufferings.

Before, he was faithful and truthful, but he fixed his eyes, his heart and his mind on his friends, so he fell into a kind of frustration and was occupied with defending himself against the accusations directed at him by his friends. But now the Spirit lifted him up as to heaven and brought him in as to the throne of grace, and he saw the Messiah the Saviour coming, and his soul found rest in Him.

He began with a delightful introduction that reveals his surpassing heavenly peace, which he longs for every believer to enjoy. Therefore he says: "Oh that my words were now written! oh that they were printed in a book!" It is as though he says: would that all would forget all that I said before; words came from me that were the fruit of my human wisdom and my human weakness, but now the Spirit of God leads me. Would that all might hear His voice with me and share with me in what I enjoy. I try to write it in letters, but words fail to express it. I will draw it in a book, perhaps the language of drawing will be more able than the language of letters!

* What prophecy is clearer than this? No one since the days of Christ has spoken plainly of the resurrection as he did (Job) before Christ. He longed that his words should remain for ever, that time should not blot them out, engraving them on a plate of lead and carving them on the rock (Job 19:23). He hopes for the resurrection. No, rather he saw Christ his Redeemer living, rising from the earth. The Lord had not yet died, and he saw the struggles of the Church, his Redeemer risen from the tomb. When he says: [And I shall put on again my skin, and see God in my flesh](f), I do not think he speaks as one who loves his body, since it had decayed and dissolved before his eyes, but in the certainty of his rising again, and through the consolations of the future he lit up his wretched present.
St. Jerome That they were graven with an iron pen and lead in the rock for ever [24].

He wishes to direct the words to all the coming generations, and that they should remain a constitution for mankind for ever. He longs that they be engraved on stone with an iron pen and then lead be poured into the engraving, so that time may not wear them away and they may not escape the eyes of any man. Let them be an inscribed monument bearing witness to God's work in the believer throughout the generations.

Records were kept in three ways: 1. By writing them in a book of cloth or skin or leaves of trees such as papyrus. From the latter word came the English word paper. Sometimes the inner bark of trees was used for writing. The Latin expression Liber was used for a book, and from it came the word "Library." 2. Lead tablets, which are very ancient. In 1699 Montfaucon bought in Rome a very ancient book made of lead: a collection of lead tablets fastened with lead nails and hinges. The book contains Egyptian Gnostic figures with Greek and Etruscan inscriptions.

In a temple in the city of Cnidus a monument of hell was found dating from the fourth century B.C., on which women appear depositing thin sheets of lead on which were written the names of the persons they hated together with their evil deeds. Curses that would fall on those who had wronged them were also engraved on the lead tablets. Many of these tablets were discovered in 1858 A.D. during the excavations in the ruins of the temple, and they are now deposited in the British Museum.

Righteous Job refers here to lead tablets or (tree) leaves with inscriptions on them. Perhaps he alludes here to the custom of engraving letters on stone and pouring molten lead into the engraving. 3. Stone monuments: the Law was engraved on two tablets of stone by the finger of God (Ex 31:18). Another set of two stones was written by Moses by divine command (Ex 34:4, 8). Also Joshua wrote a copy of the Law of Moses before the children of Israel on stones (Josh 8:32).
Job wanted his feelings to be engraved on stones so that coming generations might benefit from them.
For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth [25].

[I know that my redeemer liveth.] He believed in the coming Redeemer, and that He is his life. "And that he shall stand upon the earth (at the latter day)." He awaits the coming of the Messiah, the incarnate Word of God, who comes in the fullness of time incarnate to walk among us on our earth.
Some hold that he speaks here of His last coming, when He comes on the clouds, and meets us human beings as earthly creatures, and brings us into the fellowship of His glories.

The word [redeemer], as it appears in the Law (Lev 25:25), is the one who has the right to redeem what his brother has sold or pledged. Our heavenly inheritance was sold because of sin, and One came to restore it to us, redeeming it with His blood as the price. Our Christ is the living Redeemer, who alone is able to pay our debt, remove the pledge and restore to us the eternal inheritance.
He will come on the clouds, but as upon the earth, where He commands the dead, and they rise from their graves, and He brings them into immortality and incorruption.

* "For I know that he is eternal who saves me on the earth, he will raise up my skin which endures all these things" [25]. This is the reason Job said: [My words are written for the coming generations], for after the sufferings they will learn the resurrection... It is clear that the body that receives sufferings rises.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [I know that he is eternal, who saves me on the earth] [25]. This means that He who leads me on the earth is God. And what does this mean? If God is immortal, why do you want these words to be written, and their memory to remain for ever in an immortal way? Notice the state of the souls of those who are in distress. They seek not only eyewitnesses of it, but that those who come later should also become witnesses of their misfortunes, in a way by which they obtain sympathy from every side. It is like the case of the rich man mentioned in the Gospel (Lk 16:19), who thought that he wanted those on earth to know his distress and the state he had come to. These were those who in those days were in prosperity.

* [And I shall rise in the last day from the earth] [25]. This is because the resurrection that he announced in his own person He will one day bring about in us also... He gave us its pledge so that the members may follow the glory of their head (Christ). Our Redeemer passed through death, so we do not fear death. He showed the resurrection, so that we might have a firm hope that we too are able to rise.

St. John Chrysostom * This man in truth abstained from every evil work, for he did not allow the sin in him to master him, and when an unseemly thought rose in him he did not allow it to ascend to the head, and consequently did not allow it to be practised in act. For the presence of sin is one thing, and refusing to obey its desires is another.
St. Augustine And though after my skin is destroyed, yet without my flesh shall I see God [26].

Job was sure of the perishing of his body in the grave, and he spoke of it without concern: [and after my skin is destroyed here]. Without this body he sees God. It is as though he says to them: you have fixed your eyes on my body with all its afflictions, but I know that it will surely become food for worms, and even my skin will end like my flesh, but what delights my soul is that I see God.

St. Augustine holds that the word "skin" refers to our acceptance of death. The destruction of our skin points to our being rid of the state of inner mortification and inner corruption, that we may receive the resurrection of the soul and its incorruption. By this we enjoy the sight of the eternal, all-holy God. In other words, by the Holy Spirit of God we put off the works of our outer man until it perishes, and put on the works of the new man, who is after the image of his Creator, so that our Christ is revealed before our inner sight.
Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another; my reins yearn within me [27].

In the spirit of prophecy he beheld the coming of the Lord Christ, the incarnate Word of God, when He can be seen with the eyes of the body. He Himself, in His divinity, is not seen by the body, but the depths of the soul long for Him.
"Whom I shall see for myself," that is, I shall see Him and rejoice in Him, for He is the secret of my soul's happiness.

I shall see Him as He is (1 Jn 3:2) and not another. On the last day we shall see the Messiah, the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. He is the One for whom my soul groans within me in longing.

* Every mind is lifted up and shaped in prayer according to its purity. If it is concerned with material, earthly things, it carries this outlook before it, and this outlook remains before the inner eyes of its soul in its vision of the Lord Jesus, whether when He came in His humility in the flesh, or at His coming in His majesty. Such as these cannot see the Lord Jesus coming in His kingdom, for they are held by a kind of Jewish weakness (that is, the material outlook), and cannot say with the Apostle: "Yea, though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now henceforth know we him no more" (2 Cor 16:5).

But those who rise above earthly, lowly works and thoughts, and ascend the high mountain of solitude (seclusion), freed from the disturbance of all earthly troubles and thoughts, safe from the intrusion of sins, glorifying with strong faith, these can look with pure eyes upon His divinity, and in the heights of virtue they discover His glory and the image of His exaltation...

Jesus reveals Himself to those who are in the cities and villages and farms, that is, those who have work to do, but not with the splendour with which He appears to those who ascend with Him the aforementioned mountain of virtues... For in solitude (seclusion) God appeared to Moses and spoke with Elijah.
Fr. Isaac * Be careful of the purity of your body and the soundness of your heart, for if you make sure of obtaining them you will see God your Lord.
Mar Ephrem the Syrian
But ye should say, Why persecute we him?
Seeing the root of the matter is found in me [28].
Be ye afraid of the sword: for wrath bringeth the punishments of the sword.
That ye may know there is a judgment [29].
Job tells them what they ought to say: "Why persecute we him?" Why do we grieve him and provoke him by our criticism of his dealings, for the root of the matter is in me.
As he reveals his joy at seeing his Redeemer, whom his soul desires, he warns them to fear the day of His coming lest they be judged because of their judging of their brethren (Mt 7:1; Jas 2:1).

* [For ye say: What shall we say before him, and thus we find the root of the word in him] (Job 19:28) LXX. It is clear that under the influence of the work of the spirit of prophecy Job says this about the Pharisees and scribes and others in authority among the Jewish people. For they look to find something to say against Him (Mt 26:59)(g). That is, they wanted to find a pretext to criticize and blame Him, whether for His words or for His conduct. But what does He say to them? Do you beware of deceit? For since I uncover what is hidden and proclaim the mysteries, you deserve many chastisements not only because of your words but also because of your thoughts, so that you may not be asked about this afterward.

"For wrath will come upon the wicked, and then they will know where their being is" (Job 19:29). Who is wicked like the Jewish people, who crucified the Giver of the Law with lawbreakers, and killed Him among robbers (Mt 27:38), He who preached contempt for riches? But wrath came upon them, when the city was burned with fire, and the temple was destroyed, and their pride was extinguished...
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem
Who can support me but You!
* I believe that You are the Ruler of all; nothing will happen without Your will, or without Your permission.
* In the midst of my distress, I see even the members of my household turning into enemies.
I cry out to You from my depths:
Have You become an enemy to me, that You give me over to such distress?
How hard it is to see those who are mine become against me!
* In the midst of my trial, I was looking for tenderness from my loved ones!
The doors of their hearts were shut, that I might find the doors of Your heavens open before me.
In the midst of the bitterness of the trial I find sweetness in enjoying Your care.
* If the tongues of friends have become exceedingly biting, the tongues of Your own have turned into a deadly sword.
They aimed their accusations like spears against You!
If they stand against me, I remember how Your own stood against You, O Saviour of the whole world!
If they exalt themselves over me, who am dust and ashes, dust exalted itself over You, O Creator of heaven and earth!
If nets are wound about me, and snares are set in my path, the leaders conspired with the people against You!
* I often suffer from the feeling of isolation, but I see You, one with Your Father, crying out in my name:
My God, my God: why hast thou forsaken me?
Instead of the glory that by Your will You gave up for my sake, they put on You a crown of shame, and held You in contempt.
If they desire to kill me, I see You hanging on the Cross, and buried in the tomb, bearing me in Yourself, O Firstborn of the dead, so that I may pass through You into Your Father's bosom.
* At last I praise You and glorify You, You who have turned my bitter trial into the sweetness of contemplating You!
With every tribulation You carry me on the wings of the Spirit, that I may see You, and my soul rejoices!
Glory to You, who turn the crucible of trials into a new Mount Tabor.
I see You transfigured, occupied with nothing but speaking of the Cross, that I may ascend by it to You!

1 Then answered Zophar the Naamathite, and said, 2 Therefore do my thoughts cause me to answer, and for this I make haste. 3 I have heard the check of my reproach, and the spirit of my understanding causeth me to answer.
Then answered Zophar the Naamathite, and said [1]:
Therefore do my thoughts cause me to answer, and for this I make haste [2].
It seems that Zophar was greatly offended by what Job had said, and thought that he was justifying himself although Zophar was sure of his wickedness.

Zophar was vexed that Job spoke of his hope in heaven and of salvation as though he were a righteous and good man. So he attacked him violently, saying that his thoughts drove him to not remain silent about what Job had said, but to be obliged to answer him.

Zophar confessed that anxious thoughts had filled his mind and that agitation had mastered him. Perhaps here he expresses the inner turmoil and anger within himself and within his two companions. This anger stops the ears from hearing the truth, and the eyes from seeing the truth however plain it may be, so that they saw in Job nothing but a mass of hidden evils, covered with hypocrisy, false giving and feigned tenderness. This is what drove Zophar to biting criticism and harsh rebuke, and bitter threats of the evils that would befall Job.
* Anger lets the tongues loose and makes speech uncontrolled. Physical violence, acts of ridicule, abuse, accusations, beating and countless other evil deeds are born of anger and wrath.
St. Basil the Great * The sick mind does not control its judgments, and so it thinks that everything anger suggests to it is right.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
I have heard the check of my reproach.
And the spirit of my understanding causeth me to answer [3].
"I have heard the check of my reproach" is rendered by some: "I have heard you repel my rebuke."

They counted Job's words an insult, and that he was not worthy of their speaking to him or offering him counsel. Perhaps they had set it in their hearts to stop the dialogue, because it is of no use with an evil man like this. But Zophar's heart provoked him greatly, so he was compelled to speak.

entries.section: 2. The success of the wicked is temporary

paragraphs.text: 4 Knowest thou not this of old, since man was placed upon earth, 5 That the triumphing of the wicked is short, and the joy of the hypocrite but for a moment? 6 Though his excellency mount up to the heavens, and his head reach unto the clouds; 7 Yet he shall perish for ever like his own dung: they which have seen him shall say, Where is he? 8 He shall fly away as a dream, and shall not be found: yea, he shall be chased away as a vision of the night. 9 The eye also which saw him shall see him no more; neither shall his place any more behold him.
Knowest thou not this of old, since man was placed upon earth: [4]

Zophar resorted to Job's own knowledge before the trials came upon him, counting that it matched what they were saying to him, whereas now he objects to it and rejects it. It is a fixed principle that Job himself used to repeat before, and the experiences of the generations have confirmed it from of old. This truth is engraved in the mind of every man since the beginning of creation: the wickedness of the wicked destroys them.

* "Knowest thou not this of old, since man was placed upon earth?" By saying it in this manner Zophar abused Job, counting him ignorant of this truth (or ignoring it), although Job had declared it in particular in his next statement.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * It is clear that Zophar, puffed up with his knowledge, distorted the statements he made against the wicked, since his aim was to rebuke blessed Job. For he saw that Job had walked first in the straight ways and afterward suffered punishment, and so he counted all that he had seen before to have been practised by Job as a form of hypocrisy, for he did not believe that a righteous servant could fall into distress by a just God.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

What have we received since the fall of our first parents, Adam and Eve, except that we need the work of God, to tear down all evil in us, and to build all that befits His righteousness? So we should not wonder if God's call to His men is to root out and destroy, and to throw down the wicked peoples and corrupt kingdoms, which point to evil, in order to build and to plant what belongs to God, as it was said to the prophet Jeremiah at his call to service (Jer 1:10). Evil must be torn down for righteousness to stand; and if the wicked persist in clinging to evil, they perish with the evil.

We have no choice except between two things, with no third: either our depths are a divine garden bearing the fruit of the Holy Spirit that gladdens the heart of God, or a playground for the enemy of good to lie in and dwell. Either our hearts are a temple in which the Holy Spirit dwells, or a stage on which the enemy of good practises his evils!

* "To root out, and to pull down" (Jer 1:10). There is a building of Satan and there is a building of God. The building "upon the sand" is of Satan, because it is not founded on anything solid and firm, but the building "upon a rock" is of God. See what is said to the believers: "Ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building" (1 Cor 3:9).

So the word of God is directed [to the nations and to the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down]. If we root out and do not destroy the thing rooted out, that thing remains; and if we pull down but do not remove the foundation stones, what was pulled down still remains. It is a mark of God's goodness and love that after He roots out, He destroys, and after He pulls down, He wipes out what has been pulled down.

As for the things rooted out and destroyed, read carefully how they are destroyed: [Burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire, and gather the tares to be burned, and cast them into the fire](a). This is the manner of wiping out and destruction after the rooting out. Would you also see the destruction that comes upon corrupt buildings after they are pulled down? That house which was pulled down because of leprosy turns to dust, and then this dust is taken and cast outside the city (Lev 14:41), so that not one stone remains(b), as in the saying: [I will beat them small as the dirt in the streets](c), or (I will level them with the ground).

Corrupt things must not remain at all; rather they are destroyed to avoid using their remains in building new buildings that Satan makes, and corrupt things are rooted out so that Satan may not find in them other seeds to plant again; therefore they are destroyed, that there may be no opportunity for Satan to sow tares among the wheat...

Therefore the first thing is that we uproot and pluck out all that is evil from our souls; for God cannot build where there are corrupt and evil buildings. [For what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?](d) Evil must be rooted out from its foundation. The building of the evil one must be pulled down completely from our souls, so that the words of God may do the work of building and planting in us.

For I cannot understand that statement in any other way: "Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth"(e). Why? "To root out, and to pull down, and to destroy"(e). Yes, they are words that root out nations. Words to pull down kingdoms, but not the material kingdoms of this world; rather you must understand in a lofty way what is meant by the words that root out and the words that pull down.

And then power is granted from God, as it is written: [The Lord giveth the word: great was the company of those that published it](f), a power that roots out whatever unbelief (hypocrisy) or vice it meets. A power that destroys and pulls down if idols are found set up inside the heart, so that when the idol is pulled down a temple of the Lord is set up in its place, and in this temple the glory of God is seen and appears, and tares no longer grow, but a paradise of God in the temple of God, in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Origen How great is the difference between the planting of the enemy of good and the planting of the Lord, and between the building of the devil and the building of the Holy Spirit. The enemy of good sows grass, which appears quickly and dries quickly, and its portion is the fire. And the planting of the Lord is calm; He plants His Cross, the tree of life, in us, plants it by the streams of the Holy Spirit's waters, it bears fruit, and its fruit is eternal.

The success of the wicked is swift and temporary, but the success of the righteous is hidden, for trials surround them so that their crowns may shine all the more, and they may become bright stars accompanying the Sun of Righteousness in the very heaven.

entries.section: 2. The success of the wicked is temporary

paragraphs.text: That the triumphing of the wicked is short, and the joy of the hypocrite but for a moment! [5]

The triumph of the wicked will not last. They exult, but only for moments, then their shouting turns to wailing and lamentation. The wicked may prosper and feel secure, and you see them triumphant and glad, boasting of their wealth, power, greatness and success, but all this is for a time, and soon passes away in this world.

This principle is sound, but God has His judgments and dispensations, which differ with each person according to what is for his edification. On the other hand, Zophar was not pure in thought, nor was he defending a particular theological principle; most likely all he meant was to affirm Job's wickedness.

* "The mirth of the wicked is a sign of falling, and the joy of the hypocrite is destruction!" [5 LXX]. Zophar speaks in this statement with impudence, for he abuses Job severely and slanders him as his other two friends did. He blackened his reputation for the following reason: from the beginning, since the human race has existed, there has been joy and mirth over the fall of the wicked, and destruction for the ungodly, among whom is Job, as Zophar saw.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem The wicked lose not only their passing worldly joy, but even the earth grieves and mourns (Jer 12:4), and nature groans because of them, and heaven too with its angels grieves over them. This is the effect of evil, which deprives man of true joy, and because of it many groan over him.

* "How long shall the land mourn, and the herbs of every field wither, for the wickedness of them that dwell therein?" (Jer 12:4). The prophet speaks here as though the earth were a living being, saying that it mourns because of the wickedness of those who walk upon it.

For each one of us the earth is either mourning because of our wickedness or rejoicing because of our virtues. And what is said of the earth is said without doubt of all things. Likewise I can say that the angel in charge of the water (as an example) rejoices or mourns; we must know that for the whole universe to be ordered and administered, there is an angel in charge of the earth, another in charge of the water, another of the air and another of the fire. Lift up your mind to contemplate the order prevailing among the animals, the plants and the heavenly bodies; there is an angel in charge even of the sun, another of the moon, and others of the stars.
All these angels who accompany us throughout our life on earth either rejoice for us or mourn over us when we sin.

Jeremiah says that the earth mourns because of those who dwell in it: by the word "earth" he means the angel dwelling in it, for it was also said: "But the idol made with hands is cursed, as well as he that made it" (Wis 14:8), not that the curse falls on the lifeless thing itself, but by the word "idol" he means the devil dwelling in it, who takes the "idol" as his name. In the same way I can say that "earth" means the angel in charge of the earth, and "water" the angel in charge of the water, of which it is written: [The waters saw thee, O God, the waters saw thee; they were afraid: the depths also were troubled. The clouds poured out water: the skies sent out a sound: thine arrows also went abroad] (Ps 77:17-18).
* You, O sinner, must taste now this extreme bitterness that God brings upon you, so that you may turn back from your way and be saved.

entries.section: 2. The success of the wicked is temporary

paragraphs.text: Origen Though his excellency mount up to the heavens, and his head reach unto the clouds [6]

Zophar supposed that the success of the wicked man had reached a height that no one could imagine, rising even to heaven. And if he grew until it seemed that his head touched the clouds, such would be his loftiness and arrogance that no one would think of a man approaching him or taking a stand of resistance toward him.
* If you have committed a sin, your adversary is the word of God... It is the enemy of your will until the Word becomes the security of your salvation. What a saving and helping enemy!
St. Augustine Yet he shall perish for ever like his own dung.

entries.section: 2. The success of the wicked is temporary

paragraphs.text: They which have seen him shall say, Where is he? [7]

He who attains all this greatness perishes like his own dung (his excrement or manure). Those who were amazed at his indescribable greatness look at him, and behold, he is not there; he has perished completely! All that remains is his smell, which cannot be borne or endured.

* It is said of the pride of the hypocrite that it lifts him to heaven, as his haughty thought seems to lead him to the heavenly life. It is as though his head had reached the clouds, when the leading member, his thinking mind, is supposed to be equal to the merits of the saints who went before him. But [he shall perish at last like a dunghill], because at his death, when he is led to torments, being full of the dung of evil habits, he falls under the feet of the evil spirits. For the delights of the present life, which the wicked think a great good, the righteous look upon as dung. Therefore it is written: [A slothful man is pelted with the dung of oxen] (Sir 22:2). For whoever does not follow God becomes sluggish in the love of eternal life...
"They which have seen him shall say, Where is he?" [7]. This usually happens when the life of the hypocrite is exposed by all men in the end, to be an object of eternal judgment...

Those who saw him active in their days will say of him at his death: where is he? For he is no longer seen here, where he used to go about at large, nor is he found in the eternal rest where he was expected to be...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Observe these proud, reckless people, observe the ox being prepared for slaughter, left to roam in freedom, destroying what it wishes, until the day of its slaughter... Scripture refers to it elsewhere as a sacrifice, and says that it is left to an evil freedom (Prov 7:22).

* These flourish in the prosperity of this world, and perish by the power of God. They do not perish in the very thing in which they flourish; for they flourish for a time and perish eternally. They flourish in unreal goods and perish in real torments.

entries.section: 2. The success of the wicked is temporary

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine He shall fly away as a dream, and shall not be found: yea, he shall be chased away as a vision of the night [8].

He passes away with all the greatness, wealth and honour he has attained, and he is like a dream which a man searches for on waking and finds no trace of it; he becomes like a phantom that passed and has no existence!

* Such, my brethren, is our life, we who live a temporal life. Such is the game we play on earth. We came into being from nothing, and after we exist we dissolve. We are dreams without substance, visions not grasped, like a bird that passes and flies, and like a ship that leaves no trace on the sea (Wis 5:10-11); we are a speck of dust, a vapour, the morning dew, a flower that grows in a moment and in a moment withers. The days of man are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth (Ps 15:103).
Well did David, inspired by the Spirit, discuss our weakness, and say: [Make me to know the measure of my days](g), and he knew that the days of man are as a handbreadth (Job 39:4-5).
St. Gregory of Nazianzus * It is like a dream or a vision of the night. Zophar abuses Job with the same impudence.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * What is the life of the hypocrite but a vision of fantasy (daydreams) that appears in an outward show and possesses nothing in truth? Therefore it is justly likened to a dream, since every praise or glory is as though it had left him.

Often in "the vision of the night" some poor people are amazed to become rich, they see honours poured upon them, they see heaps of wealth, and crowds attending, garments of great beauty, and an abundance of food served to them... But suddenly, when they awake, they find the emptiness of all the joy they were feeling, and they grieve that they awoke, since real need forces them to wake. So it is with the minds of hypocrites: what they do is one thing, and what they appear to be before men is another... and while they are praised by men to excess, they think that what they delight in makes them famous among their fellow creatures.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* The Lord teaches us that whoever gives himself over to shameful works is stripped of a garment that is not made of wool but of living virtue, for the garment of virtue is eternal, not temporal.

entries.section: 2. The success of the wicked is temporary

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose The eye also which saw him shall see him no more; neither shall his place any more behold him [9].
Those who saw him as a very prominent figure, successful, rich and powerful, no longer see him. They look for him where he used to be, and behold, the place is completely empty of him.

* Although Zophar says this concerning all the wicked without referring to anyone, it is clear that he refers to Job in all his words. For the "eye" of his other friends and acquaintances left him in contempt, even though (their eyes) had seen beforehand all that was in the beginning, even when they look at him again.
"His place" means those who were originally with him in "his place," and from his country, no longer recognize him. For they see the extent of his prolonged sorrows and are struck dumb.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * What is the "place" of the hypocrite but the heart of those who flatter him? For he rests in the place where he finds those who love him... But as long as he lives he does not cease to teach his followers the very things he practises, and through the boldness of his sinful way he begets others also after the pattern of his own false deceit.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Evils remove a man from his place of rest, so that he becomes as though he did not exist. This is what happened with Korah and his company, who in their wickedness presumed against the divine commandment and wanted to seize the priesthood by force, and the earth swallowed them up, and they became as though they did not exist (Num 16:32).
* (Concerning Korah, Dathan and Abiram) They separated themselves from the holy congregation. The earth swallowed them alive, as a visible symbol of the invisible punishment.
St. Augustine

10 His children shall seek to please the poor, and his hands shall restore their goods. 11 His bones are full of the sin of his youth, which shall lie down with him in the dust. 12 Though wickedness be sweet in his mouth, though he hide it under his tongue; 13 Though he spare it, and forsake it not; but keep it still within his mouth: 14 Yet his meat in his bowels is turned, it is the gall of asps within him. 15 He hath swallowed down riches, and he shall vomit them up again: God shall cast them out of his belly. 16 He shall suck the poison of asps: the viper's tongue shall slay him. 17 He shall not see the rivers, the floods, the brooks of honey and butter. 18 That which he laboured for shall he restore, and shall not swallow it down: according to his substance shall the restitution be, and he shall not rejoice therein. 19 Because he hath oppressed and hath forsaken the poor; because he hath violently taken away an house which he builded not; 20 Surely he shall not feel quietness in his belly, he shall not save of that which he desired. 21 There shall none of his meat be left; therefore shall no man look for his goods. 22 In the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits: every hand of the wicked shall come upon him. 23 When he is about to fill his belly, God shall cast the fury of his wrath upon him, and shall rain it upon him while he is eating. 24 He shall flee from the iron weapon, and the bow of steel shall strike him through. 25 It is drawn, and cometh out of the body; yea, the glittering sword cometh out of his gall: terrors are upon him. 26 All darkness shall be hid in his secret places: a fire not blown shall consume him; it shall go ill with him that is left in his tabernacle. 27 The heaven shall reveal his iniquity; and the earth shall rise up against him. 28 The increase of his house shall depart, and his goods shall flow away in the day of his wrath. 29 This is the portion of a wicked man from God, and the heritage appointed unto him by God.
His children shall seek to please the poor, and his hands shall restore their goods [10].
Here he gives us examples of the evils that the hypocrite commits in secret in this world, and the punishment they bring upon him:

* "May the lowly ones destroy his sons" [10 LXX]. Perhaps Zophar in this manner refers to the demons, for they are "lowly" in relation to human beings, because of their fall from on high. For these are the ones who shattered and destroyed the house in which Job's children died (Job 1:19).
"And his hands kindle the fires of sorrow" when Job was scraping his sores with a potsherd.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * "His sons seek to please the poor." It is written: [Wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul] (Wis 1:4). And the psalmist declares: [The rich have lacked, and suffer hunger] (Ps 34:10). So the sons of the hypocrite [fall down in want] (Job 20:10), because those who are born in hypocrisy in superficiality, since they do not receive the substance of truth, become nothing, suffering from poverty of heart.
[And his hands restore his sorrow]. What does he mean by hands but works? So his hands restore his sorrow, because he reaps a just eternal judgment from his evil life.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* If anyone says that he does not want the Kingdom of God but seeks only eternal rest, he deceives himself. For there are two places and no third. If someone is not made worthy to reign with Christ, he will surely perish with the devil.
Caesarius, Bishop of Arles

11 His bones are full of the sin of his youth, which shall lie down with him in the dust. 12 Though wickedness be sweet in his mouth, though he hide it under his tongue; 13 Though he spare it, and forsake it not; but keep it still within his mouth: 14 Yet his meat in his bowels is turned, it is the gall of asps within him.
His bones are full of the sin of his youth (strength), which shall lie down with him in the dust [11].
He falls into the youthful passions that fill his bones, and they hold him and do not leave him until the day of his death.

* (Zophar thinks that) the corruption that issues from Job corrupts his bones with the decay of his body, and so spoils the beauty of Job's "youth." His bones sleep with him in the dust, for Job becomes dust from the pus and the dung of the dunghill where he was cast.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * What is the "youth" of the hypocrite but the beginning of the evil of his youth, when he longed and desired to embrace the passion of glory?... What he began with evil he increases daily and is strengthened through evil habit... Therefore it is written in Proverbs: "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it" (Prov 22:6). These very bones lie down with him in the dust, because evil practices continue with him until they draw him down to the dust of death.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* The body in itself is not an obstacle, but rather because of our wickedness we cannot inherit the Kingdom of God.
St. John Chrysostom Though wickedness be sweet in his mouth, though he hide it under his tongue [12].
He finds the passions sweet, so evil becomes sweet in his mouth, and he hides it under his tongue so that the pleasure may not leave him, as the choicest thing he finds.

* "Though wickedness be sweet in his mouth... but he cannot sustain it" [12]. In this statement Job is warned. He means that Job finds his wickedness sweet by his words, in other words, he covers it and hides it by his style, by the words with which he expresses himself... Thus he cannot sustain himself. Because of the evils that have come upon him he appears as a wicked man; and he rebukes him, since he wishes to hide his conduct from outside, and has not considered that it is impossible to hide it.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * "When evil becomes sweet in his mouth, he hides it under his tongue" [12]. Evil is sweet in the mouth of the hypocrite, since he finds evil sweet in his thought. For the mouth of the heart is the thought, as it is written: [Flattering lips speak with a double heart] (Ps 12:2). Now the sweet evil in the mouth of the hypocrite is hidden under the tongue, since the violence of evil conduct lies hidden in the mind, concealed under the soft garment of the mind...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Sins harm the soul with greater gravity than worms harm the body. And yet we do not perceive their corruption, nor do we feel the urgent need of being cleansed from them. It is like the drunkard who cannot tell how loathsome the taste of the wine is, while the sober man can easily discern it. So with sins: whoever lives soberly easily discerns the mire and corruption, but whoever lives in evil is like one drunk with strong drink and does not realize that he is sick. This is the worst thing about sin, that it does not allow those who fall into it to perceive the state of grave sickness they are in, but they are like those who lie in the mud and think that they are enjoying perfumes. They have not the slightest desire to be set free. And while the worms work in them, they boast like those who have precious stones. Therefore they do not want to kill (sin), but to revive it and multiply it until it carries them across to the worm in the life to come.
St. John Chrysostom Though he spare it, and forsake it not; but keep it still within his mouth [13].

If pleasure takes hold of him he hides it within him, as one who keeps it shut under his tongue. He is like the harlot of whom it was said: "Yet she multiplied her whoredoms, in calling to remembrance the days of her youth, wherein she had played the harlot" (Ezek 23:19).
Hiding the pleasure and keeping it under the tongue shows the effort he makes to conceal his desire, which is very dear to him.
But He who knows what is in the heart and the thought also knows what the wicked man hides, the pleasure he hides under his tongue.

* [He spares it, and forsakes it not, but keeps it within his throat] [13]. He spares the evil in which he delights. Since he does not practise repentance, it hunts him within. Therefore it is also added: [and forsakes it not], for if he had any thought of leaving it, he would not spare it but would pursue it closely. Now [he keeps it within his throat], for he holds it back in his thought, and will never utter it in his speech.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Yet his meat in his bowels is turned!
It is the gall of asps within him [14].

Since passion becomes his daily food that fills his bowels, it turns into a deadly poison in his depths. While he thinks that in pleasure lies the secret of his life and happiness, and that without it he has no life, behold, it strikes him dead with its poison that he hid within him.

* "His meat in his bowels is turned into the gall of asps within him" [14]. Zophar calls the poison of evil "the gall of the asp," for when the gall of the asp spreads in the bowels it can no longer be avoided, for it kills the one in whose bowels it spreads. This is plain and known to all. So the poison of evil works in all who conceal it.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * There are two kinds of food, one that serves salvation, and the other that suits the perishing... It is fitting that we not misuse the Father's gifts... let us use them in detachment and keep them under our control. Surely we were commanded to be masters and lords of food and not its slaves.

St. Clement of Alexandria * Bread in the belly is like being filled with earthly pleasures in the mind. Therefore let the hypocrite now be completely filled with the praise that he cannot resist! Let him revel in honours!

"His meat in his bowels is turned into the gall of asps" [14], because fullness with temporal pleasures turns on the day of final judgment into bitterness, so what passes here as praise of greatness is revealed to be "the gall of asps," that is, the swelling pride of evil spirits... The joy of temporal pleasure is sweet when it is tasted here by the chewing of the teeth, but it turns into bitterness in the belly when the joy passes and is swallowed to the destruction of the person.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
15 He hath swallowed down riches, and he shall vomit them up again: God shall cast them out of his belly. 16 He shall suck the poison of asps: the viper's tongue shall slay him.
He hath swallowed down riches, and he shall vomit them up again.
God shall cast them out of his belly [15].

In his love for the world he gathers riches and stores them, like one who swallows food greedily because he is hungry. There is in him no sufficiency or fullness, but it is said: "The horseleach hath two daughters, crying, Give, give. There are three things that are never satisfied, yea, four things say not, It is enough" (Prov 30:15). He is like one who fills his stomach, but constantly vomits up all that he ate, so that he remains hungry continually.

* "The wealth gathered unjustly he will vomit up"... For it is impossible to make amends without harm... the reward of the wicked is kept for the life to come (Col 3:25). Therefore what is gathered unjustly he will vomit up with great cries and great ruin of the soul, when the wealth gathered unjustly is demanded for judgment.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * The hypocrite desires to know the revelations of God, but does not practise them. He wants to speak wisdom, but does not live wisely. Therefore, since he does not practise what he knows he ought to do, he loses even what he knows. Since he does not join pure practice to his knowledge, despising the purity of true practice, he loses the knowledge itself. Therefore the wealth of the holy Law that he "swallowed" by reading, he vomits up by forgetting it, and God casts it out of his belly. In this, since he does not care to keep the practice, by a just judgment God uproots it from his memory, so that he refrains from keeping the commandments of God on his tongue, as long as he does not keep them in his life. So it was said by the prophet: "But unto the wicked God saith, What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth?" (Ps 50:16).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* The wicked are scattered in bitterness (like light chaff), while the righteous are saved like heavy wheat. Therefore notice what the Lord says to Peter: "Behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not" (Lk 22:31-32). Those who are scattered like chaff perish, but he who does not perish is like the seed that falls and grows and increases and brings forth much fruit (Lk 8:8)... Evil is likened to chaff, which burns quickly and turns to dust.
St. Ambrose He shall suck the poison of asps.
The viper's tongue shall slay him [16].

As the hypocrite draws from the love of the world, he sucks the poison of serpents against which no charm avails, and than which nothing is more deadly and fatal. This is what the lover of the world gathers for himself. He takes into his depths the serpent of sin, which kills him with its tongue.

* "The viper's tongue also shall slay him" [16]. This is he who from the beginning subjected Adam and Eve (Gen 3:4-5), and now does not cease to enslave sinners, teaching them to find pleasure in evil deeds.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * "He shall suck the poison of asps: the viper's tongue shall slay him" [16]... For at first (the unclean spirit) steals into them gently, but afterward he drags them away violently. So "he shall suck the poison of asps" where at first a hidden suggestion is offered that arises in the heart, but "the viper's tongue shall slay him" where afterward he kills the captive soul with the poison of violent temptation. Pope Gregory (the Great)

17 He shall not see the rivers, the floods, the brooks of honey and butter. 18 That which he laboured for shall he restore, and shall not swallow it down: according to his substance shall the restitution be, and he shall not rejoice therein.
He shall not see the rivers, the floods, the brooks of honey and butter [17].

* They do not see the gain from the flock that is pastured, and they do not receive milk and butter in the age to come. For they cannot enjoy pleasure in the things in which they boast here. For the instruction of such, the words of the Lord are fitting: [Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?] (Lk 12:20).

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [He shall not see the brooks of the river of honey and the rushing butter] [17]. The Lord says in the Gospel: "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water" (Jn 7:38). And the Evangelist continues: "(But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive.)" So the "channels of the river" are the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Love is a channel of the river, and faith is a channel of the river, and hope is a channel of the river. But no hypocrite loves God or his neighbour when he makes the glory of the world his goal, therefore he does not see the channels of the river, since he is not watered by the overflow of love.

The only-begotten Son of the Most High Father, who is God over all, became man among all, and, supplying us with the sweetness of His divine nature and the mystery of His incarnation, satisfied us with honey and butter.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Evils offer honey and milk or butter, hiding deadly poison. But our Christ, who forgives sins, offered us the honey of sweet peace, our inner peace with ourselves as with God and His angels and His saints. Deliverance from sin by the work of redemption restores us not to the garden of Eden with Adam and Eve, nor to Canaan that flows with milk and honey, but to surpassing reconciliation with heaven.
* Whoever seeks peace seeks Christ, for He is our peace (Col 1:20), who maketh both one (Eph 2:14), making peace by the blood of His cross, whether on earth or in heaven.
St. Basil the Great * The earth was split from heaven, and the angels became enemies to men, when they saw the Lord insulted by them...

What Christ did on the Cross was to lift up to heaven the (sinful) human nature that was in bondage to the evil one. Thus in fact He brought the enemy hated by the angels. Not only did He make what is on earth to be at peace, but He brought to them the one who had been their enemy. By this the peace became very deep. The angels appeared again on earth, because humanity on its part appeared in heaven.
St. John Chrysostom That which he laboured for shall he restore, and shall not swallow it down: according to his substance (and the gain of his merchandise) he shall not rejoice therein [18].

He expects to draw from the world as from brooks and channels that flow honey and milk, so he does not cease working night and day to store up the riches of the world. But soon he finds that he is poor, that he does not possess what he hoped for, and joy does not steal into him, for he finds no happiness in all that he has acquired.
Whoever gathers money unjustly returns what he gathered, willingly or unwillingly, so that nothing remains with him, but he becomes destitute.

* "He labours in vain and without profit, who clings to the wealth that he shall not taste" [18 LXX]. What is the use of the grandeur of a palace dripping with gold if the wicked man himself is buried six feet under (the earth)? What is the use of a multitude of festive garments and a variety of clothing to a person whom the worms strip?

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem The wicked man will discover that he came out of the world naked, because he does not put on Christ Himself, our righteousness. And his nakedness will be exposed on the day of judgment, and he will go off with the enemy of good, who stripped himself and his angels and his followers among the sons of men. All have lost what covered them with joy!
* His garment was taken from him (Joseph) (Gen 39:12), but he was not naked, because he was still covered with the garment of purity.
No one is naked except the man whose guilt is exposed.

In the first times we have this truth, that Adam, when he disobeyed the commandment of God and became indebted by a grave sin, became naked; for this reason he said: "I heard thy voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself" (Gen 3:10). Adam affirms that he is naked because he lost the adornment of divine protection. And he hid because he had not the garment of faith, which he cast aside by his disobedience.
You see an important truth: Adam was naked although he had not lost his robe, and Joseph had his garments taken from him, which he left in the hand of the adulteress, and was not naked.
Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles
Because he hath oppressed and hath forsaken the poor; because he hath violently taken away an house which he builded not [19].

In his love for the world he walks in a spirit of cruelty and injustice, so he crushes the poor and leaves them, and plunders houses and seizes them for himself, as Ahab seized the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, and so seized for himself death and shame.

When covetousness masters a man, not only does he not give from what he has to those in need, but he takes what belongs to another, so he breaks into the houses of the poor and strips them; he is not ashamed to shatter them by violence.
Whoever gives alms from money by which he wronged his brethren carries in his almsgiving neither spiritual love nor even human love, for he gives to one man and wrongs another.
* If you offer to God a part of what you acquired unjustly and by seizure, God will not accept your gift...

Rather have mercy on the one you wronged, doing him mercy and love, acting with goodness, and thereby you offer mercy and truth. For God does not share in our greed, nor does He share with robbers and plunderers; He is able to feed the poor whom He entrusted to us, but He seeks the fruits of righteousness and love for men.
Pope Athanasius the Apostolic * If you have seized money and given it to others... what is your excuse?
Would you know the measure of the evil you do? Hear what Solomon says, that whoever offers a sacrifice from the goods of the poor is like one who kills his son before his father's eyes!
St. John Chrysostom

20 Surely he shall not feel quietness in his belly, he shall not save of that which he desired. 21 There shall none of his meat be left; therefore shall no man look for his goods. 22 In the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits: every hand of the wicked shall come upon him. 23 When he is about to fill his belly, God shall cast the fury of his wrath upon him, and shall rain it upon him while he is eating. 24 He shall flee from the iron weapon, and the bow of steel shall strike him through. 25 It is drawn, and cometh out of the body; yea, the glittering sword cometh out of his gall: terrors are upon him. 26 All darkness shall be hid in his secret places: a fire not blown shall consume him; it shall go ill with him that is left in his tabernacle. 27 The heaven shall reveal his iniquity; and the earth shall rise up against him. 28 The increase of his house shall depart, and his goods shall flow away in the day of his wrath. 29 This is the portion of a wicked man from God, and the heritage appointed unto him by God.
Surely he shall not feel quietness in his belly, he shall not save of that which he desired [20].
In all his unceasing striving his depths (his belly) know no peace of mind (contentment), but anxiety besieges him and masters him. He may obtain much, but he himself is not saved.
* We must control the belly and keep it under the direction of heaven. For God will in the end destroy all that belongs to the belly, as the Apostle says.
St. Clement of Alexandria There shall none of his meat be left; therefore shall no man look for his goods [21].
What he obtained flees from him, like one who eats but is not satisfied by the food because he vomits it up...

* Because the wicked man eats without giving thanks (Rom 14:6), tastes without blessing, and the poor man has no place at his table (Lk 16:21). [He has no provision] [21]. Since the wicked man has no remnant, David himself adds: [The remnant of the wicked shall be utterly destroyed].
[His goods do not last]; why? Because his goods have no root, and they produce evil fruits.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * "His goods do not last"... because he runs after everything and does not fear the Judge, and when he departs from this life he goes naked to the Judge.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
In the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits.
Every hand of the wicked shall come upon him [22].

After Zophar described the perplexities that befall the cruel oppressor, he shows his complete ruin. For with obtaining what he desired in one way or another, the hands of the wretched turn to his paths. What he did is done to him. As his hand was unjust upon others, the hands of the wicked are stretched out against him.

* [In the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits] [22]. First he runs panting to heap up the things he gathers by covetousness, and when he has gathered very much, as in the belly of covetousness, "in the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits," for he is filled with anxiety about how to keep what he has obtained, so his fullness becomes the subject of his distress. When the field of a certain rich man brought forth a great harvest, and he had no place to store it, he said: [What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits? And he said, This will I do: I will pull down my barns, and build greater] (Lk 12:17-18). So this man, who was in straits with abundance of goods, said: "What shall I do?" He was in care, as though the multitude of food pressed upon him.

* "He is burned with the heat, and every woe falls upon him" [22]. After acquiring gifts of wealth, he achieves what he desired, and another disturbance comes to him. Fear and anxiety come upon him to keep safe what it cost him boundless troubles to obtain. On every side he is terrified of conspirators, and fears lest what he did to others be done to him. He fears lest he be subjected to violence by someone stronger than he. When he sees a poor man he looks at him as a thief. He fears the very things he has stored up, lest through the weakness of his inherited nature they be lost through neglect. In all these matters, because of the very fear of punishment, the wretched man suffers severely from fear of what he may suffer.
But it is a wonderful security for the heart that does not seek what is not ours, but is content with what it receives day by day.
Fr. Gregory (the Great)

* "When he reckons himself satisfied, he falls into anxiety" [22 LXX]. This means that fruit rots when it ripens. But as we have said many times, what Job's friends said was not to abase the wicked and the ungodly, but rather to shake Job's patience.

And since the wrestler bore the sorrows that had come upon him with a great soul, confident in the benefits that patience brings, he (Zophar) threatened him that the future would be worse than the past.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem *Truly, a man's life does not consist in his possessions, through the abundance he has; rather, he is counted blessed and possessed of a glorious hope who is rich toward God.
St. Cyril of Alexandria * When we gain a farthing we are filled with joy, and when we lose half a farthing we sink into sorrow.
St. Jerome When he is about to fill his belly, God shall cast the fury of his wrath upon him, and shall rain it upon him while he is eating [23].

Nothing stirs up the fury of God's wrath against a man like his wronging his brother. While he thinks that he is filling his belly by wronging his brother, the fury of divine wrath rains fire and brimstone upon him. "Upon the wicked he shall rain... fire and brimstone" (Ps 11:6).
It takes him by surprise in the moments of his enjoyment of feasts, as he takes his food. Perhaps Zophar is pointing here to the death of Job's sons and daughters while a feast was being held.

He also points here to what happened in the days of the Flood, and to the destruction that came upon Sodom and Gomorrah, as the Lord Christ says: "They did eat, they drank, they married wives, they were given in marriage, until the day that Noah entered into the ark, and the flood came, and destroyed them all. Likewise also as it was in the days of Lot; they did eat, they drank, they bought, they sold, they planted, they builded; but the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed them all" (Lk 17:27-29).

* [To fill his belly, so that God casts his wrath upon him, and rains his war upon him] [23]... [The rain of God's war] is the striking of hearts that exalt themselves against Him, and the wounding of the hateful soul with the arrows of His judgment... Whereas it would have been fitting for (the covetous man) to remind himself how he coveted what was not his, and with a greater evil set it in himself to gather the things he desired. And at another time he will grieve that he will be parted from the things he gathered.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
He shall flee from the iron weapon,
and the bow of steel shall strike him through [24].

Their destruction will be certain, without any possibility of escaping it. "He shall flee from the iron weapon." Fleeing points to iniquity, for the wicked man does not think of confessing his sins in humility before God to be reconciled with Him, but all he thinks of is escaping the vengeance that pursues him, yet in vain. For if he escapes the sword, "the bow of steel shall strike him through," or a bow of tempered steel. It is as though God uses the sword for those who think that they fight against Him by their own strength, and the bow for those who think that they are able to flee from Him by their cunning. For whoever thinks that he is able to escape one punishment finds another punishment pursuing him.
