* "Behold, I know your thoughts, and the devices which ye wrongfully imagine against me" [27]. As it is written: "For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him?" (1 Cor 2:11)... But the spirit of man is unknown to others unless it appears in words or deeds. It is written: "By their fruits ye shall know them" (Mt 7:20). By what happens outside, what is hidden within is seen. So also it was rightly said of Solomon: [As faces shine in water, so the hearts of men are clear to the wise] (Prov 27:19)...
Pope Gregory (the Great)
For ye say, Where is the house of the prince?
and where are the dwelling places of the wicked? [28]

As though he says to them: I know that you will answer me saying: Where is the house of the usurper? Where is the tent of the wicked? And you mean me by the usurper as you mean my sons by the wicked. You judge me to be a tyrant, and my children wicked.

If we remove the evil intention of Job's friends, and their desperate attempt to distort his character, then what they say does apply to ruthless tyrants and usurpers. For though they live all their days in wealth, honor and authority, they die and return to their dust. Then it is rightly said: "Where is the house of the prince?" He who thinks that the whole world is his settled house, which he controls and governs as the master of a house who lives in it forever, and none can drive him out or pull down the house. Tyrants through the generations died who counted themselves gods, but they became dust, and their kingdoms were utterly overthrown. In folly they lived in the world as in unstable tents, and behold, the tents have vanished and their authority has vanished with them.

* It is said of the wicked after their death: "Where are the dwelling places of the wicked?" If we look closely at this, can you deny that there is recompense from divine justice? The first (the righteous) has happiness flooding his heart, and the second misery. The first by the witness of his own soul is innocent of guilt, and the second a criminal. That man is happy in his departure from the world, and the second is sorrowful over it. Who can pronounce innocence on one who is not innocent in the eyes of his own conscience? He says: [Where is the covering of his tent, his memorial shall not be found] (cf. Job 21:28). The life of the criminal is a dream. No, even the very rest of the wicked while they live here is an illusion; they are now in hell, for they go down to Gehenna while still alive.
St. Ambrose * The weak desire success in the wealth of the world, and fear blows as though they were exceedingly grave evils, and they stumble at the punishment of those whom they see struck.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"Have ye not asked them that go by the way? and do ye not know their tokens?" [29]
That the wicked is reserved to the day of destruction? they shall be brought forth to the day of wrath. [30]
Job knows that dialogue is futile with people who do not bear a sincere and honest intention, so he asks them to question any neutral person. Ask those who pass by the road, whoever they may be.

He did not say ask the saints as Eliphaz said (Job 5:1), for the matter does not even need the experiences of the saints, but is known to every unbiased person, since all humanity agrees with Job that sinners do not necessarily receive their recompense here, but it may be deferred to the great day of the Lord. [When the wicked flourish, it is that they shall be destroyed for ever] (Ps 92:7).

Perhaps by his calling them to ask any passerby he means that they should look for anyone who perceives the truth of this temporal life as a passing road, for such a man will surely speak the truth, with wisdom and sincerity. A man's perceiving the truth of his life, that it is a passing as over a bridge, gives him a realistic view of temporal life and the eternal life to come, so his judgment of matters is balanced and true!

*He calls [one who passes by the way] him who holds in his mind that the present life is for him a road and not a homeland. He counts it a base thing for him to fix his heart in love of the present passing state, longing not to remain occupied with viewing temporal things, but to reach with his heart the eternal world...

When Moses sought the glory of heavenly contemplation he said: "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight" (Ex 3:3). For unless he withdraws the traces of his feet from the love of the world he cannot understand the things above.

When Jeremiah besought that the sorrow of his heart be considered he said: "All ye that pass by the way, behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow" (Lam 1:12). For those who do not pass through the present life as through a road, but think it their homeland, have no experience to see with the eyes of the mind the sorrow of the heart of the elect. Does the prophet look to them that they may see his sorrow?
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Who shall declare his way to his face? and who shall repay him what he hath done? [31]

The wicked man bears a kind of boldness and might, so he finds none to stand before him and confront him with his wickedness, nor anyone to punish him for his deeds. He sins and plunders while secure. No one rebukes him or terrifies him. The wise man says: [the prosperity of fools shall destroy them] (Prov 1:22), as they count themselves above the law, with none able to confront them with their wickedness, or to move them toward repentance and return to the true God.

Pope Gregory (the Great) noted that Job turned his speech about the wicked from the plural form to the singular. He sees in the plural (the wicked) a reference to human beings who have become like many members of the body of the devil, and in the singular (the wicked man) a reference to the devil as the head of the wicked. As believers are members of the body of Christ, the holy Head, so the wicked are members of the body of the devil, the evil head!

* "Who will denounce his way to his face? and who will repay him for his work?" [31]... While Job was speaking of all the wicked, suddenly he turned his words to the head of all the wicked. For he saw, at the end of the world, Satan entering into a man, whom Holy Scripture calls "the antichrist," who exalts himself proudly, supported by such authority as to be lifted up with signs and wonders displaying a (deceptive) holiness, and who cannot be accused by any man. By the authority of terror he unites the signs of outward holiness. He says: "Who will denounce his way to his face?" meaning, who of mankind dares and rebukes him...? But Elijah and Enoch alone will be present at once to rebuke him. Then all the elect will rebuke his way to his face, showing contempt; and while he is proud in thought they resist his evil. And since they do this by divine grace and not by their own strength, it is rightly said now: "Who will denounce his way to his face?" Who does this but God, by whose help the elect receive authority to stand before him? For the Lord alone can do that by His power. Rightly it is said of him: [Whom the Lord shall consume with the spirit of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming] (2 Thess 2:8)...
[Who will repay him for his work?] Truly who but the Lord, who alone will repay that perishing man for what he does with eternal judgment?
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Yet shall he be brought to the grave, and shall remain in the tomb [32].

The wicked man knows that he will surely die like the rest of men, but he prepares greatness for himself even in his death, so he sets up a memorial monument over the grave he prepares for himself, and arranges a splendid funeral procession for himself.

While many of the wicked care for temporal honor even after their passing from this world, caring for their bodies after death or the tomb or the erection of a memorial to them, the righteous are occupied with nothing but meeting the heavenly Bridegroom. They long to depart to be with Christ, which is better for them than every work however valuable.

* "He shall be brought to the graves, and shall keep watch over the heap of dead bodies" [32]... There are few righteous in the world and a multitude of the wicked. Therefore it is rightly said: "heap of dead bodies," as it points to the multitude of the wicked. "Because wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat" (Mt 7:13). Thus Satan keeps watch over the heap of dead bodies, practicing the deceits of his wickedness in the hearts of the sons of perdition.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
The clods of the valley shall be sweet unto him (the mud of the valley).
and every man shall draw after him, as there are innumerable before him [33].
As he refers to the antichrist as the representative of the evil devil, who sets himself up as God in the temple of the Lord, Job sees him as nothing but a mortal man who becomes dust and ashes.

By his saying [the clods of the valley shall be sweet unto him], Job sees that his death and return to dust is better for him than his life, because he usurps divine glory, and counts himself immortal, and leads a movement of rebellion and persecution against the Church of the Lord Christ.

Perhaps he points here to the wicked man's preparing everything for the embalming of his body and the pouring of spices on his corpse though he has nothing but the clods of the valley in which he is buried. He takes no warning from death, and does not remember that he is not the only one who faces death, but countless numbers have preceded him, and every man will come after him; all die without exception.

* "He draws every man after him, and there are innumerable before him" [33]. In this place the word "man" means one who tastes human things... Our ancient enemy, entering the man of perdition, draws all the carnal whom he finds under the yoke of his authority.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
How then comfort ye me in vain, seeing in your answers there remaineth falsehood? [34].
Job ends his speech by returning to the plural form, that is, to speaking with the wicked. What befalls the wicked of destruction and ruin will not exempt them from judgment.
If the wicked claim to desire to comfort the suffering, their consolation is vain.

Job rejects their dialogue and their arguments because they come from insincere hearts, but carry a spirit of betrayal of friendship, and because their claims are vain, as they concentrate on his repentance so that he might enjoy returning to the state of prosperity he was in before the calamities came.
There is no room for consolation when it comes from hearts that bear no love!

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the dialogue of these friends caused him pains, and instead of binding up his wounds the wounds increased. On one side the righteous man suffers from their lack of faithfulness and sincerity, not because of the accusations in themselves, but because of their insincerity and the betrayal of the friendship that existed between him and them.

His soul suffers and is embittered, because he is a lover of the truth and desires the salvation of all, and finds the odor of the sin of death rising from their depths. His soul groans over their destruction more than his bitterness over the accusations directed against him!

* "How then comfort ye me in vain, seeing your answers show that they are against the truth" [34]. Job's friends were not able to comfort him, they who in their dialogue oppose the truth. When they called him a hypocrite or wicked they committed the crime of the sin of lying, and surely added troubles to the righteous man, and to his wounds. For the minds of the saints, being subject to the truth, suffer because of the sins of deceiving others. As much as they strongly perceive that the crime of falsehood is grave, they hate it not only if they commit it but also if others commit it.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
My soul trembles at the destruction of the wicked!
* Many are occupied with asking: Why does God prosper the way of the wicked?
But what occupies me is their eternity!
Yes, the wicked may prosper and flourish, they may enjoy positions of power!
They think they are secure, and that they are above every law!
All that is around them gives them reassurance and peace.
* My soul grieves not at their success, but because they insult God's longsuffering and forbearance.
They count worship a waste of their time and energies.
Their life is not in the hand of the Almighty.
But I see their lamp suddenly go out.
* My heart groans as it sees them like stubble before the wind, and like chaff in the midst of a whirlwind!
Their days pass like a passing moment, their tents collapse completely.
* I wonder how they will stand before the judgment seat?
Wretched are those who have lost the glory!
They ask the mountains to fall on them, and the hills to cover them!
With Jeremiah the prophet I cry:
The walls of my heart pain me!
It is melted like wax within me.
My evils give me a momentary pleasure, accompanied by destruction of my whole being.

entries.section: 1. The accusation that he criticizes God's actions

paragraphs.text: 1 Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said, 2 "Can a man be profitable unto God, as he that is wise may be profitable unto himself? 3 Is it any pleasure to the Almighty, that thou art righteous? or is it gain to him, that thou makest thy ways perfect? 4 Will he reprove thee for thy piety? will he enter with thee into judgment?"
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said [1]:
"Can a man be profitable unto God,

entries.section: 1. The accusation that he criticizes God's actions

paragraphs.text: as he that is wise may be profitable unto himself?" [2]

Previously the three friends accused Job of hypocrisy, since they could not find any sin they could lay hold of against him. They insisted that he must certainly have been a hypocrite who did evil in secret. The sign of his hypocrisy, in their view, was that the successive calamities that had befallen him were a sign of God's anger against him. Now Eliphaz sets out a series of accusations, the first of which he tried to draw out of Job's words during the dialogue by interpreting them from their own point of view. The first of these accusations is that Job complains of God's actions and criticizes them, as though he were judging God to be unjust.
In Eliphaz's view, Job's complaint about the multitude of his calamities amounts to accusing God of injustice. This is a false accusation, for Job was as far as could be from thinking in this way.

If we set aside Eliphaz's intention in accusing Job, his speech carries a true side: that God is not in need of man's righteousness and has no benefit in it, but the benefit falls upon man, who is the object of God's love, concern and care. Prudence, or wisdom, is for the building up of man, and the source of wisdom is God.
"But wisdom is profitable to direct" (Eccl 10:10). "Godliness is profitable unto all things" (1 Tim 4:8). "If thou be wise, thou shalt be wise for thyself" (Prov 9:12).

* "Can a man be compared with God, even if he has perfect knowledge?" [2] Those who sink to the depths in bringing certain accusations, since they contradict the words of truth, often repeat what is well known, lest by holding their tongue they should seem to be defeated. So Eliphaz, pressed by the words of blessed Job, uttered things known to everyone.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* The wicked man strikes himself first, indeed he strikes no one but himself, for it is said: [He alone shall bear it] (see Prov 9:12). His soul is always full of grief, and his thoughts are always tangled, whether concerning what he hears or what he says. He does everything while complaining, bringing accusations.

entries.section: 1. The accusation that he criticizes God's actions

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom "Is it any pleasure to the Almighty, that thou art righteous? or is it gain to him, that thou makest thy ways perfect?" [3]

Man, in his weakness and limitation, is unable to offer any benefit to God, the all-perfect, who increases in nothing. Can a candle benefit the sun in any way? Can a drop of water in a cup affect the ocean?

If our ways became perfect in every respect, could they benefit God? And what pleasure would that Almighty One have if we became righteous? He is the source of peace, blessedness and joy. If He tells us in our human language that He is pleased with us, this only reveals His love for us and His longing for our salvation and glory, without His benefiting in anything of His own from our righteousness and sanctification.

* "Is there any profit to God if you are righteous? Or any gain if you set your ways right?" [3] In all this we do well, working for our own good, not for the good of God. Therefore it is said by the Psalmist: [O my soul, say to the Lord: You are my God, You have no need of my goods] (Ps 16:2). He is truly our Lord, for He is also certainly the God who has no need of anyone to serve Him, but who returns the good that He receives, so that the good things that are offered do not profit Him but those who first received them, and return again to them. The Lord says at His coming for the judgment: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me" (Mt 25:40). He says this with surpassing tenderness and sympathy for His members.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* If He did not love us, why did He create us? Is He in need of us? Do we supply Him with anything? By what service? Does He need something that we offer Him? Hear what the prophet says: [I said to the Lord, You are my Lord, my good is nothing apart from You] (Ps 16:2).

* He does not need our services as masters need their servants, but our very works return to us for our own benefit. With regard to them, masters profit from the service of the servant, but with regard to our service as servants the Master does not profit by it, rather the servant enjoys the benefit, as the Psalmist says: "my good is nothing apart from You" (Ps 16:2). Tell me: what is God's profit if you are righteous, or what happens to Him if you are unjust? Is not His nature incorruptible, never to be touched by harm, higher than all suffering?

entries.section: 1. The accusation that he criticizes God's actions

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom "Will he reprove thee for thy piety? will he enter with thee into judgment?" [4]

When God rebukes us so that we may become godly, He does not do this because of any harm that has befallen Him, but as a Father who wants us to enter into fellowship with Him, so that we become a living icon of Him, and this for our own glory. He rebukes for our sake. He does not enter into judgment like one who has been wronged, but to give us an opportunity for dialogue, so that we may sense His condescending love and His care for our salvation.

* "Is it for fear of you that He rebukes you? Or enters with you into judgment?" [4] Who thinks like this unless he has lost his senses, as though the Lord reproves us out of fear or passes sentence on us out of dread? But those who do not know how to weigh their words slip without doubt into vain speech... So Eliphaz, who uttered vain words, suddenly uttered corrupt and violent words.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. The accusation that Job is a dangerous wicked man

paragraphs.text: "Is not thy wickedness great? and thine iniquities infinite?" [5]

From time to time the three friends hinted at their accusation of Job, but now Eliphaz felt that it was no time for hinting but for open confrontation. He directs Job to his conscience to judge himself as a man whose wickedness is great and whose iniquities have no end.

Eliphaz portrays for us his view of Job: not merely that he is a hypocrite who hides his evils and covers over his iniquities, but that he sees him as wicked, with great wickedness and iniquities without end. It is as though he were saying to him: Language fails me to depict the evil that you are; your picture is exceedingly hideous!

* "Is not your wickedness great, and your iniquities without end?" [5] Notice how from a dead heart there come forth vain words, and from vain words he goes on to a hideous lie, and his heart was inflamed so that his tongue uttered insults. This is the degradation that comes with the increase of sin: when the tongue is not restrained, it does not stop but descends continually to what is worse.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"For thou hast taken a pledge from thy brother for nought, and stripped the naked of their clothing" [6].

Eliphaz portrays Job for us in the image of a brute. He sees him as a man who knows no mercy, with not one human touch in him. He does not take things from his brother as a pledge to secure the repayment of a loan he gives him, but takes his brother himself in pledge and holds him as a lowly hostage and as a slave who loses his freedom.

In a grave and painful exaggeration Eliphaz depicts Job as stripping the naked, who have no clothes, of their clothing! That is to say, instead of giving clothes to the naked to cover them and warm them, or at least ignoring their nakedness and the dire poverty they suffer and the cold they endure, he knows how to strip clothes from those who have none!

He accused Job of having taken some persons as hostages, put them in prison and enslaved them, because they had nothing with which to pay a debt; and of having stripped them of their garments and left them naked, which both the natural law and the Law of Moses forbid (Ex 22:26; Deut 24:13).
To bring out Job's brutality to the full, he accuses him of having enslaved not (only) a stranger, which is brutal enough, but also his brother, who is a member of his household or of his own kind.
Eliphaz did not mention the names of any persons against whom Job committed this violence, and had it been true, God Himself would not have described him as upright.

* "For you have taken a pledge from your brother for nothing, and stripped the naked of their clothing" [6]. In the Holy Bible the word "pledge" (a security or earnest) is used to refer to the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and sometimes to the confession of sin. It is used for the gift of the Holy Spirit when Paul says: [and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts] (2 Cor 1:22). For we receive the earnest so that we may have the assurance of the promise that was given us. The gift of the Holy Spirit is called an earnest because our souls are strengthened by the assurance of the inner hope.

Again, by the word "pledge" is meant the confession of a sin, as it is written in the Law: [If your brother becomes a debtor to you in anything and you take a pledge from him, you shall return it to him before the going down of the sun] (see Ex 22:26). For our brother is a debtor to us when he sins against his fellow creature in a matter that is against us. For we call sins "debts" (Mt 18:32). And in the Lord's Prayer we pray every day: [Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors] (Mt 6:12).

* "And stripped the naked of their clothing" [6]... One who is naked cannot be stripped of anything, but we ask: why are they referred to as naked and then afterwards stripped? It is necessary to know that everyone who enjoys purity of mind has not the garment of deceitful dealing (with two faces), and so he is naked. And there are some among the heretics who truly have purity of heart, and who nevertheless still hold to corrupt doctrines in their teaching. These are naked in their purity and are clothed, as it were, with the teaching of men.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. The accusation of opposing the doing of good

paragraphs.text: "Thou hast not given water to the weary to drink, and thou hast withholden bread from the hungry" [7].

After portraying him as a brutal man who enslaves his brother and spares no effort to strip the naked of a garment they do not have, he now presents him as a man without feeling, who gives no water to the thirsty, though water is the common property of all humanity, and who, if he sees a man giving bread to the hungry, prevents him from doing the work of mercy. So he neither does good nor lets others practice good.
He described him as a man who never did good to the poor, even those who had reached hunger and thirst, and who did not give a cup of water to the thirsty, which would have cost him nothing.

* "You have not given water to the troubled, and you have withheld bread from the hungry" [7]. For the heretics themselves think that they give water to the troubled, when they offer the cup of their errors to persons who suffer under their earthly burdens.

These consider themselves not to have withheld bread from the hungry. When they are asked, they answer with pride and boldness even about things that are unseen and beyond comprehension. They present themselves as learned above all men, even when they wretchedly dare to speak about things unknown.

But the Holy Church, when she sees someone hungry for something that is not to his advantage, either holds him back with restraint, if these matters are indeed known to her, or, if they appear to be unknown, she confesses this in humility. She recovers a sense of humility by good management when she instructs each one of them through her preaching: [not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think soberly] (Rom 11:20)... Thus when we see the Holy Church keeping weak minds from probing deeply into the truths, it was said to blessed Job: "You have withheld bread from the hungry."
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"But as for the mighty man, he had the earth; and the honourable man dwelt in it" [8].

After distorting Job's image and presenting him as a dangerous wicked man, with limitless iniquities, brutal in nature, enslaving his brother, doing no good and preventing others from practicing it, he accuses him of showing partiality, so that if a rich or great man committed an injustice, he would not ask him about his crime.

* [that thou observe these things without preferring one before another, doing nothing by partiality] (see 1 Tim 5:21). Act without partiality, with justice, among those who are on trial, and judge them yourself, so that your mind is not occupied beforehand with anyone, nor do you lean beforehand toward anyone.

St. John Chrysostom * This was said concerning the love that it is fitting for a man to show to his neighbor. Let us be occupied with these things without committing transgression, and let us do nothing by partiality or to the shame of others, but let us love the poor as servants of God, and especially visit them.

St. Clement of Rome * "Where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work. But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality" (see Jas 3:16-17). What blessedness will not be gained by the man who prays asking for this wisdom and receives it from the Lord?
St. Augustine

entries.section: 6. He insults widows and crushes orphans

paragraphs.text: "Thou hast sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless have been broken" [9].
He accused him of sending the poor widows away empty from the door of his house, and, instead of helping the orphans, of crushing their arms, so that they became unable to help themselves.

This accusation is grave, for it is counted as directed against God Himself. In the Old Testament God is reckoned a judge of the widows and a father of the fatherless. Perhaps even before the Law, those who believed in God understood this, either through the natural law or through the tradition handed down through the ages. Whoever despises a widow puts himself in a difficult position with the judge of the widows and their defender, and whoever crushes the arms of orphans is as one who has directed the blows against their heavenly Father, who prides Himself on being the Father of the fatherless.

This accusation carries a symbol of what is done by the heretics who abstain from marriage as though it were uncleanness, and from partaking of foods that God created, such as meats, as though they were defiled (1 Tim 4:3), as some of the Gnostics proclaimed. For they want to destroy the sanctity of marriage and to defile God's good creation. Souls are then turned into widows who have lost their heavenly Bridegroom, our Lord Jesus, and they have taken from her the rejoicing of the wedding, the joy of the Spirit and fellowship with the Savior. On the other hand, they want to deprive souls of the heavenly food, the bread of angels, so that they become like orphans whose arms are broken and crushed, unable to practice spiritual works.

Our Christ came to bring us back from the state of widowhood and to take away our orphanhood, since He became for us the spiritual Bridegroom and the heavenly Father. But the enemy of the good works through the wicked to return us to widowhood and orphanhood!
10 "Therefore snares are round about thee, and sudden fear troubleth thee; 11 Or darkness, that thou canst not see; and abundance of waters cover thee."
"Therefore snares are round about thee, and sudden fear troubleth thee" [10].

This is a new accusation, namely that it was fitting for Job not to complain of what had befallen him as though it were the fruit of God's injustice to him, because all the calamities that had come upon him are from the nets that Job himself set for himself by his injustice to others and his disregard of the poor, the widows and the orphans. All his troubles are the fruit of the deeds that Eliphaz supposed him to have practiced.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that this accusation is directed by the heretics against the Church throughout all ages. They claim that they know the truth and enjoy it, and they mock the true believers who practice daily repentance, saying that they terrify themselves and set for themselves deadly snares.

* "Therefore snares are round about you, sudden fear overtakes you" [10]... When the heretics look at the believing people as those who are sinking in the sins of unbelief, they accuse them that snares are around them.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"Or darkness, that thou canst not see; and abundance of waters cover thee" [11].

Eliphaz ascribes blindness to Job, saying that he was in darkness before the trials came, since he set the snares around himself by his wickedness, and here he falls into them and cannot be delivered from them. The trials pour out upon him like waterfalls that overwhelm him, and there is no one to rescue him from them.

* "And you think that you have not seen darkness, and that you have not been swept down by the force of the rushing waters" [11]... Eliphaz calls trials and sorrows rushing waters, since they rush in as one company after another, like waters that rise with wave following wave.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

12 "Is not God in the height of heaven? and behold the height of the stars, how high they are! 13 And thou sayest, How doth God know? can he judge through the dark cloud? 14 Thick clouds are a covering to him, that he seeth not; and he walketh in the circuit of heaven."
"Is not God in the height of heaven?
and behold the height of the stars, how high they are!" [12]

Eliphaz enumerates false accusations against Job, of which he is innocent. This new accusation has come: that although he claims to be devout and offers sacrifices for his children, he practices practical atheism.

Eliphaz says truly that Job believes that God is in the height of heaven, higher than all the stars, but he is a practical atheist, how? Even if God exists, He does not care about human beings and is not occupied with their sins or their righteousness; human life does not occupy God's mind. Thus Job thought it permissible to commit many great evils without end, since there is no fear of God in him.
How did Eliphaz discover the atheism of righteous Job?

Although Eliphaz has no particular names with whom Job practiced injustice and ingratitude, he reckoned himself, as a man of understanding who perceives the secrets of things, to know that there is no sin for which God punishes in this way except the sin of injustice, cruelty and lack of mercy.

Perhaps in Eliphaz's opinion Job sinned because, although he practiced certain outward behaviors to assure those around him that he was a man of God, a believing leader, his works reveal what he hides in his mind, which is that he believes that God is not in the heights of heaven and that nothing is hidden from Him. Had Job known that, he would not have ascribed injustice to God, and would have established the fear of God in his heart, and would not have said that the eye of God does not see the world (Ezek 8:12), and would have been committed to working with uprightness and mercy.
"And thou sayest, How doth God know?
can he judge through the dark cloud?" [13]

Perhaps Eliphaz sees that Job realizes that God is in the heights of heaven, but instead of offering Him the reverence due Him he made light of Him, because in the heights He cannot see through the mist and does not concern Himself with what goes on among men on earth.
Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on this phrase, clarifying the following truths:
a. God is truly in the heavens, as though hidden from mankind behind the mist, which does not allow human eyes to behold Him.
b. He is wholly present personally with each one, and wholly present with the community. His being wholly present with individuals does not negate His being wholly present with all.
c. God's heavens are on high, and yet by His divine providence He cares for every man on earth.

d. God appears as though He departs from those who sin, not because He is absent from any place, for there is no place in which God is not, but He departs from the wicked who persist in their evils, that is, His grace departs from them, so that they find no divine help to support them, because He does not work without our consent. He is absent in respect of offering help to those who reject His work in them, but He is present to them in condemning them, especially on the great day of the Lord.
e. God is wholly present in the heavenly things, and wholly on earth in the lower things. His presence on earth does not mean His departing from the heavenly things.

f. God is hidden from men, in that they cannot see Him with bodily eyes, but He is visible through His surpassing divine works. He is not comprehended by ordinary sight, but He is touched through His works and His judgments.

g. God, who is not comprehended by the bodily senses, condescends so that men may perceive Him by His illuminations in our minds, but with all that we enjoy we are reckoned as unable to comprehend Him as He is.

* "Do you consider God to be in the heights of heaven, higher than the height of the stars? And you say: How does God know?" [12-13] Very many are so foolish that they cannot fear anything except what they see in a tangible way. So they do not fear God, because they cannot see Him...
He is truly almighty at all times... He is present to each one personally, present in a certain way to everyone, so that His presence is not diminished for all together.
For although He leaves persons when they sin, He is nevertheless present to those same persons for judgment, even if He is seen as though not present to support them.

So He surrounds what is outside and fills what is within... He governs the heavenly things above without neglecting the depths below. He is present in a certain way in the lower parts without departing from the heavenly.

He is hidden in a certain way with regard to His appearance, yet He remains known through His works; He is known in His work, and yet He remains impossible to comprehend by the reckonings of the one who knows Him. He is thus in a certain way present, yet He remains impossible to see. In a certain way it is impossible to see Him, yet His judgments remain witnesses to His presence. He subjects Himself that He may be perceived by us, and the ray of His perception of Himself remains clouded over. Again, when we are gripped by the darkness of ignorance, He remains shining in our mind with the rays of His splendor.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* "Give ear to my words, O Lord" (Ps 5:1). As she (the Church) calls on the Lord, who is her helper, she passes through this evil world and reaches Him. [Consider my meditation] (Ps 5:1); the Psalmist rightly shows that this cry is from within, from the chambers of the heart, reaching God without bodily utterance, because the bodily voice is heard, but the spiritual is understood. For this is the hearing of God, not with a bodily ear, but because He is present everywhere in His majesty.
St. Augustine "Thick clouds are a covering to him, that he seeth not; and he walketh in the circuit of heaven" [14].

Perhaps Eliphaz falsely ascribes to Job that he looks upon God as having hidden Himself with thick clouds so that He is not seen by men, and as walking on the circuit of heaven as one occupied with his own glory, who does not care for the earthly creation.

It is as though Eliphaz were demanding that Job turn back from the evils he used to practice in secret, supposing that those around him did not see or perceive them, and that God Himself was not concerned with them, and therefore the trials came upon him so that Job might review himself and confess his great sins and his iniquities without end. It is fitting for Job, in Eliphaz's eyes, to realize that he has become a disgrace, not because of the calamities in themselves, but because of the disgrace behind them, on earth as in the heavens.

entries.section: 9. A comparison of Job's state with the ancient world

paragraphs.text: 15 "Hast thou marked the old way which wicked men have trodden? 16 Which were cut down out of time, whose foundation was overflown with a flood: 17 Which said unto God, Depart from us: and what can the Almighty do for them? 18 Yet he filled their houses with good things: but the counsel of the wicked is far from me. 19 The righteous see it, and are glad: and the innocent laugh them to scorn. 20 Whereas our substance is not cut down, but the remnant of them the fire consumeth."
"Hast thou marked the old way which wicked men have trodden?" [15].

After Eliphaz supposed that by his wisdom and experience he had opened Job's eyes to see his sins and iniquities, he now offers him warnings, lest his fate be the fate of the wicked men of old, such as those whom the Flood overwhelmed in the days of Noah. He accuses Job of walking in the same way as they, and his life will end as theirs ended.
The way that Job walks, in Eliphaz's opinion, is not a new way, but an old way, broad and well trodden, whose end is destruction.

If Eliphaz calls Job to leave the way he is walking, which many walked long ago and perished, the Lord of glory, unlike Eliphaz, did not follow the negative way, but presented Himself as the divine Way who grants sinners forgiveness through repentance and carries them to the gates of heaven, open to them and awaiting them.

Here it is fitting for us to set a contrast between Eliphaz, who destroys others, and the Lord Christ, who gives hope to the whole world. In pride and haughtiness Eliphaz claimed to be a wise man of understanding who leads Job to recognize his sins that he had hidden from men and from God, and which he tried to ignore, so that a flood of calamities and a deluge of afflictions came upon him that will not cease until he perishes completely. But the Lord Christ is the eternal Wisdom of God, who came in humility to take the hands of the wicked without wounding their feelings, carrying them in Himself and entering with them into the divine embrace, supporting the weak and granting them His Holy Spirit, the giver of love, joy, peace, goodness and self-control.

Eliphaz tried to destroy Job's soul with false accusations. But the Lord of glory Jesus bore the accusations directed against mankind, granting them fellowship with Him in the divine nature to lift up their souls, and granting them health of body, soul and spirit on an eternal level, where man is glorified in his entirety on the great day of the Lord.

* "Will you give a sign of the old way that the wicked tread?" [15] Since the way of our Redeemer is humility, the way of the world is pride. And so the wicked tread the way of the world, where by the lusts of the world they walk in self-conceit.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* If we also, beloved brethren in Christ, if we put Him on, if He is the way of our salvation, we who follow Christ in the steps of salvation, let us walk imitating Him as the Apostle John teaches us: "He that saith he abideth in him ought himself also so to walk, even as he walked" (1 Jn 2:6).
Martyr St. Cyprian * He is the house to which we go; He is the way by which we go. Let us go by Him to Him; so that we do not lose the way.

St. Augustine * Hold fast first to what they bore witness of themselves, saying: "As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in him" (Col 2:6)... For He is the way that leads to the Father; do not walk in the angels, for this way does not reach there.
St. John Chrysostom "Which were cut down out of time?"

entries.section: 9. A comparison of Job's state with the ancient world

paragraphs.text: "whose foundation was overflown with a flood" [16].

The Flood overtook the wicked suddenly while they were unprepared, thinking they would live many years, so they were drowned and perished as though it were before the time. The Flood hastened their lives suddenly. They had made the earth their foundation, and built their hopes upon it, and thought they were secure as upon a rock foundation, but the flood poured out upon this their foundation. [the flood upon the world of the ungodly] (2 Pet 2:5).
Some may ask: Is not the span of man's life known beforehand to God, so how is it said that the wicked are cut down before their time?
Do they die before the appointed time set for them? And do the days of the righteous' lives lengthen beyond what God appointed for them?

First: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that every man has a span of life that is fitting for him, that suits or deserves him. But God also knows beforehand that it is better for this wicked man to die early so that he does not cause the righteous to stumble, or He leaves him to a longer life to give him an opportunity that perhaps he may repent.

So what is said about a man's life being shortened or lengthened does not mean that God changes His mind about what He knew before, but that man receives a longer life or has his life shortened for a divine wisdom, whether with respect to the person himself or those around him, and He also knows beforehand what is fitting, whether to add to or subtract from a certain person's life as he needs to be according to nature or according to his deserving.

Second: Origen sees that the measures of life differ among men from what they are with God. As the Psalmist says, [One day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day](a). On the great day of the Lord we shall be surprised by little children who are reckoned as persons who lived many years, and by old men whom we see as little children.

To illustrate this, if we compare the unborn John the Baptist when he leaped with joy in the womb of his mother, St. Elizabeth, we find that by the human measure he had not yet been born, and the time of his stay in the womb is not counted as part of his age, whereas in God's sight and by His measures he is counted as a mature man, older than the high priest, the priests, the scribes, the Pharisees and so on at that time, because they are counted as dead men who did not bear witness to the Lord Christ in spite of their knowing the prophecies intellectually.

Righteous men may die as children and be reckoned as having lived thousands of years in the eyes of the Lord, and the days of wicked tyrants may be prolonged and their days be reckoned as nothing. [Their spirit goes forth, they return to their dust](b).

When we hear the Lord's commandment: "Honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long upon the land," we are not astonished if a son or daughter dies at an early age in spite of their honoring their parents, for this son (or daughter) is reckoned as one whose life was long on earth, because one day of his life is reckoned with the Lord as a thousand years. This is the spiritual, symbolic interpretation that Origen adopted in many places when he spoke of man's life on earth.

According to this interpretation the wicked are cut down before their time because their lives are without fruit; they did not benefit from the opportunities of repentance to enjoy fellowship with God, the Giver of life. By their death they are reckoned as dead men who lost life and did not take care to enjoy it.

* "Who were taken before the time, when the flood poured out upon their foundation"... Every man is taken from this life at a time known beforehand, before the ages, by divine authority. But it is necessary to know that Almighty God, in creating us and ordering our affairs, appoints the limits (of our life) according to the deserving of each one. It may be necessary for the wicked man to live a short time, lest he harm many who walk uprightly, and it may be necessary for the good man to remain a longer time in life, so that he may be a help in good works to many.

Again, the wicked man must remain a longer time in life so that he may add evil deeds to his deeds. And so the righteous man may practice a sincere life that is purified by his trial, or it may be necessary to take the good man away more quickly, lest, if he lived longer, he might corrupt his innocence.

But let it be borne in mind that it is God's compassions that give sinners an opportunity for repentance. In any case, times may be granted to them, and they do not return to bear the fruits of repentance but serve evil, and by God's mercy they receive the times in the hope that they may abandon their ways.

Although Almighty God knows beforehand the time of death of each one, when his life ends, no one can die before his time, but at the time appointed for his death, for if fifteen years were added to Hezekiah's life (2 Kgs 20; Isa 38), then the time of his life truly increased beyond the end that he deserved, and God had already known his time at this moment and the time at which afterwards He would take him from the present life.

This is how it is: what does [the wicked are cut off before their time] mean but that all those who love the present life prepare themselves for longer periods of that life? And when death draws them out of the present life, the long periods of their life that they were accustomed to imagine are taken from them; they are cut to pieces. Rightly it was said of these: [their foundation was overflown with a flood]...

Cain is described as the first to found a city on the earth (Gen 4:17), and by this he clearly confirmed that he was a stranger, since he was a stranger to steadfastness in the eternal world, and so he laid a foundation on the earth. Being a stranger to the heavenly things, he set his stability in a foundation of lower things, and set the stability of his heart in earthly pleasure.

Just as with the collapse of daily time the state of death in the present life itself runs toward its end, and shatters the dedication of the sons of perdition by removing these very persons, rightly it was said of the wicked: [their foundation was overflown with a flood], that is, the same change casts into them the instability of the wicked's constructions.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"Which said unto God, Depart from us:

entries.section: 9. A comparison of Job's state with the ancient world

paragraphs.text: and what can the Almighty do for them?" [17]

The sin of these wicked is that they ask God: "Depart from us," since they want to live without God, so that their consciences do not rise up and they do not lose their dullness. They ignored Him, saying: "The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil" (Zeph 1:12).
They had heard of Him that He is the Almighty, but in their eyes what authority has He over them?

As we said before, atheism is of two kinds: either denial of the existence of God, or, while knowing that He exists, they think that He does not feel for them, far from them in His heavens, or they ask Him to depart from them, since they consider Him unable to give them the happiness they seek or to fulfill for them what they desire.
"Yet he filled their houses with good things:

entries.section: 9. A comparison of Job's state with the ancient world

paragraphs.text: but the counsel of the wicked is far from me" [18].

What increases the condemnation of the wicked is that they enjoyed good things that were from the Almighty, and they misused them. Those who were drowned in the Flood [were eating and drinking, they married wives, they were given in marriage, they bought, they sold] (Lk 17:27). They had no justification for asking "What can the Almighty do for them," for they were living in His abundant good things, and they had no reason to call upon the Maker of good things to depart from them. Their houses were full of good things, but their hearts were empty of divine grace, and therefore they perished.
Here Eliphaz agrees with Job in the desire: "the counsel of the wicked is far from me" (Job 21:16).

* "But he fills the houses of the wicked with good things" [18]. The Lord fills the houses of the wicked with good things, even for the ungrateful, for He does not withhold His gifts, so that they may be ashamed of the compassion of their Creator and return to goodness, or they may despise returning, and that will be a cause of their punishment with greater severity, since they repay God's surpassing goodness with evil, and so harsh woes come upon them afterwards...
"May their judgment be far from me." This too blessed Job expressed, when he says: [let their counsel be far from me] (Job 21:16).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 9. A comparison of Job's state with the ancient world

paragraphs.text: "The righteous see it, and are glad: and the innocent laugh them to scorn" [19]

The righteous are not to be reckoned thus, as though they were pleased with the death of the wicked and mocked them; rather they groan and pray for them. But on the Day of Judgment, when opportunities were given to the wicked and they persisted in their wickedness, turning their backs on the Giver of life and preferring sonship to the devil instead of sonship to God, then, as destruction comes upon them, which is the work of their free evil will and conduct, the righteous are glad, since there is no longer any place for evil in them, but they live in the heavenly holy Jerusalem with the holy God.

The righteous do not gloat over the wicked at their perdition, for they carry the will of their Father that all be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth, but they rejoice at the annihilation of the authority of evil and injustice so that the weak may not stumble, as they are glad at the glory of God, which does not admit corruption.

The righteous find the opportunity to reveal the futility, weakness and transience of evil, and the foolishness of the wisdom, cunning and malice of the wicked. The righteous are glad at the collapse of the devil and his kingdom, and at the destruction of sin, not of the sinner. For the righteous man knows nothing but love, even toward sinners.

* "The righteous see it and rejoice, and the innocent laugh them to scorn" [19]. When the righteous see the wicked sinning here, they do not rejoice at the fault of people who destroy themselves. For if they rejoiced at the fault they would no longer be reckoned righteous... The Pharisee lost his righteousness because he was pleased, reckoning himself higher than the tax collector, saying: [I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican](c).

Again, if we say that the righteous man can triumph with complete joy over the death of the wicked, what kind of joy is this for the sake of vengeance on the wicked in this world, in which the life of the righteous is not secure?

Let us distinguish between the times of terror and those of glory. The righteous see the wicked now and become wasted because of their evils. And when they see them being smitten, they do not trust in their own lives either... Now the righteous see the sons of perdition and groan, and at the final judgment they will see them and laugh in derision.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 9. A comparison of Job's state with the ancient world

paragraphs.text: "Were not our adversaries destroyed, and the fire has consumed their remnant?" [20]

Perhaps he refers here to Lot, who tormented his righteous soul with the lawlessness of the wicked, for though he lost everything he possessed, he desired the salvation of the people of Sodom and Gomorrah as he rejoiced at the destruction of corruption and lawlessness (2 Pet 2:7-8).

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that those who oppose the righteous and are hostile to the divine truth will be cast into the fire of Gehenna that is not quenched, which burns souls with bodies. Just as the body shared with the soul in opposing God and they cooperated together in practicing the works of the devil and submitting to him, so it is fitting that they share the devil's fate, the eternal fire.

* Although the wicked depart from here from their dead body, they receive it again in the resurrection, so that in the same body they burn, the same body with which they committed sin. Since their sin was in the mind and the body, so the punishment will be in the spirit and the body alike.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

The righteous believer rejoices when he sees the opponents of the divine truth, that is, the evil thoughts that want to creep inside and gain control over the inner man. Such evil thoughts are burned by the fire of the Holy Spirit, as thorns are burned by fire. So everything that is foreign to the pure nature that God created in us is burned, to kindle the fire of divine love.
The believer rejoices in the fiery work of the Holy Spirit in him, who destroys and builds!

entries.section: 10. Repentance is getting acquainted with God

paragraphs.text: "Acquaint now thyself with him, and be at peace:
thereby good shall come unto thee" [21].

It is difficult to judge this attitude of Eliphaz, for although he wronged Job by directing bitter accusations against him, and tried to confirm them in spite of his inability to find practical proofs of his accusations, here he opens before him the door of hope.

Eliphaz reveals the blessings of returning to God by repentance. If we set aside Eliphaz's intention to confirm Job's wickedness, his words here are a strong source of hope in returning to the Almighty, so that he may find in the Almighty Himself his good, his righteousness, his treasure and all his satisfaction.

Eliphaz offers good counsel: [Draw near to God, get acquainted with Him, and be at peace with Him!] There is no remedy but drawing near to God, uniting with Him and entering with Him into inner peace.

* There is none who grieves us like the one who has fallen into sin, who remembers his sins to take pleasure in earthly fleshly things, instead of his mind being occupied with the beautiful ways of knowing God!

For Adam hid himself when he learned of God's presence, wishing to hide when God called him, with that matter by which he wounded his soul (not meeting the Lord), saying to him: "Adam...: Where art thou?" (Gen 3:9). That is, "Where are you hiding yourself? Why do you conceal yourself? Why do you flee from God, whom you longed to see?!
St. Ambrose "And be at peace": that is, be at peace with God, or with yourself, where you find rest in Him, for evil is a source of inner anxiety.

What is the "good" that Eliphaz looks to as a fruit of entering into peace with God? If he means the heavenly blessings, his counsel is sincere and constructive, but if his eyes are fixed on the temporal goods that Job lost, then he has not been right in his counsel!
* "We have peace with God" (Rom 5:1), through our Lord Jesus Christ, who reconciled us with God through the sacrifice of His blood...
Christ came to destroy the enemies, to make peace, and to reconcile us with God, from whom the barrier of evil that we erected by our sins had separated us.
Origen

entries.section: 11. Repentance is a personal enjoyment of the Word

paragraphs.text: "Receive, I pray thee, the law from his mouth, and lay up his words in thy heart" [22].

He who enters into peace with God finds the divine commandment sweet, issuing as though from His divine mouth directly into his heart, and in sweetness and delight man cries out: "Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?" (Acts 9:6).

When we hear the commandment from the mouth of a servant of God, or read it in the Holy Bible, or hear it from the mouth of a friend or from a book, we truly sense a personal relationship with God, as though He were speaking to us directly. We hear His divine voice within us, and our depths respond to His love, for there is no place fitting for the divine Word like the heart, because it is the treasury of love and the temple of the Holy Spirit.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that what Eliphaz uttered, though it represents sincere counsel, was mistaken in that he supposed himself to be righteous, more righteous than the wicked Job, as he thought, and so took the position of a teacher, a wise man and a proud leader. He represents the heretics of all ages who make light of the Church of God and accuse her of ignorance together with evil, and who want to present her with teachings as righteous teachers, possessors of understanding and knowledge and bearers of righteousness!

* There is a sin in a man's teaching someone better than himself, the crime that heretics often commit, teaching while they hold mistaken concepts... This applies also to such persons, as he adds: [I ask you to receive the law from his mouth], for they imagine that what they think out of their own minds comes from the mouth of God.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 12. Repentance is a return to the Almighty

paragraphs.text: "If thou return to the Almighty, thou shalt be built up,
thou shalt put away iniquity far from thy tabernacles" [23].

Eliphaz presents a correct, positive and effective understanding of repentance. Repentance is not merely turning back from sin, for this negative side does not satisfy the soul, but its positive side is that it is a return to the Almighty, and this satisfies the depths and builds them up. For the Almighty alone, by His Holy Spirit, can renew the heart continually without interruption, until it is formed to become truly the icon of God.

When man draws near to the divine light he does not allow darkness, especially injustice, to creep into him, because there is no fellowship between light and darkness. Therefore Eliphaz says: [If you put away iniquity from your tabernacle]. Here he refers to the tent of the family or household as a whole, just as the tent refers to the body in which the soul dwells as in a tent.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Eliphaz had learned some true things from his friend Job, but he had deviations from the straight line, or from the truth. So we find in the heretics some true concepts that they learned from the Church of Christ, but they mixed what is evangelical truth with the falsehood of their own.

* Since Eliphaz was the friend of a blessed person, he perceives some things truly, but on some points he left the straight line and became like the heretics. Therefore he did not realize that Job had been struck with trials because of good qualities. He thought that this man whom he saw stricken had sinned, and so he promised him that if he returned to Almighty God iniquity would be removed from his tent.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 13. Repentance is the way of riches

paragraphs.text: 24 "Then shalt thou lay up gold as dust, and the gold of Ophir as the stones of the brooks. 25 Yea, the Almighty shall be thy gold, and thou shalt have plenty of silver" [24].

Eliphaz sees that when man cleaves to God, the source of good things, he becomes very rich, so that gold nuggets become for him as plentiful as dust, or gold is laid up with him like dust, and he has much silver.

Eliphaz imagined that Job had gathered his wealth by injustice and therefore lost it, but if he cleaves to God, He will give him good things and riches that he will not lose. Perhaps he did not refer here to wealth in livestock and land, but to gold and silver, because what he obtained before was the wealth of farmers and shepherds, whereas what he will obtain by his cleaving to the Lord is the wealth of kings, in gold and silver.

With the abundance of gold nuggets and the gold of Ophir, he does not put these treasures in storehouses under strict guard, because he does not fear losing them, nor does he put them in his bosom, because they do not occupy his heart, but sees them as dust and pebbles that do not occupy his thought and heart.

This can be interpreted spiritually: whoever returns to God casts gold nuggets on the dust, because he possesses God and so counts everything as refuse for His sake, and he casts pure gold among the stones of the brooks, since gold is not valuable in his eyes but is like the little stones and pebbles that fill the valleys, worth nothing.

entries.section: 13. Repentance is the way of riches

paragraphs.text: "Yea, the Almighty shall be thy gold, and thou shalt have plenty of silver" [25].

When the righteous cast the gold nuggets of this world into the dust and its gold of Ophir into the brooks among the stones, they find God to be their nuggets and their heavenly gold. He becomes their treasure which will not be stolen from them.

Silver in the Holy Bible often refers to the word of God, therefore it is fitting for believers to acquire this spiritual silver, which gives them surpassing spiritual riches, and strength against the coming enemy of good, and inner joy and exultation, so that they share the heavenly beings in their praises. By the divine Word the believer becomes rich, a good soldier of the Lord Christ and a psalmist full of joy.

And as the people of the world delight in their wealth, but only for a time, the righteous are glad in God, their true treasure, wealth, honor and strength forever. [The LORD is my strength and song] (Ex 15:2; Ps 118:14; Isa 12:2).

Whoever possesses silver in his heart pleads with the word of God and is fortified against the powers of darkness, but if he submits to evil and to the powers of darkness and surrenders to them, he does not perceive the mysteries of God which the divine Word proclaims.

* What other enemies do we submit to more than the evil spirits, who besiege us in our thoughts, storm the city of our minds and gain control of it, and take us captive under the yoke of their authority?
The Psalmist testifies that the name "silver" refers to divine inspiration, as he says: [The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times] (Ps 12:6).

Often our souls do not enjoy divine inspiration when we submit in a dangerous way to the deceptions of the evil spirits, who sprinkle on our minds the dust of earthly thoughts so that our inner eyes grow dark and do not enjoy the light of inner vision. This is what the Psalmist suffered when he said: [Depart from me, ye evildoers: for I will keep the commandments of my God] (Ps 119:15), teaching us clearly that he could not search into God's commandments when he was suffering in his mind from the snares of the evil spirits.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

In the parable of the son who returned to his father, the Lord Christ revealed the riches that we enjoy through repentance, for we delight in the greatest position, namely adoption by God, by which He does not hold back from offering us the best robe, the ring of sonship and the shoes, that we may walk in the way of truth in safety and bear witness to God's tender fatherhood.
* He brings you the robe, the ring and the shoes.

The robe is the garment of wisdom with which the Apostles covered the nakedness of their bodies, and with which every man is clothed. They took the robe in order to cover the weaknesses of their bodies with the power of spiritual wisdom, and of wisdom it was said: "he washed his garments in wine" (Gen 49:11). The robe is the spiritual clothing and the wedding garment.
The ring is nothing other than the deed of true faith and the seal of truth.
The shoes refer to the preaching of the Gospel.

St. Ambrose * The best robe is the honor that Adam lost, and the servants who brought it are the preachers of reconciliation... The ring on the hand is the earnest of the Holy Spirit because of the fellowship of grace, for the Spirit is rightly indicated by the finger...
The shoes on the feet are the readiness to preach the Gospel, that we may not touch earthly things.
St. Augustine

entries.section: 14. By repentance the face is lifted up to God

paragraphs.text: "For then shalt thou have thy delight in the Almighty, and shalt lift up thy face unto God" [26].

The righteous man enjoys boldness before God: "thou shalt lift up thy face unto God," so that he is not terrified and his heart is not broken, but with gladness of heart and confidence he appears before God, speaks with Him and seeks a life of fellowship with Him.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Eliphaz spoke the truth if this speech were directed to a wicked man unable to lift his inner face toward God. But he erred, because he presented what is true without wisdom, presenting it in order to direct an accusation against righteous Job.

People know us by looking at our faces, and so they distinguish us from one another. One who does not lift up his face before people and appear before them is not known by them. So when man returns by repentance to God, he finds his delight in Almighty God and lifts his inner face to God, and so becomes known to Him and not a stranger to Him. Therefore in every Divine Liturgy the priest cries out: "Lift up your hearts," or "Where are your hearts?" and by the power of the Spirit the people answer: "We have them with the Lord." It is as though they were declaring that their inner faces are lifted up to the Lord, who is pleased with them, and that union with Him gives them awe.

* Lifting up the face to God is lifting up the heart, searching for what is highest of all. Just as by the bodily face we are known and distinguished among men, so by the inner form we are known before God. But when we are weighed down with the iniquity of sin and sink to the earth, we fear to lift up the face of our heart to God, since we do not stand with any confidence in good works. The mind is filled with fear as to looking toward the heavenly things, because conscience itself accuses it. But by the tears of repentance sin is washed away, and man laments the things that were committed so that he no longer commits what he laments, and so we enjoy confidence in the mind, and the face of our heart is lifted up to contemplate the delights of the reward.

Eliphaz is reckoned to have spoken the truth, if he were counseling a weak person, but when he looks with contempt upon a righteous man because of his blows, what is this but pouring out words of knowledge without knowledge?
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 15. Repentance opens the gates of heaven

paragraphs.text: 27 "Thou shalt make thy prayer unto him, and he shall hear thee, and thou shalt pay thy vows. 28 Thou shalt also decree a thing, and it shall be established unto thee: and the light shall shine upon thy ways."
"Thou shalt make thy prayer unto him, and he shall hear thee, and thou shalt pay thy vows" [27].
When Eliphaz calls Job to repent of his evils and return to God, he assures him that through his repentance he will pray to God and He will answer him.

This is true speech, for repentance opens the gates of heaven and gives us boldness before God, and God inclines His ear to hear us, and our prayers smell like the fragrance of good incense rising before Him.

The penitent enters into a dialogue of love with God, and finds himself before the throne of grace, and offers his vows as a response to God's answering of his prayers. He offers vows of thanksgiving and praise.

What Eliphaz aimed at by these words, which no blemish touches except Eliphaz's evil intention, was to accuse Job of not being a man of God. The prayers that he offered to God all the days of his life were not accepted, because they came from an unrepentant heart and a soul that does not return to God, and his vows he will not pay even if he offered sacrifices for his children to this extent and gave countless offerings, because his heart is not pure.

What his words carried of divine truth, which suits every soul to return to God, Eliphaz used as a sword with which to strike the soul of righteous Job to shatter him and bring him into the hell of despair.

* As for those who count the Lord's commandments as nothing, they offer prayers and the Lord never hears them. Therefore it is written: [He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination] (Prov 28:9). Since Eliphaz believes that blessed Job was not heard, he insists that he has practiced some wrong.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Repentance is a fire that consumes all human weakness, removes negligence, laziness and the heaviness of the body, and gives the soul a wing with which it flies toward heaven, and shows it, from this high summit, the vanity of this present life.

One who does not rise to the observation post cannot take a true picture of the earth and its contents. For many things darken the field of vision, deafen the ears and make the tongue stammer. Therefore it is fitting for man to wrest himself from this clamor, to keep away from the smoke, and to enter into solitude, to find deep peace, calm and stillness with enlightenment.

When the eyes are fixed on the love of God, and the ear no longer hears anything but His words as though they were a sweet spiritual symphony, the soul becomes a captive (of God) and feels disgust for food and sleep.

It is true that the noise of the world and material concerns glide over the soul, but they do not enter it, and with the soul's rising in this way it no longer cares about the crackling of earthly storms.

And as the dwellers on the mountains no longer hear the sounds of the city nor see what goes on in it, but count all this like an indistinct din, so those who have left the world of their own will and set out flying in the heights of philosophy (wisdom) no longer perceive anything of the world's affairs, because all their senses are directed toward heaven.
Therefore let us seek not only the solitude of the wilderness but the solitude of inner desire. Let us hide on the highest summit of the soul, where nothing earthly dwells.
The power of repentance is like a wind that drives away dust and sweeps away passions faster than smoke.

entries.section: 15. Repentance opens the gates of heaven

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom "Thou shalt also decree a thing, and it shall be established unto thee: and the light shall shine upon thy ways" [28].

The penitent man finds inner rest in the management of all his outward affairs: "Thou shalt also decree a thing, and it shall be established unto thee." And as it was said of the righteous man who walks in the law of the Lord: "whatsoever he doeth shall prosper" (Ps 1:3).

"The light shall shine upon thy ways," that is, God will guide you. For whoever returns to the Lord by repentance finds the word of God a lamp that lights the way for him, as the Word brings him into the Kingdom of light.
"When men are cast down, then thou shalt say, There is lifting up;
and he shall save the humble person" [29].

The Jesuit translation has: "and to him who humbles himself you will say: Rise up," when despair tries to creep into the hearts and thoughts of the penitent and almost swallows them, they find the grace of God within them strengthening them, that they may enjoy the sublime, successful life: [I will cause thee to ride upon the high places of the earth] (Isa 58:14). True repentance gives true humility, as it gives man a return to God, who lifts up the humble.

Sadly, what Eliphaz means here is not to offer counsel to every man to enjoy true humility, but to assert that the complete collapse to which Job had come, so that his place was on the dunghill, was merely the fruit of his pride and arrogance even before God, so that he prepared himself for destruction.

* "For he who is humbled will be glorified, and he who lowers his eyes will be saved" [29]. This phrase does not contradict the mouth of truth, who said: "for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted" (Lk 14:11). So it was said of Solomon: "Before destruction the heart of man is haughty, and before honour is humility" (Prov 18:12).

Fittingly it was said: "he who lowers his eyes will be saved," because pride is discovered through the service of the members, for its first announcement usually appears in the eyes. It is written: "thou wilt bring down high looks" (Ps 18:27)... So "lowering the eyes" does not mean that a man looks downward, but that he reckons himself less and beneath all that is visible.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* It is more fitting (for the sick man to tell his physician), confessing the faults into which he fell, than to keep his wounds hidden and to be fanatical, boasting and exposing the wounds of others. It is no wonder that the tax collector went away healed, since he was not ashamed to show the place of his pain.
St. Augustine * Where will you be when the demons come near you? For humility brings them down from their rank.
When they see you humble they flee from you.
Humility is the house of divinity, and where it is, God dwells in it.
Look: in whom do I dwell but in the meek, the humble, who fears my words?
Let your soul be humbled, and the King will come and dwell in you, and the whole power of the enemy will not overcome you.
For the house of the King is not robbed by thieves, because His soldiers guard its doors carefully.
If you are humble He will dwell in you in that kingdom, and thieves will not rob you.
If you humble yourself you will uproot the tree of evil, and plant in its place the blessed tree of our Lord.
If love of His divinity is kindled in you, it makes you deaf, and all the evils (that come upon you) will be as good things.
You look upon insult and mockery and all bitter abuse as though they were good things and not evils...
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh

entries.section: 17. By repentance we intercede for our brethren

paragraphs.text: "He delivereth him that is not innocent: and it is delivered by the pureness of thine hands" [30].

Eliphaz ended his speech by directing a harsh rebuke to Job. For if Job had been accustomed to offer sacrifices for his children, in case they had sinned even in thought against God (Job 1:5), reckoning himself and the members of his household more righteous than others, then God did not hear him, and did not deliver him or rescue his children, and this is a sign of his wickedness. The man who returns to God asks even for others who are not innocent, and He delivers them, for the sake of the cleanness of the hands of the righteous man who lifts his hands in prayer. It is as though he were making light of Job, saying to him: If your hands were clean your prayers and your sacrifices for yourself and your family would have been accepted, but because they are evil they have brought evil upon all!
Truly the godly man does not enjoy God's work in him alone, but as he prays for others with a wide heart God answers him, as the Apostle Paul did when he was in the ship (Acts 27:24).
Eliphaz did not realize that what he said would actually be fulfilled, when Job prayed for him and for his two companions (Job 42:8).
Perhaps Eliphaz prophesies, without knowing it, about the Lord Christ, the Intercessor and Atoning One. Who is this one with clean hands but the Lord Christ, who alone is without sin?

He stretched out His hands on the Cross, asking: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" He rose by His power, granting guilty humanity the possibility of salvation and victory over death, and deliverance!
Truly our Christ alone, by His blood, delivers the man who is not innocent, by the power of His blood shed on the Cross.
Let me return to You by repentance,

1 Then Job answered and said, 2 "Even to day is my complaint rebellion: my stroke is heavier than my groaning. 3 Oh that I knew where I might find him! that I might come even to his seat! 4 I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments. 5 I would know the words which he would answer me, and understand what he would say unto me."
Then Job answered and said [1]:
"Even to day is my complaint rebellion: my stroke is heavier than my groaning" [2].

Job says that his complaint is bitter. His friends reckoned it rebellion against God, but Job gives a justification for his complaint, which is that however much he groans, the groanings of his heart cannot express how heavy his calamities are. The wounds of his body and soul are exceedingly severe, and they justify his complaint.

* The pains of the afflicted man ought to be healed by the comfort of his friends, but because their comfort carried deceit, the pains of the stricken man became harsher than they were. Eliphaz did not hide his intention, as he promises better things if he repents; this was like a poisoned remedy, and the wound grew worse.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* "A faithful friend is the medicine of life" (Sir 6:16).

There is no remedy so effective in healing pains as the sincere friend who comforts you in your afflictions, manages your problems, rejoices in your success and grieves in your calamities. Whoever has found such a friend has found a treasure. For a faithful friend has no equal, and no weight of gold and silver can balance the goodness of his faithfulness (see Sir 6:14-15).

* Nothing establishes love so strongly as sharing in joy and pain. Do not, because you are far from troubles, isolate yourself also from sharing with others. When your neighbor is in distress, reckon the distress as your own. Share his tears to support his crushed spirit, and share his joy so that the joy in him becomes deep and rooted.

Establish love, for by this you serve yourself more than you serve him. By your tears you become merciful, and by feelings of gladness you purify your soul from envy and gloom... If you cannot remove evils from him, share them with him by your tears, and you will remove half the evil from him; and if you cannot increase his goods, share his joy and you will add something great to him.

St. John Chrysostom "My stroke is heavier than my groaning"; and in Pope Gregory (the Great) it came: "The hand of my stroke is heavier than my groaning." Here he means the blow that struck him at the hands of his friends who opposed him, for it is more violent than the trials that came upon him and drove him to groan. It is as though his friends, instead of comforting him to calm his groanings, inflamed the wounds, for their hands came more violently than what had befallen him. The son of Sirach says: "There is a companion who rejoices with his friend in prosperity, and in adversity becomes his enemy" (Sir 37:4).
