Again he affirms that whoever ascribes wisdom to himself is not thankful to God, and therefore does not bear the fear of the Lord and is not godly; he is foolish and not wise.

* "Behold, godliness, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding" (Job 28:28). Here is the distinction (between wisdom and understanding), for we must understand that wisdom belongs to contemplation, and understanding belongs to action. In this place by wisdom he means the worship of God... And what is the worship of God but love for God, by which we long to see Him, and believe and hope to see Him in part? As we progress we see as in a mirror, in a riddle, but then the vision will be in clarity... As for departing from evil, which Job says is understanding, it undoubtedly concerns temporal matters. For with regard to time (in this world) we are in evil, from which we must cease until we attain the eternal goods.

* There is another kind of wicked, who when they knew God, glorified him not as God, neither were thankful (Rom 1:21). In this "I also fell, but thy right hand held me up" (Ps 18:35), and bore me far away, and set me where I could be healed. For You said to man: "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom" (Job 28:28), and "be not wise in thine own eyes" (Prov 3:7), for "professing themselves to be wise, they became fools" (Rom 1:22). But now I have found the pearl of great price, for which I needed to sell all and buy it (Mt 13:46), but I hesitated.

* If knowledge is of the right kind, it is the handmaid of love, for without love "knowledge puffeth up" (1 Cor 8:1), but where love is, it fills the heart with edification, so that knowledge finds nothing empty that it could puff up. Add to this that Job shows useful knowledge by defining it afterward when he says, "the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom," adding, "and to depart from evil is understanding."
* "Behold, the worship of God is wisdom." Then the mind is wise, not by its own light, but by participation in that exalted light, which is eternal, in which it reigns in blessedness.

St. Augustine * "Behold, godliness, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding" [28]. There is nothing like this practical training, nothing stronger than this wisdom. "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge, and a good understanding have all they that do his commandments" (see Prov 1:7). This is the greatest of possessions. The honoring of God is the supreme wisdom.

St. John Chrysostom * O man, return to yourself. Examine the secrets of your heart, and if you find that you fear the Lord, it is truly evident that you are full of wisdom... This wisdom, which is awesome in itself even to the angels, is called in you "the fear of the Lord." For you truly possess wisdom if you fear the Lord.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
May I acquire You, O divine Wisdom!
* You gave man a mind, that he might search and work.
By human wisdom he is able to search for precious metals, but in foolishness he does not seek the mysteries of the Kingdom of God.
Grant me to discover the silver of Your pure wisdom, and to acquire the gold, the pledge of the heavenly life.
* Man brings silver and gold out of the dust and the stones.
Let there come forth from me, who am dust, a witness to You, and let me become in Your eyes more precious than every precious stone!
You are able to turn dust into heaven,
and the heart of stone into a heart enlarged with love.
* You are the worker of wonders and miracles.
You brought forth from Saul of Tarsus a unique apostle,
and from the wicked people of Nineveh a repentant people,
and from the Gentiles a holy Church.
You made man out of dust, and from the earthy sinner You raise up a being like the angels!
* Behold, I am in Your hands; establish Your Kingdom within me.
Embrace me, as it were, among the ranks of Your angels,
that I may be in touch with Your love, and know Your divine mysteries.
You are the way that brings me into the bosom of the Father.
You are my riches and my joy!
* May I acquire You, O divine Wisdom!
In You I enter into the mysteries of heaven, and enjoy partaking of the divine nature.
In You my eyes are opened, and I see what no eye has seen.
* For the sake of acquiring wealth, man learned the craft of mining,
and because of hunger the lion came to know the ways of the forests and the wilds,
and for the sake of being fed, the eagles see the prey from lofty distances.
And for the sake of love I acquire You, and You present to me the surpassing divine mysteries.
* Your wisdom is mighty and surpassing.
You bring me into the impossible, and reveal to me wonders beyond measure!
You lift the humble up to heaven.
You turn stones into children of Abraham!
And You shake those who hold authority and power!
You cause a spring of sweet waters of love to well up from my rocky heart!
You make me very precious in Your eyes, O Lover of mankind!
* May I acquire You, O wondrous Wisdom of God,
that I may carry within me the treasure of all wisdom, knowledge and understanding.
You are my wondrous treasure.
No gold, nor silver, nor precious stones can be compared with You.
* Behold, all of nature with all its creativity cries out to me:
Acquire Creativity itself, Beauty itself, the Creator of all and the Maker of everything!
* How marvelous You are, hidden and present.
Your mysteries are hidden even from the Cherubim, who cover their faces because of the greatness of Your splendor!
You hid Yourself from me for a time, not to deprive me of You, but to inflame my heart with longing for You.
You became incarnate and came down to me, so that I find You within me!
You are very near to me!
My depths cry out to You:
Show me Your glory!

entries.section: 1. His former happiness in the Lord

paragraphs.text: 1 Moreover Job continued his parable, and said, 2 "Oh that I were as in months past, as in the days when God preserved me; 3 When his candle shined upon my head, and when by his light I walked through darkness; 4 As I was in the days of my autumn, when the favour of God was upon my tabernacle; 5 When the Almighty was yet with me, when my servants were about me; 6 When I washed my steps with milk, and the rock poured me out rivers of oil.
Moreover Job continued his parable, and said: [1]

entries.section: 1. His former happiness in the Lord

paragraphs.text: "Oh that I were as in months past, as in the days when God preserved me" [2].

Here we see the sick, grieving and bewildered man remembering the days of his success and comfort, and telling us how God preserved him, and how all people respected him, stood up for him when he went out, and made him a leader over them. But now people, even the lowest of them in the eyes of society, despise him and mock him. He affirms that he was not guilty of sensual sins, that he did not wrong the poor and the widow, that he did not withhold food from the fatherless, and that he committed no secret sins. He rejected lying, deceit, injustice, stinginess, greed, idolatry, malicious joy at another's misfortune, miserliness, hypocrisy, exploitation, and so on. By this he declares his innocence. But this is not due to any merit of his own, but to God's care for him. For the secret of the uprightness of his life is God's preserving him.

Job looked at his past and compared it with what he now was, and longed for time to return and for his state to remain as it had been. In this he does not ascribe his happiness, wealth and success to his own efforts, nor to his abilities and gifts, but to the mercies of God, saying, "God preserved me." He did not see his wealth as a stronghold for himself (Prov 10:15), nor did he trust in the abundance of his riches (Ps 52:7), but "the name of the Lord is a strong tower" (Prov 18:10) for him. Job confesses that God is a wall of fire around him and a hedge that keeps him; God is the secret of his security.

* "Then Job resumed his opening discourse: Oh that I were as in my former state for a month." What does he say? I would like to live for a month the good life that I had in former times, so that I might stop your mouths and show you what I was. He asks for one month like the former months and days. He did not ask for anything extraordinary, but to live for thirty days in the happiness of other times, and to enjoy the good things that no one had given him...

Note the piety of the man, for he ascribes everything to God. A man deprived of help from above cannot remain in an upright life. He says, "God preserved me in them," for his looking back to his former good life is only to bear witness to the providence of God.

* (The Apostle Paul) wants to say that God is the spring and source of all good things, and has no need of a partner or counselor. He is the beginning, the foundation and the maker of all good things; He is the Creator. He called that which did not exist into being. He governs all things, arranges them and keeps them according to His will!

entries.section: 1. His former happiness in the Lord

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom "When his candle shined upon my head, and when by his light I walked through darkness" [3].

The light that shone from him was the light of God, who lit his lamp upon his head, as though Job were a lighthouse, worth nothing without the divine lamp. He owes everything to God, "the true Light," who led him through the darkness, gave him divine comforts in the midst of sorrows, and kept him from stumbling.

In a spirit of humility and with thanksgiving to God, Job presents himself as a lighthouse: whatever its metal, and whatever its shape, the secret of its power is the light placed at its summit, by which ships are guided from many miles away. Job confesses that even if he is a lighthouse, the light upon his head is the light of God and not his own. It is the lamp of the Lord, the true light.

The prophet David sees in the word of God "a lamp unto my feet" (Ps 119:105) that shines for him, so that he walks through the darkness of this world, but Job sees in the word of God a divine light fixed, as it were, upon his head to lead many ships toward the harbor!

It is fitting for the believer to bow before God, that He may fill his life with the work of His Holy Spirit, the Giver of enlightenment, and so he sings, saying, "In thy light shall we see light" (Ps 36:9). He did not say "I see," but "we see," for when the believer is enlightened he draws many with him to enjoy the divine light.

* When Job explained the goodness of his works, he added: "When his candle shined upon my head" (Job 29:3). This lamp is lit with the oil of good works for each one of us. But if we practice evil, and our works become evil, we not only fail to shine, but we also put out the lamp that is ours, and the saying of Scripture is fulfilled: "He that doeth evil walketh in darkness, and he that hateth his brother is in darkness" (see 1 Jn 2:11). Does it not appear to you that whoever extinguishes the light of love has extinguished the lamp? But whoever loves his brother (see 1 Jn 4:21) abides in the light of love, and can say with assurance: "But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God" (Ps 52:8), "thy children like olive plants round about thy table" (Ps 128:3).

Origen * "By the expression [candle] he means the light of Holy Scripture, of which (the Apostle Peter) says: 'We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts' (2 Pet 1:19). And the Psalmist says, 'Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path' (Ps 119:105). Now because the upper part is the mind, and the mind is rightly called the head, it was said by the Psalmist: 'Thou anointest my head with oil' (Ps 23:5), as if he were saying plainly: You fill my soul with the fatness of love. Now the lamp shines upon the head of the Church, where the holy commandments enlighten the darkness of our minds, for in the darkness of this present life we receive the light of the word of God.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Scripture enlightens the eyes of the soul, so read it, O wise one, and be filled with love for it. For from the reading of the Holy Scriptures the sun rises upon the minds that feed on them with discernment.
God placed the Holy Scriptures in the world as a lamp of light to illuminate its darkness. He who loves his soul is enlightened by reading, and walks by its guidance.
Approach Scripture with love, and contemplate its beauty. For you will not benefit without love, because love is the entrance to understanding.
Scripture demands your love; if you do not love it, do not read it.
It speaks to you, and if you grow weary of reading it, it deprives you of its hints.
You must love it, open it, read it and contemplate its beauty; otherwise do not read it, for if you do not love it you will not benefit from it.

entries.section: 1. His former happiness in the Lord

paragraphs.text: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh "As I was in the days of my autumn, when the favour of God was upon my tabernacle" [4].

The text came as it appears in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great): "And God sat with me in my tent." This phrase reveals God's surpassing humility and His wondrous love for man! Perhaps it points to the Incarnation of the divine Word, who became as one in our tent when He took on humanity.

Job looked at the days of his youth and counted them the days of his autumn, in which he had sensed God's favor upon his tent. In other words, he realized that in his youth he did not walk according to the desires of the flesh, but entered, as it were, into friendship with God, and God found His delight in the tent of Job, meeting with him, caring for him and leading him until He brought him across to the eternal dwelling.
* "As I was in the days of my youth, and God sat with me in my tent" [2]... Whoever meditates in silence on the commandments of God, in him God dwells secretly in his tent.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Job did not say that he enjoyed the sweetness of life in the days of his youth when he sat with his wife and his small children, or when the great men visited him in his tent and honored him, but what he remembered was that God overshadowed his tent like a special, cherished son, and came down to his tent to sit with him. What a wonderful picture of a man of God, whose whole concern is God's favor upon him, and His love for him, and His condescension to sit with him, speak with him and listen to him!

If God made of Job a lighthouse bearing a flame of divine light to guide ships to the safe heavenly harbor, then on the other hand He made of his tent a second heaven. It is as though God delights to come down and sit with His beloved Job!

If we look at our bodies as tents in which souls dwell during their journey in this world, then God, the Creator of the body, will not be disgusted by them or despise them, for they are the work of His hands. He sanctifies our bodies with all their emotions, senses and energies, dwells in them, and guides them so that we may enjoy the eternal, immortal glories.

entries.section: 1. His former happiness in the Lord

paragraphs.text: "When the Almighty was yet with me, when my servants were about me" [5].

In his youth Job felt the love of God, and this was the secret of his sufficiency and satisfaction. He felt as though he were in a heavenly palace, not occupied with wealth, nor prestige, nor authority, but with his servants everyone was in fellowship with God, the true Lord of the house.

* Why do you refuse to imitate the holy men and women of the Old Testament? Tell me! Especially you, mothers, think of Hannah as an example; look at what she did. She brought her only son Samuel to the temple when he was still a child!

Which of you does not want her son to be like Samuel, who is better than a king over the whole world ten thousand times over? You say: This is impossible! My son will not be as great as he! Why is it impossible? Because in truth you do not want it. Entrust him into the hands of the One who is able to make him great. And who is this? God! For Hannah entrusted Samuel into the hands of God.

The high priest Eli was not truly able to shape him, for he failed in shaping his own two sons. It was the mother's faith and zeal that made everything possible. He was her firstborn and only son. She did not know whether she would have another son besides him, and yet she never said, "I will wait until he grows up and tastes the pleasures of the world, at least in his youth." No, she rejected all such thoughts. She had one aim, how from the beginning she could consecrate the joy of her heart to God.

Be ashamed, O men, before the wisdom of this woman. She offered Samuel to God, and with the Lord she left him. By this her marriage was blessed all the more, because her first aim was spiritual things. She consecrated the firstborn of her womb to God, and afterward received many children. She saw Samuel honored even in this life.
If men return honor for honor, will not God return much more to the one who honors Him? He gives abundantly even to those who do not honor Him at all!

How long shall we remain thus as lumps of flesh? How long shall we cling to the earth? Let everything come second to our care for our children, so that we bring them up in "the nurture and admonition of the Lord" (Eph 6:4).

entries.section: 1. His former happiness in the Lord

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom "When I washed my steps with milk, and the rock poured me out rivers of oil" [6].

God gave him everything in abundance, so that from the multitude of his flocks it seemed to him as if he washed his feet with milk, and from the abundance of the fruit of the olive trees it seemed as if the rocks around him overflowed with oil.

To what does the washing of a man's steps with milk or richness, and the rock's pouring out rivers of oil for him, point, if not to the believer's sense of inner satisfaction, so that he has streams of milk in which he washes his feet, and streams of oil, so that not only are the members of his soul anointed with a smear of oil, but he becomes as one whose soul is immersed and drawn into streams of holy oil? Here he points to the stone olive press, from which oil flows like a river. "Then will I make their waters deep, and cause their rivers to run like oil, saith the Lord God" (Ezek 32:14). In the song of Moses before his departure it is said: "And he made him to suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock" (Deut 32:13).
The Psalmist sings, saying: "The eyes of all wait upon thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season. Thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing" (Ps 145:15-16).

Moreover, since Job points to the Church, in preaching the Gospel of Christ she offers the world abundance and inner satisfaction. It is the preaching of the Crucified One, rejected by the world, yet in Him are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, in Him are all the treasures of heaven!
* "When I washed my feet with butter" [6]... The feet are washed with butter when the holy preachers are filled with the richness of good works.

"And the rock poured me out rivers of oil" [6]. By the rock he means Christ, as the great preacher affirms: "And that Rock was Christ" (1 Cor 10:4). This rock now pours out rivers of oil, which the holy Church uses, for the Lord speaks in her, and presents the preaching with the inner oil.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Do you not want to be satisfied? And how can that be?! The body longs to be satisfied, but hunger returns to it again after digestion; therefore the Lord Christ says: "Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again" (Jn 4:13).

Then let us hunger and thirst after righteousness, that we may be filled with it... Let our inner man hunger and thirst, so that he may have the food and drink that suit him. (The Lord) said: "I am the bread which came down from heaven" (Jn 6:41). This is the bread of the hungry!
Let us also long to drink as the thirsty, "for with thee is the fountain of life" (Ps 36:9).
The Spiritual Elder * Ah! I shall not be satisfied until Your glory is revealed before me!
Yes, my God. For You alone are able to restore to me my happy life.

To You I confess my misery, at the passing of the day in which I was drowned among the many vanities of the world, deprived of You, the sole object of my love. That day in which my fleshly longings were scattered among deceptive delights. And how many of these delights carry in their pleasure countless toils! These delights promised me many things, and yet they brought upon me nothing but poverty. I moved from one to another, hoping that one of them might satisfy my soul, but they were unable, for my soul still lived only in You!
Truly, in You is beauty, You who alone are everlasting, exalted, and perfect always!
Whoever follows Your footsteps will never go astray! Whoever reaches You is overtaken by no despair!

Whoever possesses You has all his desires satisfied! But how hideous is my misery! Woe is me, my God, for my heart inclines to flee from You, You who are the true riches and the true joy, in order to follow a world in which there is nothing but sorrow and pain.
St. Augustine

7 "When I went out to the gate through the city, when I prepared my seat in the street! 8 The young men saw me, and hid themselves: and the aged arose, and stood up. 9 The princes refrained talking, and laid their hand on their mouth. 10 The nobles held their peace, and their tongue cleaved to the roof of their mouth.
"When I went out to the gate through the city, when I prepared my seat in the street!" [7].

His surpassing happiness in his house did not distract him from caring for others, so he would go out to the gate of the city to preside over the court of justice, not out of love of greatness, but so that all might enjoy justice and the spirit of injustice be lifted from those who suffered.

* "When I went out to the gate of the city, and in the street they prepared a seat for me"... It was the custom among the ancients that the elders sat at the gates and judged the cases of those entering the city, so that the people in the city might be safe, and those who were in dispute were not allowed to enter it. Now, while we honor the historical interpretation, we recall that Job did all this for the sake of preserving justice.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"The young men saw me, and hid themselves: and the aged arose, and stood up" [8].

He had great awe, so that those who walked in immaturity, like reckless youths, feared him. These saw him and hid from him, lest their evils be exposed. But those who walked as experienced, wise elders stood in reverence and respect for him. As the Apostle says: "Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour" (1 Tim 5:17). "Render therefore to all their dues... fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour" (Rom 13:7).

* "The young men saw me, and hid themselves: and the aged arose, and stood up" [8]. If we look to the historical interpretation, we believe what he says. If we take what he said in a symbolic sense, then those whose souls are not weighed down with the weight of counsels are called "young men." Holy Scripture usually calls those who have weight (experience from the past) in their characters elders, not only because they have become mature through the number of years... One of the wise says: "For honourable age is not that which standeth in length of time, nor that is measured by number of years. But wisdom is the gray hair unto men, and an unspotted life is old age" (Wis 4:8-9)...

Now [the young men see] the holy Church and hide, and the elders arise and stand, because the immature fear her activity and uprightness, while the elders glorify her. The trifling in thought flee, while the serious and the perfect praise her by rising to be worthy of her life. The imperfect blame her order and her perfect love. [The young men see her and hide], because they fear that their hidden conduct will be discovered.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"The princes refrained talking, and laid their hand on their mouth" [9].
"The nobles held their peace, and their tongue cleaved to the roof of their mouth" [10].

Job had a strong personality founded on his wisdom, abilities and gifts, so he was the object of honor from the great and the noble. In his presence all fell silent to listen to him, and to benefit from his wisdom and his surpassing experience. Perhaps when the great and the noble quarreled over a matter or differed in opinion, they would find the decisive solution with Job.

* "The princes refrained talking, and laid their hand on their mouth. The voice of the rulers is hushed, and their tongue cleaveth to the roof of their mouth" [9-10]. Who are those understood here as leaders or nobles but those who spread heretical evils? Of these it is said by the Psalmist: "He poureth contempt upon princes, and causeth them to wander in the wilderness, where there is no way" (Ps 107:40). For such persons do not fear to interpret the dispensation of God in a wrong sense, and certainly they draw the flocks subject to them into a wilderness without a way, and not into the Way, which is Christ. Upon these contempt (strife) is rightly poured out, and then they are like those who lay their fingers on their mouths....

Their tongue cleaves to their mouth, since they do not dare to utter what is evil in unrestrained speech, but they cover over all that they do within themselves, lest they propose anything untrue against the true faith... "The voice of the rulers is hushed, and their tongue cleaveth to their mouth." It is as if the Church says plainly: When I am given the opportunity to preach in a loud, public voice, every man who is not subject to the truth is afraid of me.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

To the extent that God gives His children honor, they fear falling into pride, so they work in a spirit of humility, but they do not lag behind in working with burning zeal. If their works appear, it is for the glory of God, and if they are hidden, it is for their preservation in the fortress of humility, full of safety.

* It is among the marks of the saints to hide the good works they have done, lest they bring upon themselves a fall into boasting. Therefore the Truth says: "Take heed that ye do not your righteousness before men, to be seen of them" (Mt 6:1). So also, when He gave sight to the two blind men sitting by the way, He commanded them, saying, "See that no man know it" (Mt 9:30). Yet it is said of them that they "departed, and spread abroad his fame in all that country"... It was fitting for them to hide for the sake of some purpose, and to make it known out of necessity.

Let their hiding be for the preservation of their souls, and let their making it known be for the benefit of others. For this reason it is written: "Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house. Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven" (Mt 5:15-16). There are times when saints are obliged to practice good works even in the presence of their fellow creatures, or to tell them what they are doing, but not with the aim that they themselves be glorified by these works, but that their Father who is in heaven be glorified...
For this reason good preachers avoid honor, and yet they wish to be honored so that others may imitate them.

In the same way, certainly, when the Apostle Paul spoke with his disciples he fled from honor, and yet he shows how much he deserves to be greatly honored. For he said to the Thessalonians: "Nor of men sought we glory, neither of you, nor yet of others, when we might have been burdensome, as the apostles of Christ, but we were gentle among you" (1 Thess 2:6-7). Again, in his epistle to the Corinthians, avoiding honor, he says: "For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord" (2 Cor 4:5)... Therefore he showed in a marvelous way the grace of humility, and sought an abundance of benefit, as one who declares himself the servant of his disciples, and proves that he is better than his enemies.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

11 "When the ear heard me, then it blessed me; and when the eye saw me, it gave witness to me: 12 Because I delivered the poor that cried, and the fatherless, and him that had none to help him. 13 The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me: and I caused the widow's heart to sing for joy. 14 I put on righteousness, and it clothed me: my judgment was as a robe and a diadem. 15 I was eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame. 16 I was a father to the poor: and the cause which I knew not I searched out. 17 And I brake the jaws of the wicked, and plucked the spoil out of his teeth.
"When the ear heard me, then it blessed me;
and when the eye saw me, it gave witness to me" [11].

This honor did not rest on his wealth, nor on his authority, but on his practical conduct, for all bore witness to him through the ear's hearing of his wisdom and his judgments, and the eye's seeing of his love and tenderness. He imitated the just God, the Lover of mankind, and so all bore witness to him.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in the person of the blessed Job a symbol of the blessed Church, for the Church has her esteem, honor and blessing from all who listen to her and see her holy life. The Church remains persecuted by her opponents, but she is blessed, awesome and honored.
"Because I delivered the poor that cried, and the fatherless, and him that had none to help him" [12].
The blessing of all upon him rested on his works of love, for he would not rest until the poor man found his rest, and no food pleased him until the orphan found help in him.

St. Basil the Great asks us to imitate righteous Job, who became a father to orphans and a helper to them (Job 29:12). He presented a deep spiritual understanding of this fatherly work. The adoption of orphans does not stop at supporting them materially, but extends to embracing the little ones in order to consecrate their hearts and lives to the Lord. In his answer to the question: "At what age is a person permitted to dedicate himself to God, and at what time is the vow of virginity considered safe?" he answers thus: [Since the Lord says, "Suffer the little children to come unto me" (Mk 10:14), and the Apostle commends the one who knows Holy Scripture from childhood (2 Tim 3:15), and the one who directs his children to be brought up "in the nurture and admonition of the Lord" (Eph 6:4), it seems to us that all times of life, even the very early, are suitable for acceptance into discipleship (monasticism). Truly we must receive those children who are deprived of their parents under our care, and so become fathers to the orphans, imitating Job (Job 29:12).]

* To make clear why they declare him blessed, he cites his good works, saying: [Because I delivered the one who cried from the hand of those who oppressed him], but this comes after he first ascribes the merit to God, who kept and preserved him, so that "he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord" (1 Cor 1:31).

* See, he does not boast that he turned aside from evil, nor that he offered sacrifices as the Jews did, but boasts that he fulfills what God wants (the rescue of the poor). He says: "Judge the fatherless, plead for the widow" (Isa 1:17). Note that he does not abuse his authority, but uses it when there is a need for it. He was a father and a defender to all. He did not use his riches for injustice, nor his glory for boasting, nor his wisdom for evil, but to rescue those who were weighed down by the pressure of the wicked.

St. John Chrysostom * Now the holy Church shows these works of tenderness on the material side, and does not cease to show them spiritually. She rescues the poor man who cries out when she forgives the sins that the sinner commits and he asks forgiveness for them. Of this poor man it is said: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Mt 5:3). The cry of such poor is the cry of those who say with the voice of the Psalmist: "Let thy tender mercies speedily prevent us: for we are brought very low" (Ps 79:8).

Now she rescues [the fatherless who has none to help him], when each one flees from the desires of the persecuting world... and runs to the bosom of the holy Church, and finds in her the help of counsel. Perhaps by "the fatherless" is meant any believer who, through the death of the good father, becomes an orphan, deprived of him for a time, but not deprived of consolation.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me: and I caused the widow's heart to sing for joy" [13].

Those under destructive pressures found their rescue in him and were saved, and their blessing came upon him, for they did not cease to pray for him, and the broken hearts of widows were gladdened and rejoiced at his works of love and tenderness.

If God attributes to Himself the despised, the needy and the broken-hearted, as the Father of the fatherless and the Judge of the widows, then Job found his delight in caring for all these suffering groups.

* How highly the holy Job esteemed the dignity of death, when he said: [May the blessing of him who drew near to death come upon me] (Job 29:13)... If we see any poor person at the moment of death, let us help him at our own expense. Let each person say: [May the blessing of the person who was near death come upon me]. If we see anyone in weakness, let us not abandon him. If we see anyone in his last sufferings, let us not leave him... May everyone, as he dies, praise you; everyone who dies of old age or of a serious wound or suffering from illness, at the moment of death. This saying has brought blessing to very many... May the last words a person utters before his death be to repeat your name, and as his soul departs from his body, may his blessing come upon you.

* If it is our duty to show mercy to all, should we not rather show it to that good man (the believer who is suffering imprisonment)?! And if he receives nothing from you at the time of danger when he is being led to death, and you think that your money is better than the life of the man who is dying, what a sin you commit! Therefore Job says his wonderful saying: [May the blessing of him who is on the way to destruction and death come upon me] (Job 29:13).

St. Ambrose * And "the blessing of him that was ready to perish" came upon her (that is, upon the Church, who cares for his salvation), when she anticipates the perishing of the sinner, and by her holy counsels turns him back from the pit of sin. It is written thus: "He which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sins" (Jas 5:20). It is a matter deserving great reward to be saved from the death of the body, which will die sooner or later; how much more does he deserve who frees a soul from death, to live in the heavenly city without end?
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"I put on righteousness, and it clothed me:
my judgment was as a robe and a diadem" [14].

His tender conduct, in that he did not allow anyone to be wronged or insulted, nor a needy person to be humiliated, was not a certain role he was bound to play, but was his garment that he never took off. He counted these works not a secondary matter in his life, but a necessity, without which he would be stripped bare before God Himself, and would return to the state of his parents Adam and Eve, sheltering under the fig tree in fear and trembling, with nakedness and shame!

He counted the works of righteousness not a gift from himself that he bestows on others, but a divine gift that clothes him with glory. It is a royal turban (crown)! He did not wear the crown of kingship for boasting and honor; rather his crown was justice and mercy. His honor was not in the royal purple robe, nor the crown, nor the scepter, but his honor and warmth were in the garment of righteousness and the crown of truth.

St. John Chrysostom sees that Job put on righteousness like a cloak, or like one who puts on the garment of a judge. No one appointed him judge over the people, but his virtuous, holy life impelled him to this work, and made the people willingly accept his judgment in their cases. Just as the virtuous life of Moses prepared him for the work of leadership, so for Job, his practice of judicial work came naturally from his virtuous life.

* He says, "I put on righteousness," for there are persons who have a greater standing than others, but they often practice injustice. This was not the case with Job, for he lived always in the way of righteousness.

[I put on righteousness like a cloak], that is, it is my garment for adornment. Some are displeased with this work, murmur, and feel that it is wearisome and hard, but I am not so... And yet who appointed him as judge? This came from his own person, because of his virtue, as with Moses. This is how men ought to be. But as for him who denies virtue, governors are set over him.

St. John Chrysostom * We are obliged to condemn ourselves, so that even when the matter is against us it turns to our favor, as we become accusers of ourselves and condemn our sins. And Scripture says: [The righteous is first in his own cause] (see Prov 18:17). And again he says: "I put on righteousness, and it clothed me as a robe" (Job 29:14). Our present garment is usually, without doubt, an armor for war rather than a garment of peace, as long as we are still subject to desire; but it is different when our last enemy is scattered, and righteousness is full and complete, with no enemy to harass us.

St. Augustine * The man who wanted to harm Jacob was not able to send him away empty (Gen 31:29). For the wise person will never be empty, but always wears the garment of prudence, and is able to say, as Job said: [I clothe myself with righteousness, and put on justice] (Job 29:14). Truly this is the inner tunic of the spirit, and no one can strip it from him unless the man himself takes it off by his erring conduct. Truly Adam was found naked and stripped (Gen 3:10-11), while Joseph was not found naked even when his outer garment was taken from him, since he was wrapped in the safe garment of virtue. For this reason the wise man will not be found empty. How could he be empty? His soul is in fullness, being guarded in the garments it has received.

St. Ambrose * The way to wisdom is not like a man coming out of water into the air, who at the moment he rises above the surface of the water suddenly breathes freely, but like a man coming out of darkness into light, upon whom the light dawns gradually as he advances. So as long as this is not fully achieved, we speak of man as one who enjoys the light gradually. As he approaches the mouth of the cave, whatever light he has comes from the light into which he is advancing, and whatever darkness remains in him comes from the darkness he is leaving. For this reason it is rightly said that in the sight of God "shall no man living be justified" (Ps 143:2). And yet "the just shall live by his faith" (Hab 2:4); so on one side the saints put on righteousness, and on the other side no one lives wholly without sin. Some sin much and others less, and the best of men is he who sins very little.

St. Augustine * [I put on righteousness, and it was my clothing] [14]. Certainly when we put on a garment we are surrounded on every side. In the same way, he who clothes himself with righteousness as with a garment defends himself on every side by good practice, and leaves no part of his conduct bare to sin. For whoever is righteous in some works and unjust in others is like one who has covered one side and left the other side naked. Good works that are afterward defiled by evil deeds do not produce good. It is said by Solomon: "He that offendeth in one thing destroyeth much good" (Eccl 9:18) (Vulgate). And James says: "For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all" (Jas 2:10). And he carefully explained this saying by adding: "For he that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill. Now if thou commit no adultery, yet if thou kill, thou art become a transgressor of the law" (a).

Thus we look with the eyes of the heart in every direction, and so we are careful with all diligence on every side. Therefore it is rightly said also by Solomon: "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life" (Prov 4:23). Before "diligence" he first added "all." Certainly it is fitting for everyone to examine himself diligently from this side and that. And as long as he is in this life he knows that he is set in a battle in which he fights against spiritual enemies, lest he lose the reward which he obtains through one set of works by another. Lest on one side he shut the door in the face of the enemy, but open a door to him on another side. For if a city has great protective barricades against deceiving enemies, and is fortified with strong walls, and is guarded on every side by sleepless watchmen, but a single unfortified opening is found through negligence, the enemy will certainly enter...

Take that Pharisee who went up into the temple to pray; let us hear how he had fortifications for the city of himself, for he says: "I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess." He who says, "I thank thee," certainly set up extraordinary fortifications. But let us see where he left an undefended opening toward the plans of the enemy. ["I am not as this publican"] (Lk 18:11-12). Behold, you see how he opened the city of his heart to the plans of the enemy through his praise of himself, the city which he had closed up in vain with fasting and almsgiving.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"I was eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame" [15].

God granted him to be eyes to the blind, offering good counsel to those who were perplexed. And he was feet to the lame, for it did not stop at giving advice, but in love he undertook everything to be feet that lead the lame in the way of truth, bringing them in practice to the life of rejoicing in the Lord.

* "I was eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame" [15]. He did not say, "I lightened their sorrows," nor "I hid from them their sense of blindness," but [I was their eyes]... In every place I turned their darkness into light.
St. John Chrysostom * By saying these things he indicated unmistakably that he stretched out his hand to one, and carried the other...

* By preaching the Church enlightens the blind, while she supports the lame with her help. For the blind man is the one who does not see where he is going, and the lame man is the one who has no ability to go to the place he sees. Sin is often committed either through ignorance (blindness) or weakness (lameness); either a man does not know what he ought to desire, or he is not able to do all that he desires.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"I was a father to the poor: and the cause which I knew not I searched out" [16].
He was not only a defender of the poor and generous toward them, but offered a sincere fatherhood, for though a king he did not disdain to call himself a father to the poor.

If a case was brought to him he did not hasten to judge, but took care to listen to all the parties and to examine all sides precisely, for he would not answer a matter before he heard it (Prov 18:13), nor issue judgment at first glance merely on appearance. "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him" (Prov 18:17).

Through Job's tender fatherhood he cared not only for the one who asked him to rescue him from injustice, but also for the one who did not ask him. He found his delight in searching for broken souls to rescue them, so he examined the causes that had not been presented to him nor known by him.

Someone may ask: If we wish to show some kind of tenderness or fatherhood toward others, should we care for their bodily affairs, when the Lord Christ asked the one He called to work with Him to let the dead bury their dead, and to devote himself to spiritual service (Lk 9:60)? Pope Gregory (the Great) answers this question, saying: [Above all, those who shine with spiritual gifts must not entirely ignore the affairs of their weak brethren, but they should entrust this matter to others, so that one suited to it may manage it.]

* Truly, blessed is he who does not send the poor man away from his house empty-handed. There is none more blessed than he who feels the needs of the poor and the distress of the weak and helpless. For on the day of judgment he receives salvation from the Lord, who counts Himself a debtor to him for the works of mercy he has shown.

St. Ambrose * "And the cause which I knew not I searched out" [16]. Look, for his role as an advocate (rescuer) does not consist in giving money only, or food or clothing, but extends to preserving them from dangers as well. In a battle that is not mine I take the front position. In the matter that concerns me I search like a skilled hunter. It is not in the things known to me... I refused to abandon them as some do today, and not only do I not refuse those who are present, but even if there is no one seeking him I seek him out myself, as though my work were digging. So I work continually to observe with all care whether anyone has been oppressed.

St. John Chrysostom * But if anyone wants to learn how we call God "Father," let him listen to Moses, the excellent teacher, when he says: ["Is not he thy father that hath bought thee? hath he not made thee, and established thee?"] (Deut 32:6). And the prophet Isaiah also says: "But now, O Lord, thou art our father; we are the clay... and we all are the work of thy hand" (Isa 64:8). The prophetic gift has declared most clearly that we call Him Father not according to nature, but by the work of God's grace in adoption.

And so that you may learn more precisely from the divine Holy Scripture that not only is he who is a natural father called "father," but others also, hear what the Apostle says: ["For though ye have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel"] (1 Cor 4:15). Paul was a father to the Corinthians, not because he begot them according to the flesh but through teaching, and he begot them again according to the Spirit.
Hear also Job: "I was a father to the poor." He called himself a father, not because he begot them all, but because of his care for them.
St. Cyril of Jerusalem "And I brake the jaws of the wicked, and plucked the spoil out of his teeth" [17].

As much as he offered tender fatherhood to the poor, he did not fear the violence of the wicked, unjust and proud. "I brake the jaws of the wicked." He did not say that he takes revenge on them or kills them, but he shatters the powers of evil and violence, and takes the prey from between their teeth, and delivers it with courage, as David rescued the lamb from the mouth of the lion.
* "I brake the jaws of the wicked." This is what the Apostle commands: ["He that ruleth, with diligence"] (see Rom 12:8).

"And plucked the spoil out of his teeth." Note the difficulty of the work. Those who have already been preyed upon and seized, he sets their affairs right... Note also that his virtue is incomparable in every case. If the situation called for it he punished, and if the situation called for it he supported others.

St. John Chrysostom * See what prey the Church snatches from the mouth of Satan, for she took Saul the plunderer at his conversion! While he was still breathing out threatenings on his way to Damascus with letters to persecute the believers, he was gathering prey for Satan, but he himself was gathered for Christ's account when he received the faith (Acts 9:1-19). The Church often snatches the prey from the mouth of the wicked one, and often rescues the soul from the grip of error by preaching...

By the jaws the hidden plans (of the devil) are shown, and by the teeth the open practice of sin is shown. The Psalmist said of these jaws and teeth: "Break their teeth, O God, in their mouth: break out the great teeth of the young lions, O Lord" (Ps 58:6).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Who can contemplate in quietness, perceiving the glory of the divine majesty, during this work? For he is "he that delivereth the poor from him that is too strong for him, yea, the poor and the needy from him that spoileth him" (Ps 35:10), "I brake the jaws of the wicked, and plucked the spoil out of his teeth" (Job 29:17). Who, while caring for the poor... is able to contemplate the greatness of blessedness, and while he is occupied with the needs of the present life for their sake, to have his heart always lifted above the filth of the earth?!... Which of men, even if he were the chief of the righteous saints, do we think could at any time, while bound by the fetters of this life, reach this chief good without ceasing from holy contemplation? Is he not drawn away, if only for a short time, from Him who alone is good by earthly thoughts? Does he not care, if only for a while, about food or clothing or other bodily matters, or about receiving the brethren, or changing his place, or building his cell...?
Father Theonas

entries.section: 4. His hopes for the continuance of his happiness

paragraphs.text: 18 "Then I said, I shall die in my nest, and I shall multiply my days as the salamander. 19 My root was spread out by the waters, and the dew lay all night upon my branch. 20 My glory was fresh in me, and my bow was renewed in my hand. 21 Unto me men gave ear, and waited, and kept silence at my counsel. 22 After my words they spake not again; and my speech dropped upon them. 23 And they waited for me as for the rain; and they opened their mouth wide as for the latter rain. 24 If I laughed on them, they believed it not; and the light of my countenance they cast not down. 25 I chose out their way, and sat chief, and dwelt as a king in the army, as one that comforteth the mourners.
"Then I said, I shall die in my nest, and I shall multiply my days as the salamander" [18].

Job counted himself in a nest to which he flees and where he dwells securely, or a nest in which he settles as at the top of a tree, safe from any dangers that might befall him until the moment comes to give up his spirit. He thought that he would spend all his days in peace, far from any storms that could shatter his nest or shake his lodging.

It is wondrous that Job looks at his life as being like the sand (the salamander) that is on the seashore, as though he thought his life would be very long, and did not realize that it is like the grains of sand that fall from the hourglass and run out in a short time.

* "And I said, I shall die in my nest, and like the palm tree I shall multiply my days" [18]... The likening of the life of the righteous to the palm tree is fitting, because the palm tree is rough to the touch below, and in a way is wrapped in dry bark, but above it bears fruit. Below it is compressed by its spread-out bark, but above it is spread out with great greenness. So is the life of the chosen, despised below, and beautiful on high...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. His hopes for the continuance of his happiness

paragraphs.text: "My root was spread out by the waters, and the dew lay all night upon my branch" [19].
Job considered himself like a tree planted by the streams of water, always watered, which makes it fruitful and flourishing, so that it never withers.
[The dew lay all night upon his branch]: if Job was planted like a tree enjoying the richness of the earth, he receives the blessings of heaven as dew. He is the delight of God who cares for him.

* "My roots are open to the waters" [19], when the thought of the mind spreads secretly to receive the streams of truth. In Holy Scripture roots point to hidden thought. Therefore we open our roots to the waters when we spread the hidden thought of our heart to the inner waters...
The Psalmist says: "He shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water" (Ps 1:3)...

["And the dew lay all night upon my harvest"]... The dew falls from above, but the harvest is gathered from below. So the dew rests upon the harvest, for the grace that comes down from on high makes us persons fit to be gathered in the world from below. By the same grace that waters us from above we bear the fruit of good work. So Paul rightly says: "But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain" (1 Cor 15:10)... As we look at the harvest growing under the dew, we hear him say: "His grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all" (1 Cor 15:10).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. His hopes for the continuance of his happiness

paragraphs.text: "My glory was fresh in me, and my bow was renewed in my hand" [20].

With every new day he carried a new thought in the life of righteousness, for he loved love and tenderness; therefore his honor did not grow old. He says, "My glory was fresh in me"; it will never wither. He does not grow weary of striving with all his strength for the oppressed, for he says, "My bow was renewed in my hand."

* "My glory was fresh in me, and my bow was renewed in my hand" [20]... All who know what is true realize that oldness (aging) is usually among the marks of evil, while newness is among the marks of virtue. Therefore Paul says: "Seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds; and have put on the new man" (Col 3:9-10)... As for our zeal (enthusiasm), when we are among our spiritual enemies or among our various kinsmen in the flesh, we are to some extent absorbed in their habits and so grow old, and we defile the form of our newness which we received through prayer and reading and the good life, through earnest sufferings and daily vigil, yet in our old age we are renewed and refreshed. So when our life is washed with tears, practices good works, and is filled with holy meditations, it recovers its newness without ceasing...

The "bow" in the Holy Scriptures sometimes points to the plans of the wicked, as when it says: "[They] bend their bows to shoot their arrows, even bitter words" (Ps 64:3). The same Psalmist referred to the day of judgment: "Thou hast shewed thy people hard things: thou hast made us to drink the wine of astonishment. Thou hast given a banner to them that fear thee, that it may be displayed because of the truth, that they may flee from the bow" (Ps 60:3-4)...

Sometimes the bow is used in Holy Scripture for good things. This one is of the bow of the Church, and that one of the bow of the Lord, from which the arrows, the terrifying words, go out to the hearts of men. The Psalmist rightly said: "He hath bent his bow, and made it ready. He hath also prepared for him the instruments of death; he ordaineth his arrows against the persecutors" (Ps 7:12-13)...

The bow in the hand is Holy Scripture in action. He holds a bow in his hand who practices in deed the divine declarations that he has learned with understanding. So [the bow is renewed in the hand] in that all we learn concerning the holy declaration by study is accomplished by practicing it in deed...

The blessed David tells us of his circumstances, and foretells our circumstances, and while he points to his sorrows, he speaks equally of what concerns the holy Church and her circumstances in the same sense.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. His hopes for the continuance of his happiness

paragraphs.text: "Unto me men gave ear, and waited, and kept silence at my counsel" [21].

Since his fatherhood to the poor was blended with courage and struggle for the oppressed, together with wisdom and dignity, he became the foremost counselor; when he spoke, all fell silent and listened to him, knowing that nothing could be found fault with in him and nothing was lacking in him.

* ["They that heard me waited for my judgment, and they that listened were silent at my counsel"]... We miss this reverence which those under him offer; it is directed toward the blessed Job. The holy Church also, who suffers bitterly from heretics or from the carnal, remembers the former days too, when all the faithful with whom she spoke listened to her with fear. She laments the boldness of those who oppose her, and says: [They that heard me waited for my judgment, and they that listened were silent at my counsel].
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. His hopes for the continuance of his happiness

paragraphs.text: "After my words they spake not again; and my speech dropped upon them" [22].

When he spoke, everyone felt there was no further need to inquire into the matter, for Job was distinguished by the precision with which he examined things. Therefore there was no one to speak again after his words or to add anything to them.

Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on the saying of the blessed Job, ["And to my words they added nothing"], by saying that the faithful did not dare to add anything of their own to the words of the holy Church, as the heretics did, who dared to add something to her words, as though they were busy correcting the uprightness of the Church's teachings and preaching.

entries.section: 4. His hopes for the continuance of his happiness

paragraphs.text: "And they waited for me as for the rain; and they opened their mouth wide as for the latter rain" [23].

All were like a wasteland in need of rain falling from Job's lips, that their wilderness might be turned into a fruitful garden. They were a land thirsty for rain. All realized the value of the wisdom coming out of his mouth; they waited for it and drank it in, so that it might bear fruit within them as in their outward conduct.

* "And they waited for me as for the rain, and they opened their mouth wide as for the latter rain" [23]. We submit to the words of holy preaching like rain when, in true humility, we recognize the dryness of our hearts and long to drink the draughts of holy preaching. Rightly it is said to God by the Psalmist: ["My soul thirsteth after thee, as a thirsty land"] (Ps 143:6). The prophet commands us to be refreshed by the streams of teaching, saying: "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters" (Isa 55:1).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. His hopes for the continuance of his happiness

paragraphs.text: "If I laughed on them, they believed it not; and the light of my countenance they cast not down" [24].

When he smiled at someone, that person was in surpassing happiness, so that he thought he was as in a dream. All sought his favor and pleasure, for he put aside formality, smiling and laughing. He gave those around him an atmosphere of warmth and joy. Those present did not abuse his simplicity, nor did they lessen their respect for him, but looked to the radiance of his face with rejoicing, without frowning.

* "If I laughed on them, they believed it not; and the light of my countenance did not fall to the ground" [24]. If we understand this through the historical interpretation, we should imagine that the holy man shows himself in a certain way to those under him, that even in his laughter he is able to be awe-inspiring. He related that he was a father to the poor, and a comforter to widows. This matter needs great discernment, how, with this firmness in action, he also shows such great kindness and tender sympathy in it...

So we should learn here that a man should govern himself in his relation to others by the following measure: that when he laughs he should be dignified, and when he is angry he should be lovable. In his excessive merriment he should not be trifling, and his anger should not be without limit, making him hated. We often crush those under our care when we exaggerate the keeping of justice beyond its bounds. Then it is not justice. It does not keep itself under such exaggerated discipline...

Let us see how Paul bears a smile through the grace from on high... even in the midst of his fears and afflictions... He was caught up to the third heaven above him, and carried into Paradise, where he heard unspeakable words (2 Cor 12:2). And yet he remained fearful, for he says: "But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway" (1 Cor 9:27). You see how, when divine grace smiles upon him, he is filled with assurance and hope, and yet does not trust in relying on himself.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. His hopes for the continuance of his happiness

paragraphs.text: "I chose out their way, and sat chief, and dwelt as a king in the army, as one that comforteth the mourners" [25].

In simplicity he smiles with dignity to pour out the spirit of cheerfulness upon those present, and at the same time he does not abandon steering the ship of their lives, for he is the captain of the ship. "I chose out their way, and sat chief."

His smile does not remove his awe as a king and a commander in battle: "And dwelt as a king in the army." When he gave a command, all obeyed him as soldiers obey the commander of the army. He says to this one, Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh; and to his servant, Do this, and he doeth it" (Mt 8:9).

His leadership does not cause distress or resentment, for he does not love authority; he leads only to comfort the mourners by the tenderness of his heart and his support for all in the truth mingled with love.

* [I chose out their way, and sat chief (head)] [25]. In the hearts of perishing sinners the works of the flesh hold the first place, and the works of the soul the next place. Certainly in their thoughts Christ does not sit first, but holds the last place. But the chosen man cares for eternal things above everything. If there is a temporal matter, he manages it as a secondary matter, and it holds less of his attention. The voice of Truth says: "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you" (Mt 6:33)...

["When I sat as a king surrounded by an army, yet I was a comforter of the mourners."] The Lord sits as a king in the heart, for He rules the noisy emotions of the heart in our thoughts. In the soul in which He dwells He gives zeal to the sluggish, restrains the restless, inflames the cold, tempers the fiery, softens the hard, and binds the dissolute, so that by this variety of thoughts He is surrounded by a kind of army. Or certainly He sits as a king surrounded by an army, because that King rules over the minds of the chosen in the midst of a host of virtues.

He is also [the comforter of the mourners], through the promise He gave, saying: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted" (Mt 5:4). Again: "But I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh from you" (Jn 16:22)...

The hearts of the mourners are also comforted by the holy Church, as she guides the souls of the chosen. She is weighed down by the woes of the present journey, and gladdens them with the promise of the eternal city...

The holy Church mingles hope and fear together for those who believe in her, so that they come into contact with the tenderness and justice of the Saviour in her continual service. She does this so that they may not rely on mercy and become lax, nor lose hope through terror of justice. So she gladdens those who are warned by the words of her Head, saying: "Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom" (Lk 12:32). Likewise she warns the presumptuous: "Watch ye and pray, lest ye enter into temptation" (Mk 14:38). And she gladdens those in terror, saying: "Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven" (Lk 10:20). But those who rely on themselves she terrifies, saying: ["I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven"].

She gladdens those in terror, saying: "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: and I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand" (Jn 10:27-28)...

* Tenderness is mingled with severity (firmness)... This truly appears in the ark of the covenant, where the rod and the manna are found together beside the tables of the Law, there where the knowledge of Holy Scripture is in the breast of the good ruler, with the rod of severity (firmness), let there be sweetness too. So David says: "Thy rod and thy staff they comfort me" (Ps 23:4).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Just as a sick man who is concerned for the healing of his body accepts with full willingness every remedy the physician prescribes for him, even if it is very bitter, and in this he does not complain or become distressed, nor does he suspect ill intent in the physician, so it is with the humble man who desires his spiritual growth. He accepts with full willingness the reproofs and counsels of the superior, without imagining that the superior does this out of hatred and harshness.

If for bodily healing we accept bitter, loathsome medicines, and risk the cutting off of limbs and cauterization by fire, and in this we thank the physicians and surgeons who care for us despite the painful treatments, how much more does right reason call us to do this for the salvation of our souls, even if the remedy, counsel and reproof, is bitter?!

St. Basil the Great * (Laxity toward sinners) is not virtue but weakness. Nor is it love or meekness but neglect; indeed it is cruelty toward those souls that are overlooked, and perish without being warned of their ruin.
St. Augustine * He who shepherds the sheep should be neither a lion nor a ewe.
St. John Climacus
Your care for me is the subject of my praise!
* I look to the past, and I touch Your hand that has kept me.
If there is any goodness in me, it is from the riches of Your grace upon me!
* You counted me as a lighthouse, and Your lamp shone upon my head.
You are the true Light.
Your word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light to my mind.
You set me up as a lighthouse to bear Your light.
I bear witness to Your care, and so You draw many to You through me.
* You have blessed my nature in Yourself, You who became incarnate for me.
Let me stand in amazement before Your love, You who sit with me in my tent.
* I stand in the midst of my family, and I see You blessing us at once.
How my soul longs to stand with all mankind, and to see You revealed with Your love and care in the midst of all!
* By Your care You give us everything in abundance, for with You present with us nothing is lacking to us.
You cleanse us and wash us as with milk, and You cause streams of oil to overflow from the rocks!
* I am satisfied in You, and so I long to serve all!
I seek not what is for myself, nor what is for my honor, but what is for Your beloved ones!
* Your care for the Church is surpassing!
You give her Your wisdom, so she speaks Your words and bears Your wondrous thought!
You judge among men, not as one who condemns, but as one who supports and shows compassion.
You give her honor, not that she may exalt herself, but that she may bow down and wash feet.
* In Your care You allow even heretics their full freedom.
They trouble Your Church, but in the midst of affliction she enjoys heavenly blessedness.
And in the midst of opposition she draws many to Your heavens!
You are the Good One who brings forth food out of the eater, and from evils You raise up what is for the edification of many.
* You stretched out Your arms to me, the orphan!
And the Father became a Father to me, so my orphanhood was transformed by the surpassing practical sonship.
Grant me to have compassion on every orphan; when shall I see all mankind enjoying practical sonship to God?!
* When shall we return the souls that have become orphans to their heavenly Father, and so enjoy their blessings upon us?
* Grant me to be covered by Your righteousness, so that I do not cease giving.
Grant me to be adorned with Your crown: that is, with righteousness and mercy!
Your righteousness has become the subject of my sweetness; I acquire it, and so I show compassion to every human being!
Let the world take its garment from me, as the Egyptian woman did with righteous Joseph, but do not allow the devil to strip off Your garment that You gave me!
It is not his right to seize it as long as I cherish it!
* Grant that Your righteousness may cover my whole being, and that the enemy of good may have no way into my depths!
He will find in me no breach as long as I am kept by Your righteousness.
* Grant me by Your grace to become eyes to the blind.
You enlighten me, and make of me a light for others.
You remove my darkness, and in You I support those who sit in darkness.
* Grant me the spirit of tender fatherhood, O Father of all mankind.
That I may have compassion on all, and care, if possible, for everyone!
* Grant me Your grace from above like the dew, and water my life on earth with the waters of Your Holy Spirit.
So that my spiritual youth may be renewed like the eagle's, and my soul may not grow old with a spirit of helplessness and weakness.
* Grant me, O Lord, to walk in the Spirit.
If I rejoice and laugh, may I carry the spirit of firmness.
And if I become firm, may I carry the spirit of tenderness.
May my merriment be completed by my firmness, and my firmness be completed by my tenderness!
* Grant me the spirit of cheerfulness, so that in You I may be a source of joy.
And in my cheerfulness I will not be slack in working earnestly.
Grant me the spirit of leadership without arrogance, so that I work not in a spirit of domination, but in a spirit of fatherhood!
I support all, so that they may bear the spirit of earnest leadership!
“For destruction from God was a terror to me, and by reason of his highness I could not endure” [23].

After speaking of his exceeding tenderness toward all the deprived classes, and his esteem for all who were rejected by society, even the slaves, he lifts his eyes with all reverence toward God and wonders why God allowed him to suffer these harsh trials.
When Job felt the weight of the afflictions he was filled with terror, and felt that the hand of God had become heavy upon him.

entries.section: 11. His trust is in God, not in his wealth

paragraphs.text: 24 “If I have made gold my hope, or have said to the fine gold, Thou art my confidence; 25 If I rejoiced because my wealth was great, and because mine hand had gotten much;
“If I have made gold my hope, or have said to the fine gold, Thou art my confidence” [24].

Had he relied on his wealth and possessions, there would have been a reason for all this to be taken from his hand. But he had focused all his feelings, emotions and intentions on the Creator and not on the creature, so why were these blessings taken from him?
* It happens that a man stops placing his hope in the Creator, so that hope in the creature takes His place.

That rich man fixed his hope on uncertain things when he said: [Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry] (Lk 12:19). But the voice from on high rebuked him, saying: “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?” (Lk 12:20)... For God stands forever, and all these things pass away. What, then, is this, that we fly from Him who alone stands, and cling to passing things?
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 11. His trust is in God, not in his wealth

paragraphs.text: “If I rejoiced because my wealth was great, and because mine hand had gotten much” [25].

St. John Chrysostom sees that the victory won by righteous Job during his trial was not the product of the moment, but the fruit of practical spiritual training that he lived by divine grace even before the trial came, among which was his training in despising temporal blessings and earthly wealth.

* Such was blessed Job. Had he not trained himself well before entering the struggles, he would not have shone in splendor in this way. Had he not experienced freedom from despondency, he would have uttered words in a rush when his sons died. But as he was before, so he stood against all the assaults: against the destruction of his wealth and the great ruin that came upon him, against the loss of his sons, the consolation of his wife, the plague that struck his body, the reproaches of his friends, and the insults of his servants.

If you also want to see his ways on the (spiritual) path, listen to him telling how he despised wealth, saying: “If I rejoiced because my wealth was great, if I gathered gold in huge quantities, if I trusted in precious stones” (Job 31:25, 24) LXX. Therefore he was not troubled when he lost these things, because he did not desire them when he had them.

* Job was rich, but he did not serve the demon of greed, mammon; rather he reigned over wealth and mastered it, so he was a lord and not a slave. Therefore he possessed all these things as a steward of another’s money, not only not seizing from others, but giving what was his to the needy. And what is more, when he had these possessions they did not make him glad, for he declared, saying: [If I rejoiced when my wealth was great] (Job 31:25), nor did he grieve when they were gone from him.

St. John Chrysostom * The saints, in this pitiable journey, long for that appearing of their Creator which they cannot now contemplate, and so they count the whole fullness of the present life as if it were poverty. Nothing outside God satisfies the mind that truly seeks after God.

Such persons often count abundant goods an excessive burden, for they carry many things with seriousness while they hasten toward their homeland. Therefore they devote their energy so that their needy relatives may share with them...
The elect will not rejoice in many goods, because out of love for the heavenly inheritance they give away and distribute what is in their hands, despising it and renouncing it.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

26 If I beheld the sun when it shined, or the moon walking in brightness; 27 And my heart hath been secretly enticed, or my mouth hath kissed my hand: 28 This also were an iniquity to be punished by the judge: for I should have denied the God that is above.
“If I beheld the sun when it shined, or the moon walking in brightness” [26].

As his wealth was not his trust, but the Giver of wealth, so the sun and the moon, with their beauty and splendor, took no place in his heart; rather he was enlightened by God, the Creator of the sun and the moon, the true eternal Light.
The sun and the moon were objects of worship for many in the days of Job, who honored them as soldiers of heaven. This act was counted the height of evil and ingratitude toward God the Creator.
* Job tells us that he did not look at the sun as it rose, nor at the moon as it walked in brightness, showing that he did not seek the present light.

As the soul pours itself out in contemplation outside itself, so much the more does it do so in order to return to inward things. Thus all who have wise hearts avoid falling toward outward things through the bodily senses. Instead they make continual effort to gather themselves within by hidden discipline, guarding their own selves, so as to be found wholly in what is inward.
Jeremiah bound himself to the depths of his heart in earnest discipline, and fled from longing for the outward life, when he said: [I did not desire the day of man, thou knowest] (cf. Jer 17:16).
* Just as the “gold” of understanding did not make Job proud, so also the light of outward works did not make him exalt himself before the eyes of men...

The sun in its brightness is the good works displayed outwardly. It is written: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mt 5:16). Again: “Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning” (Lk 12:35). For what is said in this passage about the rising sun means the Gospel, which is indicated by the burning lamps. When good works shine among unbelievers, the lamp is lit in the night; and when they shine in the Church, the sun shines in the day.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Many have strayed from the One in many ways. Some deified the sun, so that when it set they dwell at night without a god.
And some worshiped the moon, so that they have no god by day.
And some worshiped the parts of the rest of the world.
And some worshiped the arts.

And some worshiped various kinds of foods, and some their pleasures, and some took delight in women, so they set up a statue of a naked woman and called her Aphrodite, and worshiped their lusts in a visible form.
And some were dazzled by the glitter of gold and worshiped it, and others worshiped other kinds of these things.
St. Cyril of Jerusalem “And my heart hath been secretly enticed, or my mouth hath kissed my hand” [27].

Righteous Job affirms that idols, gold, precious stones and abundant wealth could not, all of them, deceive his heart in secret; that is, not only did he not practice any kind of arrogance, pride or idolatry in deed, but none of it even crept stealthily into his heart.

Putting the hand to the mouth and kissing it is a custom practiced by many when their hearts are occupied with something very dear to them or when they greatly admire it, and so they express what is in their hearts by sending kisses from the mouth through the hand, pointing to whom or what they love. Thus neither wealth nor idols occupied him, nor did he love these things, nor send them his kisses.

* Stretching the hand to the mouth is the harmony between voice and practice. He who praises what he does kisses his hand with his mouth, and so bears witness to his speech by the merits of his practical deeds. In this case, who is the despiser if not the one who receives the very same gifts for doing them (and ascribes them to himself)? The great Preacher says well: “What hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?” (1 Cor 4:7). Now the saints themselves know that they are of the stock of a corrupt origin, since from the fall of our first father it is grace that changes us for the better in desires and works... They perceive that they have received strength for the struggle. So blessed Job tells of the good things that he practices, but he never ascribes them to his own work. On the contrary, he praises his Creator, and denies that he kissed his hand with his mouth.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
“This also were an iniquity to be punished by the judge: for I should have denied the God that is above” [28].

The love of the world did not creep into Job’s heart, nor did idol worship creep into it. Had he fallen into either, he would have deserved what came upon him as a divine punishment. He did not deny his God by clinging to creation or by deifying it.

entries.section: 13. No thought of gloating enters him

paragraphs.text: 29 “If I rejoiced at the destruction of him that hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him: 30 Neither have I suffered my mouth to sin by wishing a curse to his soul.
“If I rejoiced at the destruction of him that hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him” [29].

Job was careful not to deny his Creator, nor to wrong his brother or hate him, even if his brother hated him. No thought of gloating over an opponent or one who hated him crept into his mind.
