When we think that we are not seen, we keep our eyes closed to the light of the sun, meaning we shut it out from us, and do not shut ourselves out from it.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
For he will not lay upon man more than right; that he should enter into judgment with God [23].

Some see that the meaning here is: God does not call man again to trial; He does not look into a case twice, for His judgments are just and need no appeal; the sentence is issued and there is no one to appeal for a fresh pleading.

And some translate it: "Behold, no man is given a set time to come to judgment with God." Man's time is not in his hand, nor is his lot fulfilled by his wisdom and strength. When God sees that the time is right, He judges man.

entries.section: 1. Job thinks he is more righteous than God

paragraphs.text: Elihu answered and said:
Thinkest thou this to be right?
Thou saidst, My righteousness is more than God's [1-2].

Elihu addresses Job, asking: Do you think it right to say that you are more righteous than God? This is blasphemy! Job did not say this, either openly or by implication. But perhaps Elihu sensed it in Job's talk about his sincerity and the uprightness of his life, and that he had committed no crime that would qualify him for these calamities (see Job 9:17, 30-35; 10:13-15; 16:12-17; 34:18-19). He interpreted all this to mean that Job thinks himself more righteous than his Creator.

Pope Gregory (the Great) holds that Elihu did not grasp what was in Job's mind or what lay behind his words. Though Job seemed to justify himself before the Lord, Elihu took him to be calling himself more righteous than the Lord. In truth, Job did not yet understand that his trials were meant to prove him more and more for the sake of receiving greater glories, and were not a punishment for sins. So he asks: What sins have I committed that all these trials, which have not come upon anyone else, should come upon me? It is a question rather than a justification of himself!

entries.section: 1. Job thinks he is more righteous than God

paragraphs.text: * “Thinkest thou this to be right, that thou saidst, My righteousness is more than God's?” [2]... It should be noted that the blessed Job did not say that he was more righteous than God. But he says: [Let justice contend with me, and my trial will result in victory] (see Job 23:7).

In examining Job's life and the reasons for his being struck, we often notice that he believed his scourgings were to remove his sins and not to increase his merits. Therefore he was confident that his trial would result in victory, since he found nothing in himself that deserved the blows that had befallen him. Indeed, the Lord Himself said of him to Satan: “Thou movedst me against him, to swallow him up without cause” (Job 2:3).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

What Job did even before the Law, many have done even in the age of grace, asking: “Why does God permit afflictions for the saints?” Many of the Fathers of the Church faced such a question. We mention as an example the sixth Conference of St. John Cassian with Abba Theodore (Tadros), which we have already published, and from which we quote the following:

* Some asked: Why are these men of great merit and abundant virtues slain by these robbers?! Why does God permit crimes to be committed against His servants, so that they fall into the hands of the wicked?!

In our grief we came to St. Theodore, who excelled in the (grace of) discernment. This Father lived in the region of the Cells, Calle, between Nitria and Scete, five miles from Nitria and eight from the desert of Scete where we were dwelling. When we came before him, distressed because of their death, and showing our astonishment at God's great long-suffering in permitting these men to be killed in this way, those who by their holiness were able to keep others from such trials, yet could not themselves be saved from falling into the hands of the wicked, we asked him: Why does God permit such crimes against His servants?!
Abba Theodore (Tadros)
In the introduction to his treatise “No One Can Harm a Man Unless He Harms Himself,” St. John Chrysostom wrote:

[Just as it is impossible to count the waves of the sea, so it is impossible to count the victims who fall under the burdens of plots, insults and sufferings. Neither by amending the law, nor by terror through the courts, nor by anything of the kind, can anyone stop the course of this plague and confusion; rather, evil increases more and more every day, until the sighs, laments and weeping of the sufferers have become a common and familiar thing...

And there are those who cling to a new kind of folly, accusing the providence of the Lord when they see the chaste man often held captive under violence, beaten and shamefully treated, while the shameless, cruel and base man pours countless troubles upon those who are chaster than he, and wrongs those in the city, in the country, in the desert, at sea and on land.
This discourse that I deliver is necessary in order to correct what they claim... proving that whoever has sinned is harmed only by his own hands, and no other man has driven him to sin.]

entries.section: 2. Is righteousness of no profit, and evil of no harm?

paragraphs.text: 3 For thou saidst, What advantage will it be unto thee? and, What profit shall I have more than by my sin? 4 I will answer thee, and thy companions with thee. 5 Look unto the heavens, and see; and behold the clouds which are higher than thou. 6 If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him? or if thy transgressions be multiplied, what doest thou unto him?
For thou saidst, What advantage will it be unto thee?
What profit shall I have more than by my sin? [3]
Some think that Job is speaking to himself, asking: What have you gained (O my soul)? And what do I gain by not practicing sin?
Others think that Job is saying to God: My righteousness does not profit You in anything, and it does not profit me.
Perhaps he took this from what Job said (Job 9:30-31; 10:15). The psalmist expressed this too in the Psalm (Ps 73:13).

Job did not say this openly. What he said was that he had expected these calamities not to befall him because of his upright conduct, yet this conduct did not spare him, as though he had gained nothing from it (see Job 19:28).
St. John Chrysostom made clear that nothing harms a man except his own evil, and nothing profits him except the uprightness of his life.

* What, then, is man's good? Man's good does not lie in wealth, that we should fear poverty; nor in bodily health, that we should dread sickness; nor in the way people look at you, that you should beware of what people say evilly about you; nor in life here for its own sake, that you should tremble at death... Rather, his good lies in holding fast to the true teachings and in uprightness of life, which no one, not even Satan himself, can take from a man as long as he guards it as he ought.

And this is fully understood even by the most wicked and fierce of the demons. Therefore Satan stripped Job of his possessions, not to make him poor, but to compel him to utter a word of blasphemy against God. He tormented his body, not to humble him by sickness, but to frustrate the goodness of his soul. But when he had exhausted all his devices, and had made this rich man poor... and deprived him of his children... and tore his body with a savagery that torturers could not equal, for instruments of torture cannot rend every side of the body as the worms that were in his body did, and Satan ruined his reputation, so that his friends who were with him declared that this was the recompense for the sins he deserved, directing many accusations against him, and drove him out of his city and his home, not to another city, but the dunghill of his city became his home...
None of this harmed Job; on the contrary, he was glorified the more because of these plots which Satan poured out against him.

Satan took much from him, but he did not rob him of any of his goodness. Rather, he drove him the more to increase the strength of his goodness. For after these things befell him, he enjoyed greater confidence, in proportion to the strength of the adversary who fought him.

Now if one who endured sufferings such as these, which were not the work of a man but of Satan, who is more wicked than all humankind, suffered no harm, would you say that some man has harmed or destroyed you...

If Satan, filled with such great cunning, after emptying all that was in his bag, using all his weapons, and pouring all his evils against a man of exalted standing in his family, and righteous, yet caused him no harm, but rather, as I have said, benefited him, how can you accuse one man or another of bringing harm in his hands upon another, and not upon himself?!

entries.section: 2. Is righteousness of no profit, and evil of no harm?

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom I will answer thee, and thy companions with thee [4].

I will show you the evil that the wrong way causes, or that sin causes, and the blessings that righteousness causes, and I will bring forward what your friends did not mention in their discussion with you.
Look unto the heavens, and see; and behold the clouds.

entries.section: 2. Is righteousness of no profit, and evil of no harm?

paragraphs.text: Which are higher than thou [5].

God created the heavens that you might look at them, and they would bear witness to you that God's wisdom and His boundless loftiness are beyond your understanding. Look at the clouds and you will perceive the perfections of God.

Here Elihu begins to answer Job, showing that it is impossible for him to comprehend God's wisdom, as the height of the heavens bears witness. It is as though he asks him: Can you soar in the heavens and reach the clouds? For God, who is their Creator, is higher, greater and loftier than the heavens and the clouds.
Thus Elihu, like Eliphaz, shows that God is loftier than nature, which itself rises above the thought of man.
He who cannot look with his eyes at the heaven and comprehend its secrets, how can he reach with his mind the throne of God and understand the secrets of His plan?

“For the works of the Lord are for the most part hidden; who shall declare the works of His justice, or who shall endure them? For the covenant is afar off, and the examination of all is at the end” (Sir 16:22).
“O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!” (Rom 11:33)
“For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts” (Isa 55:9).
* The works of our Creator must always be honored without examination, for they will never be unjust.
For whoever searches for the cause of His secret counsel is counted as nothing other than a man resisting His counsel in pride.

So when man cannot discover the motive of God's works, we must be silent in humility, submitting to His works, because the bodily senses are not on a level that can penetrate the secrets of His majesty...
Paul adds later: “Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus?” (Rom 9:20)
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Elihu speaks of God's surpassing loftiness. For man's conduct, whether good or evil, does not affect God [6-8]. Though man's righteousness or evil is not to serve God and does not offend Him, yet both have their effect on human life. Therefore there is no need to treat righteousness as though it were a sin that must be punished.
If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him?

entries.section: 2. Is righteousness of no profit, and evil of no harm?

paragraphs.text: Or if thy transgressions be multiplied, what doest thou unto him? [6]
Nothing of your practice of sin will hurt Him, even if you multiply it many times over (Jer 7:19; Prov 8:36).
* Such words ought not to be said to the blessed Job, who knows greater truths; yet what was said is true, namely that our sins do not harm God, nor do our good works help Him in anything.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. God has no need of our righteousness

paragraphs.text: 7 If thou be righteous, what givest thou him? or what receiveth he of thine hand? 8 Thy wickedness may hurt a man as thou art; and thy righteousness may profit the son of man. 9 By reason of the multitude of oppressions they make the oppressed to cry: they cry out by reason of the arm of the mighty.
If thou be righteous, what givest thou him? or what receiveth he of thine hand? [7]
God will gain nothing from your practice of righteousness; you have nothing that God needs for you to give Him (Ps 16:2; Prov 9:12; Lk 17:10).

entries.section: 3. God has no need of our righteousness

paragraphs.text: Thy wickedness may hurt a man as thou art; and thy righteousness may profit the son of man [8].

Your evil harms you as a man, and does not harm God, because your evil separates you from God, the source of happiness. As a man you harm yourself, and you may harm other human beings, by your evil; and by your righteousness, as a son of man, you profit and benefit your brethren.
* The evil of man harms the one whom evil corrupts by leading him astray; again, our righteousness profits the one who turns from his evil.

* When the wicked grieve the righteous, they set them free the more from the desires of this world. While they heap savage deeds upon them here, they urge them on to hasten toward heaven... This is the reason why the righteous are allowed to be wronged by the wicked, so that they may listen to the blessings to come and long for them, and bear the dreadful evils of the present; and while love calls them, the sufferings draw them into a swift flight.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* What then?! Is the man who is slandered and suffers the plundering of his goods not harmed, deprived of his possessions, driven from his inheritance, and struggling in crushing poverty?!

No, he is rather profited, if he is dignified. For did these things harm the Apostles? Did they not always struggle with hunger, thirst and nakedness?! And because of these things they became glorified and renowned, and gained for themselves more help from the Lord?!
* I have not said that no one harms another, but that no one is harmed by another. And how can no one be harmed by another, when many harm others...?!
The brothers of Joseph, for example, wronged Joseph, but Joseph himself was not harmed.
And Cain cast his nets for Abel, but Abel did not fall into them. And this is the reason why disciplines and punishments exist.

For God does not lift the punishment from the one who devised the harm merely because of the goodness of the one who bore it, but confirms his punishment because of the evil of the doer of iniquity. For although those upon whom the evil falls become more glorified because of the plots devised against them, this was not in the intention of those who devised the evil, but is due to the courage of those who are their victims. Therefore crowns of wisdom are prepared for the latter, but for the former, the recompense of their evils.

Have your possessions been taken from you? Remember those words: “Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither” (Job 1:21). And add to them the words of the Apostle: “For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out” (1 Tim 6:7).

Has your reputation been wronged, and have some loaded you with countless insults? Remember the saying: “Woe unto you, when all men shall speak well of you!” (Lk 6:26). And also: “[If they] say all manner of evil against you... rejoice, and be exceeding glad” (Mt 5:11-12).
Have you been taken into exile? Remember that you have no place here, but if you are wise you must look upon the whole world as a land of sojourning.
Have you been struck with a serious illness? Recall what the Apostle says: “Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Cor 4:16).
Is a man suffering a violent death? Let him remember John, whose head was cut off in prison and taken on a platter and given as a reward for the dancing of a harlot.

Consider the reward you receive on account of these things, for all these sufferings, when they fall unjustly from one man upon another, take away our sins and our evil (since we accept the injustice without murmuring, believing in God and hoping for the other life, and these things work to prove us). Great, then, is the benefit of these labors for those who bear them courageously!
St. John Chrysostom By reason of the multitude of oppressions they make the oppressed to cry.

entries.section: 3. God has no need of our righteousness

paragraphs.text: They cry out by reason of the arm of the mighty [9].

Though evil does not harm God at all, it harms the children of men, for the oppressed cry out in the midst of the crowds because of the violence of the powerful, those who hold authority (the mighty). The wicked rich press with their violent hands upon the poor and wretched, who cry aloud from their persecutors, and there is no one to calm their souls, because they do not turn to God.

It is difficult to connect this statement with the preceding discourse. But it seems that Elihu is reviewing a general question in society, to which Job himself had referred (Job 24:12), where he sees that God does not intervene quickly to rescue the poor from the hands of the cruel wicked. Many are crushed by tyrants, and God does not intervene. Job considered that this general question touched him personally, since his friends had almost crushed him under their feet. And Elihu considered this thought an insult directed against Almighty God, His care and His love. He found himself obliged to give an explanation of this phenomenon.

Elihu answers the question: Why does God not respond to the cries of the suffering righteous, to help them against the oppressors? Elihu declares that the secret of God's not answering prayer is that the one who prays does not care about enjoying God; all that concerns him is to benefit from God. It is not true prayer, whose aim is to enjoy the light of the divine Presence, but a natural cry that comes out of pain, as the bird and the animal cry [10-11]. Our prayers for deliverance from the wicked are empty prayers [12-13].
When a man cries out in his distress he supposes that God does not hear; but He hears, and He may not answer because of the pride of the one crying out, or his falsehood.

* Rightly we may call the wicked “oppressors,” not only those who corrupt our outward goods, but also those who strive by their evil habits and the example of their corrupt life to scatter our inner treasures. They do not attack the things around us, but seek to devour us from within.

He who attacks our virtues by his evil conduct is a more dangerous oppressor than he who harms our goods by violent injustice against us. For though he takes nothing of our resources, he sets before us examples of destruction.

He practices a heavier injustice, for he stirs our quiet hearts with temptation. Even if he does not compel us to fight his evil conduct, he presses upon us by stirring up temptation, so that we suffer severe injustice from his life, suffering within by things that we overcome with difficulty.

Since the life of the wicked man, bound to the world, harms us, it was well said: [By the multitude of oppressors they cry out] [9]... [They wail by reason of the arm of the tyrants] [9]... For he who wishes to terrify us in order to push us into sin rages against us with the arm of a tyrant. To urge toward vice through the conduct of (an evil man) is one thing, and to compel to it by terror is another.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. Let us cry out to God in distress

paragraphs.text: 10 But none saith, Where is God my maker, who giveth songs in the night; 11 Who teacheth us more than the beasts of the earth, and maketh us wiser than the fowls of heaven?
But none saith, Where is God my maker, who giveth songs in the night? [10]

The secret of this problem, that is, of God's not intervening to rescue the poor from the hands of the oppressors, is that they do not turn to God, but turn to complaint and murmuring against God, and to reliance on human arms. Elihu says that none of those who have fallen under the feet of the cruel in bitter calamities cries out, saying: Where is my God who made me, that He may turn the night of calamities into a joyful feast and a song that fills my heart with gladness?

God is ready to intervene, but He does not force Himself in; rather He waits to be called upon by the poor, that He may give them His divine consolations and break the snares set for the poor (see Acts 16:25; Ps 126:1-2).
Night in the Holy Bible sometimes signifies sin, and sometimes the afflictions and calamities that turn a man's life into a dark and frightening night.
The Septuagint reads: “Who appoints the watchers of the night,” that is, He sends His angels in the midst of the night of calamities to rescue those who take refuge in Him.
He who takes refuge in God in his joys and in his afflictions enjoys heavenly peace by day as by night, and his life is turned into a joyful symphony and a ceaseless praise.

entries.section: 4. Let us cry out to God in distress

paragraphs.text: Who teacheth us more than the beasts of the earth, and maketh us wiser than the fowls of heaven? [11]

Elihu grieves over the state to which rational man has come by ignoring his Creator, the giver of understanding and wisdom, who is able to save to the uttermost. In folly he rejects God's teaching, guidance and leadership, and so has become less than the beasts of the earth and the fowls of heaven.

The Lord says through Isaiah: “The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib: but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider” (Isa 1:3). The beasts of the earth, the birds, and sometimes the fish know the hand that is stretched out to feed them and give thanks for it; but rational man, who receives much from his Creator, pays no heed to Him and does not look to His compassionate hands.
The Holy Bible calls us to learn even from the ant, which sometimes behaves with more wisdom than man, who has a mind and surpassing abilities.

The blows of the enemy of good are dangerous. He wishes to draw us to temporal pleasures and enslave us to lusts through the carnal life; and if we do not respond to him and seek true knowledge, he strikes our hearts with pride, and so corrupts our understanding and wisdom. Therefore the psalmist stresses the need for understanding and wisdom together with humility: “Man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish” (Ps 49:20). And on the other hand the Apostle Paul says: “Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened”... Therefore “God also gave them up to uncleanness through the lusts of their own hearts, to dishonour their own bodies between themselves” (Rom 1:21, 24).
* The beasts of the earth are those who seek lower things through the carnal life, while the fowls of heaven are those who seek higher things in the zeal of arrogant curiosity.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 5. Let us cry out in humility without murmuring

paragraphs.text: 12 There they cry, but none giveth answer, because of the pride of evil men. 13 Surely God will not hear vanity, neither will the Almighty regard it. 14 Although thou sayest thou shalt not see him, yet judgment is before him; therefore trust thou in him. 15 But now, because his anger does not punish, neither does he regard the multitude of transgressions, 16 therefore Job openeth his mouth in vain; he multiplieth words without knowledge.
There they cry, but none giveth answer [12].
Sadly, these poor afflicted by calamities cry out and are not answered, because they do not cry out to God in a spirit of humility, but in complaint and murmuring, in evil pride.

Here he gives us another reason for God's not intervening: the first, as we saw, is that they do not cry out to Him; the second is that they cry out, but in a spirit of murmuring, and so they obtain nothing. God does not hear them until humility takes the place of pride in their hearts, and they offer prayers of contrition and repentance (Ps 10:4; Jer 13:17).

* It often happens that, when they are engulfed in temptation, they expect heaven to give them consolation even during their lifetime. They desire deliverance, not for their own sake, but for the sake of their opponents. They want Almighty God to deliver them from the dangers surrounding them by working a miracle, so that God may show His power even to the unjust. They long that God should save their adversaries eternally by the same means by which He saves one like them in this world. As the prophet also says in the person of the martyrs: [Deliver me because of my enemies] (Ps 69:18). It is as though he says: “For my own sake I do not ask deliverance from temporal trial, but I ask deliverance for the sake of my opponents.”
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Prayer has conditions for it to be answered, among them:

That our request be according to the will of God (Mt 26:39), with perseverance and importunity (Lk 11:8), and that we realize it is God's will that we amend our ways before the answer comes (Isa 1:15).
Among them also is the sense of our unworthiness of what we ask (1 Job 17:4), or the unworthiness of the one for whom we ask (Jer 14:11).
Among them too is that not being answered is better than being answered (2 Cor 12:7)... But if all the conditions are met, there is no doubt that God answers our prayer.

entries.section: 5. Let us cry out in humility without murmuring

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great Surely God will not hear vanity, neither will the Almighty regard it [13].

Surely God does not listen to vain or false cries or requests, or to ungrateful, thankless hearts. Where there is no sincerity, faith or thanksgiving, the petition does not rise to God. The prophet says: “Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity” (Hab 1:13).

entries.section: 5. Let us cry out in humility without murmuring

paragraphs.text: Although thou sayest thou shalt not see him, yet judgment is before him; therefore trust thou in him [14].

Elihu asks Job to trust in God. Here he seems to refer to an observation Job made (Job 23:8), where he said that he could not approach God, nor present his case to Him. He went east, west, north and south, and could not see Him, nor did he find an opportunity to present his case before Him. Here Elihu makes clear that in truth God is unseen, but this does not mean that He does not care about the affairs of men, or that He does not deserve our trust and love. God cares for humanity and judges with justice and righteousness, and all things are open before Him. It befits us to wait patiently, for He will surely judge at the proper time.

* Because the Lord does not wish to look upon faults, being Almighty, He observes all who practice deeds against the Law, and saves me. You plead before Him if you are able to praise Him, which is possible even now (see Job 35:13-14). For the Lord not only does not wish to examine faults, but does not even wish to look upon them, as another prophet says: “You who have eyes that are purer than to behold evil, and cannot look upon wrong”(a)... See what divine care this is! What protection! What tenderness! For He does not take vengeance, nor is He disgusted by the deeds!

entries.section: 5. Let us cry out in humility without murmuring

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom But now, because his anger does not punish, neither does he regard the multitude of transgressions [15].

Some think that the meaning here is that what befalls a person in the way of calamities seems as nothing beside the punishment that man deserves. If God visits man in anger through the chastisements He permits, these are very light and small compared with the transgressions we commit.

“Neither does he regard (know) the multitude of transgressions”: here the talk is of God, who does not repay here for all the transgressions we commit, as though He overlooks them or does not know them, lest the hand of chastisement grow heavy upon us. In His chastening of us He is tender and compassionate, even if we count this chastening very harsh.

* God, who judges forever, is long-suffering for a long time. If He is long-suffering in bringing His wrath, it is because He keeps it to pour out later without end. Pain here is the portion of the elect, to prepare them to receive the heavenly reward. It is our portion to receive scourgings here, for He keeps eternal joy for us.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Rejoice while you are under the scourgings, for the inheritance is kept for you, because He does not cast off His people. He chastens for a while, and does not condemn forever.

St. Augustine * I choose that the Lord visit my sins and correct my transgressions here in this world, so that Abraham may say to me there what he said about poor Lazarus in his talk with the rich man: “Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented” (Lk 16:25). For this reason, when the Lord rebukes and chastens us, we must not be ungrateful. Let us understand, then, that our rebuke in the present time is so that we may receive comfort in the future. And as the Apostle says: [But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world] (1 Cor 11:32). For this reason Job also accepted all his sufferings willingly, saying: “What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” (Job 2:10).

entries.section: 5. Let us cry out in humility without murmuring

paragraphs.text: Origen Therefore doth Job open his mouth in vain; he multiplieth words without knowledge [16].

Elihu came to this conclusion, that Job opened his mouth and cried out, but by his murmuring his words and cries were counted vain and without understanding. Job's complaint, in Elihu's eyes, is worthless babble, without knowledge or understanding, because it carried accusations against God's dispensation.
Why has Your hand been heavy upon me?!
* In my human weakness I often ask:
Why has Your hand been heavy upon me?
Why do You permit affliction for Your believers?
Why do You permit the wicked to triumph and exult?
* You answered me, O All-loving One, in the language of deed, not of dialogue; in my name and on my behalf You entered the garden of Gethsemane.
And You, the Ruler of all, began to be amazed and sorrowful.
In my stead You said: My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death.
You fell on the ground, You before whom all the heavenly powers bow down.
You said to God Your Father: Abba, Father, all things are possible unto You; take away this cup from me.
“Nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt” (Mk 14:36).
* Establish me in You, that I may utter what You uttered, and ask what You asked, and bear Your mind within me!
Then I will accept affliction with You, even the shame of the Cross!
I will accompany You on the road to Golgotha, and my soul will find rest.
* What do You ask of me in the midst of the furnace of affliction?
You ask to see my face and hear my voice.
I confess to You: I have turned my face to the world.
May Your Holy Spirit turn it back, that it may look to You.
I turned my converse to men; I thought they were able to save me, but their spirit goes forth, and they return to their dust.
Let me cry out to You, for You are my strong tower.
Affliction surrounds me, but it does not steal into my soul!
Outwardly there is bitterness and gloom, but inwardly there is exultation in You, O Heavenly One!

* In humility You cried out, O only-begotten Son, though You are one with Your Father in the same essence, and Your will is the same as His will; You surrendered Your will to Him, that He might do His will in You.
Grant me the spirit of humility, that my heart may cry out to You:
Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth!
* Welcome to affliction, as long as it is by Your permission.
I experience fellowship in the sufferings and the Crucifixion with You.
I taste the turning of my face to You; I see You and exult, and no power can separate me from You!
I cry out to You from my depths, asking that You do Your will in me!
Glory to You, O wonderful in His goodness, and all-wise in Your plans toward me!
